Step 1: R(12) means "12 < 30". That is a proposition, and it is true.

Step 2: ∃t R(t) claims at least one measured time is under 30. The value 12 is a witness, so the statement is true.

Step 3: ∀t R(t) claims every measured time is under 30. [missing step]

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: It is false, because 41 is a counterexample: "41 < 30" fails.
It is true, because two of the three times are under 30, which is most of the domain.
It is true, because the witness 12 already showed that R holds.
It is neither true nor false, because t is a variable and has no fixed value.
questions.why: A universal claim must hold for every value in the domain, so the single counterexample 41 makes ∀t R(t) false.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a proposition?
choices: "Is 9 a prime number?"
"The number 9 is prime."
"Restart the database server."
"y + 2 = 7", where y has not been given a value
questions.why: "The number 9 is prime" is a declarative statement with exactly one truth value (false), while a question, a command and an open statement with an unfixed variable have no truth value.

questions.prompt: Consider the statement ∀x (2x > x). What is its truth value over the positive integers {1, 2, 3, ...}, and over all integers?
choices: It cannot be evaluated in either domain, because x is a variable.
True over the positive integers, but false over the integers, where x = -1 is a counterexample since -2 > -1 fails.
False over both domains, because x = 1 is a counterexample.
True over both domains, because doubling a number always makes it larger.
questions.why: Every positive integer doubled is larger, but the integer domain includes -1, a counterexample, which shows the same statement can change truth value when the domain changes.

questions.prompt: A storage team runs 8 disks. They want an alert whenever at least one disk is more than 90% full, but they wrote the rule as "alert if every disk is more than 90% full." What happens on the running system?
choices: The alert fires too rarely: if one disk fills up while the others are fine, nothing fires, because they used a "for all" claim where they needed "there exists."
The alert fires too often, because a "for all" claim becomes true as soon as one disk is full.
Nothing changes, because "every disk" and "at least one disk" mean the same thing when there are only 8 disks.
The alert never evaluates, because "disk usage > 90%" is a predicate and so has no truth value.
questions.why: The intended condition is an existential claim (some disk is over 90%), but the rule uses a universal claim that needs all 8 disks to be full, so a single full disk goes unreported.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a proposition and a predicate, and how ∀ and ∃ turn a predicate into a proposition. Include one limit or pitfall, such as what changes when the domain changes.
lessons.modelAnswer: A proposition is a statement that is simply true or false, like "10 is even." A predicate has a variable in it, like E(x): "x is even." A predicate has no truth value on its own, because the answer depends on x. You get a proposition back in two ways. You can plug in a value: E(10) is true and E(3) is false. Or you can quantify. ∀x E(x) says every x in the domain is even. It is false over the integers, because one counterexample, 3, breaks it. ∃x E(x) says at least one x is even. It is true, because one witness, 10, is enough. The pitfall is the domain. The same quantified statement can flip truth value if you change the set x ranges over. So you must always state the domain. Also, never call a bare predicate true or false.
rubricPoints: Defines a proposition as a statement with exactly one truth value.
Defines a predicate as a statement with a variable whose truth depends on the value.
Explains that substitution or quantification turns a predicate into a proposition.
Distinguishes ∀ (one counterexample makes it false) from ∃ (one witness makes it true).
Names a pitfall such as the domain changing the truth value, or treating a predicate as already true or false.

suggested.rationale: The unit's core skill is reading symbolic notation and restating it in plain language, so explaining propositions, predicates and quantifiers back is the most direct practice.

lessons.plain: A truth table is a grid that lists every possible combination of true and false for some simple statements, then shows whether a bigger statement built from them comes out true or false in each case. Two statements are logically equivalent when their tables give the same answer in every single row. It is like checking two recipes by cooking every possible mix of ingredients. If both dishes always taste identical, you can swap one recipe for the other. Engineers use this to rewrite conditions safely and to check arguments without relying on gut feeling.
lessons.guessPrompt: A friend says, 'If it rains, the ground will be wet.' It did not rain, but the ground is wet anyway (someone ran a sprinkler). Was your friend's statement false?
lessons.teach:
A proposition is a statement that is either true (T) or false (F). Connectives build bigger statements from smaller ones. NOT P (written ¬P) flips the value. P AND Q (P ∧ Q) is true only when both parts are true. P OR Q (P ∨ Q) is true when at least one part is true. 'If P then Q' (P → Q), called an implication, is false only when P is true and Q is false. A truth table gives one row to each combination of values for the variables, which means 2^n rows for n variables, and works out the compound statement in every row. Two statements are logically equivalent (written ≡) when their final columns match in every row.

This works because a compound statement's value depends only on the values of its parts. There are only finitely many combinations, so checking every row is a complete proof.

Worked example: is ¬(P ∧ Q) equivalent to ¬P ∨ ¬Q?
Row 1, P=T and Q=T: P∧Q is T, so the left side is F. ¬P and ¬Q are both F, so the right side is F. They match.
Row 2, P=T and Q=F: the left side is ¬F, which is T. On the right, ¬Q is T, so the right side is T. They match.
Row 3, P=F and Q=T: the left side is T. On the right, ¬P is T, so the right side is T. They match.
Row 4, P=F and Q=F: the left side is T and the right side is T. They match.
All rows agree, so the two are equivalent. This is a De Morgan law. Its twin is ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

Common mistake: assuming P → Q means the same as its converse, Q → P. Take P=F and Q=T. P → Q is true (a false premise makes an implication true), but Q → P is false. So they are not equivalent. The contrapositive, ¬Q → ¬P, does match P → Q in every row.

In a running system, rewriting 'not (logged_in and is_admin)' as 'not logged_in and not is_admin' looks harmless. In fact it fails to deny a logged-in non-admin, which silently opens an access hole.

questions.prompt: A shipping company states a rule: 'If a parcel weighs over 20 kg (P), then a surcharge applies (Q).' An analyst checks whether P → Q is logically equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q by building a truth table. Row 1, P=T and Q=T: P → Q is T. ¬P is F and Q is T, so ¬P ∨ Q is T. They match. Row 2, P=T and Q=F: [missing step]. Row 3, P=F and Q=T: P → Q is T. ¬P is T, so ¬P ∨ Q is T. They match. Row 4, P=F and Q=F: P → Q is T. ¬P is T, so ¬P ∨ Q is T. They match. Conclusion: every row agrees, so the two statements are equivalent. Which choice correctly completes Row 2?
choices: P → Q is F. ¬P is F and Q is F, so ¬P ∨ Q is F. They match.
P → Q is T. ¬P ∨ Q is T because one part is true. They match.
P → Q is T because the premise is true. ¬P is F and Q is F, so ¬P ∨ Q is F. They do not match.
P → Q is F. ¬P ∨ Q is T because an OR only needs to be checked on Q. They do not match.
questions.why: An implication is false only when P is true and Q is false, and an OR with both parts false is false, so both sides are F and the row matches, which the conclusion requires.

questions.prompt: A network team writes a truth table for a firewall condition built from three propositions: A (port is open), B (source is trusted), and C (traffic is encrypted). How many rows does a complete truth table need?
questions.why: A truth table has 2^n rows for n variables, and 2^3 = 8.

questions.prompt: A building's safety spec says: 'If the sensor reports smoke (P), then the sprinkler turns on (Q).' Treating this as the implication P → Q, which situation makes the statement false?
choices: No smoke is reported and the sprinkler turns on.
Smoke is reported and the sprinkler turns on.
Smoke is reported and the sprinkler stays off.
No smoke is reported and the sprinkler stays off.
questions.why: An implication is false only when its premise is true and its conclusion is false, which here means smoke reported but no sprinkler.

questions.prompt: A streaming service blocks content when 'not (is_paid or is_trial)'. A developer rewrites this as 'not is_paid or not is_trial'. Which assignment of values shows that the two conditions are not logically equivalent?
choices: is_paid = T, is_trial = T
No assignment works; the two are equivalent by De Morgan's law.
is_paid = T, is_trial = F
is_paid = F, is_trial = F
questions.why: With is_paid true and is_trial false, the original is ¬(T) = F but the rewrite is F ∨ T = T, so the final columns differ in that row; the correct De Morgan rewrite is 'not is_paid and not is_trial'.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would prove that two logical statements are equivalent using a truth table, and name one limit of this method.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I list every variable and write out every combination of true and false, which gives 2^n rows for n variables. Then I compute each statement column by column, applying NOT, AND, OR and implication by their rules. If the two final columns agree in every row, the statements are logically equivalent, so I can safely substitute one for the other. That is useful when simplifying an if-condition in code. If even one row differs, they are not equivalent, and that row is a concrete counterexample. A good example is P → Q versus its converse when P is false and Q is true. The method's limit is size. Rows double with each new variable, so ten variables already need 1,024 rows. At that scale, algebraic rules like De Morgan's laws, or a program, are more practical. Truth tables also only handle propositions with fixed true or false values, not statements with variables ranging over many objects.
rubricPoints: Defines a truth table as listing every combination of truth values, one per row.
States that equivalence means the final columns match in every row.
Notes that a single mismatching row is a counterexample that disproves equivalence.
Applies the connective rules correctly, including that an implication is false only when the premise is true and the conclusion is false.
Names the limit that row count grows as 2^n, making large tables impractical.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine drills propositional logic, so the most useful practice is reasoning through exam-style situations: building tables, spotting non-equivalent rewrites, and catching the converse trap.

lessons.plain: A set is a collection of distinct things, called elements, where only membership matters. Order does not matter, and listing something twice adds nothing. Think of a guest list: what matters is whether a name is on it, not where it appears. Set operations combine lists. Union puts two lists together. Intersection keeps only the names on both. Difference keeps names on the first list that are missing from the second. Complement means everyone in the whole crowd who is not on the list. These ideas show up whenever you merge, compare or filter groups, such as users, files or permissions.
lessons.guessPrompt: Team A knows Python, Go and SQL. Team B knows SQL and Java. Which languages does at least one team know, and which languages do both teams know?
lessons.teach:
A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects, called elements. We write sets with braces, so A = {1, 2, 3}. The symbol ∈ means "is an element of", so 2 ∈ A means 2 belongs to A. The symbol ∉ means it does not. The empty set, written ∅ or {}, has no elements. A ⊆ B means A is a subset of B, so every element of A is also in B. The universal set U is the agreed collection of everything under discussion. The cardinality |A| is the number of elements in A. Because only membership counts, {1, 2} and {2, 1, 1} are the same set.

There are four core operations. The union A ∪ B holds every element that is in A, in B, or in both. The intersection A ∩ B holds the elements that are in both. The difference A \ B, also written A − B, holds the elements of A that are not in B. The complement of A, written Aᶜ or A′, holds the elements of U that are not in A.

Worked example: let U = {1, …, 8}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}.
Step 1: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
Step 2: A ∩ B = {3, 4}.
Step 3: A \ B = {1, 2}, while B \ A = {5, 6}.
Step 4: Aᶜ = {5, 6, 7, 8}.
Step 5: Check the counting rule |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B|. That gives 4 + 4 − 2 = 6, which matches Step 1. The rule subtracts the shared elements because simply adding the two sizes counts them twice.

Common mistake: confusing ∈ with ⊆. It is true that 3 ∈ A and that {3} ⊆ A, but writing "3 ⊆ A" is wrong, because 3 is an element, not a set. A second mistake is assuming difference is symmetric. It is not, because A \ B and B \ A are usually different sets.

In a running system, effective permissions are often computed as granted \ revoked. If someone reverses the order of that difference, users receive the wrong access, which is a real security fault.

questions.prompt: A clinic tracks staff on two shifts. The universal set is U = {Ana, Ben, Cai, Dev, Eli, Fay, Gus}. The day shift is D = {Ana, Ben, Cai, Dev, Eli} and the night shift is N = {Dev, Eli, Fay}. Step 1: D ∪ N = {Ana, Ben, Cai, Dev, Eli, Fay}, so |D ∪ N| = 6. Step 2: D ∩ N = {Dev, Eli}, so |D ∩ N| = 2. Step 3: N \ D = {Fay}, the night staff who do not work days. Step 4: Dᶜ = {Fay, Gus}. Step 5 is missing: check |D ∪ N| with the counting rule |D ∪ N| = |D| + |N| − |D ∩ N|. Which line correctly completes Step 5?
choices: 5 + 3 − 2 = 6, which matches Step 1
5 − 3 + 2 = 4, subtracting the night shift instead
5 + 3 − 4 = 4, subtracting both shared people twice
5 + 3 = 8, so the union has 8 people
questions.why: |D| = 5 and |N| = 3. Dev and Eli are in both sets, so they are counted twice when the two sizes are added. Subtracting |D ∩ N| = 2 once gives 6, which matches the union found in Step 1.

questions.prompt: Let S = {red, blue}. Which statement is written correctly and is true?
choices: red ⊆ S
red ∈ S
{red} ∈ S
S ⊆ {red}
questions.why: red is an element of S, so the element symbol ∈ is the right one. The subset symbol ⊆ compares two sets, so it cannot be used with a single element like red. S ⊆ {red} is false because blue is not in {red}.

questions.prompt: A file-sharing service computes each user's effective permissions as granted \ revoked. A user has granted G = {read, write, delete, share} and revoked R = {delete, export}. What are the user's effective permissions?
choices: {delete}
{read, write, share}
{export}
{read, write, delete, share, export}
questions.why: G \ R keeps the elements of G that are not in R. Removing delete leaves {read, write, share}. Reversing the order to R \ G would give {export}, which is the security fault the text warns about.

questions.prompt: A sensor log records readings into the set T = {7, 9, 9, 7, 11}. What is the cardinality |T|?
questions.why: A set has only distinct elements, and only membership counts, so repeated values are not counted again. That means T is the same set as {7, 9, 11}. Its cardinality is 3.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what union, intersection, difference and complement do, using a small example of your own. Then name one limit of modelling data as a set, or one thing you must agree on before taking a complement.
lessons.modelAnswer: A set is a collection of distinct items where only membership counts. Say on-call = {Ana, Ben, Cy} and trained = {Ben, Cy, Dee}. The union, on-call ∪ trained, gives everyone in either group: {Ana, Ben, Cy, Dee}. The intersection gives the people in both: {Ben, Cy}. The difference on-call \ trained gives the people on call who still need training: {Ana}. Reversing it to trained \ on-call gives {Dee}, so order matters for difference. A complement means "everything not in the set", so it only makes sense once we agree on the universal set, such as all staff. There are two limits to watch. Sets discard duplicates and order, so if you need counts, such as how many times someone logged in, or a sequence, a plain set loses that information. Also, the size of a union is not just the two sizes added together, because you must subtract the overlap.
rubricPoints: Defines a set as distinct, unordered elements where only membership matters.
Correctly describes union, intersection and difference with a concrete example.
Notes that difference is not symmetric, so A \ B usually differs from B \ A.
States that a complement depends on an agreed universal set.
Names a limit, such as losing duplicates or order, or double-counting the overlap in a union.

suggested.rationale: The unit's core skill is reading set notation and reasoning about results, so working through short exam-style situations that mix notation, worked operations and counting checks builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: A relation is a way of saying which things are connected to which, like a list of who follows whom online. Each connection is a pair: this item goes with that item. A function is a stricter kind of relation. It is a rule where every input gets exactly one output, like a vending machine where each button always gives one specific snack. Two buttons may give the same snack, but no button gives two snacks or nothing. Many programming ideas are functions in this sense, including dictionaries that map a key to a value.
lessons.guessPrompt: Every person has one birthday, but many people can share the same birthday. Is 'person to their birthday' a rule that always gives one clear answer? What about the reverse, 'birthday to person'?
lessons.teach:
A relation from set A to set B is any collection of ordered pairs (a, b), with a taken from A and b taken from B. An ordered pair is two items where order matters, so (1, 2) is not the same as (2, 1). The set of all possible pairs is the Cartesian product A × B. That makes a relation simply a subset of A × B. Writing a R b means the pair (a, b) is in relation R.

A function f: A → B is a relation with one extra rule: every element of A is paired with exactly one element of B. A is the domain, meaning the allowed inputs. B is the codomain, meaning where outputs may land. The range is the set of outputs actually produced. The rule works because it guarantees that f(a) always names a single answer.

A function is injective (one-to-one) if different inputs never share an output. It is surjective (onto) if every element of the codomain is hit. It is bijective if it is both, which means it can be reversed.

Worked example: let A = {alice, bob, carol} and B = {Mon, Tue}, with R = {(alice, Mon), (bob, Mon), (carol, Tue)} meaning 'on-call day'. Each person has exactly one day, so R is a function. It is not injective, because alice and bob share Mon. It is surjective, because both Mon and Tue are used. Now reverse it to 'day to person'. Mon pairs with two people, so the reverse is not a function. Birthdays behave the same way: 'person to birthday' is a function, but 'birthday to person' is not.

A common mistake is believing a function must use every codomain element or must have distinct outputs. Neither is required. The only rule is one output per input, and an input with no output breaks that rule.

In software, a dictionary or a database key acts as a function from keys to values. If you wrongly assume such a mapping is injective and reverse it, you silently lose data.

questions.prompt: A hosting team has servers A = {web1, web2, db1, cache1} and racks B = {R1, R2, R3}. The placement relation is P = {(web1, R1), (web2, R2), (db1, R3), (cache1, R1)}. Step 1: Each server appears in exactly one pair, so every input has exactly one output, and P is a function. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: R1, R2 and R3 all appear as outputs, so every codomain element is hit, and P is surjective. Step 4: P is not both injective and surjective, so it is not bijective and cannot be reversed into a 'rack to server' function. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: P is not injective, because web1 and cache1 share the output R1.
P breaks the function rule, because R1 is paired with two different servers.
P is injective, because each server appears in exactly one pair.
P is injective, because every rack in B is used by at least one server.
questions.why: Injective means different inputs never share an output, and the two different inputs web1 and cache1 both map to R1, so P is not injective.

questions.prompt: A relation R from set A to set B is any subset of A × B, the set of all ordered pairs. What extra condition makes R a function from A to B?
choices: Every element of B is paired with at least one element of A.
Every element of A is paired with exactly one element of B.
Every element of A is paired with at least one element of B.
No two elements of A are paired with the same element of B.
questions.why: The only rule for a function is one output per input, so each element of the domain A must have exactly one partner in B. Using every codomain element or having distinct outputs is not required.

questions.prompt: Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {x, y, z}. The relation g = {(1, y), (2, z), (3, x)}. Which description of g is correct?
choices: g is a function but not injective, because outputs repeat.
g is not a function, because the pairs are listed out of order.
g is injective but not surjective, because x is never hit.
g is bijective, because outputs never repeat and every element of B is hit.
questions.why: Each input has one output (a function), the outputs y, z and x are all different (injective), and all of B is covered (surjective), so g is both injective and surjective, which is bijective.

questions.prompt: A help-desk app stores a dictionary that maps ticket IDs to assignees: T101 to dana, T102 to dana, T103 to omar. An engineer builds a reverse dictionary from assignee to ticket ID so that each assignee looks up a single ticket. What happens?
choices: One of dana's tickets is silently lost, because the original mapping is not injective.
It fails only because the original mapping is not surjective onto all staff.
Nothing is lost, because reversing any relation always gives a function.
It works without loss, because the original dictionary is a function.
questions.why: Two different keys share the output dana, so the mapping is not injective, and reversing it forces one of dana's tickets to overwrite the other without any warning.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a relation and a function, and say what you lose or risk when you try to reverse a function that is not injective.
lessons.modelAnswer: A relation is just a set of ordered pairs linking items in one set to items in another. Formally, it is any subset of the Cartesian product A × B. A function is a relation with one strict rule: every input in the domain has exactly one output. Outputs can repeat, and not every codomain value has to be used. Injective means no two inputs share an output. Surjective means every codomain value is reached. Bijective means both, and only then can you cleanly reverse the function. Here is the tradeoff: if I reverse a non-injective mapping, like user-to-team, one team points to many users. The result is not a function anymore. If I force it into a dictionary, later entries overwrite earlier ones, and I quietly lose data.
rubricPoints: Defines a relation as a set of ordered pairs, a subset of A × B.
States that a function gives exactly one output for every input in the domain.
Distinguishes domain, codomain and range.
Defines injective, surjective and bijective correctly.
Explains that reversing a non-injective function fails or loses information.

suggested.rationale: The unit's core skill is translating notation such as f: A → B into plain language, so explaining the definitions and their limits back is the most direct practice.

lessons.plain: A direct proof is a way of showing that an 'if this, then that' statement is always true. You start from what you are given, then take small steps, each backed by a definition or a known fact, until you arrive at what you wanted to show. It works like following a recipe from ingredients to finished dish, where every step is one a skeptical cook would accept. Checking a few examples is not enough. The proof has to work for every case the statement covers, so you reason about a general case rather than particular numbers.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you add any two even numbers, is the result always even? How could you convince a doubtful friend without checking every possible pair?
lessons.teach:
A direct proof shows that a conditional statement, 'if P, then Q', is true. You assume P and move one justified step at a time until you reach Q. P is the hypothesis, meaning what you are given. Q is the conclusion, meaning what you must show. Every step must be justified by a definition, a fact proved earlier, or basic algebra.

Why it works: a conditional is false only when P is true and Q is false. If every situation where P holds forces Q, no counterexample can exist, so the statement is true. You never need to look at cases where P is false.

Worked example. Claim: if n is an odd integer, then n² is odd. Start with the definitions. An integer is even if it equals 2k for some integer k. It is odd if it equals 2k+1 for some integer k.

Step 1: Assume n is odd, so n = 2k+1 for some integer k.
Step 2: Square it: n² = 4k² + 4k + 1.
Step 3: Factor out a 2: n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1.
Step 4: Let m = 2k² + 2k. Sums and products of integers are integers, so m is an integer.
Step 5: Then n² = 2m+1, which is the definition of odd. The proof is complete.

The pattern is to unpack the hypothesis with a definition, do the algebra, then repack the result into the definition the conclusion needs.

Common mistake: testing examples (3² = 9, 5² = 25) and calling that a proof. Examples only suggest a pattern. The claim covers infinitely many integers, so you must use a general variable like k. A second mistake is starting from the conclusion and working backward. Unless every step reverses, that proves the converse, 'if Q then P', which is a different statement.

Why it matters in practice: engineers argue that code is correct the same way. You assume the input meets a stated condition, trace each operation, and show the output meets the required condition. A skipped step is exactly where bugs hide.

questions.prompt:
Claim: if a and b are odd integers, then a + b is even. Here is a direct proof with one step missing.

Step 1: ______
Step 2: Add them: a + b = 2j + 2k + 2.
Step 3: Factor out a 2: a + b = 2(j + k + 1).
Step 4: Let m = j + k + 1. Sums of integers are integers, so m is an integer.
Step 5: Then a + b = 2m, which is the definition of even.

Which statement correctly fills Step 1?
choices: Assume a and b are odd, so a = 2j and b = 2k for some integers j and k.
Take a = 7 and b = 11, which are both odd numbers.
Assume a + b is even, so a + b = 2m for some integer m.
Assume a and b are odd, so a = 2j + 1 and b = 2k + 1 for some integers j and k.
questions.why: A direct proof starts by assuming the hypothesis and unpacking it with the definition of odd (2 times an integer plus 1), using general variables, which is exactly what Step 2's algebra relies on.

questions.prompt: Consider the conditional statement: if x > 5, then x² > 25. Which situation, if it could happen, would make this statement false?
choices: x is not greater than 5 and x² is not greater than 25
x is not greater than 5 and x² is greater than 25
x is greater than 5 and x² is greater than 25
x is greater than 5 and x² is not greater than 25
questions.why: A conditional 'if P, then Q' is false only when P is true and Q is false; cases where P is false never make it false.

questions.prompt: Claim: if n is an even integer, then n + 6 is even. A direct proof so far reads: assume n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k. Then n + 6 = 2k + 6 = 2(k + 3). Which step correctly finishes the proof?
choices: Rewrite it as n + 6 = 2(k + 3) + 1, so n + 6 is odd.
Let m = k + 3, an integer because sums of integers are integers, so n + 6 = 2m, which is even.
Let m = k + 3. Because n + 6 is even, m must be an integer, so we are done.
Since 4 + 6 = 10 and 8 + 6 = 14 are both even, the claim holds.
questions.why: The proof must repack the result into the definition of even (2 times an integer), justifying that k + 3 is an integer from known facts rather than from the conclusion itself.

questions.prompt: A teammate wants to show: if n is a multiple of 4, then n is even. They check n = 4, 8, 12, and so on up to 400, find every one even, and declare the claim proved. What is the best assessment?
choices: Not a proof: they also need to check odd numbers, since cases where the hypothesis is false must be examined.
It is a proof, because 100 checked cases with no counterexample is enough to be certain.
Not a proof: examples only suggest a pattern; they must use a general n = 4k and show n = 2(2k).
It is a proof, but only for numbers up to 400, which is all a direct proof can ever cover.
questions.why: The claim covers infinitely many integers, so a direct proof must use a general variable and definitions; testing examples, however many, does not rule out a counterexample.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a direct proof works, using your own small example, and name one limit or pitfall of the method.
lessons.modelAnswer: A direct proof shows that 'if P then Q' is true. You assume P, the hypothesis, and chain together steps that are each justified by a definition, a known fact or algebra, until you reach Q, the conclusion. For example, to show the sum of two even numbers is even, write them as 2a and 2b for integers a and b. Their sum is 2a + 2b = 2(a+b). Since a+b is an integer, the sum fits the definition of even. This works because a conditional can only fail when P is true and Q is false, and the chain rules that case out. One limit is that it proves only that direction, not the converse. Another pitfall is mistaking examples for proof: you must reason with general variables, because a few checked cases never cover every possibility.
rubricPoints: States that a direct proof assumes the hypothesis P and derives the conclusion Q.
Says each step must be justified by a definition, a prior fact or algebra.
Gives a correct small example that uses general variables from definitions.
Explains why it works: the only way a conditional fails is P true and Q false.
Names a limit or pitfall, such as examples not being proof or the proof not covering the converse.

suggested.rationale: Building and explaining a step-by-step argument is the core skill, and no current mission or planned engine practises formal proof.

lessons.plain: Proof by contradiction is a way to show something is true by showing that its opposite cannot be true. You pretend, just for the sake of argument, that the claim is false, then reason carefully from that assumption until you hit something impossible, like a number that is both even and odd. Since correct reasoning cannot lead to nonsense, the assumption must have been wrong, so the original claim is true. It is like a detective saying: suppose the butler did it; then he was in two rooms at once, which cannot happen, so the butler did not do it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Someone insists there is a largest whole number. Without listing every number, how could you convince them they are wrong?
lessons.teach:
Proof by contradiction shows a statement P is true by assuming its negation, "not P", and deriving a contradiction. A statement is a sentence that is either true or false. Its negation is the statement that is true exactly when the original is false. A contradiction is a statement that cannot be true, such as "Q and not Q" (for example, "n is even and n is odd").

Why it works: valid reasoning from true assumptions never produces a false conclusion. So if assuming "not P" leads, by valid steps, to something impossible, then "not P" must be false. A statement is either true or false, so P is true.

Worked example. Claim P: there is no largest integer (an integer is a whole number such as -2, 0, or 7). Step 1: assume the negation, "there is a largest integer", and call it N. By assumption, every integer is less than or equal to N. Step 2: consider N + 1. Adding 1 to an integer gives an integer, so N + 1 is an integer. Step 3: N + 1 is greater than N. Step 4: now we have an integer greater than N, yet we assumed every integer is at most N. Both cannot hold, so we have a contradiction. Step 5: the assumption is false, so there is no largest integer.

Common mistake: negating the claim incorrectly. The negation of "every x has property A" is "at least one x lacks property A", not "no x has property A". If you assume the wrong negation, your contradiction proves nothing about the original claim. A second mistake is reaching a "contradiction" through an arithmetic or logic slip of your own. The method only works when every step is valid.

The same reasoning appears in engineering. Suppose a system has an invariant, a rule meant to always hold, such as "a balance never goes negative". You can argue that a bad state cannot be reached by assuming it is reached and showing that this breaks a rule the code enforces.

questions.prompt: A data center team wants to prove this claim: "If 4 backup jobs are assigned to 3 servers, then at least one server gets 2 or more jobs." They use proof by contradiction. Step 1: [MISSING]. Step 2: If each server has at most 1 job, the 3 servers together hold at most 3 jobs. Step 3: But there are 4 jobs, and every job is assigned to some server, so the servers hold exactly 4 jobs. Step 4: The servers cannot hold at most 3 jobs and exactly 4 jobs at once. That is a contradiction. Step 5: So the assumption is false, and at least one server gets 2 or more jobs. Which choice correctly fills in Step 1?
choices: Assume that no server gets any job at all.
Assume that every server gets at most 1 job.
Assume that every server gets 2 or more jobs.
Assume that some server gets at most 1 job.
questions.why: The claim says at least one server has 2 or more jobs, so its negation is that no server has 2 or more, which means every server has at most 1 job, and that is exactly what Step 2 uses.

questions.prompt: In a proof by contradiction of a statement P, why does reaching a contradiction show that P is true?
choices: A contradiction shows that P and "not P" are both false, so P is true by default.
Any statement that leads to a contradiction is automatically true, so "not P" being contradictory means P was the assumption all along.
Reaching a contradiction proves that the reasoning steps were invalid, which makes the original claim P true.
Valid reasoning from true assumptions never produces something impossible, so the assumption "not P" must be false, and since P is either true or false, P is true.
questions.why: Since valid steps from a true assumption cannot reach an impossible statement, the assumption "not P" must be false, and a statement that is not false is true.

questions.prompt: An engineer wants to prove by contradiction that "every order in the warehouse database has a shipping address." What should the engineer assume at the start of the proof?
choices: Every order in the database has two shipping addresses.
At least one order in the database lacks a shipping address.
No order in the database has a shipping address.
Every order in the database lacks a phone number.
questions.why: The negation of "every x has property A" is "at least one x lacks property A", not "no x has property A".

questions.prompt: A student tries to prove a claim Q about a parking garage by contradiction. They assume "not Q". Partway through, they compute 12 + 15 = 28 and use that result to reach the statement "the garage is full and the garage is not full." What can be concluded about Q?
choices: Nothing about Q is established, because the contradiction came from an arithmetic slip rather than valid steps.
Q is proven true, because a contradiction was reached.
"Not Q" is proven true, because the contradiction is about the garage rather than about Q.
Q is proven false, because the student's reasoning contained an error.
questions.why: Proof by contradiction only works when every step is valid, and 12 + 15 is 27, so the contradiction came from the student's own mistake and says nothing about Q.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain proof by contradiction to a teammate in your own words, using a short example. Include one limit or pitfall of the method, such as what goes wrong if the negation is stated incorrectly.
lessons.modelAnswer: Proof by contradiction proves a claim by temporarily assuming it is false and showing that this assumption leads to something impossible. For example, to prove there is no largest integer, I assume there is one and call it N. Then N + 1 is also an integer and is bigger than N, which clashes with N being the largest. Valid reasoning can't produce an impossibility from true starting points, so the assumption was false and the claim holds. The big pitfall is the negation. I must assume exactly the opposite of the claim. The opposite of "all servers are healthy" is "at least one server is unhealthy", not "no server is healthy". Every step also has to be valid, because a contradiction caused by my own mistake proves nothing. One drawback is that the method shows the claim is true without always showing how to build an example.
rubricPoints: States that you assume the negation of the claim you want to prove.
Explains that you derive a contradiction, something that cannot be true.
Explains why this works: valid steps cannot lead from true assumptions to an impossibility, so the assumption is false.
Gives a correct short example with each step traced.
Names a pitfall, such as negating the claim wrongly or reaching a contradiction through an invalid step.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine practises writing proofs, and laying out the assume-negation, derive-contradiction structure in your own words is the core skill this objective builds.

lessons.plain: Mathematical induction is a way to prove that a statement holds for every whole number, even though there are infinitely many, without checking them one by one. Picture an endless row of dominoes. If you can show that the first domino falls, and that any falling domino always knocks over the next one, then you know every domino in the row falls. Induction works the same way. You prove the statement for the first number. Then you prove that whenever it is true for one number, it must also be true for the next. Those two facts together cover every number.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you know two things about an endless row of dominoes: the first one gets pushed over, and every domino that falls always knocks over the one right after it. Do all the dominoes fall? Now drop one of those two facts. Can you still be sure they all fall?
lessons.teach:
Mathematical induction is a proof method for showing that a statement P(n) is true for every whole number n from some starting value onward. P(n) is a predicate, meaning a sentence containing a variable that becomes true or false once you plug in a number. An induction proof has two parts. The base case shows P is true at the starting value, usually n = 0 or n = 1. The inductive step shows that for any k at or above the start, if P(k) is true, then P(k+1) is true. The assumption that P(k) is true is called the inductive hypothesis.

Why it works: the base case gives you P(1). The step turns P(1) into P(2), then P(2) into P(3), and so on. No number is ever skipped, so every n is eventually reached.

Worked example. Claim: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 for all n ≥ 1. Base case, n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side is 1·2/2 = 1. True. Inductive step: assume 1 + ... + k = k(k+1)/2. Add the next term, k+1, to both sides. That gives 1 + ... + k + (k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1). Factor out (k+1) to get (k+1)(k/2 + 1), which equals (k+1)(k+2)/2. That is exactly the formula with n = k+1, so P(k+1) holds. Both parts are done, so the formula holds for every n ≥ 1. A quick check: for n = 4, 1+2+3+4 = 10 and 4·5/2 = 10.

A common mistake is skipping the base case. Take the claim n + 1 = n. Its inductive step seems to work: assume k + 1 = k, add 1 to both sides, and you get (k+1) + 1 = k + 1. Yet the claim is false for every n, because nothing starts the chain. Another mistake is assuming P(k+1) itself instead of deriving it from P(k). That reasoning is circular.

In software, the same reasoning proves a loop or a recursive function correct. You show a property holds before the first iteration, then show that each iteration keeps it true. If either half is missing, the code can fail on inputs nobody tested.

questions.prompt: Claim: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 1) = n² for all n ≥ 1 (the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared). Base case, n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side is 1² = 1, so it is true. Inductive step: assume the inductive hypothesis 1 + 3 + ... + (2k − 1) = k². [MISSING STEP] The right side is now k² + 2k + 1, which equals (k + 1)². That is exactly the formula with n = k + 1, so P(k + 1) holds and the proof is complete. Which choice fills in the missing step?
choices: Add the next odd number, 2k + 1, to both sides, so the left side becomes 1 + ... + (2k − 1) + (2k + 1) and the right side becomes k² + 2k + 1.
Check n = 2: 1 + 3 = 4 = 2², which together with n = 1 shows the pattern continues.
Add the last odd number already in the sum, 2k − 1, to both sides, so the right side becomes k² + 2k − 1.
Assume 1 + 3 + ... + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)² directly, because that is the statement we are trying to reach.
questions.why: The next term after 2k − 1 is 2(k + 1) − 1 = 2k + 1, and adding it to both sides of the inductive hypothesis turns k² into k² + 2k + 1 = (k + 1)², deriving P(k + 1) from P(k) rather than assuming it.

questions.prompt: In an induction proof that some statement P(n) holds for all n ≥ 0, what is the inductive hypothesis?
choices: The proof that P(0) is true.
The assumption that P(k) is true for some k at or above the start, used to show P(k + 1) is true.
The assumption that P(k + 1) is true, which the step then confirms.
The final conclusion that P(n) is true for every n ≥ 0.
questions.why: The inductive hypothesis is the assumption that P(k) holds, and the inductive step uses it to derive P(k + 1). Assuming P(k + 1) itself would be circular.

questions.prompt: A student wants to prove that n² + n is odd for every n ≥ 1. Their inductive step reads: assume k² + k is odd. Then (k + 1)² + (k + 1) = (k² + k) + (2k + 2), which is an odd number plus an even number, so it is odd. What is the correct verdict on this attempt?
choices: The claim is proven, because a valid inductive step is enough on its own to cover every n.
The claim is not proven. The base case fails, because at n = 1 the value is 1 + 1 = 2, which is even, so nothing starts the chain.
The claim is not proven, because the inductive step assumed P(k + 1) instead of deriving it.
The claim is proven, because the inductive step works for every k, including k = 1.
questions.why: Induction needs both parts. Here the step is valid, but P(1) is false, so the chain never starts and the claim is not established (in fact it is false).

questions.prompt: A loop adds up the prices in a shopping cart. It starts with total = 0, and on each pass it adds the next item's price to total. You want to prove by induction that after i passes, total equals the sum of the first i prices. Which statement plays the role of the base case?
choices: Testing a cart with 3 items gives the right total, so the loop is correct.
Before the first pass (i = 0), total is 0, which equals the sum of zero prices.
After every pass, if total was correct before the pass, it is still correct after adding the next price.
After the last pass, total equals the sum of all prices in the cart.
questions.why: The base case shows the property holds at the starting value, which for a loop is before the first iteration. The 'each pass keeps it true' statement is the inductive step, not the base case.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a proof by induction works and why its two parts together prove a statement for every whole number. Name at least one limit of the method or one way it goes wrong.
lessons.modelAnswer: Induction proves a statement about whole numbers, like a formula for 1 + 2 + ... + n, for every n at once. It has two parts. First, the base case: check the statement directly for the starting number, usually 1. Second, the inductive step: assume the statement holds for some number k, and use that assumption to show it holds for k+1. Together these form a chain. The base case covers 1, and the step carries truth from 1 to 2, from 2 to 3, and on forever, so no number is missed. Both parts are required. Without the base case, you can prove false things, like n + 1 = n, whose step seems fine. You also cannot assume the k+1 case itself, because that is circular. One limit: induction only verifies a claim you already have. It does not tell you what the formula should be, and it applies to step-by-step structures like the whole numbers, not to every kind of statement.
rubricPoints: States that the base case proves the claim directly for the starting number.
States that the inductive step shows truth for k implies truth for k+1.
Explains that the two parts chain together so every whole number is reached.
Notes that skipping the base case, or assuming the k+1 case, breaks the proof.
Names a limit, such as induction only verifying a known claim or applying only to step-by-step sequences.

suggested.rationale: Induction is a reasoning structure with no matching hands-on mission, so the core skill is building the two-part argument and explaining why it covers every case.

lessons.plain: Recursion is when a function solves a problem by handing a smaller copy of the same problem to itself, and it keeps doing that until the problem is tiny enough to answer outright. That tiny, answer-directly situation is called the base case, and it is what stops the chain. Think of Russian nesting dolls: you open each doll to find a smaller one inside until you reach the solid doll that does not open. Tracing recursion means following each step by hand. You go down through the dolls, then come back up while you put each answer together.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function count(n) works like this: if n is 0 it stops and prints nothing; otherwise it prints n and then calls count(n - 1). What do you think count(3) prints, and what would happen if you called count(-2)?
lessons.teach:
Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function has two parts. The base case is an input small enough to answer directly, with no further self-call. It is where the chain stops. The recursive case covers every other input: the function calls itself on something closer to the base case, then uses that answer to finish its own work. Tracing means following the calls by hand. For each call you write down the input, note the call it makes, wait for that call's answer, and then complete the work that was left pending.

Why it works: suppose three things hold. The base case gives the right answer. Each recursive case builds a right answer from a right answer to a smaller input. Every input eventually shrinks down to the base case. Then the whole function is correct. This is the same reasoning as proof by induction.

Worked example: sum_to(n) returns 0 when n is 0 (the base case). Otherwise it returns n + sum_to(n - 1). Trace sum_to(3):
Step 1: 3 is not 0, so it needs 3 + sum_to(2) and pauses.
Step 2: sum_to(2) needs 2 + sum_to(1) and pauses.
Step 3: sum_to(1) needs 1 + sum_to(0) and pauses.
Step 4: sum_to(0) hits the base case and returns 0.
Now the paused calls finish in reverse order. sum_to(1) returns 1 + 0 = 1. sum_to(2) returns 2 + 1 = 3. sum_to(3) returns 3 + 3 = 6. A trace always has two phases: calls going down until the base case, then results coming back up.

Common mistake: writing a base case that some inputs never reach. sum_to(-1) skips past 0 and calls -2, -3, and so on forever. The same thing happens if the recursive case forgets to shrink the input, for example by calling sum_to(n) again. A safer base case here is n <= 0.

In a running system, each paused call holds memory. Unbounded recursion therefore crashes the program; Python, for example, raises a RecursionError. It does not quietly return a wrong answer.

questions.prompt:
A function mult(a, b) multiplies two whole numbers using only addition. If b is 0, it returns 0 (the base case). Otherwise it returns a + mult(a, b - 1). Here is a trace of mult(4, 3).

Calls going down: mult(4, 3) needs 4 + mult(4, 2) and pauses. mult(4, 2) needs 4 + mult(4, 1) and pauses. mult(4, 1) needs 4 + mult(4, 0) and pauses. mult(4, 0) hits the base case and returns 0.

Results coming back up: mult(4, 1) returns 4 + 0 = 4. mult(4, 2) returns ____. mult(4, 3) returns 4 + 8 = 12.

What goes in the blank?
questions.why: mult(4, 2) was paused waiting for mult(4, 1), which returned 4, so it finishes 4 + 4 = 8.

questions.prompt: A function halvings(n) counts how many times a positive whole number can be halved, rounding down, before it reaches 1. If n is 1, it returns 0. Otherwise it returns 1 + halvings(n // 2), where // means divide and round down. Which part is the base case?
choices: The addition 1 + halvings(n // 2), because it builds the final answer
The first call the program makes, such as halvings(16), because the trace starts there
The rule that returns 0 when n is 1, because it answers directly with no further self-call
The call halvings(n // 2), because it makes the input smaller
questions.why: The base case is the input answered directly without calling the function again, which here is n equal to 1.

questions.prompt: A function tick(n) returns 0 when n is 0. Otherwise it returns 1 + tick(n - 2). A program running in Python calls tick(5). What happens?
choices: The input goes 5, 3, 1, -1, and so on, skipping 0, so the calls never stop and the program crashes with a RecursionError
It quietly returns a wrong answer such as 0
It returns 3, because 5 needs three steps of 2 to get near 0
It stops at tick(1) and returns 2, because 1 is the closest value to the base case
questions.why: Odd inputs jump past the base case of 0, so recursion is unbounded; each paused call holds memory and Python raises a RecursionError instead of returning a wrong answer.

questions.prompt: A function length(items) returns 0 if the list is empty. Otherwise it returns 1 + length(rest), where rest is the list without its first item. You trace length([7, 8, 9]). Which call is the first to actually return a value?
choices: length([9]), because it holds the last item
length([]), the empty list, because it hits the base case while every earlier call is still paused
length([7, 8, 9]), because it was called first
length([8, 9]), because it is in the middle of the chain
questions.why: A trace first goes down until the base case returns, and only then do the paused calls finish in reverse order, so the empty-list call returns first.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how you would trace a recursive function and how you would check that its base case is right. Include one way a base case can fail and what that costs a running program.
lessons.modelAnswer: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of that problem. The base case is the input it can answer directly without calling itself again. To trace a call, I write down each call and the input it got. I note that each call pauses while it waits for the smaller call, and I keep going down until I hit the base case. Then I work back up, filling in each paused call's result in reverse order. For sum_to(3) that gives 0, then 1, 3 and 6. To check the base case, I confirm that it returns the right value and that every possible input actually shrinks toward it. The limit is that a base case of n == 0 misses negative inputs, and so does a recursive step that never shrinks n. Then the recursion never stops, and each paused call eats memory until the program crashes.
rubricPoints: Defines the base case as the input answered directly without a further self-call.
Defines the recursive case as calling itself on a smaller input and using that result.
Describes tracing as going down to the base case, then combining results on the way back up in reverse order.
Checks that every input actually reaches the base case, not just that one exists.
Names the failure: an unreachable base case or a non-shrinking input causes endless recursion and a crash.

suggested.rationale: Tracing recursion is learned by predicting the output of small recursive functions and then running them to check, which a Python drills engine would let the learner do repeatedly.

lessons.plain: Every time a function calls another function, the computer needs to remember where it was and what its local values were, so it can pick up again when the inner call finishes. It keeps these notes in a region of memory called the call stack, piling one note on top of the last, like a stack of sticky notes on a desk. Recursion, a function calling itself, adds one note per call. If the calls go very deep before any of them finish, the pile gets tall, and if it gets taller than the space allowed, the program crashes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function sums the numbers 1 to n by calling itself on n-1 until it reaches 0. If you call it with n = 5, how many calls are waiting, unfinished, at the deepest moment?
lessons.teach:
The call stack is a region of memory the program uses to track active function calls. Each call pushes a stack frame, a block holding that call's arguments, local variables, and the return address (where to resume in the caller). When a call returns, its frame is popped and the memory is freed. Call-stack growth means how many frames pile up at once, which is the maximum recursion depth, not the total number of calls.

Why it works this way: a caller cannot finish until its callee finishes, so every unfinished caller must keep its frame. Frames only disappear once the base case (the input that stops recursion) is reached and calls start returning.

Worked example: sum(n) returns 0 if n is 0, else n + sum(n-1). Call sum(3). Push sum(3), which needs sum(2): push. That needs sum(1): push. That needs sum(0): push. Now four frames sit on the stack, the peak. sum(0) returns 0 and pops; sum(1) returns 1 and pops; sum(2) returns 3; sum(3) returns 6. Stack space grows as O(n), meaning in proportion to n.

Contrast merge sort on n items: it makes about 2n calls in total, but each branch finishes before its sibling starts, so depth is only about log2(n). For a million items that is roughly 20 frames. Quicksort's depth depends on the pivots, the values used to split the list. With balanced splits it is about log n. With consistently bad pivots, such as always picking the smallest value, depth can reach n.

Common mistake: equating total calls with stack use. Total calls measure time. Peak depth measures stack space.

Consequence in a running system: the stack has a fixed limit. Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 calls, and threads often get only a few megabytes of stack. Exceeding the limit raises a stack overflow or recursion error and can crash a service on an unusually large input. The fix is to convert deep recursion into a loop, or to bound the depth, for example by recursing on the smaller half first.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-processing tool at a small helpdesk uses a recursive function count(tickets) that returns 0 if the list is empty, otherwise 1 + count(rest of the list without the first ticket). It is called on a list of 7 tickets. Here is the trace of call-stack growth, with one step missing.
Step 1: count(7 tickets) cannot finish until count(6 tickets) returns, so it keeps its frame and a new frame is pushed.
Step 2: The same happens for 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 tickets, each pushing one more frame.
Step 3: ___
Step 4: The empty-list call returns 0 and pops, then each caller adds 1, returns and pops, until count(7 tickets) returns 7.
Step 5: Stack space grows in proportion to the list length, O(n).
Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Each frame is popped as soon as the next one is pushed, so only 1 frame is ever on the stack.
The peak is 14 frames, because each of the 7 calls pushes one frame going down and one coming back up.
count(1 ticket) is the base case, so the peak is 7 frames and nothing more is pushed.
count(empty list) is pushed as the base case, making the peak 8 frames on the stack at once.
questions.why: The empty list is the input that stops recursion, so it also gets a frame, and since no caller can finish until its callee does, all 8 frames (7 down to 0 tickets) sit on the stack together at the peak.

questions.prompt: An engineer says, "My recursive function made 3,000 calls in total, so it used 3,000 stack frames." Which statement best describes what call-stack growth actually measures?
choices: The total number of calls the function made over the whole run, which here is 3,000.
The number of base cases reached, since only base-case calls create frames.
The size of the return value, because larger results need more stack memory.
The largest number of frames on the stack at the same moment, which is the maximum recursion depth.
questions.why: Stack growth is how many frames pile up at once (the peak recursion depth); total calls measure time, not stack space.

questions.prompt: A mapping company's image tool takes a list of 4,096 map tiles, splits it in half, fully processes the left half recursively, then the right half, stopping when a piece has one tile. It makes roughly 8,000 calls in total. About how many frames are on the call stack at the peak?
choices: About 4,096, one for each tile in the list.
About 12, because the depth is about log2(4,096) and each half finishes before its sibling starts.
About 2,048, one for each pair of tiles.
About 8,000, one for each call made.
questions.why: Like merge sort, each branch finishes and pops before its sibling begins, so only one path of halvings is on the stack at once, about log2(4,096) = 12 levels deep.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a Python service that sorts shipment IDs with a quicksort that always picks the first element as the pivot. One morning it receives 50,000 IDs that are already sorted in ascending order. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: It fails only because 50,000 total calls is too many, even though few frames are ever on the stack at once.
Depth stays near log2(50,000), about 16, because quicksort always splits the list in half, so it runs fine.
Each pivot is the smallest value, so depth nears 50,000 frames, past Python's ~1000 limit, raising a recursion error.
It succeeds slowly, because frames are freed as soon as they are pushed, so recursion depth never matters.
questions.why: Always choosing the smallest value as pivot gives badly unbalanced splits, so depth grows to about n, which exceeds the fixed recursion limit and can crash the service; recursing on the smaller part first or using a loop would bound it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a recursive function can crash with a stack overflow even when its running time is fine, and name a tradeoff in fixing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each function call pushes a stack frame holding its arguments, locals, and return address. That frame stays until the call returns. In recursion, no call can return until the base case is hit, so frames pile up, and peak stack use equals the recursion depth. Running time depends on total calls, but stack use depends only on depth, and those two can differ a lot. Merge sort makes about 2n calls yet only reaches about log n depth. A naive recursive sum of n items reaches depth n, so a big enough input blows past the stack limit and crashes, even though its O(n) time is perfectly acceptable. Quicksort with bad pivots can also reach depth n. Rewriting the function as a loop keeps stack use constant, but the code is often less clear. Raising the recursion limit only postpones the crash and spends more memory.
rubricPoints: Each call pushes a frame with arguments, locals, and a return address, and the frame is popped on return.
Peak stack use equals maximum recursion depth, not total number of calls.
Frames accumulate until the base case is reached.
Example contrast: linear recursion has depth n, while merge sort or balanced quicksort has depth about log n.
Exceeding the fixed stack limit causes a stack overflow or recursion error.
A tradeoff of the fix is named, such as a loop costing clarity or a raised limit only delaying failure and using more memory.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is articulating why depth, not call count, drives stack space, and no listed mission or engine exercises recursion depth directly.

lessons.plain: Sorting means putting items in order, smallest to largest. There are many ways to do it, and they differ in how much work they need as the pile grows, how badly they behave on unlucky input, and how much extra space they need. Think of sorting a hand of playing cards. You can slide each new card into place (insertion sort), split the deck, sort each half and zip them together (merge sort), pick one card and divide the rest into lower and higher piles (quicksort), or keep pulling out the biggest remaining card (heap sort). Each habit wins in a different situation.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must sort a list that is already almost in order, with only a couple of items out of place. Would you rather slide each item into place one at a time, or split the list in half over and over? Why?
lessons.teach:
A sorting algorithm puts n items in order. We judge it by average case (typical work on random input), worst case (work on the most unlucky input), and extra memory (space beyond the list itself). O(n log n) grows only a little faster than n. O(n²) grows with the square of n, so doubling n roughly quadruples the work.

Insertion sort keeps a sorted front section and slides each new item left until it fits. It costs O(n²) on average and in the worst case (reverse order), but only about O(n) on nearly sorted input. It needs no extra memory and is fast on tiny lists.

Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. It always costs O(n log n), but merging needs an extra buffer the size of the list.

Quicksort picks a pivot (a chosen item), partitions the rest into smaller and larger groups, then sorts each group. On average it costs O(n log n) and is usually fastest in practice with little extra memory. Its worst case is O(n²), which happens when the pivot keeps landing at an extreme.

Heap sort arranges the list as a heap (a tree stored in the array where each parent is at least as large as its children), then repeatedly moves the largest item to the end. It is always O(n log n) and needs no extra buffer, but it jumps around memory, so it is often slower in practice.

Worked example: sort [1,2,3,4,5], which is already sorted. Insertion sort compares each new item once with its left neighbour: 4 comparisons, and it is done. Quicksort using the first item as pivot picks 1, so all 4 others go to one side. Next it picks 2, with 3 others, then 3, then 4. That is 4+3+2+1 = 10 comparisons, the O(n²) pattern.

A common mistake is to assume quicksort is always fast. With a naive pivot, sorted or attacker-chosen input can stall a running service. Choosing a random pivot makes this very unlikely.

questions.prompt: A parcel depot's scanner hands over 6 delivery times in exactly reverse order: [60, 50, 40, 30, 20, 10]. The software sorts them with insertion sort, which keeps a sorted front section and slides each new item left until it fits. Step 1: 50 is compared with 60 and slides in front of it, which is 1 comparison. Step 2: 40 slides past 50 and 60, which is 2 comparisons. Step 3: 30 slides past 40, 50 and 60, which is 3 comparisons. Step 4: 20 slides past four items, which is 4 comparisons. Step 5 is missing. Which choice correctly completes step 5 and the conclusion about the total work?
choices: 10 needs 1 comparison, so the total is 1+2+3+4+1 = 11. Reverse order counts as nearly sorted, so this shows the O(n) best case.
10 needs 5 comparisons, so the total is 1+2+3+4+5 = 15. This growing sum is the O(n²) worst-case pattern.
10 needs 0 comparisons because it is the smallest value, so the total stays at 10.
10 needs 5 comparisons, so the total is 15. This is the O(n log n) pattern that insertion sort always follows.
questions.why: In reverse order every new item is smaller than everything already sorted, so 10 must slide past all 5 earlier items, and the 1+2+3+4+5 sum grows with the square of n, which is insertion sort's O(n²) worst case.

questions.prompt: A sensor controller has almost no spare memory beyond the array it is sorting. It must also be guaranteed never to exceed O(n log n) work, even on unlucky input. Which algorithm fits both constraints?
choices: Heap sort, because it is always O(n log n) and needs no extra buffer
Insertion sort, because it needs no extra memory
Merge sort, because it is always O(n log n)
Quicksort, because it is usually fastest and uses little extra memory
questions.why: Heap sort is the only option here that is both always O(n log n) and needs no extra buffer. Merge sort needs a buffer the size of the list, quicksort can hit O(n²), and insertion sort is O(n²) in the worst case.

questions.prompt: An online ticket service sorts incoming order IDs with quicksort, always using the first item as the pivot (the item chosen to split the rest into smaller and larger groups). Sorting slows sharply on days when the IDs already arrive in increasing order. What is the most likely cause, and what is the fix suggested by how quicksort behaves?
choices: Sorted input forces quicksort to use an extra buffer the size of the list, so the fix is to switch to merge sort
Quicksort is O(n²) on average, so the fix is to switch to insertion sort
The data is too small for quicksort, so the fix is to add more items
The first-item pivot is always the smallest value, so each split is maximally lopsided and gives O(n²) work. The fix is to choose a random pivot.
questions.why: On sorted input a first-item pivot always lands at an extreme, which produces the O(n²) worst case. A random pivot makes that outcome very unlikely.

questions.prompt: A library catalogue of 50,000 records is kept in title order. Each night a handful of new records are added in roughly the right places, so the list is nearly sorted. Which algorithm does the least work on this nightly re-sort?
choices: Quicksort with the first item as pivot, because it is usually fastest in practice
Merge sort, because it always splits the list in half
Heap sort, because it is always O(n log n)
Insertion sort, because on nearly sorted input each item moves only a short way, giving about O(n) work
questions.why: Insertion sort runs in about O(n) on nearly sorted input. The other three do O(n log n) at best, and quicksort with a first-item pivot can fall to O(n²) on ordered data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between insertion, merge, quick, and heap sort, and name one tradeoff each one makes.
lessons.modelAnswer: All four put items in order, but they trade speed, worst-case safety and memory differently. Insertion sort slides each item into a sorted front section. It is quadratic in general, yet close to linear on nearly sorted or tiny lists and uses no extra space, so it suits small or almost-ordered data. Merge sort always runs in n log n by splitting and merging, but it needs an extra buffer as large as the input. Quicksort partitions around a pivot. It is usually the fastest in practice and light on memory, but a bad pivot, such as the first item of already sorted data, degrades it to quadratic, so use a random pivot. Heap sort guarantees n log n with no extra buffer, but its scattered memory access makes it slower in practice. If I need a guarantee and have memory, I pick merge sort. If memory is tight, I pick heap sort.
rubricPoints: States average and worst-case growth for each of the four algorithms.
Notes insertion sort is near-linear on nearly sorted or small input.
Notes merge sort guarantees n log n but needs extra memory proportional to n.
Explains quicksort's quadratic worst case comes from bad pivots and how random pivots help.
Notes heap sort guarantees n log n in place but is often slower in practice.
Matches an algorithm to a stated constraint such as memory, guarantees, or input order.

suggested.rationale: This mission already has the learner pick a sorting algorithm based on how its work grows, which is exactly this comparison.

lessons.plain: When you sort a list, two practical questions come up beyond speed. First, stability: if two items tie on the thing you are sorting by, does the sort keep them in the order they started in? Second, in-place behavior: does the sort rearrange items inside the original list, or does it need a second list of similar size as scratch space? Picture people queuing at a bank who are regrouped by ticket colour. A stable regrouping keeps everyone with the same colour in their original arrival order. An in-place regrouping shuffles people within the same room instead of renting a second room.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a list of orders already arranged by time, and you re-sort it by customer name. Two orders from the same customer were placed at 9:00 and 9:05. After the re-sort, should you expect them to still appear 9:00 then 9:05, or could they swap? What do you think decides that?
lessons.teach:
A sort is stable if items with equal keys keep their original relative order in the output. The key is the field you sort by, such as a price or a name. A sort is in-place if it rearranges items within the original array and uses only a small amount of extra memory, constant or at most logarithmic in n, rather than a second array of size n.

Stability matters because it lets you sort by several keys in passes. Sort by the secondary key first, then stable-sort by the primary key. Ties on the primary key keep the secondary order the first pass created.

Worked example. Start with records already in name order: (Ana,2), (Bo,1), (Cy,2), (Di,1). Sort by the number. A stable sort scans and finds that Bo and Di both have 1, with Bo first, so it outputs (Bo,1), (Di,1). Ana and Cy both have 2, with Ana first, so it outputs (Ana,2), (Cy,2). The groups stay alphabetical. An unstable sort could output (Di,1), (Bo,1), (Cy,2), (Ana,2). That is still correctly sorted by number, but the name order is lost.

Common algorithms have known properties. Insertion sort is stable and in-place. The usual array merge sort is stable but needs an extra buffer of about n slots, so it is not in-place. The usual quicksort is in-place, apart from its recursion stack, but not stable. Heap sort is in-place and not stable.

A common mistake is breaking stability by accident. In insertion sort, a new item should move left only past items strictly greater than it. If you write "greater than or equal", it jumps over its equal neighbours and the sort becomes unstable.

In a running system, an unstable sort can silently scramble a multi-key report, for example transactions sorted by account whose dates end up out of order. A sort that is not in-place, run on a very large dataset, can double memory use and push a service out of memory.

questions.prompt: A courier depot's delivery log is already in time order: (09:10, Oak St), (09:25, Elm Rd), (09:40, Oak St), (10:05, Elm Rd), (10:20, Oak St). A dispatcher runs a stable sort with the street as the key, with Elm Rd placed before Oak St. Step 1: The sort finds the Elm Rd records. In the original log, 09:25 comes before 10:05, so it outputs (09:25, Elm Rd), (10:05, Elm Rd). Step 2: [missing] Step 3: The two groups are joined, so the final list is grouped by street and each group stays in time order. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: It may output the Oak St records in any order, such as (09:40), (09:10), (10:20), because all three have the same key.
It outputs the Oak St records before the Elm Rd records, because Oak St appears first in the original log.
It outputs the Oak St records in their original log order: (09:10, Oak St), (09:40, Oak St), (10:20, Oak St).
It outputs the Oak St records newest first: (10:20, Oak St), (09:40, Oak St), (09:10, Oak St), because equal keys are reversed.
questions.why: A stable sort keeps records with equal keys in their original relative order, so the three Oak St records stay in their original time order.

questions.prompt: A team needs to sort an array of records. Equal keys must keep their original order, and the server cannot spare a second array the same size as the input. Of the usual array versions of these algorithms, which one meets both requirements?
choices: Heap sort
Quicksort
Merge sort
Insertion sort
questions.why: Insertion sort is both stable and in-place. Merge sort is stable but needs a buffer of about n slots, and quicksort and heap sort are in-place but not stable.

questions.prompt: A clinic wants its patient list grouped by ward, with patients in alphabetical order by surname inside each ward. It will sort the list in two passes. Which plan works?
choices: Sort by ward first, then use a stable sort to sort by surname.
Sort by ward first, then use heap sort to sort by surname.
Sort by surname first, then use a stable sort to sort by ward.
Sort by surname first, then use quicksort to sort by ward.
questions.why: You sort by the secondary key (surname) first and then stable-sort by the primary key (ward), so patients tied on ward keep the surname order from the first pass.

questions.prompt: A developer writes insertion sort but lets a new item move left past neighbours that are greater than or equal to it. The input, sorted by score, is (Pia,5), (Quinn,5). What does this version output, and what does that show?
choices: (Pia,5), (Quinn,5). This shows the sort is still stable, because both scores are equal.
(Quinn,5), (Pia,5). This shows the sort is no longer in-place, because items moved.
It gives an error. Insertion sort cannot handle equal keys when it uses greater than or equal.
(Quinn,5), (Pia,5). Quinn jumps over its equal neighbour, so the sort is no longer stable.
questions.why: With greater than or equal, Quinn moves left past Pia even though their keys are equal, which reverses their original order and breaks stability. The sort still rearranges items within the same array, so it remains in-place.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what it means for a sort to be stable and what it means for it to be in-place. Give a situation where each property matters, and name the tradeoff you face when you need both.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stable sort keeps items that tie on the sort key in the same relative order they had before sorting. That matters when you sort by multiple fields in passes. If a log is already in time order and I stable-sort it by user, each user's entries stay in time order. An unstable sort might shuffle them while still being correctly sorted by user. An in-place sort rearranges items inside the original array and uses only a little extra memory, instead of allocating a second array the size of the input. That matters when data is huge or memory is tight. The tradeoff is that the familiar fast options split these properties. Typical merge sort is stable but needs about n extra space. Quicksort and heap sort are in-place but unstable. Insertion sort has both properties but is slow on large inputs. So I either pay memory, give up speed, or add the original position as a tie-breaking key.
rubricPoints: Defines stability as preserving the original relative order of items with equal keys.
Defines in-place as rearranging within the original array using only small extra memory, not a full second array.
Gives a concrete case where stability matters, such as multi-key sorting in passes.
Gives a concrete case where in-place matters, such as large data or limited memory.
Names the tradeoff, for example that merge sort is stable but uses extra space while quicksort and heap sort are in-place but unstable.

suggested.rationale: Stability and in-place behavior are best learned by reasoning through exam-style scenarios where a stated constraint, such as preserving tie order or limited memory, rules certain sorts in or out.

lessons.plain: T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) is a short formula describing how much work a divide-and-conquer method does. It says: to handle a job of size n, split it into two halves, solve each half the same way, then spend time proportional to n stitching the answers together. Think of sorting a big stack of exam papers with a friend: you split the stack, each of you sorts your half (splitting again if it is still big), then you merge the two sorted piles by walking through them once. The formula tells us the total effort grows like n times log n, which is only a bit worse than handling each paper once.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you keep cutting a pile of 16 papers in half until each pile has one paper, how many rounds of halving does it take, and roughly how much merging work happens in each round?
lessons.teach:
A recurrence is an equation that defines a function in terms of itself on smaller inputs. Here T(n) means the running time on an input of size n. The term 2T(n/2) says the algorithm makes two recursive calls, each on half the input. The term O(n), read big-O of n, means extra work that grows at most in proportion to n, done outside the recursive calls: splitting the input and combining the two results. Merge sort is the classic example: split the list, sort each half, then merge the sorted halves in one linear pass.

To solve it, draw a recursion tree, a picture where each node is one call labelled with its own non-recursive work. The root does about cn work (c is some constant). Its two children each handle n/2, doing cn/2 each, so cn total. The next level has four calls of n/4, again cn total. Every level costs cn. Halving stops when pieces reach size 1, which takes log2 n levels. Total: cn times log2 n, so T(n) is O(n log n).

Worked example with n=8 and c=1. Level 0: one call, 8 units of merging. Level 1: two calls of size 4, 4+4=8. Level 2: four calls of size 2, 8 total. Level 3: eight calls of size 1, the base case, constant work each. Three merging levels (log2 8 = 3) times 8 gives 24, which is n log2 n.

A common mistake is reasoning that two recursive calls means the work doubles at every level and explodes.
