It does not, because each call gets half the input; the doubling of calls and the halving of size cancel, keeping each level at cn. Another mistake is dropping the O(n) term: T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(1) sums to only O(n).

The formula assumes an even split. Quicksort matches it only when pivots divide the data near the middle; consistently lopsided splits give n levels instead of log n, and running time degrades to O(n squared), which a production system feels as sudden slowdowns on unlucky inputs.

questions.prompt: A logistics team uses a divide-and-conquer routine on 16 shipment records. Each call splits its records into two halves, recurses on each half, then combines the two results in one linear pass costing 2 units per record (so c = 2). The running time follows T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n). Trace the recursion tree. Level 0: one call on 16 records, 2 x 16 = 32 units of combining. Level 1: two calls on 8 records, 16 + 16 = 32 units. Level 2: four calls on 4 records, 32 units. Level 3: eight calls on 2 records, 32 units. Level 4: sixteen calls on 1 record each, the base case, with only constant work each. Missing step: what is the total combining work, and how does it match the general formula?
choices: 5 levels x 32 = 160 units, because every level of the tree, including the size-1 base case level, does a full 32 units of combining
4 combining levels x 32 = 128 units, which equals c x n x log2 n = 2 x 16 x 4
32 + 64 + 128 + 256 = 480 units, because two recursive calls double the combining work at each level going down
32 units in total, because the root's single linear pass already touches every one of the 16 records
questions.why: Each of the log2 16 = 4 combining levels costs cn = 32, so the total is 32 x 4 = 128 units, which is cn log2 n, i.e. O(n log n). The base-case level does only constant work per call.

questions.prompt: In the recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n), what does the O(n) term describe?
choices: The number of levels in the recursion tree before the pieces reach size 1.
The number of recursive calls made at the deepest level of the recursion tree.
The total running time of the two recursive calls, each of which handles half of the input.
The work done outside the recursive calls, such as splitting the input and combining the results. This work grows at most in proportion to n.
questions.why: O(n) is the non-recursive work, the split and combine, done by a call of size n. The 2T(n/2) term covers the recursive calls.

questions.prompt: A monitoring tool finds the largest reading among n sensor values. It splits the values in half, recursively finds the largest value in each half, then compares the two answers in constant time. Its recurrence is T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(1). What is its overall running time?
choices: O(log n), because the input is halved at each step
O(n), because dropping the linear combine step to constant work makes the total sum to only O(n)
O(n log n), because any algorithm that halves its input and makes two calls is O(n log n)
O(n squared), because the number of calls doubles at every level
questions.why: With only O(1) work per call instead of O(n), the per-level cost no longer stays at cn. The whole tree sums to O(n), not O(n log n).

questions.prompt: A ticketing service sorts orders with quicksort. On a certain kind of input, every pivot ends up as the smallest remaining value, so each split leaves almost everything on one side. Why does T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) no longer describe this case, and what happens?
choices: The splits are not even, so the tree has about n levels instead of log n, and the running time degrades to O(n squared)
It still applies, because quicksort always makes two recursive calls, so the time stays O(n log n)
The tree gets shallower because one side is empty, so the running time drops to O(log n)
The combine step becomes constant, so the running time improves to O(n)
questions.why: The formula assumes halving. Consistently lopsided splits give about n levels of linear work, which is O(n squared), and the service feels this as sudden slowdowns on unlucky inputs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) means and why it works out to O(n log n), and name one assumption that, if broken, makes the result no longer hold.
lessons.modelAnswer: It describes a divide-and-conquer algorithm like merge sort: to solve a problem of size n, it makes two recursive calls on halves, plus linear work to split and combine. If you draw the calls as a tree, the top does about n work, the next level has two calls of n/2, so n again, then four calls of n/4, still n. Each level costs about n because the number of calls doubles while each piece halves. You can halve n only log2 n times before reaching size 1, so the total is n times log n. The key assumption is that the split is balanced. If one side gets almost everything, as with a bad quicksort pivot, the tree has about n levels and the cost becomes n squared. Also, the combine step must really be linear; if it were quadratic, the total would change too.
rubricPoints: States that T(n) is running time and 2T(n/2) means two recursive calls on half-size inputs.
Identifies O(n) as the split-and-combine work outside the recursive calls.
Explains that each level of the recursion tree costs about n work.
Explains there are about log2 n levels, giving O(n log n) total.
Names a limit such as needing balanced splits, with unbalanced splits degrading to O(n squared).

suggested.rationale: Interpreting this recurrence is a reasoning skill best built by walking through the recursion tree aloud and justifying why each level costs n and why there are log n levels.

lessons.plain: Any sorting method that learns about the data only by comparing two items at a time ('is A smaller than B?') must, in its worst case, make roughly n log n comparisons for n items. No cleverness gets a general comparison sort below that. Think of the game Twenty Questions: each yes/no answer can at best cut the remaining possibilities in half. A list of n items can arrive in a huge number of possible orders, and you need enough halvings to pin down which one you have. That count of halvings works out to about n log n.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must put 3 different cards in order, and the only thing you may do is ask 'is card X smaller than card Y?'. Can 2 questions always be enough, or do you sometimes need 3? Why?
lessons.teach:
A comparison sort is any algorithm that learns about the data only by comparing pairs of items. Merge sort, quicksort, heap sort and insertion sort are all comparison sorts. The objective claims their worst case is Omega(n log n). Big Omega means 'grows at least as fast as, up to a constant factor', so it states a floor on the work.

The argument uses a decision tree. This is a picture of every run the algorithm could make. Each internal node is one comparison, and its two branches are the two possible answers. Each leaf, meaning an end point, is a final sorted order. n distinct items can arrive in n! (n factorial, n×(n−1)×...×1) different orders. A correct sort must end at a different leaf for each one, so the tree needs at least n! leaves. A binary tree of height h, meaning the longest root-to-leaf path, has at most 2^h leaves. So 2^h ≥ n!, which gives h ≥ log2(n!). The height is the worst-case number of comparisons.

Worked example with n = 3. There are 3! = 6 possible orders. Two comparisons give at most 2^2 = 4 leaves, which is too few. Three comparisons give 8 leaves, which is enough. So some input always forces 3 comparisons.

In general, at least n/2 of the factors in n! are each at least n/2. That means n! ≥ (n/2)^(n/2), and so log2(n!) ≥ (n/2)·log2(n/2), which is Omega(n log n). A similar argument shows the average case has the same floor.

A common mistake is to read the bound as 'every input costs n log n'. Insertion sort finishes an already-sorted list in about n steps. The bound concerns the worst case, and the average over all orders. Another mistake is to think counting sort or radix sort break the bound. They sort by reading digits or key values instead of comparing items, so the bound does not cover them.

The practical consequence: merge sort and heap sort are already optimal up to constants. To go faster, you must exploit the structure of the keys, not look for a smarter way to compare.

questions.prompt:
A swim coach wants to rank 4 swimmers. The only tool is a head-to-head race between two swimmers, and each race says only who was faster. That makes any ranking method a comparison sort. The coach asks for the smallest number of races that some unlucky set of results could force.

Step 1: 4 distinct swimmers can finish in 4! = 4×3×2×1 = 24 possible orders. A correct method must end at a different leaf (end point) of its decision tree for each order, so the tree needs at least 24 leaves.
Step 2: Each race is one internal node with two branches. A tree whose longest path has h races therefore has at most 2^h leaves.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The coach concludes that no head-to-head method can promise a ranking in fewer races than that number for every possible set of results.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: 4 × log2(4) = 8, so every ranking will take exactly 8 races.
Each of the 24 orders needs its own race, so h must be at least 24.
We need 2^h ≥ 4, one leaf per swimmer. 2^2 = 4, so 2 races are enough.
We need 2^h ≥ 24. Since 2^4 = 16 is too few and 2^5 = 32 is enough, h is at least 5.
questions.why: The tree needs at least 4! = 24 leaves and a height-h tree has at most 2^h leaves, and the smallest h with 2^h ≥ 24 is 5.

questions.prompt: A shipping company sorts millions of parcels by 5-digit postal code. It uses radix sort, which handles the codes one digit at a time and drops each parcel into a bucket by that digit's value. It never compares two parcels with each other. A colleague says this cannot beat n log n because of the comparison-sort lower bound. What is the best response?
choices: The bound applies, but only in the average case, so radix sort can win only on its worst-case inputs.
The bound does not apply here, because postal codes contain repeated values and the bound assumes distinct items.
The bound does not apply here, because radix sort reads digit values instead of comparing pairs of items.
The colleague is right, because the bound covers every sorting algorithm whatever its method.
questions.why: The Omega(n log n) floor covers only algorithms that learn about the data by comparing pairs, and radix sort sorts by reading key digits instead.

questions.prompt: A library's catalog list is already in order. Insertion sort processes it with about n comparisons, far fewer than n log n. Does this contradict the Omega(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts?
choices: Yes. The bound says every input must cost at least n log n comparisons, so the bound must be wrong.
No. The bound only applies to sorts that use recursion, such as merge sort.
No. The bound is about the worst case and the average over all orders, not about every single input.
Yes. Insertion sort is not really a comparison sort, so it escapes the bound.
questions.why: The lower bound puts a floor on worst-case and average-case comparisons, so a lucky input like an already-sorted list can still finish in about n steps.

questions.prompt: A startup claims its new comparison-based algorithm sorts any 10 distinct items using at most 20 comparisons. Note that 10! = 3,628,800 and 2^20 = 1,048,576. Using the decision-tree argument, what should you conclude?
choices: The claim is plausible, because 20 is larger than 10 × log2(10), which is about 33.
The claim is impossible, because a comparison sort always needs at least 10! comparisons.
The claim is impossible, because 20 comparisons give at most 1,048,576 leaves, which is fewer than the 3,628,800 orders that each need their own leaf.
The claim is plausible, because the bound only limits the average case and says nothing about a worst-case promise.
questions.why: A decision tree of height 20 has at most 2^20 leaves, which is fewer than 10! distinct orders, so some input must force more than 20 comparisons.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why no general comparison-based sort can beat n log n in the worst case, and name one situation where the bound does not apply or does not mean what people assume.
lessons.modelAnswer: Picture every possible run of a comparison sort as a binary decision tree. Each comparison is a fork with two outcomes, and each leaf is a final ordering. With n items there are n! possible input orders, and each needs its own leaf, or the sort would mix two of them up. A tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves, so the worst-case comparison count h must be at least log2(n!). That grows like n log n. For 3 items, 6 orders need at least 3 comparisons, because 2 comparisons only give 4 leaves. The limits: this is a worst-case and average-case floor, not a promise about every input. Insertion sort handles already-sorted data in linear time. The bound also only covers comparison sorts. Counting sort or radix sort on small integer keys can run in near-linear time because they read the key values directly instead of comparing items.
rubricPoints: Defines a comparison sort as one that learns only from pairwise comparisons.
Uses the decision tree: each comparison has two outcomes, and each leaf is an output order.
Notes there are n! input orders, so at least n! leaves are needed and the height is at least log2(n!).
States that log2(n!) grows as n log n, giving the Omega(n log n) worst-case floor.
Names a limit: non-comparison sorts escape the bound, or some specific inputs can be faster.

suggested.rationale: The skill here is reproducing the decision-tree counting argument, so explaining it back in your own words is the most direct practice; no mission or planned engine walks through this proof.

lessons.plain: A graph is a simple picture of things and how they connect. Each thing is a vertex, also called a node: a city, a person, a server. Each connection between two things is an edge. Think of a subway map. The stations are vertices and the track segments joining two stations are edges. The map ignores the true distances and the real shape of the tunnels. It keeps only which stations are directly linked. That stripped-down view is what makes graphs useful. The same few ideas work for friendships, road networks, web links and which computer programs depend on which.
lessons.guessPrompt: Four servers: A talks to B, A talks to C, B talks to C, and C talks to D. If each server is a dot and each 'talks to' link is a line, how many lines do you draw, and which server touches the most lines?
lessons.teach:
A graph is a set of things plus the connections between pairs of them. A vertex (or node) is one thing. An edge is a connection between exactly two vertices, which are called its endpoints. Two vertices joined by an edge are adjacent, or neighbors. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges touching it. People usually write V for the set of vertices and E for the set of edges, with n for how many vertices there are and m for how many edges.

Why this works: it throws away everything except which things exist and which pairs are linked. Once that is all you keep, one toolkit fits road maps, social networks and service dependencies alike. Where you draw the dots does not matter. Only the pairs matter.

Worked example: take four servers A, B, C and D. A talks to B, A talks to C, B talks to C, and C talks to D.
Step 1: the vertices are A, B, C and D, so n = 4.
Step 2: the edges are A–B, A–C, B–C and C–D, so m = 4.
Step 3: work out the degrees. A has 2, B has 2, C has 3 (A–C, B–C and C–D), and D has 1.
Step 4: add the degrees: 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 8, which is exactly 2 × 4.
That result always holds. Every edge has two endpoints, so each edge adds one to two different degrees. This fact is called the handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges.

Common mistake: treating the sum of degrees as the edge count, or listing A–B and B–A as two separate connections when the link has no direction. Both mistakes count every edge twice. A related slip is to treat two lines that cross on paper as a new vertex. A crossing in a drawing is not a vertex.

Consequence in a running system: picture a dependency map of services. If you count each link from both ends, your estimate of storage or checking work comes out double. Degree also gives a quick warning sign. A vertex with very high degree is a service that many others connect to, so if it fails, the damage spreads widely.

questions.prompt:
A small book club has five members: Priya, Quinn, Rosa, Sam and Tess. Friendships go both ways (no direction). The friendships are Priya–Quinn, Priya–Rosa, Quinn–Rosa, Quinn–Sam, Rosa–Sam and Sam–Tess.
Step 1: the vertices are the five members, so n = 5.
Step 2: the edges are the six friendships listed, so m = 6.
Step 3: the degrees are Priya 2, Quinn 3, Rosa 3, Sam 3, Tess 1.
Step 4: ???
Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Add the degrees to get 12, which equals 2 × 6 and confirms m = 6.
Add the degrees to get 12, which should equal m, so a degree must be wrong.
Add the degrees to get 12, then halve again to get 3 real friendships.
Add the degrees to get 12, so the club has 12 friendships.
questions.why: By the handshake lemma, each friendship adds one to the degree of both of its endpoints, so the degree sum (12) is exactly twice the edge count (6).

questions.prompt: A regional rail network has 7 stations. Each track joins exactly two stations, and tracks have no direction. If you add up the degrees of all 7 stations, you get 18. How many tracks are there?
questions.why: The sum of all degrees equals twice the number of edges, so the number of tracks is 18 ÷ 2 = 9.

questions.prompt: An engineer maps an office chat system where any link between two users works both ways. For every link, she writes one entry from each user's side, such as Lee–Kim and also Kim–Lee. Her list ends up with 20 entries. What is the true number of edges?
choices: 20, because each entry is a separate connection
10, because each two-way link was written down twice
It cannot be known without the number of users
40, because each link has two endpoints
questions.why: A link with no direction is a single edge, so listing it from both ends counts every edge twice, and 20 ÷ 2 = 10.

questions.prompt: In a payment platform's service dependency graph, the degrees are: login service 9, billing service 3, email service 1, reporting service 2. Using only degree as the warning sign, which service's failure would most likely cause the widest damage?
choices: None of them, because degree says nothing about failure impact
Login service, because the most other services connect to it
Email service, because it has the fewest links to back it up
Reporting service, because it sits in the middle of the list
questions.why: A vertex with very high degree is one that many others connect to, so if it fails the damage spreads most widely.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what vertices, edges and degree are, using a system you both know. Then name one limit of this plain vertex-and-edge model: something about the real system that it does not capture.
lessons.modelAnswer: Model our microservices as a graph. Each service is a vertex. Whenever two services talk directly, we draw an edge between them, and those two services are the edge's endpoints. A service's degree is how many edges touch it, which means how many services it is directly linked to. When you count edges, count each link once. Adding up all the degrees gives twice the edge count, because every edge has two ends. A high-degree service deserves attention, since many others are connected to it. The limit is that a plain vertex-and-edge model only records whether a link exists. It does not say which side calls the other, how much traffic flows, or how slow the link is. It also ignores the physical layout. If we need any of that, we have to add more information to the edges.
rubricPoints: Defines a vertex as one thing and an edge as a connection between exactly two vertices.
Defines degree as the number of edges touching a vertex.
Notes that the sum of degrees is twice the edge count, so you must avoid double counting.
Maps the idea onto a concrete real system.
Names a limit, such as no direction, no weight or cost, or no physical layout in the basic model.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine works with graphs, and the core skill here is putting a real system into vertex-and-edge terms and explaining it clearly.

lessons.plain: A graph is a set of things (called vertices) joined by connections (called edges). Graphs come in flavours along two separate questions. First, does a connection have a direction? A friendship goes both ways (undirected), but following someone on social media can be one-way (directed). Second, does a connection carry a number? A plain road map just shows which towns are linked (unweighted), while a map with distances or travel times on each road is weighted. Picking the right flavour matters because it changes what questions you can sensibly ask, such as which route is shortest.
lessons.guessPrompt: Think of a city's streets, where some are one-way and each has a travel time. Would you describe that map as directed or undirected, and weighted or unweighted? Why?
lessons.teach:
A graph is a collection of vertices (the items) and edges (the links between pairs of items). Two independent choices describe its edges.

Directed versus undirected: in an undirected graph an edge {A, B} can be travelled either way, so A reaches B and B reaches A. In a directed graph, often called a digraph, each edge is an ordered pair (A, B), drawn as an arrow from A to B. It lets you go from A to B only. In a directed graph, a vertex's out-degree counts the arrows leaving it and its in-degree counts the arrows arriving. An undirected edge behaves exactly like two opposite arrows, which is why many programs store it that way.

Weighted versus unweighted: a weighted graph attaches a number, the weight, to every edge. The weight might be a distance, a cost or a time. An unweighted graph treats every edge as equal, so its natural measure is the number of edges, called hops.

The two choices combine freely, giving four kinds of graph.

Worked example: there are vertices A, B and C. A one-way street runs A→B taking 5 minutes. A two-way street joins B and C taking 2 minutes. A one-way street runs C→A taking 10 minutes. This graph is directed and weighted. Can you get from B back to A? Go B to C (2 minutes, allowed because that street is two-way), then C to A (10 minutes). That makes 12 minutes over 2 hops. Going A to C is possible only through B: 5 + 2 = 7 minutes. If you wrongly treated the graph as undirected, you would conclude A to C takes 10 minutes along C→A backwards, which breaks a one-way rule.

A common mistake is to ignore the weights and call the route with the fewest edges the shortest. Two cheap hops can beat one expensive hop. In a running system this matters directly. A routing service or a dependency checker that models links with the wrong direction or ignores weight will send traffic down impossible or slow paths. Fewest hops equals least cost only when all edges are unweighted, or when every weight is the same.

questions.prompt:
A small hosting company links five servers, P, Q, R, S and T. Each link has a delay in milliseconds (ms). One-way links: P→S takes 9 ms, P→Q takes 4 ms, P→R takes 1 ms, R→S takes 2 ms, P→T takes 1 ms, and S→T takes 1 ms (the arrow points from S to T). There is also a two-way link between Q and S that takes 3 ms. We want the fastest way to send data from P to S.

Step 1: Classify the graph. Some links are one-way and every link has a delay, so it is directed and weighted.
Step 2: Add up the routes that follow every arrow forward. P→S is 9 ms over 1 hop. P→Q→S is 4 + 3 = 7 ms over 2 hops (Q to S is allowed because that link is two-way). P→R→S is 1 + 2 = 3 ms over 2 hops.
Step 3: (missing) Deal with the route through T.
Step 4: The fastest route is P→R→S at 3 ms, even though P→S uses fewer hops.

Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: P→T→S would add up to 1 + 1 = 2 ms, but the link between T and S is an arrow from S to T, so data cannot go from T to S. Discard this route.
T has an in-degree of 2, so it is a dead end and can be skipped without checking its links.
P→T→S costs 1 + 1 = 2 ms, so it is the fastest route.
P→T→S has 2 hops, the same as P→R→S, so the two routes tie.
questions.why: In a directed graph you may only travel an arrow from its tail to its head, so the S→T link cannot carry data from T to S and the 2 ms total is not a real route.

questions.prompt: A university models its courses as a directed graph. An arrow from one course to another means the first course is a prerequisite for the second. Course X has arrows X→Y and X→Z, and there is also an arrow W→X. What are the out-degree and in-degree of X?
choices: Out-degree 2, in-degree 1
Out-degree 1, in-degree 2
Out-degree 3, in-degree 0, because arrow direction does not affect degree
Out-degree 3, in-degree 3
questions.why: Out-degree counts the arrows leaving X (X→Y and X→Z, so 2), and in-degree counts the arrows arriving at X (W→X, so 1).

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing app lets one user follow another without being followed back. The app stores only who follows whom and attaches no number to any link. Which kind of graph describes this follow network?
choices: Undirected and weighted
Directed and weighted
Undirected and unweighted
Directed and unweighted
questions.why: Following is one-way, so each link is an arrow (directed), and no number is attached to any link, so every edge counts the same (unweighted).

questions.prompt: A courier's routing tool always picks the route with the fewest road segments. From depot D to customer K there is one direct road of 20 km. There is also a route through two towns made of three roads of 4 km each. Which statement describes what the tool does and why?
choices: It picks the direct road, and that is correct, because one hop always costs less than three hops.
It cannot choose a route, because hop counts only work in directed graphs.
It picks the three-road route because 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 km is less than 20 km.
It picks the direct 20 km road because that route has the fewest hops. That is 8 km longer than the 12 km three-road route, because counting hops ignores the weights.
questions.why: Counting hops treats every road as equal, so the tool picks the 1-hop 20 km road. Fewest hops only equals least cost when all edges are unweighted or every weight is the same, and here the three cheap roads total just 12 km.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between directed and undirected graphs, and between weighted and unweighted ones. Give one real example of each, and name one tradeoff or limit of choosing a simpler model.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Direction asks whether an edge works both ways. An undirected edge, like two people being friends, can be travelled in either direction. A directed edge, like a web page linking to another or a one-way street, goes only from its source to its target. Weight asks whether each edge carries a number. A plain network diagram showing which servers connect is unweighted, so you count hops. Adding latency to each link makes it weighted, so you add up the latencies.

The two properties are independent, so a graph can be directed and weighted at once, like a one-way street map with travel times.

The tradeoff is that a simpler model is easier to store and reason about, and fewest hops is simple to compute. But it can give wrong answers. Treating a directed graph as undirected invents paths that do not exist. Ignoring weights can call a two-hop route shortest when a three-hop route is actually cheaper.
rubricPoints: Defines a directed edge as one-way and an undirected edge as usable in both directions.
Defines a weighted graph as having a number on each edge and an unweighted graph as counting hops.
States that direction and weight are independent properties that can be combined.
Gives a concrete real-world example for each kind.
Names a risk of oversimplifying, such as invented paths or fewest hops not being the cheapest route.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises graph modelling, and the core skill here is classifying a situation and explaining why the classification matters.

lessons.plain: A graph is a set of things (vertices) joined by connections (edges), and a computer needs some way to store it. There are two classic layouts. An adjacency matrix is a square grid with one row and one column per vertex, and a mark in a cell means those two are connected, like a mileage chart in a road atlas. An adjacency list gives each vertex its own short list of the vertices it connects to, like a contacts page per person. The grid answers 'are these two connected?' instantly but uses lots of space. The lists save space and make 'who are my neighbours?' fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: A social network has one million users, and each user has about 200 friends. Would you store the friendships as a giant grid with one row and one column per user, or as a short friend list per user? Why?
lessons.teach:
An adjacency matrix and an adjacency list are two ways to store a graph. A vertex is one item in the graph, and an edge is a connection between two vertices. V means the number of vertices and E means the number of edges.

An adjacency matrix is a V-by-V grid. The cell at row i, column j holds 1 (or the edge's weight) if there is an edge from i to j, and 0 otherwise. Because the cell location is computed directly, checking whether one specific edge exists takes constant time, O(1). The cost is space: the grid always needs V² cells, even if almost none are filled. Listing a vertex's neighbours means scanning its whole row, which is O(V).

An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours. Total space is O(V + E): one slot per vertex plus one entry per edge end. Listing neighbours takes time proportional to the degree, which is the number of edges touching that vertex. Checking one specific edge means scanning a list, which is O(degree).

Worked example: vertices A, B, C, D with undirected edges A-B, A-C, C-D. The matrix has 16 cells. A's row has 1s under B and C, and B's row has a 1 under A. Six cells hold 1, because each undirected edge appears twice. The list form is A:[B,C], B:[A], C:[A,D], D:[C], which is six entries in total. Is B connected to D? In the matrix, you read row B, column D, find 0, and you are done in one step. In the list, you scan B's list [A] and do not find D. Who are A's neighbours? The matrix scans all 4 cells of row A, while the list simply reads [B,C].

A common mistake is recording an undirected edge in only one direction, so a traversal starting from the other end never finds it.

In a running system, a matrix for a large sparse graph (one with few edges per vertex) wastes memory badly. One million vertices would need a trillion cells, which crashes or stalls the process. Lists suit sparse graphs, and matrices suit small or dense graphs where fast edge checks matter.

questions.prompt: A cycling club maps 5 rest stops, P, Q, R, S and T, connected by undirected trails P-Q, P-R, R-S and S-T. The club wants to compare the two graph storage methods. Step 1: count the vertices and edges. V = 5 and E = 4. Step 2: build the adjacency list, which gives each stop a list of its neighbours: P:[Q,R], Q:[P], R:[P,S], S:[R,T], T:[S]. That is 8 entries in total, two for each trail. Step 3: size the adjacency matrix, a V-by-V grid. 5 x 5 = 25 cells. Step 4 (missing): how many of those 25 matrix cells hold a 1?
choices: 25, because the grid is always full
4, one cell for each trail
9, one per vertex plus one per edge
8, because each undirected trail is recorded in both directions
questions.why: An undirected edge between two stops is marked in both stops' rows, so 4 trails produce 2 x 4 = 8 cells holding 1, matching the 8 list entries.

questions.prompt: A city planning team models its streets as a graph. There are 200,000 intersections (vertices), and each intersection touches only about 4 streets (edges), so the graph is sparse, meaning each vertex has few edges. Which storage choice fits best, and why?
choices: An adjacency matrix, because checking one specific street takes constant time and that outweighs memory
An adjacency list, because its space grows with V + E, while a matrix needs 200,000 squared, about 40 billion cells, almost all zero
An adjacency list or a matrix, because both need about the same memory here
An adjacency matrix, because it uses less space when there are few edges
questions.why: A matrix always needs V-squared cells no matter how few edges exist, so for a large sparse graph an adjacency list's O(V + E) space is far smaller.

questions.prompt: A warehouse robot system stores a graph of 1,000 shelf locations. Location K has degree 3, meaning exactly 3 edges touch it. The system needs to list all of K's neighbours. How much work does each storage method do?
choices: Both read only 3 items, because K has 3 neighbours
The matrix reads 3 cells directly, while the list scans all 1,000 locations
Both take constant time, O(1), regardless of degree
The matrix scans all 1,000 cells in K's row, while the list reads only K's 3 entries
questions.why: Listing neighbours in a matrix means scanning the whole row, O(V), whereas an adjacency list only reads that vertex's own list, O(degree).

questions.prompt: A delivery app stores an undirected road between Warehouse W and Depot D in an adjacency list. A developer adds D to W's list but forgets to add W to D's list. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
choices: Nothing goes wrong, because an undirected edge only needs to be stored once
The graph uses too much memory; the fix is to switch to an adjacency matrix
A traversal starting at D never finds W; the fix is to add the road to both W's and D's lists
Edge checks become slower; the fix is to sort W's list
questions.why: An undirected edge must be recorded at both ends, otherwise a search starting from the side missing the entry cannot see the connection.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list each store a graph, and tell them which one you would pick for a road map of a country's intersections and why, naming the tradeoff you are accepting.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both layouts store which vertices are connected. A matrix is a V-by-V grid where cell (i, j) marks an edge from i to j. It always costs V² space, gives an O(1) answer to 'is there an edge between these two?', but needs O(V) to list one vertex's neighbours. An adjacency list keeps, for each vertex, a list of its neighbours. That takes O(V + E) space, and listing neighbours costs only that vertex's degree, but checking one specific edge means scanning a list. For a country's road intersections I'd use lists, because the graph is huge and sparse: each intersection touches maybe four roads, so a matrix would be almost all zeros and use enormous memory. The tradeoff I accept is slower single-edge lookups. For undirected roads I must also record each edge in both vertices' lists.
rubricPoints: Describes the matrix as a V-by-V grid with one cell per possible edge.
Describes the list as per-vertex neighbour lists.
States space costs: O(V²) for the matrix versus O(V + E) for lists.
Contrasts the speed of an edge check against the speed of listing neighbours for each form.
Picks lists for a sparse graph and names the slower edge lookup as the tradeoff.
Notes that an undirected edge must be stored in both directions.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is weighing space against lookup speed for a given graph's size and density, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios rather than any existing mission.

lessons.plain: Breadth-first search, or BFS, is a way of exploring a network of connected things by visiting everything one step away first, then everything two steps away, and so on. Think of dropping a stone in a pond: the ripples spread outward in rings, and each ring reaches every spot at the same distance before the next ring starts. Because BFS works outward in these rings, the first time it reaches something is always by the fewest possible steps. That makes it the natural tool for questions like the fewest hops between two computers or the fewest introductions between two people.
lessons.guessPrompt: You want the fewest introductions needed to reach a stranger through a friend network. Should you check all your direct friends first and then their friends, or follow one chain of friends as far as it goes before trying another? Why?
lessons.teach:
BFS is a traversal, meaning a systematic visit of every reachable vertex in a graph. A vertex is a point, such as a person or a server. An edge is a connection between two vertices. BFS starts at a chosen source vertex and visits vertices in order of their distance from the source, counted in edges.

It uses two tools. A queue is a first-in, first-out line: items join at the back and leave from the front. A visited set records which vertices have already been discovered, so none is handled twice. The steps are: mark the source visited and put it in the queue. Repeat while the queue is not empty: take the front vertex, then for each neighbour not yet visited, mark it visited, record its distance as the current distance plus one, and add it to the back.

This works because the queue keeps all distance-1 vertices ahead of all distance-2 vertices, and so on. The first discovery of any vertex is therefore along a shortest path, measured in edge count.

Worked example. Edges: A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E. Start at A. Queue [A]. Take A; add B and C at distance 1. Queue [B, C]. Take B; D is new, distance 2. Queue [C, D]. Take C; D is already visited, skip. Take D; E is new, distance 3. Take E; nothing new. Visit order A, B, C, D, E, and the fewest hops from A to E is 3.

A common mistake is marking a vertex visited only when it leaves the queue. Then D would be added twice, once from B and once from C. In a large, densely connected graph this duplicates work and can bloat the queue. If the visited set is dropped entirely, cycles make the search loop forever.

Two limits matter. BFS gives shortest paths only when every edge counts the same, so it suits unweighted graphs. Its queue can hold a whole ring at once, which may need a lot of memory in wide graphs. With an adjacency list, the total work is proportional to vertices plus edges.

questions.prompt: A courier firm models six depots as vertices: P, Q, R, S, T, U. The roads between them are the edges: P-Q, P-R, Q-S, R-S, R-T, S-U, T-U. Every road counts as one hop. BFS starts at P. Queue [P]. Take P; Q and R are new, so mark each visited at distance 1 and add them to the back. Queue [Q, R]. Take Q; S is new, so mark it visited at distance 2 and add it. Queue [R, S]. Take R; [MISSING STEP]. Queue [S, T]. Take S; U is new, so mark it visited at distance 3 and add it. Queue [T, U]. Take T; U is already visited, so skip it. Take U; nothing new. Which step belongs in the gap?
choices: S is reachable from R too, so add S to the back again at distance 2. T is new, so mark it visited at distance 2 and add it.
S is already visited, so skip it. T is new, so mark it visited at distance 2 and add it to the back.
S is already visited, so skip it. T is new, so mark it visited at distance 3 and add it to the back.
S is already visited, so skip it. T is new, so mark it visited and put it at the front so it is handled next.
questions.why: R is at distance 1 and S was already discovered from Q, so only T is new, and its distance is R's distance plus one (2), added at the back of the first-in, first-out queue.

questions.prompt: A school's network team runs BFS on its building network, where vertices are switches and edges are cables, each cable counting as one hop. Why is the first time BFS discovers a switch guaranteed to be along a route with the fewest cables from the source?
choices: Because the queue releases every vertex at distance k before any vertex at distance k+1, so a vertex is first reached from the nearest possible ring.
Because BFS always follows one route as deep as possible before trying another.
Because BFS checks every possible route to each switch and keeps the shortest one.
Because the visited set sorts vertices alphabetically before they are handled.
questions.why: The first-in, first-out queue processes vertices ring by ring by distance, so the first discovery of any vertex happens from the closest ring and therefore along a shortest path in edge count.

questions.prompt: A hiking app stores trails as edges between huts, and each trail has a different walking time, from 10 minutes to 3 hours. A developer uses BFS to find the quickest route between two huts. What is the problem?
choices: BFS will visit some huts twice, because every hut needs a visited set of its own.
BFS finds the route with the fewest trails, which may not be the one with the least total walking time, because it treats every edge as equal.
BFS cannot run on a graph of huts because it only works on computer networks.
BFS will loop forever, because trail networks always contain cycles.
questions.why: BFS gives shortest paths only when every edge counts the same, so on a weighted graph it minimises hop count, not total time.

questions.prompt: A community forum has 2,000 member accounts (vertices) and 9,000 friendships (edges), stored as an adjacency list. Running BFS from one member over the whole forum takes total work roughly proportional to which number?
choices: 9,000 (edges only)
11,000 (vertices plus edges)
18,000,000 (vertices times edges)
2,000 (vertices only)
questions.why: With an adjacency list, BFS handles each vertex once and looks at each edge a bounded number of times, so the work grows with vertices plus edges: 2,000 + 9,000 = 11,000.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how BFS works and why it finds the fewest-hop path, using your own words. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: BFS explores a graph outward from a starting vertex in layers. First it visits everything one edge away, then everything two edges away, and so on. It keeps a queue, a first-in, first-out line, so that nearer vertices are always processed before farther ones. It also keeps a visited set and marks each vertex when it is first added to the queue, so nothing gets queued twice and cycles cannot trap it. Because of that layered order, the first time BFS reaches a vertex is along a path with the fewest edges. That makes it ideal for minimum-hop questions. One limit is that this shortest-path guarantee only holds when every edge counts equally. With weighted edges, fewest hops is not necessarily cheapest. A second tradeoff is memory: the queue can hold an entire wide layer at once. The total work grows with vertices plus edges.
rubricPoints: BFS visits vertices in order of distance from the source, layer by layer.
It uses a first-in, first-out queue to keep nearer vertices ahead of farther ones.
A visited set, marked when a vertex is enqueued, prevents duplicates and infinite loops on cycles.
The first discovery of a vertex gives its fewest-edge distance.
The shortest-path guarantee holds only for unweighted graphs.
The queue can use a lot of memory on wide graphs.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine traverses graphs, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios builds the unit's core skill: choosing BFS for a task and tracing its result by hand.

lessons.plain: Depth-first search, or DFS, is a way to visit every reachable point in a network by always pushing as far forward as you can before turning back. Picture exploring a maze with a piece of chalk: at each junction you take an unmarked passage and keep going until you hit a dead end or a spot you already chalked. Then you walk back to the last junction that still has an unmarked passage and try that one. The chalk marks stop you from going in circles. You are finished when every passage from every junction you reached has been tried.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are exploring a maze, always taking the first unexplored passage and only turning back at dead ends. Do you think you will reach rooms close to the entrance first, or might you reach a room far from the entrance before one right next to it? Why?
lessons.teach:
Depth-first search (DFS) is a graph traversal that starts at one vertex and follows an unexplored edge as deep as it can before backtracking. A vertex is a point in the graph and an edge is a link between two vertices. Backtracking means returning to the most recent vertex that still has unexplored neighbours. A neighbour is any vertex joined to the current one by an edge.

DFS needs two things. The first is a visited set, a record of the vertices already reached, so that cycles do not trap it. A cycle is a path that loops back to where it began. The second is a stack, a last-in, first-out pile, which remembers where to return. DFS works because the stack always resumes the newest unfinished vertex. Writing DFS as a recursive function, one that calls itself, uses the program's own call stack for this. Each reachable vertex is visited once and each edge is checked a constant number of times, so the cost is proportional to vertices plus edges.

Worked example: the edges are A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D and D-E, and neighbours are taken in alphabetical order. Start at A and mark it. A's first neighbour is B, which is unvisited, so go to B. From B, A is already marked, so go to D. From D, B is marked, so go to C. From C, both A and D are marked, which is a dead end, so backtrack to D. D's next neighbour is E, so visit E. E has nothing new, and backtracking through D, B and A finds nothing new either. The visit order is A, B, D, C, E. C was reached third even though it sits right next to A. This is DFS diving deep rather than spreading out.

A common mistake is marking a vertex only after you finish exploring it, or forgetting the visited set entirely. On any graph with a cycle, DFS then loops forever. In a running system, deep recursion on a long chain of vertices can exceed the call-stack limit and crash the program. An explicit stack avoids that crash.

questions.prompt: A small office network links routers with cables: F-G, F-H, G-H, H-J, J-K and G-K. A technician runs depth-first search (DFS) from router F to list every router it can reach, taking neighbours in alphabetical order and marking each router as visited when first reached. The trace so far: Start at F and mark it. F's first neighbour is G, which is unvisited, so go to G and mark it. From G, F is already marked, so the next neighbour H is taken; go to H and mark it. [MISSING STEP]. From J, H is marked, so go to K and mark it. From K, both G and J are marked, which is a dead end, so backtrack to J, then H, then G, then F, finding nothing new. The visit order is F, G, H, J, K. Which step fills the gap?
choices: From H, backtrack to G, because G still has an unexplored neighbour, K.
From H, go to K, because K is the next unvisited router after H in alphabetical order.
From H, F and G are already marked, so go to J and mark it.
From H, go back to F, because F is H's first neighbour alphabetically.
questions.why: DFS keeps going deeper from the current vertex while it has an unvisited neighbour, and H's only unvisited neighbour is J, so it dives to J before any backtracking.

questions.prompt: A delivery company models its depots as a graph with 2,000 vertices (depots) and 9,000 edges (roads between them). Using DFS to find every depot reachable from headquarters, roughly how much work is done, given that DFS cost is proportional to vertices plus edges?
choices: About 18,000,000 steps, because every vertex must be compared with every edge.
About 11,000 steps, because each vertex is visited once and each edge is checked a constant number of times.
About 2,000 steps, because only the vertices are visited.
About 9,000 steps, because only the edges are followed.
questions.why: DFS cost grows with vertices plus edges, and 2,000 + 9,000 = 11,000.

questions.prompt: A developer writes a DFS to explore a social network where friendships form loops (Ana knows Ben, Ben knows Cal, Cal knows Ana). The code marks a person as visited only after it has finished exploring all of that person's friends. What happens when it runs?
choices: It visits each person exactly once, just more slowly.
It loops forever, because it keeps re-entering people in the cycle who are not yet marked.
It works correctly but visits people in a different order.
It stops early and skips anyone in the loop.
questions.why: Marking only after finishing means a vertex in a cycle is reached again before it is marked, so DFS keeps going around the loop without end.

questions.prompt: A logistics service runs a recursive DFS over a supply chain that is one long chain of 500,000 linked warehouses, each joined only to the next. The visited set is in place, but the program crashes partway through. What is the most suitable fix?
choices: Rewrite DFS to use an explicit stack instead of recursion, so depth no longer depends on the program's call-stack limit.
Mark each warehouse only after its neighbours are finished.
Take neighbours in reverse alphabetical order so the recursion goes less deep.
Add a second visited set so each warehouse is checked twice.
questions.why: Deep recursion on a long chain exceeds the call-stack limit, and an explicit stack holds the return points without using the program's call stack.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how DFS explores a graph and what keeps it from looping forever. Name one limit or tradeoff, such as what DFS does not guarantee or a risk of writing it recursively.
lessons.modelAnswer: DFS starts at one vertex, marks it visited, and then picks an unvisited neighbour and moves there. It repeats this so it keeps going deeper until it reaches a vertex with no unvisited neighbours. At that point it backtracks to the most recent vertex that still has something unexplored. A stack holds that 'where to return' information. It is either an explicit stack or the call stack if you write DFS recursively. The visited set is what stops it circling forever around a cycle. Every reachable vertex and edge is handled about once, so the work grows with vertices plus edges. The tradeoff is that DFS does not explore in order of distance, so the first path it finds to a vertex need not be the shortest. A recursive version can also overflow the call stack on a very deep graph, so for big inputs I would use an explicit stack.
rubricPoints: DFS goes as deep as possible along unexplored edges before backtracking.
A stack, explicit or the recursion call stack, tracks where to resume.
A visited set prevents infinite loops on cycles.
Work grows with the number of vertices plus edges.
DFS does not give shortest paths, or deep recursion can overflow the stack.

suggested.rationale: Writing and tracing a DFS with a visited set and an explicit stack in a Python drill makes the visit order and the cycle trap concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: Traversal complexity is a way of predicting how much work it takes to visit every reachable place in a network of connected things, called a graph. Picture a building inspector who must check every room and walk every corridor once. The total effort depends on how many rooms there are and how many corridors connect them, not on rooms multiplied by corridors. Breadth-first and depth-first search, the two standard ways to explore a graph, both behave like that careful inspector. The way the map is written down still matters, because a poorly organized map makes the inspector waste time looking up corridors that do not exist.
lessons.guessPrompt: A graph has 1,000 points and only 2,000 connections between them. If a search visits each point once and looks at each connection from each end, roughly how many steps should it take: about 5,000, about 1,000,000, or about 2,000,000,000?
lessons.teach:
Traversal complexity is the time and memory a graph search needs, written in big-O notation. Big-O describes how work grows as input grows and ignores constant factors. V is the number of vertices, the points, and E is the number of edges, the connections. Breadth-first search (BFS) explores level by level using a queue. Depth-first search (DFS) goes as deep as possible first using a stack or recursion. With an adjacency list, which stores each vertex's neighbors as a list, both searches run in O(V + E) time.

This works because of the visited set, a record of vertices already reached. Each vertex enters the queue or stack at most once, so you pay V for processing vertices. When a vertex is processed, you scan its neighbor list once. The lengths of all neighbor lists add up to E for a directed graph and 2E for an undirected graph, because each edge is stored at both ends. Memory is O(V) for the visited set and the queue or stack.

Worked example: take an undirected graph with vertices A, B, C, D and edges A-B, A-C, B-D. BFS starts from A. Processing A scans 2 neighbors and adds B and C. Processing B scans A and D and adds D. Processing C scans 1 neighbor. Processing D scans 1 neighbor. That gives 4 vertex steps plus 6 neighbor checks, which is 10, matching V + 2E. With an adjacency matrix, a V-by-V grid with a cell for every possible pair, each vertex must scan its whole row of 4 cells. That gives 16 checks, so the cost is O(V²) whatever E is.

A common mistake is forgetting the visited set or calling the cost O(V × E). Without a visited set, a cycle sends the search around forever. In a running system, such as a crawler following links or a dependency resolver, a missing visited check means the program hangs or runs out of memory. Using a matrix for a huge sparse graph wastes time and memory on empty cells.

questions.prompt: A build server models 5 jobs, P, Q, R, S and T, as a directed graph (each edge points one way only). There are 6 edges: P->Q, P->R, Q->S, R->S, S->T and Q->T. Each job's outgoing neighbors are stored in an adjacency list (a list of neighbors kept for each vertex), and a visited set records jobs already reached. DFS starts from P. Step 1: Each of the 5 jobs is processed once, giving 5 vertex steps. Step 2: MISSING. Step 3: Adding the two gives 11 units of work, which matches O(V + E). Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The neighbor checks total 6, because each directed edge appears in exactly one neighbor list
The neighbor checks total 25, because each job scans a row covering all 5 jobs
The neighbor checks total 12, because every edge is stored at both of its ends
The neighbor checks total 30, because each of the 5 jobs checks all 6 edges
questions.why: In a directed graph each edge is stored once, in its source's list, so the neighbor lists add up to E = 6, and 5 + 6 = 11 fits V + E.

questions.prompt: A study-group app stores 1,000 students and 5,000 mutual friendships. A friendship goes both ways, so the graph is undirected. The data is kept as adjacency lists, and a BFS from one student reaches everyone using a visited set. Roughly how many neighbor-list entries does the BFS scan in total?
choices: 5,000, because each friendship is scanned only once
10,000, because each undirected friendship is stored in both students' lists
5,000,000, because each student checks every friendship
1,000,000, because each student scans every other student
questions.why: In an undirected graph each edge is stored at both ends, so the neighbor lists add up to 2E = 10,000.

questions.prompt: A delivery company models a city with 10,000 intersections and 25,000 roads. It stores the roads in an adjacency matrix, a V-by-V grid with one cell for every possible pair of intersections, and runs BFS over it. Which statement about the cost is correct?
choices: It costs about V + 2E, or 60,000 checks, because BFS only follows real roads
It costs about V × E, or 250,000,000 checks, because every vertex checks every edge
It costs about 2E, or 50,000 checks, because only the edges matter
It costs about V², or 100,000,000 checks, because each intersection scans its whole row
questions.why: With a matrix, every processed vertex scans a full row of V cells, so the work is O(V²) whatever the number of roads, which wastes time on empty cells in a sparse graph.

questions.prompt: A team writes a crawler that follows links between pages on a company intranet. Many pages link back to the home page. The developer leaves out the visited set, which is the record of pages already reached. What is the most likely result when the crawler runs?
choices: It finishes in O(V × E) time instead of O(V + E)
It visits each page once but uses O(V²) memory
It loops around the cycles of links and hangs or runs out of memory
It finishes in O(V + E) time, just as it would with a visited set
questions.why: Without a visited set, nothing stops pages from being added again, so a cycle sends the search around forever and the program hangs or exhausts memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why BFS and DFS cost O(V + E) and not O(V × E), and name one situation where the cost is worse than that.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both searches keep a visited set, so each vertex is processed at most once. That part costs V. When a vertex is processed, we read its neighbor list once. Across the whole search those lists add up to the number of edges, or twice that for an undirected graph. So the work is vertices plus edges, not vertices times edges, because we never rescan an edge list. Extra memory is O(V) for the visited set and the queue or stack. There is a limit, though. That bound assumes an adjacency list. With an adjacency matrix, each vertex has to scan a full row of V cells, so the cost becomes O(V²), which is wasteful when the graph is sparse. Another case is forgetting the visited check. Then a cycle can make the search loop forever.
rubricPoints: States that BFS and DFS run in O(V + E) time with an adjacency list.
Explains that the visited set ensures each vertex is processed once.
Explains that the neighbor scans sum to E, or 2E for undirected graphs.
Notes that an adjacency matrix raises the cost to O(V²).
Mentions O(V) extra memory or the infinite-loop risk without a visited set.

suggested.rationale: The unit goal is to justify a traversal's complexity, so explaining where V and E come from is the core skill, and no current mission involves graph traversal.

lessons.plain: A shortest path is the cheapest way to get from one point to another in a network of connections. Picture a map of towns joined by roads, where each road has a cost such as distance, time, or a toll. The shortest path from your town to another is the route whose costs add up to the smallest total. It is not necessarily the route with the fewest roads: three short roads can beat one long highway. Computers solve this for driving directions, network routing, and game characters, by trying routes and keeping only improvements.
lessons.guessPrompt: Town A connects straight to Town C by a 5 km road, or you can go A to B (1 km) and then B to C (1 km). Which route is shorter, and does the route with fewer roads always win?
lessons.teach:
A graph is a set of vertices (points, like towns) joined by edges (connections, like roads). In a weighted graph each edge carries a weight, a number such as distance or cost. A path is a sequence of edges leading from one vertex to another, and its length is the sum of its weights. The shortest-path problem asks for the path of smallest total weight from a source vertex to a target, or from the source to every vertex.

Two ideas make this solvable. First, optimal substructure: any piece of a shortest path is itself a shortest path between its endpoints, so good answers are built from good smaller answers. Second, relaxation: keep a distance estimate for each vertex, starting at 0 for the source and infinity for the rest. To relax an edge from u to v with weight w, check whether dist(u) + w is smaller than dist(v); if so, lower dist(v) and remember u as v's predecessor.

Worked example with edges A-B (1), B-C (1), A-C (5), source A. Start: A=0, B=infinity, C=infinity. Relax A-B: 0+1 beats infinity, so B=1. Relax A-C: 0+5 beats infinity, so C=5. Relax B-C: 1+1=2 beats 5, so C=2 with predecessor B. Following predecessors back from C gives A, B, C, total 2.

Which algorithm to use depends on the weights. If every edge counts the same, breadth-first search, which explores vertices in layers of increasing edge count, finds shortest paths directly. With nonnegative weights, Dijkstra's algorithm is the usual choice. With negative weights, Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge repeatedly (vertex count minus one rounds) and can also report a negative cycle, a loop whose weights sum below zero, where no shortest path exists because circling forever keeps lowering the cost.

The common mistake is running breadth-first search on a weighted graph: it finds the fewest edges, here A-C directly at cost 5. In a running system, a router or delivery planner built this way silently picks slower, costlier routes.

questions.prompt: A courier company has four depots: W, X, Y and Z. The roads and their travel times in minutes are W-X (4), W-Y (1), Y-X (2) and X-Z (1). The source is W. Start: W=0, X=infinity, Y=infinity, Z=infinity. Relax W-X: 0+4 beats infinity, so X=4 with predecessor W. Relax W-Y: 0+1 beats infinity, so Y=1 with predecessor W. Relax Y-X: [missing step]. Relax X-Z: 3+1=4 beats infinity, so Z=4 with predecessor X. Following predecessors back from Z gives W, Y, X, Z, a total of 4 minutes. Which choice correctly fills in the missing step?
choices: Only the edge weight 2 is compared with 4, and 2 is smaller, so X=2 with predecessor Y.
1+2=3 beats 4, so X=3 and X's predecessor changes to Y.
1+2=3 beats 4, so X=3, but X's predecessor stays W.
X already has an estimate from W, so it keeps X=4 and no change is made.
questions.why: Relaxation compares dist(Y) plus the edge weight (1+2=3) with the current dist(X) (4), and because 3 is smaller it lowers X to 3 and records Y as X's predecessor, which is what lets the final path trace back through Y.

questions.prompt: A currency-exchange desk models trades as a weighted graph: each vertex is a currency, and each edge weight is the cost of a trade. Some trades carry rebates, so a few edges have negative weights. The desk wants the cheapest sequence of trades from its home currency to every other currency, and it also wants to be warned about any loop of trades that keeps getting cheaper. Which algorithm fits best?
choices: Dijkstra's algorithm, because it is the usual choice for weighted graphs
Dijkstra's algorithm run once from every currency to cover the negative edges
Bellman-Ford, because it handles negative weights and can report a negative cycle
Breadth-first search, because it explores the currencies in layers
questions.why: The teaching text reserves Dijkstra's algorithm for nonnegative weights, and only Bellman-Ford, which relaxes every edge for vertex count minus one rounds, both handles negative weights and detects negative cycles.

questions.prompt: A bike-delivery app has a direct road from shop P to customer Q that takes 30 minutes. It also has a three-road route P-R, R-S, S-Q, where each road takes 5 minutes. The developer uses breadth-first search on this weighted map. Which route does the app pick, and why is that a problem?
choices: P-R-S-Q at 15 minutes, because breadth-first search adds up the weights in each layer
P-R-S-Q at 15 minutes, because breadth-first search always finds the cheapest path
P-Q at 15 minutes, because breadth-first search treats each road as 5 minutes
P-Q at 30 minutes, because breadth-first search minimizes edge count, not total weight
questions.why: Breadth-first search counts edges, so it chooses the one-road route at 30 minutes and quietly misses the 15-minute route, which is exactly the costlier-route failure the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: In a game map, three rooms form a loop with weights K to L (2), L to M (-3) and M back to K (-1). Bellman-Ford reports this loop. What does that mean for finding a shortest path to vertices reachable through it?
choices: The shortest path goes around the loop exactly once, then stops.
Dijkstra's algorithm should be used instead, because it ignores loops.
No shortest path exists, because the loop sums to -2 and each trip around lowers the cost further.
The shortest path simply skips the edge with weight -3.
questions.why: The loop's weights sum to 2-3-1=-2, which is below zero, so it is a negative cycle, and circling it forever keeps lowering the cost, which means no shortest path exists.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how shortest-path algorithms find the cheapest route, and name one situation where the obvious approach gives a wrong answer or where no shortest path exists.
lessons.modelAnswer: We model the problem as a graph: vertices are places, edges are connections, and each edge has a weight like time or cost. A path's length is the sum of its weights, and we want the smallest sum. The core move is relaxation: we hold a best-known distance for each vertex, starting at zero for the source and infinity elsewhere, and whenever going through a neighbor gives a cheaper total, we lower the estimate and record that neighbor as the predecessor. It works because pieces of a shortest path are themselves shortest. The tradeoff is choosing the right tool. Breadth-first search only counts edges, so on weighted graphs it can pick a single expensive edge over two cheap ones. Dijkstra needs nonnegative weights, Bellman-Ford handles negatives but is slower, and if a negative cycle exists, no shortest path is defined at all.
rubricPoints: Defines path length as the sum of edge weights between a source and target.
Describes relaxation: lowering a distance estimate when a route through a neighbor is cheaper.
Notes that fewest edges is not the same as smallest total weight, so breadth-first search fails on weighted graphs.
Matches algorithm to weights: breadth-first search for equal weights, Dijkstra for nonnegative, Bellman-Ford for negative.
Explains that a negative cycle makes the shortest path undefined.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs graph algorithms, so reasoning through exam-style route problems and tracing relaxation by hand best builds the skill of picking the right shortest-path method.

lessons.plain: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the cheapest route from one starting point to every other point in a network, where each link has a cost called a weight, such as distance or travel time. It works like spreading ink outward from the start: it always locks in whichever unvisited place is currently cheapest to reach, then never reconsiders it. That locking-in is safe only if no link has a negative cost. If a later link could subtract cost, a place already locked in might really have had a cheaper route. That is why Dijkstra requires all weights to be zero or more.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine you have already found that the cheapest known way to reach town B costs 2, and every other unexplored route so far costs at least 5. If every road cost is zero or positive, could some longer detour still reach B for less than 2? What changes if a road could have a cost of minus 4?
lessons.teach:
Dijkstra's algorithm solves the single-source shortest path problem. A graph is a set of vertices (points) joined by edges (links), and each edge has a weight (a cost). The source is the starting vertex. A shortest path is the route with the smallest total weight. Dijkstra keeps a tentative distance for each vertex. It starts with 0 for the source and infinity for every other vertex. A priority queue is a structure that always hands back the item with the smallest key. Here it repeatedly hands back the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance. That vertex becomes settled, meaning its distance is declared final. The algorithm then relaxes each outgoing edge. Relaxing means checking whether going through this vertex gives a neighbour a smaller tentative distance, and lowering it if so.

Why settling is safe: when vertex u has the smallest tentative distance, any other route to u must pass through some vertex that already costs at least as much. With nonnegative weights, adding edges can never make that route cheaper, so u's distance is truly final.

Worked example with a negative edge. Take edges A to B costing 2, A to C costing 5, and C to B costing minus 4, with source A. Step 1: settle A at 0, which sets B to 2 and C to 5. Step 2: B is smallest, so settle B at 2. Step 3: settle C at 5, then relax C to B: 5 minus 4 gives 1, which is less than 2. But B is already settled, so Dijkstra reports 2. The true answer is 1.

Common mistake: adding a constant to every weight to remove negatives. This penalises paths with more edges, so it can change which path is shortest. In this example, adding 4 makes A to B cost 6 and A to C to B cost 9, but the correct route was the longer one.

In a running system, the danger is that the algorithm does not crash. It silently returns wrong routes or costs. For negative weights, use an algorithm built for them, such as Bellman-Ford, which repeatedly relaxes every edge instead of settling vertices once.

questions.prompt: A courier firm uses Dijkstra's algorithm to find the cheapest route from its hub P to every other depot. All travel costs are nonnegative: P to Q costs 4, P to R costs 1, R to Q costs 2, R to S costs 6, and Q to S costs 1. Step 1: settle P at 0, which sets Q to 4 and R to 1. Step 2: R has the smallest tentative distance, so settle R at 1. Relaxing R to Q gives 1 + 2 = 3, which is less than 4, so Q becomes 3. Relaxing R to S gives 1 + 6 = 7, so S becomes 7. Step 3: missing. Step 4: settle S at 4, its final distance. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: Settle Q at 4, its first tentative distance, then relax Q to S to set S to 5.
Settle Q at 3, but leave S at 7 because S already has a tentative distance from R.
Settle Q at 3, then relax Q to S: 3 + 1 = 4, which is less than 7, so S becomes 4.
Settle S at 7, because it was the most recently updated vertex, then relax its outgoing edges.
questions.why: The priority queue hands back the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, which is Q at 3, and relaxing Q to S lowers S from 7 to 4 because that route is cheaper.

questions.prompt: A warehouse robot plans paths across a floor grid using Dijkstra's algorithm. Some moves cost 0 (gliding along a powered rail), and every other move has a positive cost. No move has a negative cost. Can Dijkstra be trusted to give correct shortest paths here?
choices: No, unless 1 is first added to every edge cost so that no edge is free.
Yes, because zero is nonnegative, so adding an edge can never make a route cheaper and settled distances stay final.
No, because a zero-cost edge lets a later route become cheaper than a settled distance.
Only if the source vertex has no zero-cost outgoing edges.
questions.why: Settling is safe whenever every weight is nonnegative, and zero counts as nonnegative, so extending a route can never lower its total.

questions.prompt: A loyalty-points app models trades as a graph. Starting from vertex X: X to Y costs 3, X to Z costs 4, and Z to Y costs minus 2 (a rebate). If Dijkstra's algorithm is run from X, what distance does it report for Y?
questions.why: Dijkstra settles Y at 3 before it settles Z at 4. When it later relaxes Z to Y and finds 4 minus 2 = 2, Y is already final, so the algorithm reports 3 even though the true shortest distance is 2.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking team finds that some legs in its route graph have negative costs, because partner airlines pay credits on those legs. The team currently uses Dijkstra's algorithm. Which response is the sound one?
choices: Add a constant to every leg so all costs become nonnegative, then keep using Dijkstra.
Replace each negative cost with its absolute value so the weights fit Dijkstra's requirement.
Switch to an algorithm built for negative weights, such as Bellman-Ford, which repeatedly relaxes every edge.
Keep Dijkstra, because a wrong result will make it crash, and the crash will flag the problem.
questions.why: Bellman-Ford handles negative weights by relaxing every edge many times instead of settling each vertex once. Adding a constant penalises routes with more legs, taking absolute values changes the real costs, and Dijkstra fails silently rather than crashing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Dijkstra's algorithm decides that a vertex's distance is final, why that decision depends on all edge weights being nonnegative, and what you would do if your data contained negative costs.
lessons.modelAnswer: Dijkstra starts from a source and keeps a tentative cost for every vertex. Each round it pulls the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative cost from a priority queue. It declares that cost final, then relaxes the outgoing edges, which means lowering any neighbour's cost if going through this vertex is cheaper. Declaring a cost final is safe because every other route to that vertex goes through something that already costs at least as much. If edges never subtract cost, that route can't come out cheaper. A negative edge breaks this. A vertex settled early could later be reachable more cheaply, and Dijkstra won't revisit it, so it silently returns a wrong answer. Shifting all weights up by a constant doesn't fix it, because paths with more edges get penalised more. With negative weights I'd switch to Bellman-Ford. It is slower but handles them correctly.
rubricPoints: States that Dijkstra finds the cheapest paths from one source using a priority queue of tentative distances.
Explains that the vertex with the smallest tentative distance is settled and never revisited.
Explains that settling is correct only because nonnegative edges can never lower a total later.
Gives or describes how a negative edge makes an already-settled distance wrong.
Notes that the failure is silent, and that adding a constant to all weights is not a valid fix.
Names an alternative such as Bellman-Ford for graphs with negative weights.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs graph algorithms, and the core skill for this unit is defending why the greedy settling step needs nonnegative weights, which is best practised by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Topological sorting is putting a set of tasks in an order that respects every 'this must happen before that' rule. Think of getting dressed: socks before shoes, underwear before trousers, shirt before tie. Many orders work: you could put on the shirt first or the socks first. But any order that puts shoes before socks breaks a rule. A topological sort finds one valid order. If the rules contradict each other, so that A must come before B and B must also come before A, then no valid order exists. The method can detect that and report it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You must do four chores. Wash dishes before drying them. Dry dishes before putting them away. Buy soap before washing dishes. Write one order that obeys every rule. Is your order the only correct one, or could a fifth chore with no rules be placed in several spots?
lessons.teach:
A topological sort is a linear ordering of the nodes of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) in which every edge points forward. A node is a task. A directed edge from X to Y means X must come before Y. Acyclic means you can never follow the edges and return to where you started. A node's in-degree is the number of edges pointing into it, which is the number of things it still waits on.

One common method is Kahn's algorithm. It works because a node with in-degree zero has no unmet prerequisites, so it is always safe to output next. Put every in-degree-zero node in a queue. Repeatedly remove one node from the queue and output it. Then delete its outgoing edges, lowering each neighbor's in-degree by one. Any neighbor that reaches zero joins the queue. The algorithm touches each node and each edge once, so its running time is O(V+E), where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges.

Here is a worked example. Tasks: A install compiler, B fetch source, C compile, D test, E build docs. Edges: A→C, B→C, C→D, B→E. Starting in-degrees are A0, B0, C2, D1, E1, so the queue holds A and B. Output A, and C drops to 1. Output B, and C drops to 0 and E drops to 0, so both join the queue. Output C, and D drops to 0. Output E, then D. The result is A, B, C, E, D. Five nodes were output out of five, so the graph had no cycle.

A common mistake is assuming there is one correct answer. B, A, C, D, E is equally valid, so tests should check that every edge points forward, not compare against a fixed list. Another mistake is ignoring the case where the output comes up short. If fewer nodes come out than exist, the leftover nodes sit on a cycle and no valid order exists.

In a running system, build tools, package installers and job schedulers rely on this. If a dependency cycle goes unnoticed, the scheduler silently never runs some jobs, or a deploy hangs waiting forever.

questions.prompt: A university plans the order of six courses. An edge X→Y means X must be taken before Y. Courses: M (Intro Math), N (Programming 1), O (Data Structures), Q (Algorithms), R (Databases), S (Capstone). Edges: M→Q, N→O, O→Q, O→R, Q→S, R→S. You run Kahn's algorithm, which repeatedly outputs a course with in-degree zero (no unmet prerequisites) and lowers its neighbors' in-degrees. Starting in-degrees are M0, N0, O1, Q2, R1, S2, so the queue holds M and N. Step 1: output M, and Q drops to 1. Step 2: output N, and O drops to 0 and joins the queue. Step 3: output O, and Q drops to 0 and R drops to 0, so both join the queue. Step 4: output Q, and S drops from 2 to 1. Step 5: ??? Step 6: output S. The final order is M, N, O, Q, R, S. What is Step 5?
choices: Output R. S drops from 2 to 1, so it stays out of the queue.
Output S now, because it is the only course not yet placed in the order.
Output R. S drops from 1 to 0, so S joins the queue.
Stop. S still has in-degree 1, so the course graph must contain a cycle.
questions.why: R is the only course left in the queue, and removing its edge R→S lowers S from 1 (after Q's edge was already removed) to 0, which makes S safe to output next.

questions.prompt: A recipe has four steps. An edge X→Y means X must happen before Y. Edges: W→X, W→Y, Y→Z, X→Z. Which ordering is a valid topological sort?
choices: X, W, Y, Z
W, Y, X, Z
Y, W, X, Z
W, X, Z, Y
questions.why: In W, Y, X, Z every edge points forward: W comes before X and Y, and both X and Y come before Z. Each other order puts at least one edge backward.

questions.prompt: A cluster job scheduler has 8 jobs and uses Kahn's algorithm to decide run order. It outputs 5 jobs, and then the queue of in-degree-zero jobs is empty. What should you conclude?
choices: The algorithm ran out of time, because Kahn's algorithm is slower than O(V+E) on large graphs.
The leftover jobs should be added at the end in any order, since every edge has already been handled.
The 5 output jobs are a valid complete order. The other 3 jobs had no dependencies, so they can be skipped.
