The 3 leftover jobs are caught in a dependency cycle, so no valid order exists for all 8 jobs.
questions.why: When fewer nodes come out than exist, the leftover nodes sit on a cycle, so no valid order exists. If this goes unnoticed, those jobs silently never run.

questions.prompt: An autograder checks a student's topological sort of a package-dependency graph by comparing it to one reference list. The student's order differs from the reference, but every dependency edge in the student's order points forward. What is the correct judgment?
choices: The student's order is wrong, because a DAG has exactly one correct topological sort.
The student's order is valid. The grader should check that every edge points forward, not compare against one fixed list.
The graph must contain a cycle, because two different orders came out of the same set of edges.
The student's order is valid only if it starts with the same in-degree-zero node as the reference list.
questions.why: A DAG can have many valid topological sorts. Any order in which every edge points forward is correct, so comparing against a single list wrongly fails valid answers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain topological sorting to a teammate who is writing a job scheduler. Tell them what it guarantees, how one method produces the order, and what limit or tradeoff they must handle.
lessons.modelAnswer: A topological sort takes tasks with 'must run before' rules, drawn as a directed graph, and lists them so every rule points forward in the list. One way to do it: count each task's unmet prerequisites, which is its in-degree. Start with the tasks that have zero. Each time you emit a task, decrement the counts of the tasks that depend on it, and queue any that hit zero. This takes time proportional to tasks plus edges. There are two limits to handle. First, it only works on an acyclic graph. If tasks depend on each other in a loop, some never reach zero and the output is shorter than the task list. The scheduler must check for that and report the cycle rather than hang. Second, the order is usually not unique. Tests should verify that every dependency is respected instead of expecting one exact sequence.
rubricPoints: Defines it as an ordering where every directed dependency edge points forward.
Describes repeatedly emitting a task with no remaining prerequisites and updating its dependents.
States it requires a directed acyclic graph and that a cycle leaves nodes unemitted.
Notes that multiple valid orders usually exist.
Mentions linear cost in nodes plus edges or a real use such as build or job ordering.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises dependency ordering, so tracing Kahn's algorithm by hand on an exam-style scenario, including one that hides a cycle, builds the skill most directly.

lessons.plain: Cycle detection is checking whether a network of connections contains a loop: a route that starts at one point, follows the connections, and arrives back where it began. Picture a list of chores where washing dishes needs a clean towel, the towel needs the laundry done, and the laundry needs clean dishes. Nobody can ever start, because each job waits on the next one around the circle. Computers face the same trap with software that depends on other software, programs waiting on each other's locks, or links between web pages. Cycle detection finds those circles so a system can refuse them, report them, or break them before it gets stuck.
lessons.guessPrompt: Three jobs have rules: job A must wait for B, B must wait for C, and C must wait for A. Can any job ever start? If you traced the 'waits for' arrows by hand, what would tell you that you had found a problem?
lessons.teach:
Cycle detection means deciding whether a graph contains a cycle. A graph is a set of nodes (the things) joined by edges (the relationships). A cycle is a path that leaves a node, follows edges, and returns to that same node. In a directed graph each edge points one way, such as 'A depends on B'. In an undirected graph edges work both ways, like a two-way road.

The usual tool is depth-first search (DFS), a traversal that follows one path as deep as it can before backing up. For a directed graph, give each node one of three colors. White means not visited yet. Gray means it is on the current path and still being explored. Black means it is finished. If DFS follows an edge into a gray node, it has found a back edge, which is an edge pointing to a node earlier on the current path. That edge closes a cycle. The method works because the gray nodes are exactly the ones on the path you are walking right now. Every node and edge is checked once, so the cost is O(V + E), where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges.

Worked example: take the edges A→B, B→C, C→A. Start at A and mark it gray. Move to B and mark it gray. Move to C and mark it gray. C points to A, and A is gray, so the cycle A→B→C→A is found.

Now take a diamond: A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D. A, B and D turn gray. D has no outgoing edges, so it turns black, and then B turns black. Back at A, visit C. C points to D, but D is black, meaning it is already finished. That is not a cycle.

A common mistake is to use one 'visited' flag in a directed graph. In the diamond, that version would report a false cycle at D. Undirected graphs need a different rule: any visited neighbor other than the parent (the node you just came from) means a cycle. If you forget the parent exception, every edge looks like a cycle.

This matters in real systems. A package manager that misses a dependency cycle can loop forever. A cycle among processes waiting on each other's locks is a deadlock, where no process can make progress.

questions.prompt:
A build server runs tasks with these dependencies (an arrow means 'leads to'): Fetch→Build, Fetch→Lint, Build→Test, Lint→Test, Test→Report, Report→Lint. A three-color DFS starts at Fetch.

Step 1: Fetch is marked gray. Step 2: Build is marked gray. Step 3: Test is marked gray. Step 4: Report is marked gray. Step 5: Report points to Lint, which is white, so Lint is marked gray. Step 6: Lint points to Test. ???

What happens at Step 6?
choices: Lint was first listed as a child of Fetch, so this edge is skipped until the search returns to Fetch.
Test is marked black because it now has two incoming edges, and no cycle is reported.
Test has already been visited, so Lint is marked black and the search backs up to Report.
Test is gray, so Lint→Test is a back edge, and the cycle Test→Report→Lint→Test is reported.
questions.why: Test is still gray, which means it is on the current path, so an edge into it closes a cycle.

questions.prompt: During a three-color DFS on a directed graph of microservice calls, the search is exploring from service Ledger and finds an edge Ledger→Auth. In which case does this edge prove that the graph has a cycle?
choices: Auth is white, because the search has not reached it yet.
Auth is black, because it has already been fully explored.
Auth has more outgoing edges than Ledger.
Auth is gray, because it is still on the path currently being explored.
questions.why: Only an edge into a gray node is a back edge, meaning it points to a node earlier on the current path, and that closes a cycle.

questions.prompt: Four office routers are connected by two-way cables in a straight line: R1–R2, R2–R3, R3–R4. DFS starts at R1, then moves to R2. Looking at R2's neighbors, the search sees R1, which is already visited. What should a correct undirected cycle check conclude?
choices: A cycle exists, because every two-way cable counts as a loop between two routers.
No cycle from this edge, because R1 is R2's parent, the node the search just came from.
The search must restart from R4 before it can decide anything.
A cycle exists, because R2 has a visited neighbor.
questions.why: In an undirected graph a visited neighbor only means a cycle if it is not the parent, and R1 is R2's parent.

questions.prompt: A team writes a cycle checker for course prerequisites, which are directed (an arrow means 'is required before'). Their DFS uses a single 'visited' flag and reports a cycle whenever it reaches any visited node. The prerequisites are Calc1→Calc2, Calc1→Stats, Calc2→Proba, Stats→Proba, and they contain no cycle. What will the checker most likely do?
choices: Wrongly report a cycle when Stats leads to Proba, which was already finished by the path through Calc2.
Correctly report no cycle, because a single flag works the same as three colors.
Loop forever, because it never marks any course as visited.
Miss real cycles but never report false ones.
questions.why: A single flag cannot tell a node on the current path (gray) from a finished one (black), so reaching the already-finished Proba by a second route looks like a cycle when it is not.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would check whether a set of service dependencies contains a cycle. Say why a simple 'visited' flag is not enough for directed dependencies, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd model each service as a node and each 'depends on' as a directed edge, then run depth-first search. Each node gets three states: unvisited, in progress (on the path I'm currently exploring), and done. If I follow an edge into a node that is still in progress, I've looped back onto my own path, so there's a cycle. A plain visited flag isn't enough. Two services can both depend on the same shared library, and reaching that library a second time from a different branch is fine, not a loop. The done state tells those cases apart. The check is linear in nodes plus edges, so it's cheap. One limit: it tells you a cycle exists, and you can recover that one loop, but it doesn't list every cycle or say which edge you should remove. Undirected graphs also need a different rule, which is to ignore the parent you just came from.
rubricPoints: Models the problem as a directed graph with nodes and edges.
Uses depth-first search with an in-progress state and treats an edge into an in-progress node as a cycle.
Explains why a single visited flag gives false cycles when shared nodes are reached by two paths.
Notes that undirected graphs need the parent exception instead.
Names a limit, such as finding one cycle rather than all of them, or not choosing which edge to break.
Mentions the linear O(V + E) cost or a real consequence such as deadlock or a stuck dependency install.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine runs graph traversals, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios like dependency loops or lock waits, and classifying them as traversal problems, best builds the unit's core skill.

lessons.plain: Divide and conquer is a way of solving a big problem by cutting it into smaller copies of the same problem, solving each small copy, and then stitching the small answers into the big answer. Imagine alphabetizing a tall stack of 1,000 forms. Splitting the stack in half, sorting each half separately, then merging the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking whichever top form comes first is far easier than shuffling all 1,000 at once. Each half can be split again, until every pile holds one form, which is already in order.
lessons.guessPrompt: You and a friend must put 1,000 shuffled name cards in alphabetical order. You each sort half. When you both finish, what is the quickest way to combine your two sorted piles into one sorted pile?
lessons.teach:
Divide and conquer is an algorithm design strategy with three steps. Divide: split the input into smaller subproblems, meaning smaller instances of the same task. Conquer: solve each subproblem, usually by applying the same method to it again, which is called recursion (a procedure that calls itself on smaller input). Combine: merge the subproblem answers into the answer for the whole. Recursion stops at a base case, an input so small that the answer is obvious, such as a list of one item.

It works because small problems are easy, and the combine step is often cheap. If halving the input happens repeatedly, there are only about log n levels of splitting (log n is the number of times you can halve n before reaching 1), so the total work is roughly the combine cost per level times log n.

Worked example, merge sort on [5, 2, 4, 1]. Divide into [5, 2] and [4, 1]. Divide again into [5], [2], [4], [1]; each is a base case. Combine [5] and [2] by comparing fronts: 2 first, then 5, giving [2, 5]. Likewise [1, 4]. Combine [2, 5] and [1, 4]: compare 2 and 1, take 1; compare 2 and 4, take 2; compare 5 and 4, take 4; take 5. Result [1, 2, 4, 5]. Each level merges n items, and there are log n levels, so about n log n work.

A common mistake is applying divide and conquer when subproblems overlap, meaning the same smaller problem is solved again and again. Computing Fibonacci numbers by splitting into the two previous values recomputes the same values exponentially many times; that pattern calls for remembering answers instead, which is a different strategy. Divide and conquer fits best when subproblems are independent. Another mistake is a missing or wrong base case, which in a running program causes endless recursion and a crash when the call stack runs out of memory.

questions.prompt: A delivery depot logs four daily parcel counts: [12, 30, 7, 19]. A divide-and-conquer routine finds the largest count. Divide: split into [12, 30] and [7, 19]. Divide again into [12], [30], [7], [19]. Each single-item list is a base case, and its largest value is just that item. Combine [12] and [30] by keeping the larger, giving 30. Combine [7] and [19] the same way, giving 19. What is the missing final step?
choices: Split 30 and 19 again into smaller pieces, because they are not yet base cases
Return 19, because it came from the most recently solved subproblem
Add 30 and 19 to get 49, since combining means merging both answers together
Combine 30 and 19 by keeping the larger, giving 30 as the overall answer
questions.why: The combine step must merge the subproblem answers in a way that answers the whole task, and the largest of the whole list is the larger of the two halves' largest values, which is 30.

questions.prompt: A design strategy fits best when subproblems are independent. Which of these tasks is the poorest fit for plain divide and conquer?
choices: Finding the cheapest price in a catalog by halving the list and keeping the smaller minimum
Totaling 1,000 sensor readings by halving the list and adding the two half-totals
Sorting library book IDs by halving the list, sorting each half, and merging the halves
Computing a value defined as f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) by splitting into those two smaller calls
questions.why: Splitting into f(n-1) and f(n-2) creates overlapping subproblems that get recomputed many times, which calls for remembering answers instead of plain divide and conquer.

questions.prompt: A developer at a document-indexing service writes a recursive function that keeps splitting a page range in half, but forgets to include any check that stops at a range of one page. What is the most likely result when the program runs?
choices: It finishes correctly but more slowly, because the extra splits only add some overhead
It returns an empty answer immediately, because no base case means nothing is computed
It automatically switches to a loop once the ranges become too small to split
It recurses endlessly and crashes when the call stack runs out of memory
questions.why: Without a base case the recursion never stops, so calls pile up until the call stack runs out of memory and the program crashes.

questions.prompt: A clinic sorts 64 patient records with a halving divide-and-conquer sort whose combine step handles every record once per level. Halving 64 repeatedly reaches 1 after 6 halvings. Roughly how much total work does the sort do?
choices: About 4,096 steps, from 64 records compared against all 64 others
About 6 steps, one for each level of splitting
About 64 steps, since each record is handled only once overall
About 384 steps, from 64 records per level times 6 levels
questions.why: Total work is roughly the combine cost per level (64) times the number of levels (log of 64, which is 6), giving about 384.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would recognize that a new problem suits divide and conquer, using merge sort as your example, and name one situation where the strategy is a poor fit and why.
lessons.modelAnswer: Divide and conquer means splitting a problem into smaller versions of itself, solving those recursively until they hit a trivial base case, then combining the results. Merge sort is the classic case: split the list in half until each piece has one item, then merge sorted pieces by repeatedly taking the smaller front item. Because halving gives about log n levels and each level's merging touches n items, it costs about n log n. I'd suspect divide and conquer when the problem naturally splits into independent pieces of the same shape and the combine step is cheap. It's a poor fit when the pieces overlap, like naive recursive Fibonacci, where the same subproblem gets recomputed exponentially often; there you should store answers instead. It also needs a correct base case, or the program recurses forever and runs out of stack.
rubricPoints: Names the three steps: divide, conquer recursively, combine.
Mentions a base case that stops the recursion.
Traces or describes merge sort as an example.
Explains why halving leads to roughly log n levels and n log n work.
States that overlapping subproblems make it a poor fit and points toward storing answers instead.
Flags that a missing base case leads to infinite recursion or a stack crash.

suggested.rationale: The unit's goal is classifying unfamiliar problems, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that contrast divide and conquer with greedy and dynamic programming builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A greedy algorithm builds an answer one step at a time, and at each step it grabs whatever looks best right now, without ever going back to reconsider. Think of packing a day with as many meetings as possible by always choosing the meeting that finishes soonest. Greedy reasoning is the skill of deciding whether that shortcut is actually safe for a given problem. Sometimes the locally best move always leads to the best overall answer. Sometimes it walks you into a dead end. The skill is telling the two apart and giving a reason.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have coins worth 1, 3 and 4 and must make 6 using as few coins as possible. If you always take the biggest coin that still fits, how many coins do you use, and is that the fewest possible?
lessons.teach:
A greedy algorithm makes a sequence of choices, and each choice is the one that looks best by some simple rule at that moment. It never undoes a choice. Greedy is correct only when two properties hold. The greedy choice property means some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice, so picking it never rules out the best answer. Optimal substructure means that once you make that choice, what remains is a smaller copy of the same problem, whose best answer combines with your choice to give the best overall answer.

The usual way to show the greedy choice property is an exchange argument. Take any optimal solution, swap its first choice for the greedy choice, and show the result is still valid and no worse.

Worked example, interval scheduling. The goal is to attend the most non-overlapping meetings: A 1-4, B 3-5, C 0-6, D 5-7, E 8-9. The rule is to always pick the meeting that ends earliest among those that do not clash with what you already picked. Sorted by end time, the order is A, B, C, D, E. Pick A, which ends at 4. Skip B, because it starts at 3, before 4. Skip C, because it starts at 0. Pick D, because it starts at 5. Pick E, because it starts at 8. That gives three meetings. The exchange argument works because finishing earliest leaves the most time free, so swapping any optimal schedule's first meeting for A never causes a clash.

The common mistake is trusting a greedy rule because it feels sensible. With coins 1, 3 and 4 and a target of 6, taking the biggest coin first gives 4+1+1, which is three coins. The best answer is 3+3, which is two coins. Here the greedy choice property fails, and the problem needs dynamic programming. Always test a greedy rule against small counterexamples before relying on it.

In a running system, a wrong greedy rule does not crash. It quietly produces worse schedules, wasted capacity or extra cost, which makes the fault hard to notice.

questions.prompt: A university makerspace has one 3D printer and wants to run as many non-overlapping print jobs as possible. Jobs (start-end, in hours): P 2-5, Q 1-3, R 4-6, T 3-8, S 7-9. The rule is to always pick the job that ends earliest among those that do not clash with jobs already picked. Sorted by end time, the order is Q, P, R, T, S. Step 1: Pick Q, which ends at 3. Step 2: Skip P, because it starts at 2, before 3. Step 3: Pick R, because it starts at 4, after 3; R ends at 6. Step 4: ??? Step 5: Pick S, because it starts at 7, after 6. Result: three jobs (Q, R, S). What is Step 4?
choices: Pick T instead of R, because T runs longer and uses the printer more
Skip T, because it starts at 3, before R ends at 6
Stop here, because a greedy algorithm cannot revisit jobs once one has been skipped
Pick T, because it starts at 3, which is when Q ends
questions.why: T's start time of 3 is before 6, when the last picked job (R) ends, so it clashes and must be skipped.

questions.prompt: In greedy reasoning, what does the greedy choice property say?
choices: Some optimal solution begins with the choice the greedy rule makes, so taking it never rules out the best answer
After any choice, the remaining problem can be solved by trying every possibility
Every choice the greedy rule makes is the largest or cheapest item available
The greedy rule can undo an earlier choice if a better one appears later
questions.why: The greedy choice property means picking the greedy option is always consistent with at least one optimal solution.

questions.prompt: A vending machine company issues tokens worth 1, 5 and 6 units and wants to give change of 10 units using as few tokens as possible. The engineer proposes taking the biggest token that fits each time. What should the engineer conclude?
choices: The rule is correct, because it gives 6+1+1+1+1 and any valid answer is optimal
The rule is correct, because taking the biggest token always reduces the remaining amount fastest
The rule fails: it gives 6+1+1+1+1 (five tokens) while 5+5 uses two, so the greedy choice property does not hold and a method like dynamic programming is needed
The rule is fine as long as the token values are sorted from largest to smallest first
questions.why: A small counterexample shows the biggest-first rule gives five tokens when two suffice, so the greedy choice property fails here.

questions.prompt: A delivery firm's routing service uses a greedy rule that seemed sensible but was never tested against small counterexamples, and the rule is actually not optimal. What is the most likely way this shows up in production?
choices: The service automatically switches to dynamic programming when the greedy rule fails
The service loops forever because the greedy rule keeps undoing its own choices
The service crashes with an error on the first input where the rule is wrong
The service keeps running but quietly produces worse plans, such as extra cost or wasted capacity, which is hard to notice
questions.why: A wrong greedy rule does not crash; it silently yields worse results, so the fault is hard to spot.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a greedy approach is safe for a new optimization problem, and name the risk of using greedy when it does not fit.
lessons.modelAnswer: Greedy means making the locally best choice at each step and never revisiting it. Before trusting it, I check two things. The first is the greedy choice property, which says some optimal answer begins with the greedy pick. I usually show this with an exchange argument: take any optimal solution, swap in the greedy pick, and confirm it stays valid and no worse. The second is optimal substructure, which says that after the pick, the rest is a smaller version of the same problem. Earliest-finish-first for scheduling meetings passes both checks. I also try small counterexamples. Coins 1, 3 and 4 making 6 breaks the biggest-coin-first rule, which gives three coins when two would do. The tradeoff is that greedy is fast and simple, but when it does not fit it silently returns a suboptimal answer instead of failing loudly. In that case I would switch to dynamic programming.
rubricPoints: Defines greedy as making the locally best choice without revisiting it.
Names the greedy choice property and optimal substructure as the conditions for correctness.
Mentions an exchange argument or a counterexample as the way to justify or reject greedy.
Gives a concrete case where greedy works or fails, such as interval scheduling or the coin set 1, 3, 4.
Notes the risk that a wrong greedy rule silently produces suboptimal results, and that dynamic programming is the fallback.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine exercises algorithm design, and the unit goal of classifying unfamiliar problems and defending the choice is best built by reasoning through exam-style scenarios and testing them against counterexamples.

lessons.plain: Dynamic programming is a way to solve a big problem by breaking it into smaller versions of itself, solving each small version once, and writing the answer down so you never redo it. Memoization is the writing-it-down part: before solving a small piece, check your notes; if the answer is there, reuse it. Picture a student doing a long homework set where several questions secretly ask the same sub-question. A careless student re-derives it every time. A smart student keeps a sticky note of finished answers. Same results, far less work, at the cost of keeping the notes.
lessons.guessPrompt: You can climb a staircase one or two steps at a time. To count the ways up 5 stairs, you add the ways up 4 stairs and the ways up 3 stairs, and each of those breaks down the same way. Without keeping notes, roughly how many times do you think you would end up counting the ways up 3 stairs: once, or more than once?
lessons.teach:
Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by expressing its answer in terms of answers to smaller subproblems, then making sure each subproblem is solved only once. It applies when two properties hold. Optimal substructure means the answer to the whole can be built from answers to its parts. Overlapping subproblems means the same smaller pieces come up again and again. The rule linking a problem to its parts is called a recurrence.

There are two styles. Memoization is top-down: write the natural recursive solution, but keep a cache (a lookup table, often a hash map) from each subproblem's input to its answer, and check it before computing. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table from the smallest subproblems upward, in an order where everything you need is already filled.

Worked example: count the ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps. Recurrence: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(0) = 1 and ways(1) = 1. Plain recursion for n = 5 calls ways(4) and ways(3); ways(4) calls ways(3) again and ways(2); ways(2) ends up computed three times. The call count roughly doubles with each extra stair, which is exponential growth. With memoization: ways(2) = 1 + 1 = 2, stored; ways(3) = 2 + 1 = 3, stored; ways(4) = 3 + 2 = 5, stored; ways(5) = 5 + 3 = 8. Each value is computed once, so the work is proportional to n.

Why it works: the expensive part was repetition, and the cache removes repetition by trading memory for time.

A common mistake is a cache key that leaves out part of the subproblem's state, for example caching by position only when the answer also depends on remaining budget. The cache then returns wrong answers silently. Another is using DP when subproblems do not overlap, which is ordinary divide and conquer and gains nothing from a cache. In a running system, missing memoization can turn a fast call into one that never finishes, while an unbounded cache or very deep recursion can exhaust memory or the call stack.

questions.prompt: A parking kiosk accepts only 1-dollar and 3-dollar tokens, inserted one at a time. Let f(n) be the number of different orders of tokens that add up to exactly n dollars. The last token is either a 1 or a 3, so the recurrence is f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-3), with f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 1. Using memoization, each new value is computed once and stored: f(3) = f(2) + f(0) = 1 + 1 = 2, stored. f(4) = f(3) + f(1) = 2 + 1 = 3, stored. f(5) = f(4) + f(2) = 3 + 1 = 4, stored. Missing step: what is f(6)?
questions.why: The recurrence f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-3) gives f(6) = f(5) + f(3), and both values are already in the cache as 4 and 2, so f(6) = 6.

questions.prompt: A warehouse robot finds the cheapest route to a loading dock on a grid. The cheapest cost from a cell depends on the cell and on how much battery charge remains. A developer memoizes the recursive solver using only the cell's row and column as the cache key. What is the most likely result?
choices: The solver runs faster and always returns correct costs, because each cell is computed only once
The program fails immediately, because a cache key must hold every input to the function
Nothing changes, because memoization only matters when subproblems do not overlap
The cache sometimes returns an answer computed for a different charge level, giving wrong costs with no error raised
questions.why: The key leaves out part of the subproblem's state (remaining charge), so answers for one charge level are silently reused for another.

questions.prompt: A sensor team finds the highest reading in a list of 1,000,000 values. Their recursive method splits the list into two halves, finds the maximum of each half, and returns the larger one. Each half is a different, non-shared slice of the list. A teammate proposes adding a memoization cache. What is the best assessment?
choices: Worthwhile, because every recursive solution has overlapping subproblems that a cache removes
Not useful, because no subproblem repeats; this is ordinary divide and conquer and a cache gains nothing
Not useful, because the problem lacks optimal substructure, so it cannot be solved recursively at all
Worthwhile, because the cache turns exponential work into work proportional to the list length
questions.why: Dynamic programming needs overlapping subproblems; here each slice is solved once anyway, so a cache only adds memory cost.

questions.prompt: A ticket-pricing model defines best(i), the best revenue from seat i to the end of a row of 50 seats, as a recurrence that uses best(i+1) and best(i+2). The values best(50) and best(51) are known starting values. If you solve it with tabulation (bottom-up, filling a table), which fill order works?
choices: From i = 49 downward to i = 1, so best(i+1) and best(i+2) are already filled when needed
From i = 1 upward to i = 49, since tabulation always starts at the smallest index
Only odd i first, then even i, so the two dependencies never collide
In any order, since a table lets you look up any entry at any time
questions.why: Tabulation must fill entries in an order where everything a cell depends on is already computed, and here each cell depends on larger indices.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide that a new problem calls for dynamic programming with memoization, and name one cost or limit of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I look for two things. First, can I write the answer as a recurrence over smaller versions of the same problem, so the best or total answer is built from sub-answers? That's optimal substructure. Second, when I sketch the recursion, do the same subproblems show up repeatedly? That's overlap. If both hold, I memoize: keep a cache keyed by everything that defines a subproblem and check it before computing. For counting ways to climb stairs, ways(3) gets recomputed many times in plain recursion, so caching cuts the work from exponential to linear. If subproblems don't overlap, like the halves in merge sort, it's divide and conquer and a cache is wasted. The tradeoff is memory: the cache holds one entry per distinct subproblem, and top-down recursion can hit stack-depth limits, which bottom-up tabulation avoids. Also the key must capture the full state or the cache returns wrong answers.
rubricPoints: States that DP needs optimal substructure expressed as a recurrence.
States that DP pays off only when subproblems overlap.
Describes memoization as caching subproblem answers checked before computing.
Notes the cache key must include all state that affects the answer.
Names a cost such as memory use or recursion depth, possibly mentioning tabulation as an alternative.
Distinguishes DP from divide and conquer, where subproblems do not overlap.

suggested.rationale: The unit's goal is classifying unfamiliar problems and defending the choice, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios that test for substructure and overlap.

lessons.plain: Computers store everything as long rows of tiny switches that are either off or on, written 0 and 1. Binary is the way of writing numbers using only those two digits. Long rows of 0s and 1s are hard for people to read, so engineers use a shorthand called hexadecimal, or hex. Hex uses sixteen symbols, and each one stands for exactly four switches. Think of hex as a compact nickname for a binary pattern: it carries the same information in fewer characters, so it is easier to read and copy. You will see hex in memory addresses, colour codes, error codes and network data.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine a row of 3 light switches, each either off or on. How many different on/off patterns can the row show? What happens to that count each time you add one more switch?
lessons.teach:
Binary is base 2. Each digit, called a bit, is 0 or 1. Each position is worth a power of 2. Reading from the right, the positions are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. To get a value, add up the positions that hold a 1. A row of n bits has 2^n possible patterns, because each extra bit doubles the count. So 3 bits give 8 patterns, and 8 bits give 256. A byte is 8 bits, so one byte can hold the whole numbers 0 to 255.

Hexadecimal, or hex, is base 16. It uses the digits 0 to 9, then A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14 and F=15. Each position is worth a power of 16. Hex is useful because 16 = 2^4, so one hex digit matches exactly 4 bits. A group of 4 bits is called a nibble. That means one byte is always exactly two hex digits. Prefixes mark the base: 0b means binary and 0x means hex.

Worked example: convert 0xB6. Split it into its hex digits. B = 11 = 1011, and 6 = 0110. Joined together, that gives 0b10110110. Now check it in decimal. The 1 bits sit in the positions worth 128, 32, 16, 4 and 2, and 128+32+16+4+2 = 182. The hex method agrees: B × 16 + 6 = 176 + 6 = 182. To go the other way, from binary to hex, split the bits into groups of four starting from the right, then convert each group.

A common mistake is reading hex as if it were decimal. 0x10 is sixteen, not ten. Another is grouping bits from the left, which shifts every group and gives the wrong digits.

In a running system these slips cause real bugs. If you misread an address offset of 0x10 as ten bytes, you point at the wrong memory. If you forget that one byte tops out at 255, a counter that goes past it wraps around to 0.

questions.prompt: A warehouse barcode scanner reports its status as the 7-bit value 0b1101011, and a technician wants it in hex and decimal. Step 1: split the bits into groups of four starting from the right, padding the leftmost group with a 0. That gives 0110 and 1011. Step 2: convert each group. 0110 = 6 and 1011 = 11 = B, so the value is 0x6B. Step 3 (missing): check the value in decimal using the hex positions. What is the correct decimal value?
questions.why: The first hex digit's position is worth 16, so 0x6B is 6 × 16 + 11 = 96 + 11 = 107.

questions.prompt: A small robot uses a 5-bit field to choose its movement mode. How many different bit patterns can that field hold?
questions.why: Each extra bit doubles the count, so 5 bits give 2^5 = 32 patterns. 31 is the largest value those patterns can show, not the number of patterns.

questions.prompt: A game engine's documentation says a player's health value is stored at offset 0x20 from the start of a record. How many bytes from the start of the record is that?
choices: 2 bytes
64 bytes
32 bytes
20 bytes
questions.why: 0x20 is hex, so the 2 sits in the 16s position: 2 × 16 = 32. Reading it as decimal 20 would point at the wrong memory.

questions.prompt: A ticket kiosk keeps its sales count in a single byte. The count is currently 250, and 10 more tickets are sold. What value does the byte hold afterwards?
questions.why: One byte tops out at 255. Counting up gives 251 to 255 for the first five sales. The sixth sale wraps the count to 0, and the last four bring it to 4.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why engineers write raw data in hex instead of binary or decimal, and walk through converting one byte between the three forms. Name one limit or pitfall of working in hex.
lessons.modelAnswer: Hardware stores bits, which are 0s and 1s, and binary shows them exactly. But a long binary string is easy to misread. Decimal is familiar, but it does not line up with bit boundaries. Hex is base 16, and since 16 is 2^4, every hex digit maps to exactly four bits. So a byte is always two hex digits, and you can convert in your head one nibble at a time. Take 0xB6. B is 1011 and 6 is 0110, so the byte is 10110110. Adding the place values 128+32+16+4+2 gives 182 in decimal. The limit is that hex is only a notation: it does not tell you what the bits mean, such as a signed number, text or an address. A common pitfall is reading 0x10 as ten when it is sixteen. Also remember a fixed width caps the range, so one byte holds only 0 to 255.
rubricPoints: Binary is base 2 with place values that are powers of 2, and n bits give 2^n patterns.
Hex is base 16, with A through F standing for 10 through 15.
One hex digit equals exactly four bits, so one byte is two hex digits.
Correctly traces a conversion between hex, binary and decimal.
Names a pitfall, such as reading 0x10 as ten, grouping bits from the left, or the 0 to 255 limit of a byte.

suggested.rationale: Fluency comes from reasoning through concrete conversions and spotting errors in realistic values such as addresses and byte limits, which no current mission or planned engine directly exercises.

lessons.plain: Boolean logic is the arithmetic of yes and no. Every value is either true or false, often written 1 and 0, and a few simple rules combine them. AND says yes only if both inputs say yes. OR says yes if at least one does. NOT flips a single answer. XOR (exclusive or) says yes only when the two inputs disagree. Think of a hallway light: AND is two switches wired in a row so both must be on, while XOR is the two-switch staircase light where flipping either switch changes the result. Computers build everything from tiny circuits that apply these rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: A door opens only if you have a badge and it is not after midnight. If you have a badge and it is 1 a.m., does the door open? Which words in the rule did you use to decide?
lessons.teach:
Boolean logic is a system of reasoning where every value is exactly one of two states: true (1) or false (0). An operator takes one or more of these values and produces a new one. A truth table lists every possible input combination with its output, so you can check any operator completely.

AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. NOT takes one input and outputs its opposite. XOR, short for exclusive or, outputs 1 when its two inputs differ and 0 when they match. In hardware, a gate is a small electronic circuit that performs one of these operators on voltages, with a high voltage standing for 1 and a low voltage for 0.

This works because any yes-or-no decision can be broken into these pieces, and gates can feed into other gates, so complex decisions come from wiring simple ones together.

Worked example: compute (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B) with A = 1, B = 0. Step 1: NOT B is 1. Step 2: A AND 1 is 1. Step 3: NOT A is 0. Step 4: 0 AND B is 0. Step 5: 1 OR 0 is 1. Now try A = 1, B = 1: NOT B is 0, so the left part is 0; NOT A is 0, so the right part is 0; the result is 0. This expression outputs 1 exactly when A and B differ, so it is XOR built from AND, OR and NOT.

A common mistake is treating everyday or as Boolean OR in the wrong way. In speech, "tea or coffee" often means one but not both, which is XOR. Boolean OR is inclusive: 1 OR 1 is 1. Mixing these up in a circuit or a program condition produces a check that wrongly accepts, or wrongly rejects, the case where both inputs are true. In a running system, that might mean an access rule that lets in a user who should have been blocked.

questions.prompt: A warehouse alarm circuit uses the rule: Alarm = (D AND NOT K) OR M. Here D is 1 when the dock door is open, K is 1 when a valid keycard was swiped, and M is 1 when a motion sensor trips. Tonight D = 1, K = 1 and M = 0. Step 1: NOT K is 0. Step 2: missing. Step 3: the left part is now combined with M using OR, so we compute (left part) OR 0. Step 4: the alarm stays silent. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: D AND NOT K is 1 AND 1, which is 1
D AND NOT K is 1 AND 0, which is 0
D AND NOT K is 1 AND 0, which is 1, because at least one input is 1
D AND NOT K is 1 XOR 0, which is 1, because the inputs differ
questions.why: D is 1 and NOT K is 0 from Step 1, and AND outputs 1 only when all inputs are 1, so the result is 0. That 0 OR M = 0 keeps the alarm silent.

questions.prompt: A sensor network feeds two signals into a single XOR gate. In which case does the gate output 1?
choices: Both signals are 0
Either both signals are 1 or both are 0
One signal is 1 and the other is 0
Both signals are 1
questions.why: XOR, short for exclusive or, outputs 1 exactly when its two inputs differ and 0 when they match.

questions.prompt: A city museum lets a visitor in free if they are a student OR a senior. The rule is coded with Boolean OR. A visitor who is both a student and a senior arrives. What does the rule output, and why?
choices: 1, because Boolean OR is inclusive: it outputs 1 when at least one input is 1, including when both are 1
0, because OR needs exactly one input to be 1
1, but only because the two inputs differ
0, because OR means one or the other but not both
questions.why: Boolean OR is inclusive, so 1 OR 1 is 1. The 'one but not both' reading is XOR, not OR.

questions.prompt: A research lab meant its door rule to require a badge AND a PIN. A developer wrote it as badge OR PIN instead. What happens in the running system?
choices: The door rejects everyone, including people who have both a badge and a PIN
Someone who has only a badge, with no PIN, is let in when they should have been blocked
Nothing changes, because AND and OR give the same output whenever both inputs are 1
The door opens only when the badge and the PIN disagree
questions.why: OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1, so badge = 1 and PIN = 0 gives 1. The intended AND would give 0 and block that person.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AND, OR, NOT and XOR each do, and why XOR is not the same as OR. Name one limit of Boolean logic as a model, or one place where people get it wrong.
lessons.modelAnswer: Boolean logic works on values that are only true or false, 1 or 0. AND gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1, including when both are. NOT flips one input. XOR gives 1 only when the two inputs differ. The key difference from OR is the case where both inputs are 1: OR says 1, XOR says 0. People often confuse them because spoken "or" usually means one or the other but not both, which is XOR. You can check any of these with a truth table, and you can even build XOR from AND, OR and NOT. One limit is that the model only knows two states. Anything with degrees, like "mostly" or an unknown value, has to be encoded using several bits or handled by other logic.
rubricPoints: States that Boolean values are only true or false, written 1 or 0.
Defines AND, OR and NOT correctly.
Defines XOR as outputting 1 only when the inputs differ.
Identifies the both-inputs-true case as where OR and XOR disagree.
Names a limit or pitfall, such as confusing everyday or with OR, or the two-state limitation.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine exercises logic gates, and explaining the operators and the OR versus XOR distinction back in your own words is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Boolean arithmetic is doing ordinary math, like adding and subtracting, using only true/false values (the bits 1 and 0) and simple logic rules. A computer has no idea what the number 9 is. It only has tiny switches that are on or off, and circuits that combine them. Boolean arithmetic shows how those on/off rules, applied column by column, add up to real arithmetic. Think of grade-school addition: you add one column, write a digit, and carry a 1 to the next column. A computer does exactly that, except each column holds only 0 or 1, and a small circuit decides the digit and the carry.
lessons.guessPrompt: In binary, each column can only hold 0 or 1. What do you think 1 + 1 gives in a single column, and what has to happen to the next column?
lessons.teach:
Boolean arithmetic means performing number arithmetic on binary digits (bits, each 0 or 1) using logic operations. Two operations matter most here. XOR (exclusive or) outputs 1 when exactly one input is 1. AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1.

Why it works: adding two bits has four cases. 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+0=1, and 1+1=10 (binary for two), meaning sum digit 0 and carry 1. The sum digit matches XOR exactly, and the carry matches AND exactly. A circuit built from one XOR and one AND is called a half adder. A full adder also accepts a carry coming in from the previous column, so it adds three bits. Chaining full adders, one per bit, gives a ripple-carry adder, where each carry ripples into the next column.

Worked example, 4 bits, 6 + 3 (0110 + 0011), rightmost column first. Column 1: 0+1 = sum 1, carry 0. Column 2: 1+1 = sum 0, carry 1. Column 3: 1+0+carry 1 = sum 0, carry 1. Column 4: 0+0+carry 1 = sum 1, carry 0. Result 1001, which is 9.

Negative numbers usually use two's complement: to negate, flip every bit and add 1. So 3 (0011) becomes 1100, plus 1 is 1101, meaning -3. Subtraction then becomes addition: A minus B equals A plus the negation of B, so the same adder circuit does both.

A common mistake is forgetting that hardware works at a fixed width. With 4 bits, 0111 (7) + 0001 gives 1000, which in two's complement means -8, not 8. This is overflow: the true answer does not fit. In a running system, integer overflow silently wraps around, so a counter or balance can suddenly turn hugely negative, causing crashes or security bugs.

questions.prompt: A 4-bit adder computes 5 minus 2 by adding 5 to the two's complement of 2. Negating 2 (0010): flip every bit to get 1101, then add 1 to get 1110 (-2). Now add 0101 + 1110, rightmost column first. Column 1: 1+0 = sum 1, carry 0. Column 2: 0+1 = sum 1, carry 0. Column 3: 1+1 = sum 0, carry 1. Column 4: 0+1 plus the incoming carry of 1 = ? Because the hardware is only 4 bits wide, any carry out of column 4 is dropped. What is the missing column 4 result?
choices: Sum 1, carry 1
Sum 0, carry 1
Sum 0, carry 0
Sum 1, carry 0
questions.why: 0+1+1 equals two, which is binary 10, so the sum digit is 0 and the carry is 1; dropping that carry leaves 0011, which is 3, the correct answer to 5 minus 2.

questions.prompt: A half adder adds two single bits and produces a sum digit and a carry digit. Which logic operations produce these two outputs?
choices: Sum from OR, carry from AND
Sum from AND, carry from XOR
Sum from XOR, carry from AND
Sum from XOR, carry from OR
questions.why: The sum digit is 1 only when exactly one input is 1, which is XOR, and the carry is 1 only when both inputs are 1, which is AND.

questions.prompt: Using 4-bit two's complement, what bit pattern represents -5? Positive 5 is 0101.
questions.why: To negate, flip every bit of 0101 to get 1010, then add 1 to get 1011; stopping at 1010 forgets the add-1 step.

questions.prompt: A program keeps a stock count in a 4-bit two's complement register. The count is 5 (0101) and a delivery adds 4 (0100). The adder produces 1001. What has happened?
choices: Nothing is wrong: 1001 is 9, the correct total
Overflow: 9 does not fit in 4-bit two's complement, so 1001 is read as a negative number and the count silently wraps
The extra carry was saved in a fifth bit, so the total is stored safely
The adder made a carry mistake in column 1
questions.why: In 4-bit two's complement the largest positive value is 7, so the true answer 9 does not fit; the result 1001 has its leading bit set, which makes it a negative number, and the count wraps around without any warning.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a computer adds two binary numbers using only logic gates, and how the same circuit handles subtraction. Name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Adding two bits has only four cases, and the results line up with two logic gates: the sum digit is XOR of the bits, and the carry is AND of them. That pair is a half adder. A full adder also takes the carry from the column to its right, and chaining one full adder per bit gives a ripple-carry adder that works exactly like grade-school column addition. For subtraction, we store negatives in two's complement: flip all the bits and add 1. Then A minus B is just A plus negated B, so no separate subtraction circuit is needed. The limit is fixed width: if the true result needs more bits than we have, it overflows and wraps around, so 7 + 1 in 4-bit signed arithmetic comes out as -8. Ripple carries also add delay, since each column waits for the previous one.
rubricPoints: Sum bit equals XOR and carry bit equals AND of the input bits.
A full adder adds a carry-in, and chaining them adds multi-bit numbers column by column.
Two's complement negation is flip all bits then add 1.
Subtraction is done by adding the two's complement, reusing the adder.
Fixed bit width means results can overflow and wrap around.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises gate-level adders, and tracing carries and two's complement out loud is the core skill to check.

lessons.plain: Digital circuits come in two kinds. A combinational circuit is like a calculator button press: the answer depends only on what you type right now, and the same input always gives the same answer. A sequential circuit is like a turnstile counter: what it shows depends on what you do now and on what happened before, because it remembers. Sequential circuits are built by adding memory to combinational logic, often with a steady timing signal deciding when the memory updates. Almost every computer part, from the adder to the processor's registers, is one of these two kinds or a mix of both.
lessons.guessPrompt: A box has one button. You press it and a light comes on; you press the identical button again and the light goes off. Can the light's state be worked out from the button press alone, or does the box need to remember something? Why?
lessons.teach:
A combinational circuit is a network of logic gates whose output depends only on its current inputs. A logic gate is a tiny switch that computes AND, OR, NOT or XOR on bits. Give a combinational circuit the same inputs and you always get the same output, whatever happened before. A sequential circuit's output depends on current inputs plus stored state, meaning bits it remembers from earlier. Sequential circuits combine combinational logic with memory elements, typically flip-flops. A flip-flop is a small circuit that holds one bit and updates it only on a tick of the clock. The clock is a signal that alternates steadily between 0 and 1, telling every part of the chip when to update.

Why it works: combinational logic has no loops, so signals flow one way from inputs to outputs. Memory appears through feedback, where an output is routed back into an input. That loop lets the circuit hold a value after the original input is gone, and the clock makes state change only at predictable instants.

Worked example: a half adder adds two bits, A and B. Sum = A XOR B and Carry = A AND B. With inputs 1 and 1, XOR gives 0 and AND gives 1, so carry is 1 and sum is 0 (binary 10, which is decimal 2). It gives that result every time, regardless of history, so it is combinational. Now take a toggle: one flip-flop holding Q, with a NOT gate feeding NOT Q back into it. Start with Q=0. On tick 1 it stores NOT 0, which is 1. On tick 2 it stores 0, and on tick 3 it stores 1. Every tick looks identical, yet the output alternates because it depends on stored state, so it is sequential.

Common mistake: calling a circuit sequential because its gates sit in stages one after another. Many stages without feedback or storage are still combinational. Sequential means the circuit remembers.

Consequence in a running system: signals take time to pass through gates, which is called propagation delay. The clock period must be longer than the slowest combinational path between flip-flops. Otherwise a flip-flop captures a half-computed value. That longest path is a key limit on a processor's clock speed.

questions.prompt: A 'seen-a-one' detector has one flip-flop holding Q. On each clock tick it stores Q OR In, where In is the current input bit. It starts with Q=0, and the inputs on ticks 1, 2 and 3 are 0, 1 and 0. Tick 1: it stores 0 OR 0, which is 0. Tick 2: it stores 0 OR 1, which is 1. Tick 3: ? What happens on tick 3, and what does it show?
choices: It stores NOT 1, which is 0, because a flip-flop flips its value on every tick.
It stores 1 OR 0, which is 1, but it is still combinational because only one OR gate does the work.
It stores 0, because the current input is 0 and the output follows the input on each tick.
It stores 1 OR 0, which is 1, so the output stays 1 even though the input is now 0. That shows it is sequential.
questions.why: The new value combines the stored Q=1 with the input 0, giving 1. The output depends on remembered state, not just the current input, so the circuit is sequential.

questions.prompt: A designer chains five stages of AND, OR and XOR gates to build a 3-input majority-vote circuit. Signals flow only forward, there is no feedback and there are no flip-flops. How should this circuit be classified?
choices: Sequential, because signals take time to pass through each stage.
Sequential, because the gates sit in five stages one after another.
It cannot be classified until you know the clock speed.
Combinational, because its output depends only on its current inputs.
questions.why: With no feedback and no memory elements, the output depends only on the current inputs. The number of stages does not make a circuit sequential.

questions.prompt: In a chip design, the slowest combinational path between two flip-flops takes 2.5 ns. The fastest path takes 0.8 ns. Which clock period lets every flip-flop capture a finished result?
choices: 0.8 ns
2.0 ns
1.6 ns
3.0 ns
questions.why: The clock period must be longer than the slowest combinational path, here 2.5 ns. Any shorter period lets a flip-flop capture a half-computed value.

questions.prompt: A technician tests an unlabeled circuit board. She applies the inputs 1 and 0 and reads output 1. Later, after other inputs have been applied in between, she applies 1 and 0 again and reads output 0. The board is not faulty. What does this tell her?
choices: The circuit is combinational because it contains XOR gates, which can give either value.
The circuit has no feedback, because feedback would make the output fixed.
The circuit is combinational, and propagation delay changed the result.
The circuit is sequential: its output depends on stored state as well as the current inputs.
questions.why: A combinational circuit always gives the same output for the same inputs. Different outputs for identical inputs mean the circuit remembers earlier state, so it is sequential.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between combinational and sequential logic, using one example of each, and name one limit or tradeoff that comes from mixing them in a clocked processor.
lessons.modelAnswer: Combinational logic is gates wired with no loops, so the output is a pure function of the current inputs. A half adder is the classic case: 1 plus 1 always gives sum 0 and carry 1, no matter what came before. Sequential logic adds memory, usually flip-flops that store a bit and update on a clock tick, so the output depends on the inputs and on stored state. A toggle circuit that flips its stored bit every tick is sequential, because identical ticks produce alternating outputs. Having many gates in a row does not make a circuit sequential; it needs feedback or storage. The tradeoff is timing. Combinational paths between flip-flops take real time to settle, so the clock period has to exceed the slowest path. Long paths mean a slower clock, which caps how fast the processor can run.
rubricPoints: States that combinational output depends only on current inputs.
States that sequential output depends on inputs plus stored state, via feedback or flip-flops.
Gives a correct example of each, such as an adder and a flip-flop-based toggle or counter.
Mentions the clock as what times state updates.
Names the timing limit: the clock period must exceed the slowest combinational path's propagation delay.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine simulates logic circuits, and the core skill here is distinguishing and justifying the two circuit kinds in your own words.

lessons.plain: A computer keeps data in two very different kinds of places. Registers are a handful of tiny storage slots built right into the processor, the chip that does the work; they are extremely fast but there are only a few dozen of them. Memory, usually called RAM (random-access memory), is a much larger store outside the processor where every byte has a numbered location called an address. Think of a chef: the cutting board (registers) holds only what is being worked on right now, while the pantry (memory) holds everything else. Ingredients must be carried from the pantry to the board, used, and carried back.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a program says "add 1 to the variable count", and count lives in memory, how many separate steps do you think the processor needs to make that happen, and what might each step be?
lessons.teach:
A register is a small, fixed-size storage cell inside the CPU (central processing unit), usually holding one word, meaning the chunk of bits the processor handles at once, such as 64 bits. Registers are built from flip-flops, circuits that hold a bit until told to change, so they keep state between clock ticks. Memory (RAM) is a large array of storage cells outside the CPU; each cell has an address, a number used to pick it out.

Why the split? Circuitry that is fast enough to answer within one clock tick is expensive and must sit physically close to the arithmetic hardware, so only a few registers fit. RAM is cheap and huge but takes many times longer to reach. So arithmetic is done on registers, and data moves between memory and registers with two kinds of instruction: a load copies a value from a memory address into a register, and a store copies a register's value back to a memory address.

Worked example: count sits at address 1000 holding 7, and the program wants count = count + 1. Step 1, load: the CPU copies 7 from address 1000 into register R1. Step 2, add: the arithmetic unit computes R1 + 1 and puts 8 in R1. Address 1000 still says 7. Step 3, store: the CPU copies 8 from R1 back to address 1000. Only now does memory say 8.

The common mistake is to picture a variable as living in one place and changing in place. In reality the register holds a temporary copy, and memory is unchanged until the store happens. The consequence in a running system: if two cores each load 7, each add 1, and each store 8, the final value is 8 instead of 9. One increment is silently lost, which is the root of many concurrency bugs. Registers are fast private scratch space; memory is the slower, shared, addressable record.

questions.prompt: A shop's checkout program must compute total = price + tax. In memory, price is at address 3000 and holds 20, tax is at address 3008 and holds 3, and total is at address 3016. A register is a small, fast storage cell inside the CPU. A load copies a value from a memory address into a register, and a store copies a register's value back to a memory address. Step 1: load 20 from address 3000 into register R1. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: the arithmetic unit adds R1 and R2 and puts 23 in register R3. Step 4: store 23 from R3 into address 3016. Which instruction belongs in Step 2?
choices: Add: compute R1 + 3008 and put the result in R2
Load: copy 20 from address 3000 into register R2
Store: copy 3 from register R2 into address 3008
Load: copy 3 from address 3008 into register R2
questions.why: Arithmetic works only on registers, so the tax value must first be loaded from its memory address into R2 before the add can use it.

questions.prompt: A CPU (central processing unit) does its arithmetic on registers, which are small storage cells inside the CPU. It does not work directly on RAM, the large array of addressed storage cells outside the CPU. What is the main reason for this design?
choices: Storage fast enough to answer within one clock tick is expensive and must sit close to the arithmetic hardware, so only a few registers fit. RAM is cheap and large but much slower to reach.
Registers are shared by all cores, while RAM is private to each core, so working in registers keeps data consistent.
RAM has no addresses, so the CPU must copy values into registers before it can find them again.
RAM cannot hold numbers larger than one bit, so values have to be widened in registers before any arithmetic.
questions.why: Registers are fast but costly and must be near the arithmetic unit, so there are few of them. RAM is cheap and big but slow, so values are loaded into registers for arithmetic.

questions.prompt: A warehouse program tracks a stock count at memory address 5200, which holds 40. One core has loaded 40 into its register R4 and subtracted 5, so R4 now holds 35. It has not yet run the store instruction, which copies a register's value back to memory. At this exact moment, a second core reads address 5200. What value does the second core see?
choices: 45, because the register and memory values are combined
40, because memory changes only when the store runs
0, because the address is locked while R4 is in use
35, because the subtraction already changed the variable
questions.why: The register holds a private temporary copy, so address 5200 keeps its old value of 40 until the store copies 35 back.

questions.prompt: A website's hit counter lives at a shared memory address and currently holds 10. Three CPU cores each try to add one visit. All three load 10 into their own registers before any of them stores. Each then adds 1 and stores its result back to the same address. What is the final value in memory?
choices: 10, because the stores cancel each other out
11, because every core stored the same value of 11
13, because each core added one
33, because the three results of 11 are summed
questions.why: Each core worked on its own copy of 10 and stored 11, so two of the three increments are silently lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a register and memory, walk through what really happens when code increments a variable, and name one tradeoff or limit that this design creates.
lessons.modelAnswer: Registers are a small number of storage slots inside the CPU, each holding one word, and they are fast enough to feed the arithmetic hardware every clock tick. Memory, or RAM, is a much bigger array outside the CPU where each cell has an address, but it is far slower to reach. The CPU does arithmetic only on registers, so it moves data with loads and stores. Incrementing count at address 1000 is three steps: load the value into a register, add 1 in the register, store the result back to address 1000. Until the store, memory still holds the old value. The tradeoff is speed versus size: registers are fast but scarce and expensive, memory is roomy but slow. A limit this creates is that the register copy is private, so two cores incrementing the same variable at once can both store the same result and lose an update.
rubricPoints: Defines a register as a small, fast storage cell inside the CPU holding about one word.
Defines memory as a large, slower store where each cell has an address.
Explains that loads copy memory into registers and stores copy registers back to memory.
Traces an increment as load, add, store, noting memory is unchanged until the store.
Names the speed versus size tradeoff or the lost-update risk from private register copies.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is describing the load, compute, store path between registers and memory clearly, which is best checked by explaining it back rather than by any current hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A pure combinational circuit is like a calculator that forgets everything the instant you look away: give it the same inputs and it always gives the same answer, because the output depends only on what is going in right now. State is memory: something the system keeps from earlier that changes how it answers now. Think of a light with a single push button. Pressing the button does not tell you whether the light ends up on or off. That depends on whether it was already on. The remembered 'on or off' is the state.
lessons.guessPrompt: A box has one button and one lamp. You press the button and the lamp turns on. You press the exact same button the exact same way and the lamp turns off. Can the lamp's behaviour be explained by looking only at the button's current input? What else must the box be keeping track of?
lessons.teach:
A combinational circuit is a network of logic gates whose output is a fixed function of its present inputs alone. An adder is the classic case: feed it 3 and 3 and it outputs 6, every time, no matter what happened before. State is information a circuit stores from the past. A circuit with state is called sequential, and its output depends on both the present inputs and the stored state.

State works through feedback: some of a circuit's output is routed back into its own input, so a value can hold itself in place. The smallest such storage element holds one bit and is called a latch or flip-flop. Many systems use a clock, a steady on-off signal, to say exactly when the stored value is allowed to update, so changes happen in orderly steps.

Worked example: a running-total accumulator, which is an adder whose output is stored and fed back as one of its inputs. Start with stored state 0. Step 1: input 3, adder computes 0+3, state becomes 3, output 3. Step 2: input 3 again, adder computes 3+3, state becomes 6, output 6. Step 3: input 3 again, output 9. The same input produced three different outputs because the stored total differed each time. A plain adder given 3 would have no history to draw on.

A common mistake is forgetting that state has to start somewhere. When power comes on, a storage element may hold an arbitrary value until something sets it, which is why real hardware has a reset that forces a known starting state. In a running system, an uninitialized or unexpected state produces behaviour that seems random: you repeat the same inputs and get different results, and the bug cannot be reproduced until you account for what was remembered. Combinational output can be predicted from inputs alone; stateful output also requires knowing the history or the current stored value.

questions.prompt: A parking garage uses a circuit to track free spaces. It is a subtractor whose result is stored and fed back as one of its own inputs, and the stored value updates once per clock tick. A reset sets the stored value to 50. Tick 1: the input is 4 (four cars entered), the subtractor computes 50 - 4, the state becomes 46, and the output is 46. Tick 2: the input is 4 again. [missing step] Tick 3: the input is 4 again, the subtractor computes 42 - 4, the state becomes 38, and the output is 38. Which choice correctly fills in tick 2?
choices: The subtractor computes 46 - 4, the state becomes 42, and the output is 42.
The subtractor computes 4 + 4, the state becomes 8, and the output is 8.
The output is 46 again, because the input of 4 is the same as in tick 1.
The state goes back to 50, because the stored value only changes on a reset.
questions.why: This is a sequential circuit: the stored 46 is fed back and combined with the new input, giving 46 - 4 = 42, which is also the value tick 3 starts from.

questions.prompt: Which of these circuits is purely combinational, meaning its output depends only on its present inputs?
choices: A circuit that stores the last temperature reading and outputs it until a new reading arrives.
A circuit whose output for an input of 5 differs depending on which inputs came before.
A circuit that takes two numbers and outputs whichever one is larger.
A circuit that counts how many times a button has been pressed since reset.
questions.why: Picking the larger of two present inputs needs no stored history, so the same inputs always give the same output. The other three all rely on remembered state.

questions.prompt: A warehouse installs a hardware counter that tallies boxes passing a sensor. Right after power-on, before any box has passed, the display reads 217. Tomorrow it might read a different number. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The counter is combinational, so it shows a random function of its inputs.
The sensor must have counted 217 boxes during power-on.
The clock is running too slowly for the counter to show zero.
No reset forced a known starting value, so the storage elements came up holding arbitrary values.
questions.why: Storage elements can hold arbitrary values at power-on until something sets them. A reset is what forces the known starting state of zero.

questions.prompt: What lets a latch or flip-flop keep holding a stored bit after the input that set it has changed?
choices: Using larger input values, which leave a longer-lasting effect on the output.
Feedback: part of the circuit's output is routed back into its own input, so the value holds itself in place.
A clock signal alone, which stores the bit inside each tick.
Adding more gates in a straight chain with no loops, so the signal takes longer to fade.
questions.why: State works through feedback. The clock only controls when the stored value may update, and a loop-free chain of gates stays combinational.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a circuit with state differs from a purely combinational one, using an example, and name one cost or risk that comes with having state.
lessons.modelAnswer: A combinational circuit is a pure function of its current inputs: an adder given 3 and 3 always says 6, and it remembers nothing. A stateful, or sequential, circuit stores something from the past, using feedback so a value holds itself, often updated on a clock tick. Its output depends on inputs plus that stored value. An accumulator shows the difference: feed it 3 three times and it outputs 3, 6, then 9, because the stored total keeps changing. Memory is what makes counters, registers and whole computers possible. The tradeoff is that you can no longer predict behaviour from inputs alone; you also need the history or the current state. That means you need a defined starting point, like a reset, otherwise power-on values are arbitrary, and bugs can appear that do not reproduce from the same inputs.
rubricPoints: Combinational output depends only on current inputs, so identical inputs always give identical outputs.
Stateful circuits store information from the past, and output depends on inputs plus stored state.
State is held through feedback, typically in a latch or flip-flop, often updated by a clock.
Gives a concrete example where the same input yields different outputs, such as an accumulator or toggle.
Names a cost: need for a known starting state or reset, and harder prediction and debugging.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine simulates logic circuits, and articulating why identical inputs can give different outputs is the core conceptual skill here.

lessons.plain: An instruction-set architecture, or ISA, is the official list of commands a processor promises to understand. It also sets the rules for how each command is written as a number and exactly what it does. It is the contract between software and hardware. Think of a restaurant menu. The menu tells customers what they can order and what they will get, but it says nothing about how the kitchen is organized. Two very different kitchens can serve the same menu, and a customer who knows the menu can order at either one.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a program has been translated into machine instructions for one family of processors. Do you think it will run unchanged on a processor from a different family? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An instruction-set architecture (ISA) is the specification of what a processor can be told to do. It lists every instruction, which is a single command the processor carries out. It fixes the opcode, the bit pattern that names the operation, such as add or load. It defines the operands, the inputs and outputs an instruction works on. It names the registers, a few tiny storage slots inside the processor. It also defines how memory addresses, the numbered locations in main memory, are specified. Machine code is the binary form of these instructions. Assembly language is a human-readable spelling of the same instructions.

The ISA works because it is a stable contract. Compilers, the tools that translate high-level code, only need to target the ISA. Chip designers can then build any internal design, called the microarchitecture, as long as it obeys that contract.

Worked example. Take the statement x = y + z in a toy ISA where y is stored at address 100, z at 104, and x at 108. The compiler emits four instructions. First, LOAD R1, [100] copies y, which is 5, into register R1. Second, LOAD R2, [104] copies z, which is 7, into R2. Third, ADD R3, R1, R2 puts 12 in R3. Fourth, STORE R3, [108] writes 12 to x. Each line becomes a binary number whose opcode bits say load, add, or store.

The ISA also marks some instructions as privileged. Privileged instructions, such as those that control hardware devices or memory protection, run only when the processor is in kernel mode, the mode the operating system uses. A user program that needs one of these actions uses a special system-call instruction to ask the operating system to do it.

A common mistake is to treat the ISA and the chip as the same thing. A newer, faster chip usually keeps the same ISA but has a better microarchitecture. In a running system, this distinction has a practical effect. Old binaries keep working on new chips that share an ISA, but a binary built for one ISA will not run on a different ISA unless it is recompiled or emulated.

questions.prompt: A game studio's toy ISA stores a player's score at address 300 (current value 40) and a bonus at address 304 (value 15). The compiler must turn the statement score = score + bonus into instructions. Step 1: LOAD R1, [300] copies 40 into register R1. Step 2: LOAD R2, [304] copies 15 into register R2. Step 3: ??? Step 4: STORE R1, [300] writes the new score, 55, back to address 300. Which instruction belongs in Step 3?
choices: STORE R2, [300], which writes 15 to address 300
LOAD R1, [55], which copies the value at address 55 into R1
ADD R1, R1, R2, which puts 55 in register R1
ADD R3, R1, R2, which puts 55 in register R3
questions.why: Step 4 stores whatever is in R1, so the add must place its result, 55, in R1; putting it in R3 would leave 40 in R1 and the score would never change.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a drone company is reading the instruction-set architecture (ISA) document for the processor in their flight controller. Which of these would they expect the ISA to specify?
choices: How many internal pipeline stages this particular chip model uses to speed up execution
How many transistors the chip contains and what silicon process it is built on
The opcode bit pattern for a multiply instruction and the names of the registers it can use
The exact physical layout of the circuits inside the chip, which varies from model to model
questions.why: An ISA is the contract of what the processor can be told to do, including opcodes, operands, registers and memory addressing, while internal design details belong to the microarchitecture.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a compiled inventory program, built for ISA "Alpha". It replaces its servers with two new machines: Server P has a newer, faster chip that still implements ISA Alpha; Server Q uses a chip implementing a different ISA, "Beta". Without changing the program, what happens?
choices: It runs on both, because any newer chip can execute any older binary
It runs on Server Q but not on Server P, because a faster chip changes the opcodes
It runs on Server P, but on Server Q it must be recompiled for Beta or run under emulation
It fails on both, because a new chip always requires every program to be recompiled
questions.why: Binaries keep working on new chips that share the same ISA, but a binary built for one ISA will not run on a different ISA unless it is recompiled or emulated.

questions.prompt: A photo-editing app running as an ordinary user program wants to change the computer's memory-protection settings, an action the ISA marks as privileged. What is the correct way for the app to get this done?
choices: Recompile the app for a different ISA that has no privileged instructions
Use the system-call instruction to ask the operating system, running in kernel mode, to perform the action
Execute the privileged instruction directly, since every program can use every instruction in the ISA
Write the setting into one of the processor's registers, which bypasses kernel mode
questions.why: Privileged instructions run only in kernel mode, the mode the operating system uses, so a user program must make a system call to have the OS carry them out.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an instruction-set architecture is and why it matters when you ship a compiled program. Name one limit or tradeoff that comes from having a fixed ISA.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ISA is the contract between software and the processor. It lists the instructions the chip understands, how each one is encoded in binary, which registers exist, and how memory is addressed. A compiler turns code like x = y + z into ISA instructions such as two loads, an add, and a store.
