Unlock (also called release) marks it free again so one waiting thread can proceed. The code between lock and unlock is the critical section, meaning the part that touches shared data and must not interleave with another thread's copy of the same code.

This works because acquiring the mutex is atomic. Atomic means the hardware or operating system performs the check-and-take as one indivisible step. So two threads can never both see the mutex as free and both take it. If the mutex is held, a waiting thread either spins, which means it loops and keeps checking, or it is put to sleep by the kernel until the mutex is released.

Worked example. A balance is 100, and threads A and B each withdraw 30. Each withdrawal reads the balance, subtracts 30, and writes the result. Without a lock, A reads 100 and then B reads 100. A writes 70, and then B writes 70. One withdrawal is lost. With a lock, A locks, reads 100, and writes 70, then unlocks. B was blocked the whole time. B then locks, reads 70, writes 40, and unlocks. The final value of 40 is correct.

The most common mistake is protecting only the write and not the read. The lock must cover the whole read-modify-write sequence, or the race remains. A related mistake is forgetting to unlock on an error path. When that happens, every later thread waits forever and the program hangs.

There is a performance tradeoff. A lock makes the critical section serial, so only one thread at a time can be in it. If many threads compete for one lock, which is called contention, they spend their time waiting, and adding more cores stops helping. Good practice is to keep critical sections short and to hold a lock only around the shared data it protects. Correctness comes first, but a lock held too broadly turns a parallel program into a slow, effectively single-threaded one.

questions.prompt: A concert venue's booking server has 12 seats left in one section. Two booking threads, X and Y, each try to reserve 5 seats. Each reservation reads the seat count, subtracts 5, and writes the result, and the whole sequence is protected by one mutex. Trace: X locks the mutex. X reads 12, writes 7, and unlocks. Y has been blocked while X held the lock. Missing step: what does Y do next so that the final count is correct?
choices: Y reads the count it saw before blocking, which was 12, then locks, writes 7, and unlocks
Y writes 7 without locking, because X has already finished and the mutex is free
Y locks the mutex, reads 7, writes 2, and unlocks
Y locks the mutex, writes 2 straight away without reading, and unlocks
questions.why: Y must acquire the lock and then perform the whole read-modify-write inside it, so it reads X's result of 7 and correctly writes 2.

questions.prompt: Two threads at a parking-garage control system call lock on the same free mutex at almost the same instant. Why can't both of them end up holding it?
choices: The mutex holds a copy of the shared data for each thread, so they never conflict
Each thread checks the mutex twice before taking it, which catches the collision
The operating system always runs only one thread at a time, so they can never truly try at the same instant
Acquiring a mutex is atomic: the check that it is free and the taking of it happen as one indivisible step, so only one thread can succeed
questions.why: Because check-and-take is a single indivisible operation, one thread wins and the other sees the mutex as held and must wait.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse inventory service, a function locks a mutex, updates the stock table, and unlocks. If the update fails, the function returns an error early, skipping the unlock line. What happens to the running system after the first failure?
choices: The next thread takes the lock anyway, because a failed update does not count as holding it
Every later thread that tries to lock that mutex waits forever, so the service hangs
Nothing changes, because the mutex automatically frees itself when the function returns
Only the failed update is lost; other threads continue normally
questions.why: The mutex stays marked as held with no one to release it, so all later lock attempts block indefinitely.

questions.prompt: A photo-processing program runs 16 worker threads on 16 cores. Each worker holds one shared mutex for its entire job, including resizing the image, even though only a final update to a shared counter touches shared data. Adding more cores barely speeds it up. What is the best diagnosis and fix?
choices: Heavy contention makes the work effectively serial; hold the lock only around the shared counter update
The lock is not atomic; switch the waiting threads from sleeping to spinning
The program has a race condition; remove the lock so all workers run in parallel
There are too few threads; start 64 workers so the cores stay busy
questions.why: Holding the lock too broadly serializes all the work, so keeping the critical section short, just around the shared counter, restores parallelism while staying correct.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a mutex does, why the critical section must cover the entire read-modify-write step, and what tradeoff you accept by adding a lock.
lessons.modelAnswer: A mutex makes sure only one thread at a time runs a critical section, which is the code that touches shared data. Taking the lock is atomic, so two threads can't both grab it. Everyone else waits until the holder unlocks. The lock has to wrap the whole read-modify-write. If I only lock the write, two threads can still read the same old value, and one update gets lost. For example, two withdrawals of 30 from 100 could both leave 70. I also need to unlock on every path, including errors, or the next thread waits forever. The tradeoff is performance. Inside the lock, work is serial, so heavy contention means threads sit idle and extra cores don't help. So I keep critical sections short and narrow, but I never shrink them so far that the race comes back.
rubricPoints: States that a mutex allows only one thread at a time into a critical section.
Notes that acquiring the lock is atomic, so two threads cannot both take it.
Explains that the lock must cover the full read-modify-write sequence to prevent lost updates.
Mentions releasing the lock on every path to avoid threads waiting forever.
Names the cost: serialization and contention reduce parallel speedup, so critical sections should be short.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner find a double-spend data race and fix it by protecting a critical section, which is exactly what a mutex is for.

lessons.plain: A condition variable is a way for a thread (one independent line of execution inside a program) to sleep until some fact about shared data becomes true, and to be woken when another thread changes that data. Picture a restaurant pickup counter: instead of customers staring at the counter nonstop, they sit down, and the cook rings a bell when an order is placed there. A customer who hears the bell still walks up and checks that the order is really theirs before taking it. The bell is the condition variable; checking the counter is rechecking the condition.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two threads share a queue. A consumer thread wants to take an item, but the queue is empty. If you had no special tool, how might the consumer wait for an item, and what would be wasteful about that approach?
lessons.teach:
A condition variable is a synchronization tool that lets a thread block (sleep without using CPU) until another thread tells it that shared state may have changed. It always works together with a mutex, a lock that lets only one thread at a time run a critical section, the code that touches shared data. The alternative, busy-waiting, means looping on the check and burning CPU while nothing changes.

It offers three operations. Wait: called while holding the mutex, it releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep as one indivisible step, then reacquires the mutex before returning. Signal: wakes one waiting thread. Broadcast: wakes all waiting threads. The indivisible release-and-sleep is why it works: no other thread can change the data and signal in the gap between your check and your sleep, which would cause a lost wakeup, a signal sent when nobody was yet waiting, leaving the waiter asleep forever.

Worked example, a shared queue. Consumer locks the mutex, sees the queue is empty, calls wait; the mutex is released and the consumer sleeps. Producer locks the mutex, adds an item, calls signal, unlocks. Consumer wakes, reacquires the mutex, checks the queue again, finds one item, removes it, unlocks.

The common mistake is checking the condition with an if instead of a while loop. Being woken only means the state might have changed. Another consumer may have grabbed the item first, and some systems allow spurious wakeups, wakeups with no signal at all. With an if, the woken consumer assumes an item exists and tries to remove from an empty queue, crashing or corrupting data. The correct pattern is: while the condition is false, wait. Forgetting to signal after changing state, or signaling when one waiter is woken but several could proceed, causes the opposite failure in a running system: threads that hang forever while work sits ready.

questions.prompt: A ride-share app runs a driver thread that should sleep until a ride request arrives in a shared request list. The list is protected by a mutex, and a condition variable named requestReady is used. Trace the steps. Step 1: the driver thread locks the mutex. Step 2: inside a while loop, it checks the request list and finds it empty. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the dispatcher thread locks the mutex, appends a request for a pickup at 42 Elm Street, signals requestReady, and unlocks. Step 5: the driver thread wakes, reacquires the mutex, and the while loop checks the list again. Step 6: it finds one request, removes it, and unlocks the mutex. What must happen in Step 3?
choices: The driver calls wait on requestReady, which releases the mutex and puts the thread to sleep as one indivisible step.
The driver calls signal on requestReady so the dispatcher knows a driver is free to take a ride.
The driver keeps the mutex locked and loops on the empty check until a request shows up.
The driver unlocks the mutex first, and then, as a separate later step, calls wait on requestReady.
questions.why: Wait releases the mutex and sleeps in one indivisible step, so the dispatcher can lock, add a request and signal without any gap in which the wakeup could be lost.

questions.prompt: A thread holding a mutex calls wait on a condition variable. Which statement correctly describes what wait does?
choices: It keeps the mutex locked while the thread sleeps, so no other thread can touch the shared data.
It releases the mutex and sleeps as one indivisible step, then reacquires the mutex before returning.
It wakes every other thread waiting on the same condition variable, then releases the mutex.
It repeatedly rechecks the condition in a loop, using CPU until the shared state changes.
questions.why: Wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, and it holds the mutex again by the time it returns, which prevents lost wakeups.

questions.prompt: At a shipping warehouse, 6 truck threads wait on a condition variable until the loading gate is open. A gate-controller thread locks the mutex, sets gateOpen to true, calls signal once, and unlocks. Once open, the gate lets every truck through. What happens in the running system?
choices: The program crashes immediately because signal cannot be called while gateOpen is true.
One truck wakes and proceeds, and the other 5 can stay asleep indefinitely even though they could all go.
All 6 trucks wake up because setting gateOpen to true automatically notifies every waiter.
No truck wakes up, because signal only works on threads that are not yet waiting.
questions.why: Signal wakes only one waiter, so when several threads could proceed, broadcast is needed, otherwise the rest hang while work sits ready.

questions.prompt: A concert box office has one ticket pool shared by two buyer threads. Each buyer locks the mutex and writes: if the pool is empty, wait; then remove one ticket. A seller thread adds 1 ticket and signals. Both buyers end up awake, and buyer A removes the ticket first. What goes wrong for buyer B, and what is the fix?
choices: Buyer B busy-waits and burns CPU; the fix is to replace the condition variable with a plain loop on the pool.
Buyer B deadlocks on the mutex; the fix is to call wait without holding the mutex in the first place.
Buyer B skips the recheck and tries to remove from an empty pool; using while instead of if makes B check again and go back to waiting.
Buyer B can never wake up at all; the fix is to have the seller release the mutex before adding the ticket.
questions.why: Waking only means the state might have changed, so the condition must be rechecked in a while loop or the thread acts on a ticket that is already gone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a condition variable does and why it is paired with a mutex, using a producer and consumer as your example. Name one tradeoff or limit, such as why the condition must be rechecked in a loop or the cost of signal versus broadcast.
lessons.modelAnswer: A condition variable lets a thread sleep until another thread changes shared data, instead of spinning in a loop and wasting CPU. It is always used with a mutex protecting that data. A consumer locks the mutex, and while the queue is empty it calls wait, which releases the mutex and sleeps as one atomic step, so a producer cannot slip in an item and signal in between and have the wakeup lost. The producer locks, adds an item, signals, and unlocks; the consumer wakes holding the mutex again. The limit is that waking is only a hint: another consumer might take the item first, or a spurious wakeup can happen, so the check must be a while loop, not an if. There is also a tradeoff: signal wakes one thread cheaply but can leave others stuck if several could proceed, while broadcast is safe but wakes everyone, who then compete for the mutex.
rubricPoints: A condition variable lets a thread sleep until shared state may have changed, avoiding busy-waiting.
It is always used with a mutex that protects the shared state.
Wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires it, preventing lost wakeups.
The condition must be rechecked in a while loop because wakeups can be stolen or spurious.
Signal wakes one waiter and broadcast wakes all, trading efficiency against the risk of leaving threads stuck.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission uses condition variables directly, and the core skill is explaining the wait-in-a-loop pattern and why the mutex release must be atomic.

lessons.plain: A semaphore is a shared counter that controls how many threads (independent streams of work inside a program) may use something at the same time. Picture a parking garage with a sign showing free spaces. Each car entering takes one space and the number drops; when it hits zero, the next car waits at the gate. When a car leaves, the number goes up and a waiting car is let in. Operating systems and programs use semaphores the same way: to limit access to a scarce resource, or to let one piece of work tell another that something is ready.
lessons.guessPrompt: A garage has 3 spaces and a gate counter that starts at 3. Four cars arrive one after another, and none have left yet. What do you think happens to the fourth car, and what has to happen before it can get in?
lessons.teach:
A semaphore is a shared integer plus two operations that the system guarantees are atomic, meaning each runs as one indivisible step that no other thread can interrupt halfway. The wait operation (also called P or down) decreases the counter; if the counter is already zero, the calling thread is blocked, meaning it is paused and does not use the CPU until it can continue. The signal operation (also called V or up) increases the counter and, if any threads are blocked, wakes one of them.

This works because the counter always records how many permits remain, and atomicity stops two threads from both reading 1 and both taking the last permit. A counting semaphore starts at some number N and lets up to N threads through at once. A binary semaphore starts at 1 and lets only one through, so it can guard a critical section, which is code that touches shared data. A semaphore started at 0 works as a signal: one thread waits until another thread calls signal to say work is ready.

Worked example: a database connection pool has 3 connections, so the semaphore starts at 3. Thread A waits and the counter goes to 2. B waits and it goes to 1. C waits and it goes to 0. D waits, finds 0, and blocks. A finishes and signals. The counter would rise to 1, but D is waiting, so D wakes and takes that permit, and the counter stays at 0.

A common mistake is forgetting to signal on every exit path, for example when an error makes a thread return early. That permit is lost for good. In a running system the pool slowly shrinks until every thread blocks forever and the service hangs, even though no connection is actually in use. A second mistake is assuming a counting semaphore with N greater than 1 protects shared data. It does not, because N threads can be inside together.

questions.prompt: A video site has an uploader thread and an encoder thread. The encoder must not start until a file is fully uploaded, so they share a semaphore that starts at 0 and is used as a signal. Step 1: The encoder calls wait. The counter is 0, so the encoder blocks. Step 2: The uploader finishes file #1 and calls signal. The encoder is blocked, so it wakes and takes that permit, and the counter stays at 0. Step 3: While the encoder is busy with file #1, the uploader finishes file #2 and calls signal. No thread is blocked, so the counter rises to 1. Step 4: The encoder finishes file #1 and calls wait again. What happens in Step 4?
choices: The counter drops from 1 to 0, and the encoder continues right away to file #2 without blocking.
The encoder blocks, because the signal from Step 3 was thrown away when no thread was waiting.
The encoder blocks, because a semaphore used as a signal must always start from 0 again before each wait.
The counter drops from 1 to -1 and the encoder blocks until the uploader signals twice more.
questions.why: The signal in Step 3 raised the counter to 1, recording one waiting file, so the encoder's wait can decrease it to 0 and go straight on to file #2 without blocking.

questions.prompt: An event-ticket service guards its last available seat with a semaphore whose counter is 1. Kiosk thread X and kiosk thread Y both call wait at almost the same moment. Why does it matter that the system makes wait atomic, meaning it runs as one indivisible step that no other thread can interrupt halfway?
choices: It stops both threads from reading 1 and both taking the last seat. One gets the permit and the other blocks.
It makes wait faster, so neither kiosk has to pause and the seat is assigned sooner.
It guarantees that thread X always goes first, because it called wait slightly earlier.
It lets both threads take the seat safely, because the counter can go below zero to record the overbooking.
questions.why: Atomicity makes each wait an indivisible step, so only one thread can see the counter at 1 and decrease it. The other then finds 0 and blocks.

questions.prompt: A weather-data app has a shared variable totalReadings. Many threads add to it. To protect it, a developer wraps each update in wait and signal on a semaphore that starts at 5. Updates are still sometimes lost. What is the problem?
choices: The semaphore should start at 0, because a starting value of 0 is what protects a critical section.
Wait and signal are not atomic on counting semaphores, so the counter itself becomes corrupted.
The update needs more threads, because a counting semaphore only protects data when at least 5 threads are running.
A semaphore that starts at 5 lets up to 5 threads into the critical section, the code that touches shared data, at the same time. A binary semaphore starting at 1 is needed.
questions.why: A counting semaphore with N greater than 1 lets N threads in together, so it cannot protect shared data. A binary semaphore starting at 1 lets only one thread into the critical section at a time.

questions.prompt: An image-rendering service limits work to 6 GPU slots with a semaphore that starts at 6. When a render fails with an error, the code returns early and skips its signal call. After several weeks, every new request blocks forever, yet monitoring shows all GPUs sitting idle. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Blocked threads keep using CPU while they wait, so the service ran out of CPU time.
The semaphore should have started at 0, so all 6 slots were never actually available.
The semaphore counter overflowed past 6 after too many signals and wrapped around to 0.
Each failed render took a permit with wait and never gave it back, so permits were lost until the counter stayed at 0 for good.
questions.why: Skipping signal on an early-exit path loses that permit permanently. Over time the available permits shrink to zero, and every thread blocks even though no GPU is in use.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a semaphore is and how wait and signal work, using a resource-limiting example. Name one limit or tradeoff, such as what goes wrong when a signal is missed or why a counting semaphore does not protect shared data.
lessons.modelAnswer: A semaphore is a counter of permits with two atomic operations. Wait takes a permit: it lowers the count, or blocks the thread if the count is zero. Signal gives a permit back and wakes a blocked thread if there is one. Atomic means two threads can never both grab the last permit. For a pool of 3 connections, I start the semaphore at 3. Three threads get through, and the fourth sleeps until someone signals. A semaphore starting at 1 acts like a lock, and one starting at 0 lets one thread wait for another to say work is ready. The tradeoff is that correctness depends on discipline. Nothing checks that every wait is paired with a signal, so a missed signal on an error path leaks a permit, and eventually everything blocks. Also, a count above 1 limits how many threads run at once but does not stop them from racing on shared data.
rubricPoints: Defines a semaphore as a shared counter with atomic wait and signal operations.
Explains that wait blocks when the count is zero and signal increments the count and wakes a waiter.
Distinguishes counting use (limit N users) from binary use (mutual exclusion) or zero-start signaling.
Gives a concrete example, such as a pool of N resources.
Names a limit: a missed signal leaks permits and can hang the system, or a count above 1 does not prevent data races.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine uses semaphores directly, so tracing wait and signal through a bounded-resource scenario and diagnosing a leaked permit is the most effective practice.

lessons.plain: A deadlock is a standstill where two or more running tasks each hold something the other needs, and each waits forever for the other to let go. Nobody can move, so nothing gets done, even though the computer is not busy. Picture two cars meeting on a one-lane bridge from opposite ends: each driver refuses to reverse, each is waiting for the other to back out, and traffic stops for good. Computer scientists found four conditions that must all be true at once for a deadlock to happen. Remove any one of them and the standstill cannot form.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two workers each need both a hammer and a saw to finish a job. Worker A grabs the hammer, Worker B grabs the saw, and each politely waits for the other tool without putting theirs down. What happens, and what simple house rule could stop this from ever happening?
lessons.teach:
A deadlock is a state where a set of threads (independent sequences of instructions running inside a program) are each blocked, waiting for a resource that another thread in the same set holds, so none can ever proceed. A resource is anything only so many threads may use at once, such as a lock (a marker that grants one thread exclusive access to some data), a file, or a database row.

Deadlock can only occur when four conditions hold together. Mutual exclusion: at least one resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Hold and wait: a thread keeps the resources it already has while waiting for more. No preemption: preemption means forcibly taking a resource away, and here nothing can take a held resource from a thread; it must release it voluntarily. Circular wait: there is a closed chain of threads, each waiting for a resource held by the next one. Because all four are necessary, breaking any single one prevents deadlock.

Worked example. Thread 1 locks account X, then tries to lock account Y. Thread 2 locks account Y, then tries to lock account X. Step one: Thread 1 holds X. Step two: Thread 2 holds Y. Step three: Thread 1 waits for Y, held by Thread 2. Step four: Thread 2 waits for X, held by Thread 1. All four conditions are now true, and the chain 1 to 2 to 1 is circular. The fix most engineers use is a global lock order: always lock the lower-numbered account first. Both threads then try X first, one wins, the other waits without holding anything, and the circle cannot form.

A common mistake is confusing deadlock with slowness or a busy loop. A deadlocked program typically uses almost no CPU; its threads are asleep. In a running service this shows up as requests that hang until they time out while machines look idle, and restarting only clears it until the same timing happens again.

questions.prompt: A hospital records app runs two threads on the same patient. Thread P locks the patient's lab-results file, then tries to lock the prescription file. Thread Q locks the prescription file, then tries to lock the lab-results file. Here is the trace with one step missing. Step 1: P holds the lab-results file. Step 2: Q holds the prescription file. Step 3: P waits for the prescription file, which Q holds. Step 4: ______. Result: the chain P to Q to P is closed, all four conditions hold, and neither thread can ever proceed. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Q gives up the prescription file on its own after a short wait, so that P can take it
Q loops rapidly at full CPU, checking again and again whether the lab-results file is free
Q waits for the lab-results file, which P holds, while still keeping the prescription file
The operating system takes the lab-results file away from P and hands it to Q
questions.why: Only Q waiting for P's file while keeping its own completes the circular wait with hold and wait and no preemption, which is the state the result describes.

questions.prompt: A game server adds a watchdog that can forcibly take a lock away from any thread that has held it for more than two seconds and give it to a waiting thread. Which of the four necessary conditions for deadlock does this change remove?
choices: Mutual exclusion
No preemption
Circular wait
Hold and wait
questions.why: Preemption means forcibly taking a resource away, so a watchdog that does this removes the no-preemption condition.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing service starts having requests hang until they hit a 30-second timeout. The servers show about 3% CPU use the whole time. Restarting the service fixes it for a few hours, and then the hangs come back. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The servers are too small for the traffic and need more CPU
Threads are deadlocked, each asleep waiting on a resource another holds
Requests are simply slow because each one does a lot of computation
A busy loop that keeps the threads spinning and checking for work
questions.why: Hanging requests on nearly idle machines, cleared only temporarily by restarts, matches deadlocked threads that are asleep rather than busy.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app has threads that need several storage bins at once, for example bins 7, 12 and 40. A new rule says a thread must request all the bins it needs in one go, and if any one is unavailable it takes none of them and holds nothing while it waits. Which deadlock condition does this rule break?
choices: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Circular wait
No preemption
questions.why: Because a waiting thread never keeps some bins while waiting for others, the hold-and-wait condition can no longer be true, so deadlock cannot occur.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a deadlock is and the four conditions that must all hold for one to occur, then describe one way to prevent it and the tradeoff that prevention method brings.
lessons.modelAnswer: A deadlock is when a group of threads are all stuck waiting on resources held by each other, so none can ever continue. It needs four things at once: mutual exclusion, meaning a resource can only be held by one thread; hold and wait, meaning a thread keeps what it has while asking for more; no preemption, meaning nobody can forcibly take a resource back; and circular wait, a closed loop of threads each waiting on the next. Since all four are required, breaking one prevents deadlock. The usual approach is to break circular wait by always acquiring locks in one agreed global order. The tradeoff is discipline and flexibility: every piece of code must follow the order, which is hard to enforce in a large codebase, and sometimes you must grab a lock earlier than you need it, holding it longer and reducing concurrency.
rubricPoints: Defines deadlock as threads blocked forever waiting on resources held by each other.
Names all four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
States that all four are necessary, so breaking any one prevents deadlock.
Gives a concrete prevention method such as a global lock ordering.
Names a real tradeoff such as enforcement burden, longer lock holding, or reduced concurrency.
Notes a deadlocked system tends to look idle with hanging requests rather than busy.

suggested.rationale: No current mission stages a deadlock, so reasoning through an exam-style two-lock scenario, spotting the four conditions and choosing which to break, builds the diagnostic skill this unit asks for.

lessons.plain: Persistence means data survives after the program stops or the power goes out. Memory (RAM) forgets everything when power is lost, so anything worth keeping must reach a storage device such as a disk or SSD. A file system is the part of the operating system that organizes that storage into named files and folders. It tracks where each file's bytes live and who may use them. Think of a library: the books are your data, the shelves are the disk, and the card catalogue is the file system. It lets you ask for a book by title instead of hunting shelf by shelf.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your program calls write() to save a record and gets back 'success'. One second later the machine loses power. Do you think the record is guaranteed to be on the disk? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A file is a named sequence of bytes kept on storage. A directory is a special file that maps names to files. On Unix-like systems, each file's metadata (size, owner, permissions, and where its data blocks sit on disk) lives in a record called an inode. A directory entry is just a name pointing to an inode, so one file can have several names. When a process opens a file, the kernel returns a file descriptor, a small integer the process uses in later read and write system calls.

Disks are slow compared with memory, so the kernel keeps recently used file data in RAM, called the page cache. A write() normally copies your bytes into the page cache and returns at once. The kernel flushes them to disk later. This makes writes fast, but it opens a gap where data exists only in memory. The fsync() call forces a file's cached data to storage and returns only when that is done.

Worked example: a program appends 'order 42 paid' to a log. First, write() copies the bytes into the page cache and returns success. Second, the program tells the customer the order is saved. Third, power fails before the kernel flushes. Fourth, on reboot the log has no order 42. Calling fsync() before step two closes the gap, at the cost of waiting for the disk.

A crash can also happen halfway through an update that touches several structures, such as the inode, a directory and a data block. That can leave the file system inconsistent. Journaling file systems first record the intended changes in a log called a journal, then apply them. After a crash, they replay or discard the journal, so the structure stays consistent.

Common mistake: treating a successful write() as durable. In a running system this causes data that 'was saved' to vanish after a crash. A related surprise is that deleting a file that a process still holds open does not free its space until the descriptor is closed, because the inode is still in use.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming company's server runs a recorder process that keeps a 30 GB capture file open while it writes to it. The disk fills up, so an engineer deletes the capture file, but the free-space report does not change. Trace it. Step 1: when the recorder opened the file, the kernel returned a file descriptor, a small integer the process uses for later reads and writes. Step 2: deleting the file removed its directory entry, which is the name that pointed to the file's inode (the record holding the file's size, owner, permissions and the locations of its data blocks). Step 3: ??? Step 4: the engineer restarts the recorder, its descriptor is closed, and the 30 GB is freed. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: The inode is still in use through the recorder's open descriptor, so the kernel keeps its data blocks allocated even though no name points to it.
The journal recorded the deletion but has not been replayed yet, so the disk will look full until the next reboot.
The deletion is still waiting in the page cache, the in-memory copy of file data, and is applied only when the next fsync() runs.
The recorder keeps writing new data under the old name, which recreates the file and uses up the same 30 GB again.
questions.why: A file's space is released only when no names point to its inode and no open descriptor still uses it, so the recorder's open descriptor keeps the 30 GB allocated until it is closed.

questions.prompt: On a Unix-like system, a research lab's file has two names in different directories: /data/results.csv and /archive/run7.csv. Both are directory entries, meaning names that each point to an inode, the record holding the file's metadata and data-block locations. Both names point to the same inode. A scientist edits the file through /data/results.csv. What does a colleague see when opening /archive/run7.csv?
choices: The old contents, because each name keeps its own private copy of the data blocks.
An error, because one inode can have only one name at a time.
The old contents until the colleague's process calls fsync(), which copies the edit across to the second name.
The edited contents, because both names lead to the same inode and therefore to the same data.
questions.why: A directory entry is only a name pointing to an inode, so every name for that inode reaches the same file data.

questions.prompt: A weather-station program saves each sensor reading with write() and then sends a message to a central server saying the reading is stored. write() normally copies the bytes into the page cache, the kernel's in-memory copy of recently used file data, and returns before they reach the disk. After a power cut, three readings that the server had been told were stored are missing from the station's file. Which change makes the 'stored' message trustworthy, and what does it cost?
choices: Call write() twice for each reading, so a second copy exists; this costs extra disk space but no waiting.
Call fsync() after write() and before sending the message; the program then waits for the disk, so each save is slower.
Open the file again before each write so the kernel receives a new file descriptor; this costs one extra system call.
Switch to a journaling file system, which keeps a log of intended changes; this guarantees every write() survives, with no added delay.
questions.why: fsync() returns only after the file's cached data has reached storage, which closes the memory-only gap at the cost of waiting for the disk.

questions.prompt: A library's catalogue server uses a journaling file system. A journal is a log where the file system records the changes it intends to make before applying them. The server loses power partway through creating a new file, an update that touches the file's inode, a directory and a data block. What does journaling do for this server after it reboots?
choices: It switches off the page cache, so that all later writes go straight to the disk.
It guarantees that every byte any program passed to write() before the crash is now safely on disk.
It replays or discards the logged changes, so the inode, directory and data blocks are left in a consistent state.
It retries the program's write() calls from the beginning, so the program does not need to check whether its data was saved.
questions.why: Journaling protects the consistency of the file system's own structures by replaying or discarding the logged changes; it does not make a successful write() durable, which is what fsync() is for.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what actually happens between a program calling write() and the data being safe on disk, and name the tradeoff involved in calling fsync().
lessons.modelAnswer: When a program calls write(), the kernel usually copies the bytes into the page cache, which is a copy of file data kept in RAM. It then returns success right away. The data reaches the disk later, when the kernel flushes it. Until then, a power loss or crash can erase it, even though the program was told the write succeeded. The file system tracks the file through its inode, which holds the metadata and the locations of the file's data blocks. The program refers to the open file by a file descriptor. If the data must survive a crash, for example a payment record, call fsync(). It blocks until the data is on storage. The tradeoff is durability versus speed: fsync waits on a slow device, so calling it on every write cuts throughput. Journaling keeps the file system's own structure consistent after a crash, but it does not make your un-synced data durable.
rubricPoints: States that write() usually lands in the in-memory page cache, not directly on disk.
Explains that fsync() forces data to storage and waits until it is there.
Names the tradeoff: durability costs latency and throughput.
Mentions file-system structures such as inodes, directories or file descriptors accurately.
Notes that journaling protects file-system consistency after a crash.

suggested.rationale: Freeing disk space safely makes the learner deal with files, directories and deleted-but-still-open files in practice, which ties directly to inodes and file descriptors.

lessons.plain: The relational model is a way of organizing data as a set of tables, where each table describes one kind of thing (drivers, trips, invoices) and each row records one fact about it. Every column holds one kind of value, like a name or a date. Instead of following pointers from record to record, you ask questions by describing the answer you want, and the system works out how to combine tables to produce it. Think of a well-kept filing cabinet of index cards with identical labelled boxes on each card: you can sort, filter and match cards across drawers without knowing how they are physically stored.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have one table of drivers (driver id, name) and another of trips (trip id, driver id, distance in km). Without any special software, how would you work out the names of drivers who made a trip longer than 100 km?
lessons.teach:
The relational model represents data as relations. A relation is what most people call a table: a named set of rows that all share the same shape. Each column is an attribute, a named property such as name or distance_km. Each attribute has a domain, the set of values it may hold (for example, positive integers). Each row is a tuple, one fact made of one value per attribute. The schema is the relation's name plus its list of attributes and domains; the rows present at any moment are its contents.

Two ideas make the model powerful. First, a relation is a set, so rows have no built-in order and, in the pure model, no duplicates. Second, relations are combined with a small set of operations that take relations in and give relations out: selection keeps rows matching a condition, projection keeps chosen columns, and join pairs rows from two relations whose values match. Because every result is itself a relation, operations chain freely. You state what you want; the database decides how to fetch it. This separation is called data independence: storage can change without breaking queries.

Worked example. Drivers(driver_id, name) holds (1, Ana) and (2, Ben). Trips(trip_id, driver_id, km) holds (10, 1, 140), (11, 2, 60), (12, 1, 30). Step 1, select trips where km > 100: only (10, 1, 140) remains. Step 2, join with Drivers on matching driver_id: (10, 1, 140, Ana). Step 3, project name: the result is the one-row relation {Ana}.

A common mistake is treating a table like a spreadsheet whose row order means something, for example assuming the newest row comes back last. Order is only guaranteed when a query explicitly asks for sorting. In a running system, code that relies on implicit order can work for months and then silently return rows in a different order after the data grows or the database picks a different access path, corrupting reports or pagination.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic stores Pets(pet_id, town) holding (7, Lyon) and (8, Nice), and Visits(visit_id, pet_id, fee) holding (100, 7, 45), (101, 8, 80) and (102, 7, 20). The goal is to list the visit_id of every visit for a pet from Lyon. Step 1, join Visits with Pets on matching pet_id: (100, 7, 45, Lyon), (101, 8, 80, Nice), (102, 7, 20, Lyon). Step 2, select rows where town = Lyon: the result is MISSING. Step 3, project visit_id: the result is the relation {100, 102}. Which relation belongs in the MISSING spot for Step 2?
choices: {45, 20}, the fees of the Lyon visits
Only (101, 8, 80, Nice), the one row whose town is not Lyon
Only (100, 7, 45, Lyon), because selection keeps just the first matching row
questions.why: Selection keeps every row that meets the condition with all of its columns, so both Lyon rows remain, and Step 3 then projects them down to {100, 102}.

questions.prompt: A payroll relation Staff(staff_id, team, salary) has a rule that salary may only hold non-negative whole numbers. In relational terms, what does that rule describe?
choices: The domain of the salary attribute
The current contents of the relation
A tuple of the Staff relation
A projection on the salary column
questions.why: A domain is the set of values an attribute is allowed to hold, and this rule defines exactly that set for salary.

questions.prompt: A warehouse keeps Items(sku, shelf, qty). A manager wants only the sku values of items whose qty is below 5. Which combination of relational operations produces this?
choices: A projection on qty followed by a selection where sku is below 5
A join of Items with itself on sku, and no other operation
A selection where qty < 5, followed by a projection on sku
A projection on sku alone, because projection also filters rows
questions.why: Selection keeps the rows matching the condition, and projection then keeps only the chosen column. Each result is a relation, so the two operations chain.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app shows orders 20 per page. Its query has no sorting clause, and the code assumes the rows come back in the order they were inserted. It works for months. Then, after the table grows, some orders appear on two pages and others never appear. What is the underlying cause and the fix?
choices: Duplicate rows were inserted, so a projection should be added to remove the extra columns
A join became necessary as the data grew, so the query should join the table with itself
Each row's position is stored inside its tuple and got corrupted, so the table must be rebuilt
A relation has no built-in row order, so the query must explicitly ask for sorting
questions.why: Rows in a relation have no inherent order, and the database may use a different access path as data grows. Order is only guaranteed when the query explicitly requests sorting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what the relational model is and why answering questions with select, project and join is useful, and name one limit or tradeoff of organizing data this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: The relational model stores data as relations, which are tables: each row is a tuple recording one fact, each column is an attribute with a defined domain of allowed values, and the schema fixes that shape. A relation is a set, so rows have no inherent order. We query by combining relations with operations like selection (filter rows), projection (pick columns) and join (match rows across tables on shared values), and since each result is again a relation, we can chain them. We describe what we want and the database decides how to get it, so storage can change without rewriting queries. The tradeoff is rigidity and cost: every row must fit a fixed schema, and data that is deeply connected, like many hops through a network of relationships, needs many joins, which can be slow and awkward to express. Also, never rely on row order unless you sort explicitly.
rubricPoints: Defines a relation as a table of tuples sharing attributes with defined domains, described by a schema.
States that a relation is a set, so rows have no inherent order.
Describes selection, projection and join, and that results are themselves relations that can be chained.
Explains the declarative idea and data independence: say what, not how.
Names a real limit, such as fixed schema rigidity or the cost of many joins for highly connected data.

suggested.rationale: Writing select, project and join queries against small tables in a SQL lab makes the learner build relational results step by step rather than only read about them.

lessons.plain: A primary key is the value that uniquely names each row in a table, like a student ID number that no two students share and that never goes blank. A foreign key is a column in one table that holds the primary key of a row in another table, so the two rows are linked. Think of a library: every book has a unique barcode (primary key), and each loan slip records a barcode (foreign key) to say which book was borrowed. The database can then refuse a loan slip that points to a barcode that does not exist.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop stores customers in one table and orders in another. If you wanted each order to say which customer placed it, what would you store in the order row, and why would storing the customer's name be a risky choice?
lessons.teach:
A table is a set of rows, and each row has the same columns. A primary key is a column, or a combination of columns, whose value is unique for every row and is never NULL (NULL means 'no value'). The database enforces both rules, so the key reliably identifies exactly one row. A foreign key is a column in a child table whose values must match an existing primary key value in a parent table. The rule that every foreign key value points to a real parent row is called referential integrity, and the database checks it on every insert, update and delete.

Worked example. Table customers has primary key customer_id. Table orders has primary key order_id and a foreign key customer_id referencing customers. Step 1: insert customer 7, Ana. Step 2: insert order 100 with customer_id 7; the database finds customer 7, so it accepts. Step 3: insert order 101 with customer_id 99; no customer 99 exists, so the database rejects it. Step 4: try to delete customer 7; order 100 still points at her, so the database blocks the delete unless you chose a rule such as cascade (delete her orders too) or set null (blank the link).

Keys come in two flavours. A natural key is a real-world value such as an email address. A surrogate key is a meaningless generated number. Surrogates are often preferred because they never need to change.

Common mistake: using a value that can change, like an email or a name, as the primary key. When Ana changes her email, every order that copied it must be updated, and any copy you miss breaks the link. A related mistake is linking tables by convention without declaring the foreign key constraint. Nothing then stops a bug from creating orphan rows, meaning child rows whose parent is missing. In a running system, orphans cause reports that do not add up and pages that crash on missing data. Declared keys turn these silent errors into immediate, visible rejections.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic's database has a table pets with primary key pet_id, and a table visits with primary key visit_id and a foreign key pet_id referencing pets. The foreign key uses the set null delete rule. Step 1: insert pet 31, a cat named Miso. Step 2: insert visit 500 with pet_id 31. The database finds pet 31, so it accepts. Step 3: insert visit 501 with pet_id 45. No pet 45 exists, so the database rejects it. Step 4: delete pet 31. What does the database do in Step 4?
choices: It blocks the delete, because visit 500 still points at pet 31
It deletes pet 31 and leaves visit 500 still holding pet_id 31
It deletes pet 31 and keeps visit 500 with its pet_id blanked
It deletes pet 31 and also deletes visit 500
questions.why: Under the set null rule, deleting the parent row is allowed and the child's link is blanked, so visit 500 stays but no longer points at a missing pet.

questions.prompt: A table's designer wants to pick a primary key. Which two rules must the chosen column, or combination of columns, satisfy, and which the database enforces?
choices: Its value must be a real-world fact and must be unique
Its value must be a number and must be generated automatically
Its value must be unique for every row and must never be NULL
Its value must match a row in another table and must never change
questions.why: A primary key must be unique for every row and never NULL. That is what lets it reliably identify exactly one row.

questions.prompt: A hospital is designing a staff table that other tables, such as shifts and payroll, will point to with foreign keys. Staff sometimes change their surnames, phone numbers and departments. Which primary key choice best avoids broken links later?
choices: The name of the department they work in
A combination of surname and first name
The staff member's mobile phone number
A generated staff_id number with no real-world meaning
questions.why: A surrogate key never needs to change, so the shifts and payroll rows that point to it never have to be updated when personal details change.

questions.prompt: A warehouse app stores a supplier_id column in its shipments table to show which supplier sent each shipment. The team links the tables only by convention and never declared a foreign key constraint. A bug deletes supplier 18 while shipments still list supplier_id 18. What happens?
choices: The database rejects the delete, because shipments still reference supplier 18
The database sets supplier_id to NULL in the affected shipments
The database automatically deletes every shipment from supplier 18
The delete succeeds silently, leaving orphan shipments that can break reports and pages later
questions.why: With no declared foreign key, nothing checks referential integrity. The shipments become orphan rows, and the error stays silent until reports or pages fail.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what primary and foreign keys are and what the database does with them, using a customers-and-orders example, and name one tradeoff or limit, such as choosing natural versus surrogate keys or what happens when a parent row is deleted.
lessons.modelAnswer: A primary key is the column whose value uniquely identifies each row and can never be NULL, like customer_id in a customers table. A foreign key is a column in another table, like customer_id in orders, whose values must match an existing primary key. The database enforces this referential integrity: it rejects an order pointing at customer 99 if no such customer exists, and it blocks deleting a customer who still has orders unless we chose cascade or set null. One tradeoff is natural versus surrogate keys. Using an email as the key is meaningful, but emails change, and every referencing row would then need updating. A generated surrogate number never changes, though we still need a separate uniqueness rule on email. Also, the constraint checks cost a little work on every write, which is usually worth it to avoid orphan rows.
rubricPoints: States that a primary key is unique and never NULL, identifying exactly one row.
States that a foreign key holds values that must match a primary key in another table.
Explains referential integrity: inserts with missing parents are rejected.
Describes what happens on parent deletion: block, cascade, or set null.
Names a tradeoff, such as mutable natural keys versus stable surrogate keys.
Mentions the risk of orphan rows when constraints are not declared.

suggested.rationale: Creating linked tables and watching the database reject orphan inserts and blocked deletes makes key constraints concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: Normalization is a way of organizing database tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place. Imagine a school where every class roster also lists each student's home address. If a student moves, someone has to update every roster, and if one copy is missed, the school now holds two different addresses. Normalization moves the address to a single student record that everything else points to. The levels called first, second and third normal form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) are increasingly strict checklists for removing this kind of duplication, so data stays consistent when it changes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table stores one row per item on each order: order number, product code, quantity, product name and customer city. If a customer moves to a new city, what could go wrong when you update this table?
lessons.teach:
Normalization is the process of splitting tables so that every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. A key is a column or set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. A functional dependency, written A → B, means that knowing A fixes exactly one value of B.

First normal form (1NF): every cell holds a single value and there are no repeating groups such as phone1, phone2, phone3. Second normal form (2NF): 1NF, plus no partial dependency, meaning no non-key column depends on only part of a multi-column key. Third normal form (3NF): 2NF, plus no transitive dependency, meaning no non-key column depends on another non-key column.

Why it works: duplication causes anomalies. An update anomaly is when one fact stored in many rows gets changed in some but not others. An insert anomaly is when you cannot record a fact (a new product) without an unrelated one (an order). A delete anomaly is when removing a row loses a fact you wanted to keep.

Worked example: OrderLines(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name, customer_id, customer_city), key (order_id, product_id). Step 1: quantity needs both key columns, fine. Step 2: product_name depends only on product_id, a partial dependency, so move it to Products(product_id, product_name). Step 3: customer_id depends only on order_id, so move it to Orders(order_id, customer_id). Now 2NF holds. Step 4: in Orders, customer_city depends on customer_id, a non-key column, which is a transitive dependency, so create Customers(customer_id, customer_city). Result: four tables, each fact stored once.

Common mistake: splitting by intuition about what feels like an entity instead of checking actual dependencies, which either misses a transitive dependency or over-splits into tables that need many joins.

In a running system the tradeoff is real: normalized schemas keep writes correct and cheap, but reads need joins, so read-heavy systems sometimes deliberately denormalize and accept the job of keeping copies in sync.

questions.prompt: A hospital stores staff in Employees(employee_id, employee_name, dept_id, dept_floor), key employee_id. Each department sits on exactly one floor. Step 1: every cell holds one value and there are no repeating groups, so 1NF holds. Step 2: the key is a single column, so no column can depend on only part of it; 2NF holds automatically. Step 3: ??? Result: two tables, with each department's floor stored once. What is Step 3?
choices: Every column can be found from employee_id, so the table is already in 3NF and nothing changes.
Move both dept_id and dept_floor into Departments(dept_id, dept_floor) and remove dept_id from Employees.
employee_name is a separate idea from the employee, so move it to Names(employee_id, employee_name).
dept_floor depends on dept_id, a non-key column, which is a transitive dependency, so create Departments(dept_id, dept_floor) and keep dept_id in Employees.
questions.why: dept_floor is fixed by dept_id rather than directly by the key, so it is moved to its own table while Employees keeps dept_id as the link.

questions.prompt: A clinic schedules nurses in Shifts(nurse_id, shift_date, ward, nurse_name). The key is (nurse_id, shift_date). ward needs both key columns, but nurse_name is fixed by nurse_id alone. Which normal form does this table fail?
choices: 2NF, because nurse_name has a partial dependency on only part of the multi-column key
3NF only, because nurse_name depends on another non-key column
None, because every column can be found once you know the whole key
1NF, because nurse_name is stored in more than one row
questions.why: A non-key column that depends on only part of a multi-column key is a partial dependency, and having one breaks 2NF.

questions.prompt: A veterinary practice keeps everything in Visits(visit_id, pet_id, vet_id, vet_specialty). A new vet joins, but the practice cannot record her specialty until she has seen at least one pet. What kind of problem is this?
choices: A partial dependency on visit_id
An insert anomaly
A delete anomaly
An update anomaly
questions.why: An insert anomaly means one fact, the vet's specialty, cannot be recorded without an unrelated fact, a visit.

questions.prompt: A retail chain's reporting dashboard is read far more often than its data is written. To avoid joins, the team copies store_region into every row of a normalized Sales table. What tradeoff have they accepted?
choices: Reads get slower, but anomalies are no longer possible.
Reads need fewer joins, but every copy of a store's region must be kept in sync, or an update anomaly appears.
Nothing changes, because copying a column does not affect the normal form of the table.
Writes become cheaper because each region is now stored in fewer places.
questions.why: Denormalizing speeds up reads by removing joins, but the same fact now lives in many rows, so writes must update all of them consistently.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what moving a table to 3NF fixes and what it costs, using an example of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Normalizing to 3NF means every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. 1NF removes multi-valued cells and repeating columns. 2NF removes partial dependencies, like product_name depending only on product_id inside an order-line table keyed by order and product. 3NF removes transitive dependencies, like customer_city depending on customer_id rather than on order_id. The payoff is that each fact lives in one row, so a customer move is one update, you can add a product before anyone orders it, and deleting an order doesn't erase what you know about a customer. The cost is more tables and more joins on reads, which can slow read-heavy queries. Teams sometimes denormalize on purpose for speed, but then they own the work of keeping duplicated copies consistent.
rubricPoints: States the goal: each fact stored once so changes stay consistent.
Correctly distinguishes partial dependency (2NF) from transitive dependency (3NF).
Names at least one anomaly (update, insert or delete) that normalization prevents.
Uses a concrete example showing a table being split by its dependencies.
Names the tradeoff: more joins on reads, and denormalization as a deliberate exception.

suggested.rationale: Decomposing a real table step by step and watching update anomalies disappear in a SQL lab builds the dependency-checking skill far better than reading definitions.

lessons.plain: An index is a shortcut a database keeps so it can find rows quickly without reading the whole table. Think of the index at the back of a textbook. Instead of flipping every page to find 'photosynthesis', you look it up alphabetically and jump straight to page 212. A B-tree is the most common way databases organise that shortcut. It is a wide, shallow, always-sorted tree, so even millions of entries can be found in a handful of steps. The price is upkeep. Every time the data changes, the index must change too.
lessons.guessPrompt: A phone book lists 1,000,000 names in alphabetical order. If you can open it to any page and see which names that page covers, roughly how many look-ups do you think it takes to find one name? Would it be closer to 1,000,000, 1,000, or under 30?
lessons.teach:
An index is an extra data structure a database keeps alongside a table. It lets the database find rows by a column's value without a full scan, which means reading every row. The most common index is a B-tree. This is a balanced tree whose nodes are each sized to fit one disk page, a fixed-size block of a few kilobytes that storage reads in one go. Each internal node holds many sorted keys plus pointers to child nodes. The number of children per node is called the fanout. Leaf nodes are the bottom level. They hold keys with pointers to the actual rows, and the leaves are linked to each other in sorted order. Balanced means every leaf sits the same distance from the root, called the height. So every lookup costs the same number of page reads.

Why it works: page reads are the slow part, and fanout is large, often in the hundreds. Height therefore grows as the logarithm, base fanout, of the row count, and that stays tiny.

Worked example: a users table has 1,000,000 rows and an index on email with fanout 100. Three levels cover 100 x 100 x 100 = 1,000,000 entries. To find kim@example.com, step 1: read the root and compare against its sorted keys, then follow the child whose range covers 'kim'. Step 2: read that node and repeat. Step 3: read the leaf, find the key and its row pointer. Step 4: fetch the row. That is four page reads instead of a million rows scanned. Because the leaves are sorted and linked, a range query such as emails starting with 'k' just walks along neighbouring leaves.

Common mistake: indexing every column. Every insert, update or delete must also update each index, sometimes splitting a full node in two. Writes slow down and storage grows. An index on a column with few distinct values, like a true/false flag, rarely helps, because each value still matches a huge share of the rows.

In a running system, a missing index shows up as slow queries and heavy disk reads. Too many indexes show up as slow writes.

questions.prompt: A city library keeps a catalogue table of 64,000,000 book copies, with a B-tree index on barcode and a fanout of 400. Since 400 x 400 x 400 = 64,000,000, the tree is three levels tall. A librarian looks up barcode 5521907. Step 1: the database reads the root page, compares 5521907 against its sorted keys, and follows the child whose range covers it. Step 2: it reads that internal page and does the same. Step 3: it reads the leaf page and finds the key 5521907. Step 4 is missing. Which choice correctly completes the lookup and gives the total page reads?
choices: Step 4: stop here, because the leaf page already holds the full book record. Total: 3 page reads.
Step 4: follow the leaf's row pointer and fetch the book's row from the table. Total: 4 page reads.
Step 4: walk all the linked neighbouring leaves to make sure no other copy has that barcode. Total: about 400 page reads.
Step 4: go back to the root and read all 400 of its children to confirm the right branch was taken. Total: 403 page reads.
questions.why: B-tree leaves store keys with pointers to rows, not the rows themselves, so one more read fetches the row: three tree levels plus one row fetch gives 4 page reads.

questions.prompt: A payments company has a transactions table with a B-tree index on transaction ID and a fanout of 100. The table grows from 1,000,000 rows to 100,000,000 rows. Roughly how does the height of the index (the number of levels from root to leaf) change?
choices: It grows from about 3 levels to about 4 levels, because each extra level multiplies capacity by 100.
It stays exactly the same, because B-tree height never depends on the number of rows.
It doubles from about 3 levels to about 6 levels, because the row count gained two zeros.
It grows about 100 times taller, because the row count grew 100 times.
questions.why: Height grows as the logarithm, base fanout, of the row count: 100^3 is 1,000,000 and 100^4 is 100,000,000, so 100 times more rows adds only one level.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup adds a B-tree index to all 14 columns of its shipments table so that any query will be fast. A week later, lookups are quick but inserting new shipments has become noticeably slow and the database uses far more storage. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The fanout of each index shrank to 1, turning every index into a full scan.
Every insert must also update all 14 indexes, sometimes splitting full nodes, which costs write time and space.
The indexes made the tree unbalanced, so leaves now sit at different heights.
B-tree indexes slow down reads, and the slow reads are blocking the inserts.
questions.why: Each index is an extra structure that every insert, update or delete must also maintain, so indexing every column slows writes and grows storage.

questions.prompt: A weather service stores sensor readings in a table with a B-tree index on reading time. A dashboard asks for every reading between 14:00 and 15:00 on one day. Why does the B-tree index handle this range query efficiently?
choices: The database repeats a full root-to-leaf lookup for every possible second in the hour.
The database finds the first matching leaf, then walks along the sorted, linked leaves until it passes 15:00.
A B-tree can only answer exact-match lookups, so the database falls back to scanning every row.
The index stores readings in random order, so the range can be read from any leaf.
questions.why: B-tree leaves are kept in sorted order and linked to each other, so after one lookup to find the start of the range, the database just reads neighbouring leaves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a B-tree index makes lookups fast, and name at least one cost or situation where adding an index is the wrong call.
lessons.modelAnswer: An index is a separate sorted structure the database maintains so it can jump to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. A B-tree stores many sorted keys per node, with each node about one disk page, so the fanout is in the hundreds. The tree is also balanced, so every lookup walks the same short path from the root to a leaf. With a fanout of 100, a million rows need only about three levels, so a lookup is a few page reads instead of a million row reads. The leaves are linked in order, so range queries are cheap too. The tradeoff is that every write must also update every index on that table, sometimes splitting nodes. Indexes also use extra storage. So I would not index every column. I would skip an index on low-variety columns like a boolean flag, because it barely narrows the search.
rubricPoints: Defines an index as an extra structure that avoids a full table scan.
Explains that high fanout and balance keep the B-tree shallow, so lookups take only a few page reads.
Mentions that sorted, linked leaves make range queries efficient.
Names the write cost: every insert, update or delete must also maintain each index.
Identifies a poor index choice, such as too many indexes or a low-distinct-value column.

suggested.rationale: A SQL lab where the learner times a query, adds an index and compares lookup and write speed would make the read-versus-write tradeoff concrete.

lessons.plain: A transaction is a group of database changes that must succeed or fail together, as one unit. Think of moving money between two bank accounts: taking it out of one and putting it into the other only makes sense if both happen. If the power cuts out halfway, you want neither change, not just one. ACID is a short name for four promises a database makes about transactions: all-or-nothing, the rules stay true, people working at the same time do not trip over each other, and once the database says done, the change survives a crash.
lessons.guessPrompt: You move 100 dollars from account A to account B. The database subtracts 100 from A, then the server crashes before adding 100 to B. What should the balances look like when the server comes back, and why?
lessons.teach:
A transaction is a sequence of reads and writes that the database treats as a single unit of work. It starts with a begin, and ends with either a commit (make every change permanent) or a rollback (undo every change). ACID names four guarantees. Atomicity means all-or-nothing: either every change in the transaction takes effect or none does. Consistency means the transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, so rules you declared, such as a balance never going negative, still hold afterward. Isolation means transactions running at the same time behave as if they did not see each other's half-finished work. Durability means a committed change survives crashes and restarts.

Why it works: most databases first record intended changes in a write-ahead log, an append-only file saved to disk before the main data is touched. On restart, the database replays log entries for committed transactions and discards those that never committed. That log gives both atomicity and durability.

Worked example, transferring 100 from A (balance 500) to B (balance 200). Step 1: begin. Step 2: set A to 400, logged. Step 3: set B to 300, logged. Step 4: commit, and the commit record is written to disk. If a crash happens after step 2, there is no commit record, so recovery undoes it and A stays 500, B stays 200. If the crash happens after step 4, recovery reapplies both changes: A 400, B 300. No outcome leaves the 100 missing.

Common mistake: running the two updates as separate statements in autocommit mode, where each statement commits on its own. A failure between them then really loses money. Another confusion is treating the C in ACID as the same as replica consistency in distributed systems; here it only means your declared rules hold.

In a running system, long transactions hold resources and slow others down, so keep them short and commit promptly.

questions.prompt: A city library's database records a book loan as one transaction. The book starts with 3 copies available, and member M-17 has no loan for it. Step 1: begin. Step 2: set copies available to 2; the change is written to the write-ahead log (an append-only file saved to disk before the main data is touched). Step 3: insert a loan row for M-17; this is also logged. Before any commit record reaches disk, the server loses power. Step 4, on restart: recovery reads the log and ____. Which choice correctly completes step 4?
choices: keeps copies available at 2 but drops the loan row, because only the first change finished
waits for a staff member to choose whether to keep or undo the half-finished loan
finds no commit record, so it discards both changes: 3 copies available and no loan for M-17
reapplies both logged changes, because they were saved to the log before the crash
questions.why: Recovery replays only transactions that have a commit record on disk, so an uncommitted transaction is undone completely, which is atomicity's all-or-nothing rule.

questions.prompt: A warehouse database declares the rule that stock on hand can never be below zero. A transaction that ships 12 units of a part from a bin holding 10 is accepted and commits, leaving the stock at -2. Which ACID guarantee has been broken?
choices: Isolation, because another transaction must have seen the half-finished stock count
Durability, because the committed result should have been lost in a crash
Consistency, because the transaction left the database in a state that breaks a declared rule
Atomicity, because only part of the shipment was recorded
questions.why: In ACID, consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, so declared rules like a non-negative stock count must still hold afterward.

questions.prompt: A payroll app moves 2,000 from a department budget account to a salary account. A developer writes it as two separate statements with autocommit mode on, which means each statement commits on its own. The server crashes after the first statement (subtract 2,000 from the budget) and before the second. What state does the database hold after restart?
choices: Both changes appear, because recovery finishes the second statement from the log
The budget is down 2,000 and the salary account never received it
Both accounts are unchanged, because recovery undoes the whole transfer
The salary account gains 2,000 while the budget stays the same
questions.why: In autocommit mode the first statement was already committed on its own, so recovery keeps it and the 2,000 is lost because the two updates were never one transaction.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking system tells a patient their appointment is confirmed right after the transaction commits and the commit record is written to disk. One second later the server crashes and restarts. Why is the appointment still there?
choices: Isolation hid the booking from the crash until it was safely finished
Consistency: replicas in other data centers agreed on the booking
Atomicity alone: the booking had only one step, so it cannot be lost
Durability: recovery replays the logged changes of committed transactions from the write-ahead log
questions.why: Durability means a committed change survives crashes, and the write-ahead log lets recovery reapply changes for any transaction whose commit record reached disk.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a database transaction is and what each letter of ACID guarantees, using an example from your own work, and name one cost or limit of relying on transactions.
lessons.modelAnswer: A transaction bundles several database changes so they act as one unit: you begin, make changes, then commit to keep them all or roll back to discard them all. Atomicity is that all-or-nothing rule, so a transfer never debits one account without crediting the other. Consistency means declared rules, like no negative balances, still hold after the transaction. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work. Durability means once commit returns, the change survives a crash, usually because it was written to a write-ahead log on disk first. The limit is cost: forcing the log to disk on every commit adds latency, and long-running transactions hold resources that block or slow other work. Also, these guarantees only cover changes inside one database; a call to an outside service in the middle is not rolled back.
rubricPoints: Defines a transaction as a unit of work ending in commit or rollback.
States atomicity as all-or-nothing.
States consistency as declared rules still holding, not replica agreement.
States isolation as concurrent transactions not seeing partial work.
States durability as committed changes surviving crashes, e.g. via a log.
Names a cost or limit such as commit latency, blocking from long transactions, or no coverage of outside systems.

suggested.rationale: A SQL lab where the learner begins, commits, rolls back and simulates a mid-transfer crash would make atomicity and durability concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: When many people use a database at once, their work overlaps in time. An isolation level is a setting that decides how much each person's unfinished or freshly finished work can leak into everyone else's view. Picture a shared notebook in a busy office. At the loosest setting you can read someone's half-written scribbles. At the strictest, it behaves as if everyone took turns, one after another. Stricter settings stop more confusing mix-ups, but people wait longer or must redo their work. So choosing a level is a deliberate trade between correctness and speed.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two people each check a shared calendar, see that one meeting room is free at 3pm, and each book it at the same moment. Neither saw anything wrong when they looked. What do you think a database would need to do to stop both bookings from succeeding?
lessons.teach:
An isolation level is a database setting that controls how much one transaction can see of other transactions running at the same time. A transaction is a group of reads and writes that the database treats as a single unit. Stricter levels hide more interference, but they cost more waiting, aborted work or throughput.

Levels are described by which anomalies they allow. An anomaly is a wrong-looking result caused by overlapping work. A dirty read means seeing another transaction's change before it commits, even though it might still be undone. A non-repeatable read means reading the same row twice and getting different values because someone committed a change in between. A phantom read means running the same search twice and getting a different set of rows because someone inserted or deleted matching rows.

The four standard levels, from weakest to strongest, work like this. Read Uncommitted allows all three anomalies. Read Committed blocks dirty reads only, and many databases use it as their default. Repeatable Read also blocks non-repeatable reads. Serializable blocks every anomaly and promises that the result matches some one-at-a-time order of the transactions. Real products enforce these levels with locks or with per-transaction snapshots, and their exact guarantees vary.

Here is a worked example. A hospital rule says at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. In transaction T1, Alice counts the on-call doctors, gets 2, and marks herself off. At the same moment, in transaction T2, Bob counts, also gets 2, and marks himself off. Both transactions commit, and now nobody is on call. Neither transaction saw a dirty, non-repeatable or phantom read, yet the rule broke. This anomaly is called write skew. Only Serializable reliably stops it, by blocking or aborting one transaction so that it has to retry.
