A common mistake is assuming that wrapping code in a transaction prevents every race, or that the default level is Serializable. Under weaker levels, a running system shows rare, load-dependent bugs such as double bookings, oversold stock or negative balances. Under Serializable, the application must catch serialization failures and retry them.

questions.prompt: A warehouse database runs at Read Committed. Transaction T1, a stock report, reads the quantity of part P-17 and gets 50. While T1 is still open, transaction T2 changes P-17's quantity to 12 and commits. T1 then reads P-17 again and gets 12. Step 1: T1 never saw an uncommitted value, so this was not a dirty read. Step 2: the same row was read twice and returned different values because another transaction committed a change in between, so this is a non-repeatable read. Step 3 is missing: what is the weakest standard isolation level that would block this anomaly?
choices: Read Committed, because T2's change was already committed before T1 saw it
Serializable, because it is the only level that blocks non-repeatable reads
Read Uncommitted, because T1 would then see T2's value consistently
Repeatable Read, because it adds protection against non-repeatable reads
questions.why: Repeatable Read is the first level up from Read Committed and adds blocking of non-repeatable reads, so it is the weakest level that stops this anomaly; Serializable also stops it but is stronger than needed.

questions.prompt: A finance dashboard runs the search "all invoices over $1,000 this month" twice inside one transaction. The first run returns 7 invoices. Between the runs, another transaction inserts a new $2,500 invoice and commits. The second run returns 8 invoices. No existing invoice changed its values. Which anomaly is this?
choices: Non-repeatable read
Write skew
Dirty read
Phantom read
questions.why: The same search returned a different set of rows because another transaction inserted a matching row, which is the definition of a phantom read.

questions.prompt: A couple's bank allows each of two linked accounts to go negative as long as their combined balance stays at or above $0. Checking holds $60 and savings holds $40. Transaction T1 reads the total ($100) and withdraws $80 from checking. At the same moment, T2 reads the total ($100) and withdraws $80 from savings. Neither saw a dirty, non-repeatable or phantom read, yet after both commit the total is -$60. Which choice reliably prevents this?
choices: Running both at Read Committed
Wrapping each withdrawal in a transaction at the default level
Running both at Repeatable Read
Running both at Serializable and retrying any transaction it aborts
questions.why: This is write skew, which none of the three named anomalies covers; only Serializable reliably stops it by blocking or aborting one transaction so it must retry.

questions.prompt: A ticketing team moves its seat-booking transactions from Read Committed to Serializable to stop rare double bookings. What change must the application also make so that it keeps working correctly under load?
choices: Nothing, because Serializable never aborts a transaction
Switch reads to Read Uncommitted so the extra waiting disappears
Stop using transactions, since the isolation level now handles races
Catch serialization failures and retry the aborted transaction
questions.why: Serializable enforces a one-at-a-time result partly by aborting conflicting transactions, so the application must catch those serialization failures and retry them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an isolation level is and how you would choose one for a feature like seat booking, naming the tradeoff you accept with your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: An isolation level decides how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's work. The weaker levels allow known anomalies. Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads, which means seeing uncommitted changes. Read Committed stops those but still allows non-repeatable reads, where a row changes between two of your reads. Repeatable Read stops that, but phantoms can remain, where new matching rows appear. Serializable makes the outcome equal to running the transactions one at a time, and it also catches write skew. That is the case where two transactions each check a rule, each see it satisfied, and together break it. Seat booking is exactly that check-then-write pattern, so I would use Serializable, or an explicit lock on the seat row. The tradeoff is more blocking and aborted transactions under load, so our code must retry on serialization failures. Also, the database's default is often Read Committed, not Serializable.
rubricPoints: Defines an isolation level as controlling what concurrent transactions see of each other.
Names the anomalies such as dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads and links them to levels.
Explains that Serializable equals some one-at-a-time order and also prevents write skew.
States the cost of stricter levels: blocking, aborts and the need for retries.
Notes that defaults are often weaker than Serializable, so a transaction alone does not prevent all races.

suggested.rationale: Isolation anomalies are best understood by running two overlapping transactions side by side and watching which level lets a write skew or non-repeatable read through, which a SQL lab could let the learner do.

lessons.plain: When many people use a database at the same moment, it needs a rule for what happens when two of them touch the same data. One approach is locking: you put a 'busy' sign on a row, and others wait until you are done. The other is MVCC (multi-version concurrency control): the database keeps older copies of a row, so readers look at a consistent snapshot while a writer prepares a new copy. Think of a shared document. Locking is checking it out so nobody else can open it. MVCC is letting readers keep the printed copy while you edit a fresh one.
lessons.guessPrompt: A report is reading an account balance of 100 while another user changes it to 80 and saves. Should the report wait for the change to finish, or keep reading 100? What could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
Locking and MVCC are the two main ways a database lets many transactions run at once without corrupting each other's view of the data. A transaction is a group of reads and writes that succeed or fail together.

A lock is a marker a transaction places on a row or table that tells others to wait. A shared lock lets many readers hold it together. An exclusive lock is needed to write, and it lets only one holder in while blocking everyone else. Two-phase locking (2PL) means a transaction acquires locks as it goes and releases none until it finishes. That ordering makes the combined result look as if the transactions ran one at a time. The cost is that readers block writers and writers block readers. Sometimes two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds. This is a deadlock, and the database breaks it by aborting one of them.

MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) keeps several versions of each row instead. A write creates a new version stamped with the writing transaction's ID, and the old version stays. Each transaction reads from a snapshot, which is the set of versions already committed when it started. So readers never wait for writers, and writers never wait for readers. Two writers on the same row still conflict: one waits or is aborted.

Worked example: a row holds balance=100. T1 starts and reads it. T2 updates the balance to 80, which creates version 2, and commits. Under locking, T2's exclusive lock would have waited until T1 released its shared lock. Under MVCC, T2 proceeds at once. T1 keeps seeing 100 because version 2 is newer than its snapshot. A transaction that starts afterward sees 80.

Common mistake: assuming MVCC means no locks at all. Writes to the same row still take turns. Snapshots can also allow anomalies. In one example, two transactions each check a shared condition and then write different rows, and together they break a rule neither would break alone.

Running-system consequence: old versions pile up. A long-running transaction keeps old snapshots alive, so cleanup (often called vacuum or garbage collection) cannot remove dead versions. Tables bloat and queries slow down.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site stores seats_left = 40 for a concert, in a database that uses MVCC (multi-version concurrency control: it keeps several versions of each row, and each transaction reads from a snapshot of the versions already committed when it started). A transaction is a group of reads and writes that succeed or fail together. Step 1: Transaction T7 starts, and its snapshot includes version 1 of the row (40). Step 2: T7 reads seats_left and gets 40. Step 3: Transaction T9 sells 3 seats. This writes version 2 (37), stamped with T9's ID, and T9 commits. Step 4: T7 reads seats_left again. [MISSING STEP] Step 5: Transaction T12 starts after T9 has committed and reads 37. What happens in Step 4?
choices: T7 reads 40 straight away, because version 2 was committed after T7's snapshot was taken
T7 pauses until T9's exclusive lock on the row has been released, and only then does it read the row, getting 37
T7 is aborted because its snapshot no longer matches the latest data
T7 reads 37, because version 2 is now the newest committed version of the row
questions.why: Under MVCC a transaction keeps reading from the snapshot taken when it started, so T7 never waits and still sees version 1 (40), while T12 started later and sees 37.

questions.prompt: A warehouse database uses two-phase locking (2PL): each transaction acquires locks as it goes and releases none until it finishes. An exclusive lock is the lock needed to write, and it lets only one holder in at a time. Transaction T1 holds an exclusive lock on order row 501 and now requests a lock on order row 502. At the same moment, transaction T2 holds an exclusive lock on row 502 and requests a lock on row 501. What happens?
choices: This is a deadlock, and the database breaks it by aborting one of the two transactions
Both transactions proceed, because each reads its own snapshot of the rows
Both transactions wait forever, because 2PL forbids releasing any lock before a transaction finishes
Whichever transaction started first is handed both locks and continues
questions.why: Each transaction is waiting for a lock the other holds, which is a deadlock, and the database resolves it by aborting one of them.

questions.prompt: An online shop runs an MVCC database whose orders table receives thousands of updates per hour. An analyst opens one transaction for a report and leaves it open for six hours. What is the most likely effect on the running system?
choices: The analyst's report shows each new update as soon as it commits
The database silently drops the old versions that the report still needs
Every order update is blocked until the analyst's transaction finishes
Old row versions cannot be cleaned up, so the table bloats and queries slow down
questions.why: A long-running transaction keeps its old snapshot alive. Cleanup (vacuum or garbage collection) cannot remove the dead versions that snapshot might still need, so they pile up, the table bloats and queries slow down.

questions.prompt: A clinic has a rule that at least one doctor must be on call. Two doctors are currently on call, and each one's status is stored in a separate row. In an MVCC database, each doctor starts a transaction, checks that two doctors are on call, and then sets only their own row to off call. Both transactions run at the same time. What is the outcome?
choices: One transaction is aborted, because both wrote the same row
Nothing goes wrong, because MVCC snapshots prevent every kind of anomaly
The second transaction waits for the first one's read lock before it can write
Both transactions commit and no doctor is left on call, because they wrote different rows
questions.why: Each transaction checked a shared condition in its own snapshot and then wrote a different row. Because there was no conflict on the same row, both commit, and together they break a rule that neither would break alone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how locking and MVCC differ when one transaction reads a row that another is updating. Name one cost or limit of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both approaches stop concurrent transactions from stepping on each other, but they handle a reader and a writer differently. With locking, the reader takes a shared lock and the writer needs an exclusive lock, so one of them waits. Two-phase locking holds every lock until the transaction ends, which gives clean one-at-a-time behaviour. The cost is blocking and the risk of deadlocks, where the database must abort a transaction. With MVCC, the writer creates a new version of the row, and the reader keeps reading the older version from its snapshot, so neither waits. MVCC still serializes two writers on the same row. Snapshots can also allow anomalies such as write skew. Old versions must also be cleaned up, and a long-running transaction blocks that cleanup, which causes table bloat and slower queries.
rubricPoints: Defines a lock, including shared versus exclusive, and says writers and readers block each other under locking.
Explains that MVCC keeps multiple row versions and readers use a snapshot of committed data.
States that under MVCC readers and writers do not block each other, but concurrent writers to the same row still conflict.
Names deadlock or blocking as a cost of locking.
Names version buildup, cleanup, or snapshot anomalies as a cost of MVCC.

suggested.rationale: Running two concurrent sessions and watching one block under locking, or read an older version under MVCC, makes the difference concrete in a way reading alone cannot.

lessons.plain: When you send a database a query, you describe what data you want, not how to fetch it. The query planner is the part of the database that works out the how. It considers several ways to get the answer, estimates how much work each would take, and runs the cheapest one. It is like a GPS. You give it a destination. It weighs routes using what it knows about distances and traffic, then picks one. If its traffic data is stale, it can confidently pick a terrible route.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customers table has an index on the city column, which lets the database jump straight to rows for one city. Should the database use that index when you ask for customers in a tiny town? What if the city you ask about holds 90% of all customers?
lessons.teach:
A query planner, also called the optimizer, turns a declarative query into an execution plan. A declarative query states which rows you want. An execution plan is a concrete step-by-step recipe for producing them.

The planner works in three moves. First, it rewrites the query into a logical plan made of operations such as filter, join and aggregate.

Second, it lists physical plans. Each one picks an access path for every table. A sequential scan reads every row. An index scan uses an index, a sorted lookup structure, to jump to matching rows. Each physical plan also picks a join algorithm. A nested loop takes each row on one side and looks up its matches on the other. A hash join builds a hash table from the smaller input and then probes it. A merge join walks two sorted inputs side by side.

Third, it scores each candidate with a cost model, which estimates disk reads and CPU work, and keeps the cheapest. Those costs depend on cardinality estimates, meaning guesses of how many rows each step produces. The guesses come from statistics: stored summaries such as row counts and how values are distributed.

Worked example: join orders (10 million rows) to customers (50,000 rows), keeping only customers in one city. Step 1: statistics say about 1% of customers live there, roughly 500 rows. Step 2: filter customers first, because that shrinks the input. Step 3: for 500 customers, a nested loop that probes an index on the orders table's customer column costs about 500 index lookups, which is cheap. Step 4: if the filter matched 40,000 customers instead, those lookups would pile up. A hash join that reads the orders table once becomes cheaper. The query is the same, but the best plan differs.

A common mistake is assuming an index is always used. When a filter matches a large share of rows, many scattered index lookups cost more than one straight scan, so the planner correctly skips the index.

In a running system, statistics can go stale, for example after a bulk load. The estimates are then badly wrong. The planner may choose a nested loop over millions of rows, and a millisecond query can take minutes. The first steps are to inspect the chosen plan with the database's explain command and to refresh the statistics.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointments table holds 6 million rows and has an index on its status column. A report asks for every appointment with status = 'completed'. The planner works it through. Step 1: statistics (stored summaries of the data) say about 85% of appointments are completed, so the cardinality estimate is roughly 5.1 million rows. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the planner therefore keeps the plan that reads the appointments table once from start to finish and checks each row's status. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Because the filter matches most rows, millions of scattered index lookups would cost more than one sequential scan, so the cost model scores the sequential scan lower.
Because 5.1 million rows is a large result, the planner should pick a hash join to produce them.
Because an index exists on status, an index scan is always the cheapest access path, so the planner should use it.
Because the statistics might be stale, the planner ignores the estimate and defaults to a sequential scan.
questions.why: When a filter matches a large share of rows, the cost model finds that one straight sequential scan is cheaper than millions of scattered index lookups, so it skips the index.

questions.prompt: In query planning, what is a cardinality estimate?
choices: The exact number of rows in a table, counted fresh each time a query runs.
The estimated disk reads and CPU work for a whole execution plan.
The number of indexes available on the tables in a query.
A guess of how many rows a step of the plan will produce, based on stored statistics.
questions.why: Cardinality estimates are the planner's guesses of row counts per step, derived from statistics; the cost model then uses them to estimate disk and CPU work.

questions.prompt: A logistics company joins a shipments table (3 million rows) to a warehouses table (2,000 rows) on the warehouse ID. There is no index on the join column in either table, and neither input is sorted on it. No filter shrinks either side. Which physical join choice is the planner most likely to score as cheapest?
choices: A merge join, because it walks two inputs side by side and needs no preparation.
A hash join that builds a hash table from the warehouses rows and probes it with each shipment.
An index scan on shipments, because joins always use an index.
A nested loop that, for each shipment, scans the whole warehouses table.
questions.why: With no index and unsorted inputs, a hash join built from the smaller input (warehouses) lets the planner read the large table once and probe cheaply.

questions.prompt: An online store's sales report normally runs in 40 milliseconds. The morning after a bulk import of 20 million new rows, the same unchanged query takes 7 minutes. What are the sensible first steps?
choices: Delete the imported rows, because a planner cannot handle tables that large.
Add a new index to every column the query touches, since the old ones must have broken.
Inspect the chosen plan with the database's explain command and refresh the table statistics.
Rewrite the query as a step-by-step recipe so the planner is bypassed.
questions.why: After a bulk load, statistics can go stale and mislead the planner into a bad plan, so you check the plan with explain and refresh the statistics.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a database decides how to run a query, and why the same query can suddenly get much slower without anyone changing it. Name one limit of the planner's approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our SQL only says what rows we want. The query planner decides how to get them. It builds several candidate plans, each with a choice of how to read each table and which join method to use. A table can be read with a full scan or through an index. Joins can be a nested loop, a hash join or a merge join. The planner scores every candidate with a cost model and runs the cheapest. The catch is that those costs rest on estimates of how many rows each step returns, and the estimates come from stored statistics. If the statistics are stale, the estimates are wrong, and the planner can pick a plan that is disastrous for the real data. That is the limit: it is only as good as its estimates. So a query can slow down with no code change simply because the data grew or shifted. The fix starts with looking at the plan and refreshing statistics.
rubricPoints: Queries say what data is wanted, and the planner chooses how to compute it.
The planner compares candidate plans that differ in access path, such as scan versus index, and in join algorithm.
A cost model picks the cheapest plan using cardinality estimates drawn from statistics.
Stale or misleading statistics can lead to a bad plan and a sudden slowdown.
An index is not always the best choice when a filter matches many rows.

suggested.rationale: Query planning sticks best when the learner runs queries and compares the chosen plans as data size and filter selectivity change, which a SQL lab would let them do.

lessons.plain: Replication and partitioning are two ways to spread a database across several machines. Replication means keeping full copies of the same data on more than one machine, so if one dies another can answer, and reads can be shared out. Partitioning, also called sharding, means cutting the data into pieces and giving each machine only its own piece, so no single machine has to hold or write everything. Think of a library: replication is buying three copies of a popular book for three branches; partitioning is putting authors A to M in one building and N to Z in another. Most large systems do both at once.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database server is overwhelmed by writes, and someone proposes adding three read-only copies of it. Will those copies relieve the write load? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Replication means keeping copies of the same data on more than one machine; each copy is a replica. Partitioning, also called sharding, means splitting one dataset into pieces, called partitions or shards, each stored on a different machine. Replication buys availability and read capacity. Partitioning buys room for more data and more writes. Real systems usually combine them, with each partition replicated.

A common replication setup is leader-follower. One replica, the leader, accepts all writes and sends a log of changes to the other replicas, the followers. The followers apply those changes and serve reads. In synchronous replication, the leader waits for a follower to confirm before reporting success, which is safer but slower. In asynchronous replication, the leader reports success at once and followers catch up later. That delay is called replica lag, and a read from a lagging follower returns stale (out-of-date) data.

Partitioning needs a partition key, the field that decides which shard holds a row. Hash partitioning runs the key through a hash function so rows spread evenly. Range partitioning gives each shard a continuous range of keys. This keeps range queries cheap but risks hot spots, meaning one shard gets far more traffic than the others.

Worked example: a fleet app has 4 shards, hash-partitioned by vehicle_id. Vehicle 1042 reports a position. Step 1: hash(1042) mod 4 = 2, so the write goes to shard 2's leader. Step 2: the leader stores it and asynchronously ships it to shard 2's two followers. Step 3: a dispatcher's map reads from a follower 300 ms later, but lag is 2 seconds, so the map shows the old position. Step 4: a query listing every vehicle must ask all 4 shards and merge the results, because hashing scattered the rows.

Common mistake: adding read replicas to cure a write bottleneck. Every replica still applies every write, so write capacity does not grow; only partitioning spreads writes. A related trap is range partitioning on date, which sends all of today's writes to one hot shard.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket service stores orders in 5 shards, hash-partitioned by order_id. Each shard has one leader and two followers, using asynchronous replication. Order 7713 is placed. Step 1: the hash function turns 7713 into the number 38. Step 2: ??? Step 3: that leader saves the order, reports success right away, and ships the change to its two followers. Step 4: a report that totals every order sold tonight must query all 5 shards and combine the results, because hashing spread the orders across them. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: 38 mod 5 = 3, so the write goes to shard 3's leader
The write goes to whichever shard holds the range of order IDs closest to 7713, keeping nearby orders together
The write goes to the leader of every shard so that any shard can answer later reads for this order
38 mod 5 = 3, so the write goes to one of shard 3's followers, which will forward it to the leader later
questions.why: With hash partitioning the hashed key mod the shard count picks the shard (38 mod 5 = 3), and in leader-follower replication all writes go to that shard's leader.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup's database server is overloaded because users upload far more new photos per second than one machine can write. Which change actually increases how many writes the system can handle?
choices: Partition the photos across several machines by a partition key
Switch from asynchronous to synchronous replication
Add three read replicas that copy the server's data
Move every follower closer to the leader to reduce replica lag
questions.why: Every replica still applies every write, so only partitioning spreads writes across machines and raises write capacity.

questions.prompt: A server-monitoring company stores log entries in shards using range partitioning on the log's timestamp, with each shard covering one day. Operators notice that one shard is overwhelmed while the others sit almost idle. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Range partitioning makes queries over a span of dates expensive, so reads pile up on every shard equally
Hash partitioning was used by mistake, scattering each day's logs unevenly across shards
All of today's new log entries fall in the same date range, so one shard receives nearly all writes, creating a hot spot
The followers are lagging, so the leader is forced to resend old entries to all shards
questions.why: Range partitioning on date sends all current writes to the single shard holding today's range, so that shard becomes a hot spot.

questions.prompt: A banking app uses leader-follower replication with asynchronous replication, and balance reads are served by followers. A customer deposits money, sees a success message, then immediately checks the balance and sees the old amount. What explains this, and what replication choice would have prevented the leader from reporting success before a follower had the change?
choices: The deposit landed on the wrong partition; adding more read replicas would fix it
The data was split across too many shards; merging all shards into one would fix it
The follower had not caught up yet (replica lag gave stale data); synchronous replication makes the leader wait for a follower's confirmation
The leader rejected the write; switching to range partitioning would fix it
questions.why: Asynchronous replication reports success before followers catch up, so a lagging follower returns stale data, whereas synchronous replication waits for a follower to confirm first at the cost of slower writes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between replication and partitioning, which problem each one solves, and one tradeoff or limit that comes with each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Replication keeps full copies of the same data on several machines. Usually one leader takes writes and followers copy its change log and serve reads. That gives us failover and more read capacity. It does not help with writes, because every replica still applies every write. If replication is asynchronous, followers lag behind, so a read from a follower can return stale data. Making it synchronous fixes that but slows every write. Partitioning splits the data by a partition key so each machine owns only a slice. That spreads storage and write load. The cost is that queries spanning many keys have to fan out to every shard and merge the results. A poor key, like range-partitioning by date, creates a hot shard that takes all the current traffic. In practice we partition for scale and replicate each partition for availability.
rubricPoints: Replication copies the same data to multiple machines; partitioning splits data so each machine holds a subset.
Replication improves availability and read capacity but not write capacity.
Asynchronous replication causes replica lag and stale reads; synchronous replication trades write speed for freshness.
Partitioning spreads data and writes, and depends on a well-chosen partition key.
Poor keys cause hot spots, and cross-partition queries must fan out to all shards.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose stale reads caused by replica lag, which is the central replication tradeoff in this lesson.

lessons.plain: When a database keeps several copies of the same data, often on different machines, you face a choice. You can make every read wait until the copies agree, so you always see the newest value, or you can answer quickly from the nearest copy and accept that it might be a little out of date. That is the consistency/latency tradeoff. It is like asking a group of friends for the latest news. You can wait for everyone to check in and be sure, or you can ask whoever is closest and risk hearing yesterday's story. Neither is always right. The answer depends on what a stale answer would cost.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shopping site keeps three copies of its data in three cities. Which should it show from the nearest copy, even if that copy is a few seconds out of date: the number of likes on a product review, or a customer's remaining gift-card balance at checkout? Why?
lessons.teach:
A consistency/latency tradeoff is the choice between strong consistency, where every read sees the newest write, and faster answers that may return an older value. It arises whenever data lives in several copies, called replicas.

It works this way because guaranteeing the newest value means checking with, or waiting for, enough replicas, and every extra network round trip adds delay. Skipping that coordination is quicker but risks a stale read, which returns a value that has since been overwritten. Eventual consistency promises that once writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value, but it says nothing about when. The PACELC idea sums this up. During a network Partition you trade Availability against Consistency. Else, in normal running, you still trade Latency against Consistency.

A common middle ground is a quorum. With N replicas, a write waits for W of them to confirm, and a read asks R of them and keeps the newest version. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so reads see the latest write.

Worked example: N = 3, W = 2, R = 2. A price changes from 10 to 12. Replicas A and B confirm the write, while C is slow and still holds 10. A read asks B and C, gets 12 and 10, and returns 12 because its version is newer. Since 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, the overlap is guaranteed. With R = 1, a read that happened to reach C would return 10. That read is faster, but it is stale.

A common mistake is treating all reads alike. Some paths need strong reads, such as checking a balance before a withdrawal, or read-your-writes, where a user sees their own edit straight after saving it. Other paths, like a like count, can come from fast, possibly stale copies.

The consequence for a running system follows from that choice. Strong consistency everywhere raises response time and can make requests fail when replicas are unreachable. Weak consistency in the wrong place causes double spends, confused users, and decisions made on old data.

questions.prompt: A warehouse inventory service keeps each stock count on N = 5 replicas. Each write waits for W = 3 replicas to confirm. The team wants every read to see the latest write, using the smallest possible read quorum R. Worked so far: Step 1, the rule is that the read set must always overlap the write set, which holds when R + W > N. Step 2, substitute the known values: R + 3 > 5. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, the team configures reads to ask that many replicas and keep the newest version. What is Step 3?
choices: R = 5, because every replica must be read to be sure
R = 1 is enough, because the write already reached a majority of replicas
R = 2, because 2 + 3 = 5, which matches N
R = 3, because 3 + 3 = 6, which is greater than 5
questions.why: R + W must be strictly greater than N, so the smallest R is 3, since 3 + 3 = 6 > 5 while 2 + 3 = 5 only equals N and leaves room for a read set that misses every replica holding the write.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing app stores caption text on several replicas and uses eventual consistency. What does eventual consistency actually promise?
choices: Every read returns the newest caption as soon as it is saved
Replicas will agree within a fixed time limit after each write
Reads are always faster than under strong consistency, with no stale results
Once writes stop, all replicas will converge to the same caption, with no promise about how soon
questions.why: Eventual consistency only guarantees that replicas converge after writes stop; it says nothing about when, so stale reads can happen meanwhile.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing site serves several kinds of reads from replicated data. Which read most needs a strong (newest-value) read rather than a fast, possibly stale copy?
choices: Showing how many fans marked the concert as a favourite
Checking that a specific seat is still free right before charging the buyer's card
Listing the most popular concerts this week
Showing how many people viewed the event page today
questions.why: Acting on an old seat status could sell the same seat twice, just like a double spend, while the other counts can tolerate being slightly out of date.

questions.prompt: A library catalogue stores each book's loan status on N = 4 replicas, with writes confirmed by W = 2 and reads asking R = 2. A librarian marks a book as loaned, yet a read seconds later shows it as available. What best explains this?
choices: Quorums only work during a network partition, so they do nothing in normal running
The read should have returned the older version because it arrived first
R + W equals 4, which is not greater than N, so a read can ask two replicas that never received the write
W = 2 means the write reached every replica, so the read must have hit a bug in the newest-version check
questions.why: Overlap is only guaranteed when R + W > N; here 2 + 2 = 4 equals N, so the read set and write set can be completely separate and the read returns a stale value.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a replicated database cannot give both the freshest possible reads and the lowest possible latency for free. Use the quorum rule R + W > N, and name one case where you would accept stale reads and one where you would not.
lessons.modelAnswer: When data is copied across replicas, a read is only guaranteed to be fresh if it checks enough copies to overlap with the copies that confirmed the latest write. Each extra replica we wait on is another network round trip, so freshness costs time. With N replicas, writes waiting for W and reads asking R, the rule R + W > N guarantees overlap. For example, with N=3, W=2 and R=2, a read always hits at least one replica holding the newest value. Dropping to R=1 makes reads faster but can return stale data from a lagging copy. I'd accept stale reads for a view counter or a social feed, where being a few seconds behind harms nobody. I wouldn't accept them for an account balance before a payment, or for a user reloading their own edit. The tradeoff is that stronger guarantees mean higher latency and less tolerance for unreachable replicas.
rubricPoints: Defines strong consistency versus stale or eventually consistent reads.
Explains that freshness requires coordinating with replicas, which adds network delay.
States the quorum rule R + W > N and why overlap guarantees the latest value.
Gives a case where stale reads are acceptable and one where they are not.
Notes a cost of strong consistency, such as higher latency or failing when replicas are unreachable.

suggested.rationale: In this incident, dispatchers read minute-old positions from a lagging replica, so the learner has to reason through the stale-read versus latency tradeoff on a live system.

lessons.plain: Different kinds of databases are shaped for different questions. A relational database stores data in tables, like a set of linked spreadsheets, and is best at exact, rule-checked records such as orders and payments. A graph database stores things and the connections between them, and is best at questions like 'who is connected to whom, three steps away'. A search-oriented system is built to find text quickly and rank the best matches first, like a library's subject catalogue. Think of a city: the land registry (relational), the road map (graph), and the phone book's keyword index (search). Each answers its own kind of question fast and the others' slowly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop wants three features: record each customer's order reliably, suggest 'people who bought this also bought', and let users type 'red waterproof hiking boots' into a search bar. Which feature would you give to which kind of system, and why?
lessons.teach:
A relational database stores data as tables. A table is a set of rows (records) with fixed columns, described by a schema, which is the declared structure and rules. Tables are linked by shared values, and a join is the operation that combines rows from two tables on those values. Relational systems usually offer strong guarantees that a group of changes either all happen or none do, which is why they hold money and orders.

A graph database stores nodes (things, such as a person or product) and edges (named connections, such as BOUGHT or FOLLOWS) as first-class data. Each node keeps direct pointers to its neighbours, so a traversal, meaning walking from node to node along edges, costs roughly the number of edges visited rather than a scan of whole tables.

A search-oriented system, such as Elasticsearch or OpenSearch, splits text into tokens (individual words, often lowercased and stemmed, so 'boots' matches 'boot'). It builds an inverted index, which maps each token to the list of documents containing it, and then gives each match a relevance score so the best results come first.

Worked example, the shop. Step 1: an order touches a customer, items and a payment that must agree, so it goes in relational tables. Step 2: 'also bought' means starting at product P, following BOUGHT edges back to customers, then forward to their other products. That is a two-hop traversal, which is natural in a graph. In SQL it becomes repeated self-joins that get slower with each hop. Step 3: the query 'red waterproof boots' looks up three tokens in the inverted index, intersects the lists and ranks them. A relational LIKE '%red%' scan would read every row.

Common mistake: treating the search index as the system of record. Search indexes are usually filled by copying data from the main database and lag behind it. If you write orders only to the index, you can lose or misreport them. In a running system, keep the relational database as the source of truth and feed graph or search copies from it, accepting that they may be briefly stale.

questions.prompt: A recipe website runs a search-oriented system. A visitor types 'Spicy Noodles'. Step 1: the text is split into tokens, lowercased and stemmed, giving 'spicy' and 'noodl'. Step 2: the inverted index is consulted. 'spicy' maps to recipes {2, 5, 9} and 'noodl' maps to recipes {5, 9, 12}. Step 3: ??? Step 4: each remaining recipe gets a relevance score, and the higher-scoring one is shown first. What is Step 3?
choices: Run a LIKE '%spicy%' scan over every recipe row to confirm the matches
Keep only the recipes that appear in just one list, giving {2, 12}
Combine both lists into {2, 5, 9, 12} so every recipe with either word is returned unranked
Intersect the two lists to keep only recipes containing both tokens, giving {5, 9}
questions.why: For a multi-word query the token lists are intersected, so only recipes containing both words, {5, 9}, go on to be ranked.

questions.prompt: In a search-oriented system such as OpenSearch, what does an inverted index do?
choices: It keeps direct pointers from each document to its neighbouring documents for fast traversal
It stores each document's columns in a fixed schema so documents can be joined on shared values
It maps each token to the list of documents that contain that token
It reverses the order of rows so the newest documents are read first
questions.why: An inverted index goes from token to the documents containing it, so a word lookup avoids reading every document.

questions.prompt: A fitness app wants a feature that suggests 'people followed by people your friends follow', which means starting at a user and walking FOLLOWS connections three steps out. The member table holds 2 million users. Which kind of system fits this feature best, and why?
choices: A graph database, because each user node points directly to its neighbours, so the cost tracks the number of edges walked
A search-oriented system, because tokenizing user names and ranking them by relevance finds followers of followers
A relational database, because each extra hop is just one more self-join, and self-joins stay equally fast however many hops are added
A search-oriented system, because its copies are filled from the main database and are always up to date
questions.why: Multi-hop walks along named connections are traversals, which a graph handles in time roughly proportional to the edges visited, while SQL needs repeated self-joins that slow down with each hop.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing startup saves new bookings only into its Elasticsearch index, because searching is fast there, and it has no other database for them. What is the main risk?
choices: The search index is not meant to be the system of record, so bookings can be lost or misreported
Every booking query will trigger a LIKE scan that reads every row in the index
The bookings will automatically form edges, so ticket queries turn into slow graph traversals
Bookings will be impossible to search, because Elasticsearch cannot tokenize text
questions.why: Search indexes are usually filled as copies and can lag behind, so the relational database should hold bookings as the source of truth, and the index should be fed from it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a relational, a graph, and a search-oriented system for a new feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the question the feature asks. If it needs exact, consistent records where several changes must succeed or fail together, like orders or balances, I use a relational database. Tables, a schema and joins enforce structure, but joins get expensive when I chain many hops of relationships. If the question is about connections, like friends of friends or recommendation paths, a graph database fits, because nodes point straight to their neighbours and traversal cost tracks edges visited. Its limit is weaker fit for bulk reporting across everything. If users type free text and want ranked results, a search system with an inverted index and relevance scoring is right. Its tradeoff is that it is usually a copy fed from the main store, so it can lag and should not be the source of truth. Many real systems combine all three.
rubricPoints: Relational fits structured, consistent records with joins and all-or-nothing changes.
Graph fits multi-hop relationship questions because traversal follows stored edges directly.
Search fits ranked free-text lookup using tokens and an inverted index.
Names a limit for each, such as costly deep joins, weak bulk analytics, or stale index copies.
Keeps the relational store as source of truth and feeds other systems from it.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a data model is a judgement call best practised by reasoning through exam-style use cases that mix records, relationships and text search.

lessons.plain: Linear algebra is the arithmetic of lists of numbers. A single number is a scalar. An ordered list of numbers is a vector, which you can picture as an arrow pointing somewhere in space, and a grid of numbers is a matrix. Machine learning describes almost everything this way. A house might become the vector (bedrooms, size, age), and a word or a photo becomes a longer list. Once things are arrows, you can ask useful questions. How long is this arrow? How far apart are two arrows? Do they point the same way? That last question is how a search engine decides that two pieces of text are about the same thing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Document A mentions 'cat' 2 times and 'dog' 1 time. Document B mentions 'cat' 4 times and 'dog' 2 times. B is twice as long, but are the two documents about the same mix of topics? Would you call them similar or different, and why?
lessons.teach:
A scalar is one number. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, such as a = (3, 4). A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers with rows and columns, and a 2×3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns.

The dot product of two vectors of equal length multiplies matching entries and adds the results, which gives one scalar. Matrix multiplication repeats that move. Entry (i, j) of AB is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B. So an (m×n) matrix times an (n×p) matrix gives an (m×p) matrix, and the inner sizes must match. The transpose of a matrix, written Aᵀ, swaps its rows and columns, so a 2×3 matrix becomes 3×2. It is often used to make shapes line up.

The magnitude, or length, of a vector is the square root of the sum of its squared entries. The distance between two vectors, here the straight-line or Euclidean distance, is the magnitude of their difference. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the two magnitudes. It measures only direction. A result of 1 means the vectors point the same way, 0 means they are at right angles, and -1 means they point opposite ways. It works because the dot product grows when large entries line up, and dividing by the lengths removes the effect of size.

Worked example with a = (3, 4) and b = (4, 3):
The dot product is 3·4 + 4·3 = 24.
The magnitude of a is √(9+16) = 5, and the magnitude of b is also 5.
The cosine similarity is 24 / (5·5) = 0.96, so the two point in very similar directions.
The distance is √((3−4)² + (4−3)²) = √2 ≈ 1.41.

A common mistake is to treat distance and cosine as interchangeable. The vectors (2, 1) and (4, 2) have a cosine of exactly 1, so their direction is identical, yet they are about 2.24 apart. In a running similarity search, choosing the wrong measure ranks a long document as different from a short one on the same topic. Mismatched inner sizes in matrix multiplication make the code fail with a shape error.

questions.prompt:
A music app stores each listener's taste as a vector of plays per genre. Listener u = (1, 2, 2) and listener v = (2, 0, 1). The app computes their cosine similarity.

Step 1: Dot product = 1·2 + 2·0 + 2·1 = 4.
Step 2: Magnitude of u = √(1 + 4 + 4) = √9 = 3.
Step 3: Magnitude of v = ???
Step 4: Cosine similarity = 4 / (3 · 2.24) ≈ 0.60, so the tastes point in a moderately similar direction.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
questions.why: Magnitude is the square root of the sum of the squared entries, so it is √(4 + 0 + 1) = √5 ≈ 2.24, which is also the value Step 4 uses.

questions.prompt: A warehouse system multiplies matrix A, which has 4 rows and 2 columns (4×2), by matrix B, which is 2×5, to form AB. What is the shape of the result?
choices: It fails with a shape error, because 4 and 5 differ
questions.why: The inner sizes (2 and 2) match, so an (m×n) times (n×p) product gives (m×p), which here is 4×5.

questions.prompt: A clinic's analytics script holds matrix A as 3×2 and matrix B as 3×2. A programmer wants to multiply them, and the transpose (swapping rows and columns) is available. Which statement is correct?
choices: AᵀB works and gives a 2×2 result
AB works directly and gives a 3×3 result
AB works directly and gives a 3×2 result
AᵀB works and gives a 3×3 result
questions.why: AB fails because the inner sizes are 2 and 3. Aᵀ is 2×3, so Aᵀ (2×3) times B (3×2) has matching inner sizes and gives a 2×2 result.

questions.prompt: A help-desk tool counts two keywords in support tickets. Ticket P has counts (1, 3) and ticket Q has counts (3, 9). Which statement about these two vectors is correct?
choices: Their cosine similarity is 1, yet their Euclidean distance is about 6.32, so they share a direction but differ in size
Their distance is 0 because Q is just P multiplied by 3
Their cosine similarity is 3 because Q is three times as long as P
Their cosine similarity is close to 0 because the distance between them is large
questions.why: Q points the same way as P, so the cosine is 1. The distance is the magnitude of the difference, √(2² + 6²) = √40 ≈ 6.32, which shows that distance and cosine measure different things.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what cosine similarity measures and how it differs from Euclidean distance, using a small example. Name one situation where relying on cosine alone would mislead you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each item becomes a vector, which is a list of numbers you can picture as an arrow. Cosine similarity takes the dot product of two vectors and divides it by the product of their lengths. The answer runs from -1 to 1 and tells you only whether the arrows point the same way. Euclidean distance is the length of the gap between the two arrow tips, so it cares about size as well as direction. Take (2, 1) and (4, 2). Their cosine is 1, so the direction is identical, but the distance between them is about 2.24. For comparing topics in texts of different lengths, cosine is usually what you want. The tradeoff is that cosine throws magnitude away. If size carries meaning, cosine would call two very different things identical. One example is a customer spending $10 versus $1,000 in the same proportions across categories, and in that case distance is the better measure.
rubricPoints: Defines a vector as an ordered list of numbers and cosine similarity as the dot product divided by the product of the magnitudes.
States that cosine measures direction only, with values from -1 to 1.
States that Euclidean distance is the magnitude of the difference and depends on size.
Gives a small numeric example where the two measures disagree.
Names a limit, such as cosine ignoring magnitude when magnitude matters.

suggested.rationale: Short drills that compute dot products, matrix shapes, distances and cosine similarity on tiny vectors make the learner apply each definition by hand and check the result.

lessons.plain: Probability is the math of uncertainty. It gives each possible outcome a number between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), so you can reason about chance instead of guessing. Statistics uses those ideas to summarize real data: the typical value, how spread out the values are, and whether two things tend to rise and fall together. Think of a weather forecaster. Past patterns suggest a 30% chance of rain, and dark clouds this morning push that number higher. Machine learning works the same way. Models turn data into likelihoods and update their beliefs when new evidence arrives.
lessons.guessPrompt: Only 1 in 100 emails is spam. A filter catches 90% of spam but also wrongly flags 5% of normal emails. An email gets flagged. Is it more likely or less likely than 50% that it is really spam?
lessons.teach:
A probability is a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely an event is, where an event is an outcome or a set of outcomes. A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance. A distribution lists every possible value of a random variable along with its probability, and those probabilities always sum to 1. A fair die follows a uniform distribution, with each face at 1/6. Adult heights roughly follow a normal distribution, the bell curve, clustered around a middle value.

Conditional probability, written P(A|B), is the chance of A given that B has happened. You shrink your world to only the cases where B is true. Bayes' theorem lets you flip a conditional: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). P(A) is the prior, your belief before seeing evidence. The result is the posterior, your belief after seeing it.

Worked example. 1% of emails are spam. A filter flags 90% of spam and wrongly flags 5% of normal mail. Picture 1,000 emails. Step 1: 10 are spam and 990 are normal. Step 2: the filter flags 9 of the spam emails. Step 3: it also flags 0.05 × 990 ≈ 49.5 normal emails. Step 4: P(spam|flagged) = 9 / (9 + 49.5) ≈ 15%.

The common mistake is answering 90%. That confuses P(flagged|spam) with P(spam|flagged) and ignores the low prior, also called the base rate. In a running system, this mistake means trusting an alert or classifier far more than it deserves.

Expectation, or expected value, is the probability-weighted average. For a die it is (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5. Variance measures spread: it is the expected squared distance from the mean. Standard deviation is the square root of variance, which puts it back in the original units.

Covariance shows whether two variables move together. It is positive when both tend to sit above their means at the same time, and negative when one rises as the other falls. Correlation is covariance rescaled to the range -1 to +1, so it has no units. A correlation of 0 means no straight-line relationship, which is not the same as no relationship at all. Correlation also never proves causation.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud detector is checked with Bayes' theorem. 2% of card transactions are fraudulent. The detector flags 80% of fraudulent transactions and wrongly flags 10% of legitimate ones. Picture 2,000 transactions. Step 1: 2% of 2,000 gives 40 fraudulent and 1,960 legitimate transactions. Step 2: the detector flags 0.80 × 40 = 32 fraudulent transactions. Step 3: it also flags 0.10 × 1,960 = 196 legitimate transactions. Step 4 is missing: what is P(fraud | flagged), the chance a flagged transaction is really fraud?
choices: 80%, because the detector catches 80% of fraud
questions.why: Given a flag, you shrink your world to the 228 flagged transactions, and only 32 of them are fraud, so about 14%.

questions.prompt: A game pays $10 with probability 0.3 and $0 with probability 0.7. What is the expected value, the probability-weighted average payout, of one play?
choices: $5, halfway between the two payouts
$10, the largest prize
questions.why: Expected value is 0.3 × $10 + 0.7 × $0 = $3.

questions.prompt: An analyst plots a variable y against x and sees a perfect U-shaped curve that is symmetric around x = 0. The computed correlation is about 0. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: x and y have no relationship at all
There is no straight-line relationship, but there can still be a strong curved one
x must cause y, since the pattern is so clear
The correlation must have been miscalculated, since it should be +1
questions.why: A correlation of 0 only rules out a straight-line relationship; it does not mean no relationship, and correlation never proves causation.

questions.prompt: A team models a web request as a random variable with three outcomes: fast with probability 0.6, slow with probability 0.3, and timeout with probability 0.2. Why can this not be a valid distribution?
choices: A distribution must give every outcome the same probability
A distribution needs at least six outcomes, like a die
A probability of 0.6 is too high for a single outcome
The probabilities sum to 1.1, but a distribution's probabilities must sum to 1
questions.why: A distribution lists every possible value with its probability, and those probabilities must sum to exactly 1.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why a test or classifier that is '90% accurate' can still be wrong most of the time when it raises a flag. Use conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, and name one limit of correlation while you are at it.
lessons.modelAnswer: The 90% figure is P(flag | real problem): how often the test catches a real case. What we actually want is the reverse, P(real problem | flag). Bayes' theorem connects the two, and it brings in the prior, meaning how common the problem is to begin with. If only 1% of emails are spam, then out of 1,000 emails about 9 real spams get flagged. Meanwhile about 50 normal emails get flagged by mistake, so only around 15% of flags are real. Rare events plus even a small false-alarm rate give you mostly false alarms. That's why we should check the base rate before trusting an alert. A related limit: if two metrics are strongly correlated, that only means they move together in a straight-line way. It doesn't show that one causes the other. A correlation near zero also doesn't rule out a curved relationship.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes P(A|B) from P(B|A) and says they are not equal.
Explains that the prior or base rate strongly affects the posterior.
Traces or sketches a numeric example that shows a low posterior.
States that correlation measures straight-line co-movement on a -1 to +1 scale.
Names a limit, such as correlation not implying causation or missing curved relationships.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises probability, and Bayes and base-rate problems are learned best by reasoning through short exam-style scenarios with numbers.

lessons.plain: Calculus gives machine learning a way to answer one question: if I nudge this number a little, does my error go up or down, and how fast? A derivative is that rate of change for one input. A gradient bundles those rates for many inputs into one arrow pointing uphill. Gradient descent is the habit of repeatedly stepping the opposite way, downhill, to shrink the error. Picture walking down a foggy hill: you cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. The learning rate is how big each step is.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are blindfolded on a hillside and want to reach the lowest point. You can only feel the slope under your feet. What would you do on each step, and what could go wrong if every step were enormous?
lessons.teach:
A derivative measures how fast a function's output changes when its input changes a tiny bit. For f(w) = (w - 3)^2, the derivative is 2(w - 3). At w = 0 it is -6: the output falls steeply as w increases. A positive derivative means increasing w raises the output; zero means a flat spot, often a minimum.

A partial derivative is the same idea when there are several inputs: you vary one and hold the others fixed. For g(x, y) = x^2 + 3y, the partial with respect to x is 2x, and with respect to y is 3. The gradient is the list of all partial derivatives, here (2x, 3). It points in the direction of steepest increase.

In machine learning, the function is the loss (a number measuring how wrong the model is) and the inputs are the model's weights (adjustable numbers). Gradient descent repeats one rule: new weight = old weight - learning rate x gradient. The learning rate is a small positive number controlling step size. We subtract because the gradient points uphill and we want to go down.

Worked example with f(w) = (w - 3)^2, learning rate 0.1, start w = 0. Step 1: gradient 2(0 - 3) = -6, so w = 0 - 0.1 x (-6) = 0.6. Step 2: gradient 2(0.6 - 3) = -4.8, so w = 0.6 + 0.48 = 1.08. Each step moves toward 3, the minimum, and steps shrink as the slope flattens.

A common mistake is choosing the learning rate badly. With 1.0, w jumps from 0 to 6 and back to 0 forever; above 1.0 it overshoots further each time and diverges. Too small, like 0.0001, is stable but needs a huge number of steps. In a real training job, a learning rate that is too large shows up as a loss that bounces or explodes, and one that is too small wastes compute time while the loss barely moves.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup tunes one pricing weight w for its delivery-fee model. The loss is f(w) = (w - 5)^2, so the derivative (gradient) is 2(w - 5). The learning rate is 0.2 and training starts at w = 1. Step 1: gradient = 2(1 - 5) = -8, so new w = 1 - 0.2 x (-8) = 2.6. Step 2: gradient = 2(2.6 - 5) = -4.8. What is the new value of w after Step 2?
choices: 1.64, because 0.2 x 4.8 = 0.96 is taken away from 2.6
4.2, because Step 1's gradient is reused: 2.6 - 0.2 x (-8) = 2.6 + 1.6
questions.why: The update rule is new weight = old weight - learning rate x gradient, and subtracting 0.2 x (-4.8) adds 0.96, giving 3.56, which moves w closer to the minimum at 5.

questions.prompt: A sensor-calibration model has the loss h(a, b) = 4a + b^2, where a and b are two weights. A partial derivative varies one input and holds the other fixed, and the gradient is the list of all the partial derivatives. What is the gradient at a = 2, b = 3?
questions.why: The partial with respect to a is 4, a constant, and the partial with respect to b is 2b = 6 at b = 3, so the gradient is (4, 6).

questions.prompt: During training of a fraud-detection model, one weight currently equals 4. The derivative of the loss with respect to that weight is +2.5, and the learning rate is 0.1. After one gradient descent step, what happens to the weight?
choices: It drops to 1.5, because the derivative is subtracted directly from the weight
It drops to 3.75, because 4 - 0.1 x 2.5 = 3.75
It stays at 4, because a positive derivative means the weight is already at a minimum
It rises to 4.25, because a positive derivative means you should move the weight up
questions.why: A positive derivative means increasing the weight raises the loss, so gradient descent subtracts learning rate x gradient (0.1 x 2.5 = 0.25) and lowers the weight to 3.75.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a music-streaming company watches a recommendation model train. The loss swings up and down from step to step and then grows to enormous values instead of shrinking. What is the most likely cause, and what is the sensible fix?
choices: The learning rate is too large, so each step overshoots the minimum; lower the learning rate
The gradient is being subtracted instead of added; switch the sign in the update rule
The learning rate is too small, so the steps are stuck; raise the learning rate
The model has reached a flat spot where the derivative is zero; stop training
questions.why: A loss that bounces or explodes is the sign of steps that are too big and overshoot further each time, so reducing the learning rate restores stable progress toward the minimum.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how gradient descent uses derivatives and the gradient to improve a model, and describe the tradeoff in picking the learning rate.
lessons.modelAnswer: A derivative tells you how much the output changes when you nudge one input. When there are many inputs, we take a partial derivative for each one, holding the rest fixed, and the list of those is the gradient, which points in the direction the loss rises fastest. Gradient descent trains a model by repeatedly updating every weight as weight minus learning rate times gradient, so we step downhill on the loss. Near the bottom the slope flattens, so steps naturally shrink. The learning rate is the tradeoff: too big and you overshoot the minimum, bouncing around or even diverging so the loss blows up; too small and progress is safe but painfully slow and costs a lot of compute. It also only follows the local slope, so it finds a nearby low point, not necessarily the best one overall.
rubricPoints: Defines a derivative as the rate of change of output for a small change in input.
Explains partial derivatives as varying one input at a time and the gradient as the list of them pointing uphill.
States the update rule: subtract learning rate times gradient to move downhill on the loss.
Describes the learning-rate tradeoff: too large overshoots or diverges, too small is slow.
Connects the loss to model error and the inputs to the model's weights.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine trains a model, and the unit's goal is to explain gradients in plain language and trace small examples, so explaining it back is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Machine learning is a way of building a program by showing it examples instead of writing every rule by hand. It is like teaching a child to tell apples from oranges by pointing at many fruits, rather than reciting a definition. Sometimes each example comes with the right answer attached, and the program learns to predict it. Sometimes there are no answers, and the program just looks for natural groups. Good learning means doing well on new examples, not just remembering old ones. Many methods also turn things into lists of numbers, so that similar items sit close together and can be found by measuring distance.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 1,000 emails already marked spam or not spam, and you want a program that marks new emails. Should you judge how good it is using emails it learned from, or emails it never saw? Why?
lessons.teach:
Machine learning (ML) fits a program's behaviour from examples. Each example has features, the measured inputs (size, colour). In supervised learning each example also has a label, the correct answer to predict. If the label is a category (spam or not), the task is classification. If it is a number (a price), it is regression. Unsupervised learning has no labels. Its most common task is clustering, which groups examples that resemble each other.

Training tunes a model to lower its loss, one number scoring how wrong its predictions are, such as average squared error. Data is split three ways. The training set fits the model. The validation set compares choices and settings. The test set is used once at the end to estimate performance on unseen data.

Underfitting means the model is too simple, so error is high everywhere. That is high bias: error from wrong assumptions. Overfitting means the model memorised noise, so training error is low but validation error is high. That is high variance: over-sensitivity to the particular sample. Reducing one usually raises the other, which is the bias/variance tradeoff.

An embedding is a vector, a list of numbers, learned so that similar items get nearby vectors. Vector similarity measures that closeness, for example with Euclidean distance (straight-line distance) or cosine similarity (how closely two directions point the same way). k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) labels a new point by taking the majority label of its k closest training points.

Worked example, k = 3. Training data: A(1,1) cat, B(2,1) cat, E(2,2) dog, C(5,5) dog. New point P(1,2). The distances are A = 1, E = 1, B = about 1.41 and C = 5. The three nearest are A, E and B, whose labels are cat, dog and cat, so P is labelled cat.

A common mistake is tuning choices, such as the value of k, against the test set. The test set then stops being unseen, so the reported score is too optimistic. Choosing k = 1 also tends to overfit, because one noisy neighbour decides the answer. In a running system, either mistake means the deployed model performs worse than promised.

questions.prompt:
A small orchard sorts apples with k-NN, k = 3. Each apple has two features: (firmness, sweetness). Training data: Q(4,4) ripe, R(4,6) unripe, S(6,4) ripe, T(0,0) unripe. A new apple N is at (4,5). Using Euclidean (straight-line) distance:

Step 1: distance to Q = 1 (only sweetness differs, by 1).
Step 2: distance to R = 1 (only sweetness differs, by 1).
Step 3: distance to S = ?
Step 4: distance to T = about 6.40.
Step 5: the three nearest are Q, R and S, labelled ripe, unripe and ripe, so N is labelled ripe.

Which value correctly completes Step 3?
choices: 3, found by adding the differences 2 + 1
5, found as 2² + 1² without taking the square root
About 2.24, the square root of 2² + 1²
1, found by keeping only the smaller difference
questions.why: Straight-line distance squares each coordinate difference (2 and 1), adds them to get 5, then takes the square root, giving about 2.24.

questions.prompt: A courier company has records of past deliveries. Each record lists the trip distance and the traffic level, plus how many minutes the delivery actually took. They want a model that predicts the minutes for a new delivery. What kind of task is this?
choices: Supervised regression, because the label is a number
Unsupervised regression, because no categories are given
Unsupervised clustering, because similar trips get grouped
Supervised classification, because each record has a label
questions.why: The records include the correct answer (a label), which makes it supervised, and that label is a number of minutes rather than a category, which makes it regression.

questions.prompt: A team trains a model to flag faulty sensor readings. Its error on the training set is 2%, but its error on the validation set is 30%. What best describes this model?
choices: Underfitting with high bias, since the model is too simple
Underfitting with high variance, since validation error is high
Overfitting with high variance, since it memorised noise in the training sample
A good fit, since the low training error proves it has learned
questions.why: Low training error together with high validation error means the model fitted the quirks of its training sample, which is overfitting, also called high variance.

questions.prompt: A clinic's data team tries k = 1 through k = 15 for a k-NN model and keeps whichever k scores best on the test set. They then report that test score as the expected accuracy. What is the main problem?
choices: The test set should have been used to fit the model instead of the training set
k-NN cannot be tuned at all, so any value of k gives the same score
The test set was used for tuning, so it is no longer unseen and the reported score is likely too optimistic
Trying several values of k always causes underfitting, so the score is too pessimistic
questions.why: Choosing settings belongs on the validation set; tuning against the test set means it no longer estimates performance on truly unseen data, so the deployed model will likely do worse than reported.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we split data into training, validation and test sets, using overfitting and underfitting in your answer, and name the tradeoff involved when choosing k in k-NN.
lessons.modelAnswer: We train on one slice of the data, but what we care about is new data. So we hold out a validation set to compare choices like k, and a test set we look at only once to estimate real-world performance. If we tune against the test set, it leaks into our decisions and the score becomes too optimistic. Overfitting shows up as low training error but high validation error: the model memorised noise, which is high variance. Underfitting shows up as high error on both, because the model is too simple, which is high bias. In k-NN, a small k like 1 follows every noisy neighbour and has high variance. A very large k averages over far-away points and blurs real boundaries, which is high bias. We pick k by validation error, accepting that we can't minimise both kinds of error at once.
rubricPoints: Training fits the model, validation guides choices, and test gives a final unseen estimate.
Tuning on the test set makes the reported performance too optimistic.
Overfitting means low training error and high validation error, which is high variance.
Underfitting means high error everywhere, which is high bias.
In k-NN, a small k means high variance and a large k means high bias, and k is chosen on validation data.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a web of conceptual definitions and tradeoffs, and no current mission or planned engine exercises ML. Explaining how the terms connect is the core skill to practise.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles a message so only someone holding the right key can unscramble it. In symmetric encryption, one shared secret key both locks and unlocks, like a house key you copy for a friend. It is very fast, but you must somehow hand over the copy safely. In asymmetric encryption, each person has a matched pair: a public key anyone may use to lock a message, and a private key only the owner uses to unlock it, like a mailbox slot anyone can drop letters into. It solves the handover problem but is much slower. Real systems use both together.
lessons.guessPrompt: You need to send a friend a 2 GB video secretly over the internet, and you have never met to agree on a password. Would you rather use one fast shared key, or a slow method that needs no prior meeting? Can you think of a way to get the benefits of both?
lessons.teach:
Encryption turns plaintext (readable data) into ciphertext (scrambled data) using a key, which is a secret value that controls the scrambling. Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt; AES is a common example. It is fast and cheap, even on large data. Its weakness is the key distribution problem: both sides must already share the key, and sending it in the clear lets an eavesdropper read everything.

Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a key pair. The public key can be published; data encrypted with it can only be decrypted by the matching private key, which the owner never shares. RSA is a classic example. Distribution is easy because the public key need not be secret, but the mathematics is far slower and only suits small pieces of data.

They are combined in hybrid encryption. Worked example: Alice wants to send Bob a 1 GB file. Step one, Alice generates a random symmetric key, called a session key because it lives only for this exchange. Step two, she encrypts the 1 GB file with that session key, which is fast. Step three, she encrypts just the small session key with Bob's public key. Step four, she sends both. Step five, Bob uses his private key to recover the session key, then uses the session key to decrypt the file. Asymmetric did the small, hard job (getting a key across safely); symmetric did the big, fast job.

TLS, the protocol behind HTTPS, follows the same pattern: public-key techniques during setup establish shared session keys, then all traffic is protected with symmetric encryption.

A common mistake is believing asymmetric is simply 'more secure' and encrypting all data with it. In a running system that wastes large amounts of CPU, adds latency, and hits size limits; the security comes from the right tool on each job, not from the slower algorithm.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital sends a 40 GB nightly backup archive to an offsite storage company. The storage company has published its public key and keeps the matching private key to itself. The hospital and the company have never shared any secret before. Here is how the hospital uses hybrid encryption (a symmetric key for the bulk data plus public-key encryption for that key). First, the hospital's backup server generates a fresh random session key, a symmetric key used only for tonight's transfer. Second, it encrypts the 40 GB archive with that session key. Third, it encrypts only the small session key with the storage company's public key. Fourth, it sends the encrypted archive and the encrypted session key together. Fifth, the storage company receives both. What must the storage company do next to read the archive?
choices: Decrypt the 40 GB archive directly with its private key, skipping the session key entirely
Use its private key to recover the session key, then use that session key to decrypt the archive
Decrypt the session key with its own public key, then use the session key on the archive
Ask the hospital to email the session key unencrypted so the archive can be decrypted quickly
questions.why: Only the company's private key can undo encryption done with its public key, which recovers the small session key, and that symmetric key then quickly decrypts the large archive.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm plans to protect messages between its depots using only symmetric encryption, where the same key encrypts and decrypts. The depots have never exchanged a key. What is the main weakness the firm faces?
choices: Symmetric encryption needs a public key to be published, which exposes the data
A symmetric key can only encrypt small pieces of data, such as a single password
Symmetric encryption is too slow to handle large amounts of depot data
Both depots must already share the key, and sending it openly would let an eavesdropper read all traffic
questions.why: Symmetric encryption is fast but suffers from the key distribution problem: the shared key has to reach both sides safely before use.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming startup must send about 800 MB of recorded footage every hour from cameras to a cloud server. The cameras have the server's public key but share no secret with it. Which design best fits this scenario?
choices: Encrypt all footage with the camera's own private key so only the server can read it
Encrypt footage with a random session key and send that key encrypted with the server's public key
Encrypt all footage with the server's public key, because public-key encryption is more secure
Encrypt all footage with a symmetric key and send that key unencrypted alongside it
questions.why: Hybrid encryption lets fast symmetric encryption handle the large footage while slow public-key encryption only protects the small session key in transit.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a payments company changes the API so every request and response, including large reports, is encrypted directly with RSA (a public-key algorithm) instead of the usual TLS pattern, believing this makes the system more secure. What is the most likely result in production?
choices: CPU use and latency rise sharply and large payloads hit size limits, with no real security gain
Security improves noticeably and performance stays about the same
Nothing changes, since TLS already encrypts all traffic with RSA anyway
Clients can no longer decrypt anything, because RSA cannot be used for confidentiality
questions.why: Asymmetric encryption is far slower and suited only to small data, so using it for everything wastes CPU, adds delay, and runs into size limits, while TLS gets its security from using each tool on the right job.
