lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a protocol like TLS uses both symmetric and asymmetric encryption instead of just one, and name the main limitation each type has on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: Symmetric encryption uses one shared key to lock and unlock. It is fast enough for bulk data, but its limitation is distribution: both sides need the same secret first, and you cannot safely send it over an untrusted network in the clear. Asymmetric encryption uses a public key anyone can use to encrypt and a private key only the owner can decrypt with, so no shared secret is needed in advance. Its limitation is speed and size: it is far slower and only practical for small data. So TLS uses them together. Public-key techniques at the start let the two sides establish a fresh session key securely, then all the actual traffic is encrypted symmetrically with that session key. Using asymmetric for everything would be slow; using symmetric alone would leave no safe way to agree on the key.
rubricPoints: Symmetric uses one shared key and is fast for large data.
Symmetric's weakness is safely distributing the shared key.
Asymmetric uses a public/private key pair, so the public key can be shared openly.
Asymmetric's weakness is that it is slow and suited only to small data.
Hybrid systems like TLS use asymmetric methods to establish a session key, then symmetric encryption for the bulk traffic.

suggested.rationale: The unit's goal is defending a symmetric-versus-asymmetric choice for a stated scenario, which is best built by reasoning through exam-style situations.

lessons.plain: Hashing and encryption both scramble data, but for different jobs. Hashing turns any input into a short fixed-size fingerprint that cannot be turned back into the original; it answers "has this changed?" Encryption locks data with a key so only key holders can unlock and read it; it answers "who can see this?" Think of a hash as a wax seal impression, which shows tampering but carries no letter, and encryption as a locked box that hides the letter. Neither, on its own, tells you who really sent something, and a seal impression of a very short, guessable message can be matched just by trying guesses.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website stores a fingerprint of your password instead of the password itself, and the fingerprint cannot be reversed. If an attacker steals that list of fingerprints, can they still learn common passwords like "summer2024"? How might they do it?
lessons.teach:
A hash function is a fixed recipe that turns any input into a short, fixed-length output called a digest. It uses no key and is one-way: given a digest, there is no practical way to compute the input. A cryptographic hash also makes it infeasible to find two inputs with the same digest (collision resistance), and changing one input bit changes the digest completely. Encryption is a reversible transformation that uses a key: readable data (plaintext) becomes scrambled data (ciphertext), and anyone holding the right key can decrypt it back.

So they guarantee different things. Hashing supports integrity checking: if you already hold a trusted digest, you can detect whether data changed. Encryption gives confidentiality: only key holders can read the data.

Worked example: you download a large file, and the publisher lists its SHA-256 digest. Step 1, hash your downloaded copy. Step 2, compare the two digests. Step 3, a match means your copy is byte-for-byte what was hashed; a mismatch means corruption or tampering. Nothing was hidden: the file was readable throughout.

What neither does alone: a bare hash does not prove who produced the data, because an attacker who can swap the file may also swap the listed digest; proving origin needs a secret key. Plain encryption does not by itself detect that ciphertext was altered or show who sent it, which is why modern schemes bundle an integrity check with encryption. And a hash does not hide small, guessable inputs: an attacker can hash every likely value and look for matches.

Common mistake: calling password storage "encrypting passwords", or storing passwords under a plain fast hash. Because many passwords are guessable, an attacker who steals the digest table hashes a dictionary of guesses at enormous speed and recovers many accounts. In a running system, a database leak becomes account takeover. Proper storage uses a salt (a random value stored per user and mixed into the hash, so identical passwords get different digests) plus a deliberately slow hash, never reversible encryption.

questions.prompt: A small gym's member app stores each member's 4-digit door PIN as a plain SHA-256 digest, with no salt. An attacker steals the table of 3,200 digests. Trace the attack. Step 1: the attacker notes there are only 10,000 possible PINs (0000 to 9999). Step 2: ______. Step 3: the attacker looks up each stolen digest in that list and reads off the matching PIN, recovering every member's PIN within seconds. Step 4: members who share the same PIN all have identical digests, so one match exposes all of them at once. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Search for a second PIN that collides with each stolen digest, since a collision unlocks the door
Use the hash function's secret key to decrypt each stolen digest back to its PIN
Reverse the SHA-256 recipe mathematically, working backwards from each digest to its input
Run SHA-256 on every one of the 10,000 possible PINs and record each PIN next to its digest
questions.why: A hash has no key and cannot practically be reversed, but a small, guessable input space lets the attacker hash every candidate and match digests, which is why plain fast hashes fail for PINs and passwords.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm must send its quarterly salary spreadsheet across the internet so that only the payroll team can read the figures. Which approach provides that guarantee?
choices: Compute a cryptographic digest of the spreadsheet and send the digest in place of the file
Add a random salt to the spreadsheet and hash it with a deliberately slow hash
Send the file openly along with its digest so payroll can check that nothing changed
Encrypt the spreadsheet with a key that only the payroll team holds, so they can decrypt it
questions.why: Confidentiality, meaning only key holders can read the data, comes from reversible encryption with a key; a digest only supports integrity checking and cannot be turned back into the readable spreadsheet.

questions.prompt: A volunteer-run mirror site hosts a photo-editing installer, and the digest for checking it sits on the same web page. An attacker gains control of the site. You download the installer, hash it, and your digest matches the one on the page. What does the match prove?
choices: The installer was encrypted in transit, so nobody could have read or altered it
The installer is safe, because collision resistance stops any attacker from producing a match
Only that your copy matches the posted digest, which the attacker could have replaced too
The installer definitely came from the original developers, because the digests match
questions.why: A bare hash does not prove who produced the data; an attacker who can swap the file can also swap the listed digest, so proving origin needs a secret key.

questions.prompt: A logistics company encrypts shipment orders with a shared key, using plain encryption with no integrity check bundled in. An attacker on the network flips some bits in one ciphertext before it arrives. What should the company expect?
choices: The receiver may decrypt altered or garbled data with no warning that it was changed
The attacker learns the shared key, because altering ciphertext reveals how it was made
Decryption fails safely and reports tampering, because only key holders can change ciphertext
Nothing changes, because encryption keeps the readable data hidden and therefore unchanged
questions.why: Plain encryption gives confidentiality but does not by itself detect that ciphertext was altered, which is why modern schemes bundle an integrity check with encryption.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "Hashing and encryption are basically the same, so let's just encrypt user passwords." Explain to them in your own words what each one guarantees, what neither guarantees on its own, and why that suggestion is a poor tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: They solve different problems. A hash is a keyless, one-way fingerprint: you can't reverse it, and any change to the input changes the digest, so it lets you check integrity against a digest you already trust. Encryption is reversible with a key and gives confidentiality: only key holders can read the data. Neither proves who sent something on its own; that needs a secret key used for authentication, and plain encryption doesn't detect tampering unless an integrity check is added. For passwords we never need to read them back, only to compare, so reversible encryption adds risk: steal the key and every password is exposed. But a plain fast hash isn't enough either, because passwords are guessable and attackers can hash dictionaries quickly. The right choice is a salted, deliberately slow hash.
rubricPoints: Hashing is keyless and one-way, producing a fixed-size digest used to detect changes.
Encryption is reversible with a key and provides confidentiality.
Neither alone proves who created or sent the data.
A plain hash does not protect guessable inputs, because attackers can hash guesses and compare.
Passwords should be stored with salted, deliberately slow hashing, not reversible encryption.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is distinguishing the two guarantees and their gaps clearly, which is best tested by explaining it back rather than by any current mission.

lessons.plain: A digital signature is a mathematical stamp attached to a message that lets anyone check two things: the message has not changed since it was stamped, and it was stamped by whoever holds one particular secret key. Think of a wax seal pressed with a unique ring. If the seal is intact and matches the ring's known pattern, you know the letter was sealed by the ring's holder and nobody opened it. What the seal does not tell you is who that holder really is, whether the ring was stolen, when the letter was sealed, or whether it is an old letter being handed to you twice.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you receive a message reading "transfer 100 to Bob" with a valid digital signature from Alice's key. List what you think you can now be sure of, and one thing you think you still cannot be sure of.
lessons.teach:
A digital signature is a value computed from a message and a private key that anyone holding the matching public key can check. It uses a key pair: a private key, kept secret by its owner, and a public key, shared openly. The two are mathematically linked so that only the private key can produce a signature, but the public key can confirm it.

In practice the signer first runs the message through a hash function, which turns any input into a short fixed-size fingerprint where any change to the input changes the fingerprint unpredictably. The signer then applies the private key to that fingerprint. That result is the signature. To verify, the receiver hashes the message they received, then uses the public key to check that the signature matches this fingerprint.

Worked example. Alice wants to send "pay Bob 100". Step 1: she hashes it and gets fingerprint H. Step 2: she signs H with her private key, producing signature S. Step 3: she sends the message plus S. Step 4: an attacker changes the text to "pay Bob 900". Step 5: the receiver hashes "pay Bob 900" and gets H2, not H. Step 6: checking S against H2 with Alice's public key fails, so the change is caught.

So a valid signature proves integrity, meaning the message is unchanged, and origin, meaning it was signed by whoever holds that private key. It does not hide the message, because signing is not encryption. It does not prove that the key belongs to a real person named Alice. That binding needs something extra, such as a certificate. It also cannot detect a stolen key, and it says nothing about when the message was sent.

A common mistake is treating a valid signature as "this request is fresh and legitimate". An attacker can resend Alice's genuine signed "pay Bob 100" ten times, and every copy will verify. In a running system that means duplicate payments, unless each signed message includes a unique number or timestamp that the receiver checks and records.

questions.prompt: A thermostat maker, Kelvo, ships firmware version 3.2 and wants every thermostat to refuse tampered files. Step 1: Kelvo runs the firmware file through a hash function and gets fingerprint F. Step 2: Kelvo applies its private key to F, producing signature G. Step 3: Kelvo posts the firmware file and G on its download server. Step 4: a thermostat downloads both the file and G. Step 5: (missing). Step 6: the thermostat uses Kelvo's public key, which was built in at the factory, to check G against the fingerprint from Step 5. If the check fails, it refuses to install. Which action belongs in Step 5?
choices: The thermostat uses Kelvo's public key to decrypt the firmware file so it can read the original contents
The thermostat runs the downloaded firmware file through the same hash function to get its own fingerprint
The thermostat applies its own private key to G so the signature becomes unique to that device
The thermostat asks the download server for fingerprint F and uses that value for the check
questions.why: Verification only catches tampering if the receiver hashes the file it actually received and checks the signature against that fresh fingerprint, rather than trusting a fingerprint supplied by someone else.

questions.prompt: A payroll system at Northgate Clinic receives the message "set nurse overtime rate to 42" with a digital signature. The signature verifies correctly with the HR department's public key. What does this valid signature establish?
choices: The key pair definitely belongs to a real, named HR manager
The message is unchanged and was signed by whoever holds HR's private key
The message was hidden from anyone who intercepted it on the network
The message was sent within the last few minutes and is not a repeat
questions.why: A valid signature proves integrity and origin from the private-key holder only. It does not provide secrecy, tie the key to a real person, or say anything about when the message was sent.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's port system accepts signed commands. An attacker records a genuine signed command, "release container 4471", and sends the identical copy three more times. Each copy has the original, untouched signature. What happens, and what prevents the harm?
choices: Every copy verifies. The fix is to include a unique number or timestamp in each signed command, which the receiver checks and records
Copies 2 to 4 fail verification, because a signature can only be checked once before it expires
Every copy verifies. The fix is to encrypt the command, because encryption stops a valid signature from being reused
Copies 2 to 4 fail verification, because resending a message changes its hash fingerprint
questions.why: An exact copy has the same contents and the same signature, so it verifies every time. Only a unique number or timestamp that the receiver checks and records lets it reject the repeats.

questions.prompt: Someone copies a contractor's private key from an unlocked laptop. The thief signs "grant admin access to user dmitri" and sends it to a company server. The server checks the signature with the contractor's public key, and the check passes. Why didn't the signature catch this?
choices: The server should have used the contractor's private key to check the signature instead
Signatures prove only that a message is secret, not who it came from, so origin was never checked
A signature only shows the message was signed by whoever holds the private key, so it cannot detect a stolen key
The hash function failed, because a short command like this produces a weak fingerprint
questions.why: Verification confirms that the matching private key produced the signature. It cannot tell whether the rightful owner or a thief was holding that key.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a valid digital signature on an incoming API request actually proves, and name at least two things it does not prove that your service would still need to handle.
lessons.modelAnswer: A digital signature is made by hashing the message and applying the sender's private key to that hash. We verify it by hashing what we received and checking the signature with the sender's public key. If the check passes, we know two things. The bytes weren't altered in transit, and they were signed by whoever holds that private key. That's all it tells us. It doesn't keep the request secret, because signing isn't encryption. It doesn't tell us the public key really belongs to the partner we think it does. We have to get the key from somewhere we trust, like a certificate. It can't tell us the key hasn't been stolen. It also doesn't tell us the request is fresh. Someone could replay a genuine signed request. So our service still has to include and check a nonce or timestamp, and it needs a way to revoke compromised keys.
rubricPoints: A signature is created with the private key over a hash of the message and checked with the public key.
A valid signature proves the message is unchanged since signing.
It proves the signer held the matching private key, not who that person is.
Signing does not provide confidentiality.
It does not prevent replay, so freshness needs a nonce or timestamp.
It cannot detect a stolen key, and binding a key to an identity needs something like a certificate.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is stating precisely what a signature does and does not prove, which is best practised by explaining it back, and no listed mission or engine exercises signatures directly.

lessons.plain: Key exchange is how two parties who have never met agree on a shared secret key while someone listens to every message they send. Diffie-Hellman is the classic method. Picture mixing paint. You both start with the same public colour. Each of you secretly adds your own private colour and sends the mixture across. Each then adds their private colour to the other's mixture. You both end with the same final colour. The eavesdropper saw only the starting colour and the two mixtures, and un-mixing paint is hard, so they cannot work out the final colour.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two people can only talk on a phone line that a stranger is recording. Without ever having met, can they end up agreeing on a secret number the stranger does not know? What would they need to be true about the maths for that to work?
lessons.teach:
Diffie-Hellman (DH) is a key exchange method. Two parties use it to build a shared secret, a value that only they know, over a channel an eavesdropper can read. It uses modular arithmetic. "x mod p" means the remainder after dividing x by p.

The two parties first agree in public on two numbers: a large prime modulus p and a generator g. Each then picks a private number and keeps it to themselves. Alice picks a, and Bob picks b. Alice sends A = g^a mod p and Bob sends B = g^b mod p. Alice computes B^a mod p and Bob computes A^b mod p. Both results equal g^(ab) mod p, so the two of them now hold the same value.

This is secure because computing g^a mod p is fast, but recovering a from the result is very hard when p is large. Recovering a this way is called the discrete logarithm problem. An eavesdropper sees p, g, A and B, but cannot combine A and B into g^(ab) without knowing a or b.

Here is a worked example with tiny numbers, where p = 23 and g = 5. Alice chooses a = 6, so she sends 5^6 mod 23, which is 8. Bob chooses b = 15, so he sends 5^15 mod 23, which is 19. Alice computes 19^6 mod 23, which is 2. Bob computes 8^15 mod 23, which is also 2. Their shared secret is 2. Real systems use numbers hundreds of digits long, or elliptic curves, which are a related kind of maths with smaller keys. The shared secret is then turned into a key for fast symmetric encryption.

A common mistake is thinking DH proves who you are talking to. It does not. In a man-in-the-middle attack, an attacker sits between the two parties and runs one exchange with Alice and a separate one with Bob. The attacker can then read and re-encrypt all traffic, and neither side notices. A running system therefore has to authenticate the exchanged values, for example by having them signed by a key tied to a certificate. Fresh private values for each session (called ephemeral DH) also give forward secrecy: a server key stolen later cannot decrypt past recorded sessions.

questions.prompt: Two hospital servers, Ward and Lab, set up a shared secret over a network that anyone can read. In public they agree on p = 11 and g = 2. Ward privately picks a = 3 and sends A = 2^3 mod 11 = 8. Lab privately picks b = 4 and sends B = 2^4 mod 11 = 16 mod 11 = 5. Ward computes B^a mod 11 = 5^3 mod 11 = 125 mod 11 = 4. Missing step: what does Lab compute to get its copy of the shared secret, and what is the result?
choices: Lab computes 8 × 4 mod 11 = 10, multiplying Ward's public value by its private number
Lab computes 8^4 mod 11 = 4, raising Ward's public value to its own private number
Lab computes 2^(3+4) mod 11 = 7, adding the two private numbers in the exponent
Lab computes 5^4 mod 11 = 9, raising its own public value to its private number
questions.why: Each side raises the other side's public value to its own private number, so Lab computes A^b = 8^4 mod 11 = 4, which matches Ward's result because both equal g^(ab) mod p = 2^12 mod 11 = 4.

questions.prompt: An eavesdropper records a Diffie-Hellman exchange between a bank branch and its head office. The eavesdropper captures the public prime p, the generator g, and both sent values A and B, where p is hundreds of digits long. Why can't the eavesdropper work out the shared secret?
choices: To get the secret they would need a private number, and recovering it from g^a mod p (the discrete logarithm problem) is very hard when p is large
The prime p is kept secret by both parties, so the eavesdropper cannot reduce any value mod p
A and B are encrypted with a symmetric key before they are sent, so the eavesdropper only sees scrambled data
Multiplying A and B gives the secret, but that multiplication takes too long with numbers hundreds of digits long
questions.why: The eavesdropper sees p, g, A and B, but combining A and B into g^(ab) mod p requires a or b, and finding them means solving the discrete logarithm problem, which is very hard for a large p.

questions.prompt: A laptop on a café Wi-Fi network runs a plain Diffie-Hellman exchange with a mail server. Neither side signs or otherwise authenticates the values it sends. An attacker controls the café's router. What can the attacker do, and what would stop it?
choices: Read only the public values p and g; this is harmless and needs no fix
Nothing useful, because Diffie-Hellman keeps the shared secret hidden from anyone on the path
Run one exchange with the laptop and a separate one with the server, then read and re-encrypt all traffic unnoticed; signing the exchanged values with a key tied to a certificate stops this
Recover the private numbers by watching many exchanges; using a larger prime would stop this
questions.why: Diffie-Hellman does not prove who you are talking to, so an attacker in the middle can run two separate exchanges, a man-in-the-middle attack, unless the exchanged values are authenticated, for example by a certificate-linked signature.

questions.prompt: An online retailer's servers used ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, meaning fresh private values for every session. An attacker recorded encrypted customer sessions in March. In October the attacker steals the server's long-term key. What happens to the recorded March sessions?
choices: They stay protected only if the retailer switches to elliptic curves before the theft
They can be decrypted, because ephemeral Diffie-Hellman sends the shared secret alongside the public values
They can now be decrypted, because the long-term key lets the attacker rebuild every past shared secret
They stay protected, because each session's secret came from fresh private values that the stolen key cannot reveal (forward secrecy)
questions.why: With ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, each session's secret depends on fresh private values rather than the server's long-term key, so stealing that key later cannot decrypt past recorded sessions; this property is called forward secrecy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how Diffie-Hellman lets two strangers agree on a key over a public channel, and name the main thing it does not protect against on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both sides agree publicly on a big prime p and a generator g. Each picks a private number, raises g to it mod p, and sends the result. Each then raises the value they received to their own private number. Both land on g^(ab) mod p, which becomes the shared secret. An eavesdropper sees p, g and the two public values. To get the secret they would have to undo the exponentiation, which is the discrete logarithm problem and is infeasible at real key sizes. The shared secret is then used to derive a symmetric key for the actual data. The limit is that plain DH has no authentication. A man-in-the-middle can run separate exchanges with each side and relay the traffic. So the exchanged values must be signed or tied to certificates. Using fresh values for each session also gives forward secrecy.
rubricPoints: Public parameters p and g are shared openly, and each side keeps a private number.
Each side sends g raised to its private number mod p, and both compute the same g^(ab) mod p.
Security rests on the discrete logarithm being hard to reverse even when the public values are seen.
The result is used to derive a symmetric key rather than to encrypt data directly.
Plain DH does not authenticate, so it is open to a man-in-the-middle unless the values are signed.
Ephemeral keys for each session give forward secrecy.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine performs a key exchange, and the core skill here is explaining the mechanism and its authentication gap clearly.

lessons.plain: A TLS handshake is the short opening conversation a browser and a server have before any private data moves between them. In a few quick messages they agree on how to scramble their traffic, the server proves it really is the site you asked for, and both sides end up holding the same fresh secret key that nobody listening in could work out. Think of two strangers meeting to swap documents. First they agree on a language, then one shows a government-issued ID, and finally they settle on a code word only they know. Only after that do they talk business.
lessons.guessPrompt: Before your browser sends your password to a website, what two or three things do you think it needs to check or agree on with the server first?
lessons.teach:
A TLS handshake is the opening exchange between a client (such as a browser) and a server before any real data flows. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol behind HTTPS. The handshake establishes three things. The first is the cipher suite, meaning the set of algorithms both sides will use. The second is authentication, meaning proof that the server is who it claims to be. The third is a fresh session key, a shared secret used for fast symmetric encryption, where the same key locks and unlocks the data.

Here is a simplified trace in the style of TLS 1.3. Step 1, ClientHello: the client lists the cipher suites it supports, a nonce (a one-time random value), and its half of a Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Diffie-Hellman is a method where each side combines its own private value with the other side's public value, and both arrive at the same secret without ever sending it. Step 2, ServerHello: the server picks a suite and sends its own nonce and key-exchange half. Both sides now compute the shared secret and derive session keys from it. Step 3, Certificate: the server sends its certificate. This is a document that binds a domain name to a public key and is vouched for by a certificate authority, a trusted issuer. Step 4, CertificateVerify: the server signs a hash (a fixed-size fingerprint) of the whole conversation so far with its private key. This proves it holds the key the certificate names. Step 5, Finished: each side sends a keyed check over the full transcript. If anyone altered an earlier message, the checks disagree and the connection aborts.

Why this works: the key exchange gives secrecy, and the signature ties that exchange to the real server. Because the key-exchange values are fresh each time, a later theft of the server's long-term key cannot decrypt recorded past sessions. This property is called forward secrecy.

A common mistake is believing the certificate's key encrypts your data. It only signs; your data uses the session key. Skipping certificate checks is the dangerous version of this. The connection is still encrypted, but possibly to an impostor in the middle. In production, an expired certificate makes every handshake fail and every connection errors out.

questions.prompt: A smart thermostat made by a company called CoolHome opens a TLS connection to its cloud server at api.coolhome.example. Here is what happens, mostly worked out for you. First, the thermostat sends the cipher suites it supports, a fresh random nonce and its half of a Diffie-Hellman exchange. Second, the server picks one suite and replies with its own nonce and its own key-exchange half; both sides now compute the same shared secret without either one sending it, and they derive session keys from it. Third, the server sends a certificate that binds the name api.coolhome.example to a public key and is vouched for by a certificate authority. Fourth: MISSING STEP. Fifth, each side sends a keyed check over the full conversation, the checks match, and temperature readings start flowing, encrypted with the session key. Which choice correctly fills in the fourth step?
choices: The server signs a hash of the whole conversation so far with its private key, and the thermostat checks that signature using the public key in the certificate, proving the server holds the key the certificate names.
The thermostat checks that the certificate is signed by a certificate authority; because the certificate is publicly signed, nothing further is needed to show the server is genuine.
The server encrypts the session key with the certificate's public key and sends it, so that the thermostat can unlock it with that same public key.
The server sends its private key in encrypted form so the thermostat can confirm it matches the public key in the certificate.
questions.why: A certificate is a public document that anyone could copy and replay, so the server must also sign the conversation with the matching private key to prove it really owns the certificate's key.

questions.prompt: An attacker quietly records encrypted HTTPS traffic between customers and an online bookshop throughout 2023. In 2025 the attacker steals the bookshop server's long-term private key, the one named in its certificate. The connections used a TLS 1.3-style handshake with a fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange each time. Can the attacker now decrypt the recorded 2023 sessions?
choices: Yes. The long-term private key encrypted every session key, so with that key the attacker can unlock each recorded session one by one.
Yes, but only for sessions that used the same cipher suite as the one the stolen key belongs to.
No, but only because the certificate expired before 2025; an unexpired certificate's key would decrypt the old sessions.
No. Each session key came from fresh key-exchange values that were never sent and are gone now, so the long-term key alone cannot rebuild them. This property is called forward secrecy.
questions.why: Session keys come from per-connection Diffie-Hellman values, and the long-term key only signs, so stealing it later does not reveal past session keys.

questions.prompt: A developer on a payments team keeps getting certificate errors when one internal service calls another. To make the errors go away, they switch off certificate checking in the calling service, and the connection now succeeds over TLS. What is the real consequence?
choices: None worth worrying about. The traffic is still encrypted with a session key, so nobody else can read it.
The traffic is still encrypted, but the service no longer knows who it is talking to, so it could be sending payment data, encrypted, to an impostor sitting in the middle.
Every handshake will now fail, because a certificate check is needed to compute the session key.
The connection stops being encrypted, because the certificate's key is what encrypts the data.
questions.why: Encryption comes from the key exchange, while the certificate check is what proves the other side is genuine. Skipping it keeps the secrecy but loses the authentication.

questions.prompt: A clinic's laptop starts a TLS connection to a patient-records server. Along the way, a tampering network device edits the laptop's opening message to delete the strongest cipher suites, hoping to force a weaker choice. Neither endpoint notices at first. What happens when the handshake finishes?
choices: The connection continues, but the session key is regenerated automatically using the strongest suite.
The handshake completes on the weaker suite, because the server can only pick from what it was shown.
The keyed checks that each side sends over the full conversation do not match, because the two sides saw different messages, so the connection aborts.
The server's certificate is rejected, because certificates list which cipher suites are allowed.
questions.why: The final checks cover the whole transcript, so any change to an earlier message makes them disagree and the connection is ended.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what a TLS handshake establishes and in what order. Then name one thing it does not protect against, or one way it can break in a running system.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before any app data moves, client and server run a handshake that settles three things. First, the client offers algorithms, a random nonce and its half of a Diffie-Hellman exchange. The server picks an algorithm set and sends its own half, and now both compute the same secret without ever sending it. Next, the server sends its certificate, which binds its domain name to a public key and is backed by a certificate authority. It then signs a hash of the conversation so far, proving it owns that key. Finally, both sides exchange Finished checks over the whole transcript, so any tampering aborts the connection. After that, traffic uses fast symmetric session keys. Its limit is that it only proves you reached whoever holds that certificate. If the client skips validation, or a trusted authority misissues a certificate, you get encryption to an impostor. Operationally, an expired certificate breaks every connection.
rubricPoints: States that the handshake agrees on algorithms (the cipher suite).
Explains that a key exchange gives both sides a shared secret that is never sent over the wire.
Explains that the certificate plus a signature over the transcript authenticates the server.
Notes that Finished checks over the transcript detect tampering with earlier messages.
Says bulk data uses symmetric session keys, not the certificate's key.
Names a limit or failure mode, such as skipped validation, a misissued certificate, or expiry.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine walks through a TLS handshake, so the core skill is tracing and explaining the message sequence and what each step guarantees.

lessons.plain: Public key infrastructure, or PKI, is the system that lets you trust that a public key really belongs to the website or server it claims to belong to. A certificate is a small digital document that says, in effect, this name goes with this public key. A certificate authority is an organisation that checks the claim and vouches for it. Think of a passport: you trust it not because you know the traveller, but because you trust the government that issued it. Your computer arrives already trusting a short list of issuers, and that trust is passed down a chain to millions of sites.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your browser has never seen a particular shopping website before, yet it can tell whether the site's public key is genuine. Where do you think that confidence comes from, if not from the site itself?
lessons.teach:
A public key is the half of a key pair you can share openly. Its partner, the private key, is kept secret by its owner. A certificate is a file that binds a name, such as shop.example, to a public key. It also records who issued it and when it expires. A certificate authority (CA) is a trusted party that checks the requester controls that name and then signs the certificate. A signature here means the CA used its own private key to stamp the certificate so anyone holding the CA's public key can detect forgery or tampering.

CAs are layered. A root CA is a top-level authority whose certificate is preinstalled in your operating system or browser trust store, the built-in list of issuers you trust. Roots usually sign intermediate CAs, which sign the leaf certificate, the one the website actually presents. The chain of trust is the path from leaf up to a trusted root.

Worked example: you visit shop.example. The server sends its leaf certificate plus the intermediate. Step one: your browser checks the leaf names shop.example and has not expired. Step two: it checks the intermediate's signature on the leaf. Step three: it checks the root's signature on the intermediate. Step four: it finds that root in the trust store. Every link holds, so the browser accepts shop.example's public key.

What this proves is narrow: a CA you trust confirmed that whoever holds this key controls this name. It does not prove the site is honest, safe or well run. A common mistake is reading the padlock as a statement that the business is legitimate; a scam site can hold a perfectly valid certificate.

In a running system, chains break in ordinary ways. An expired certificate makes every client refuse to connect, causing an outage. A server that forgets to send the intermediate may work in one browser that cached it and fail in others. A stolen private key needs the certificate revoked, meaning the CA declares it no longer valid before its expiry.

questions.prompt: A payroll app connects to api.ledgerline.example. The server sends three certificates: its leaf, Intermediate B (which signed the leaf), and Intermediate A (which signed Intermediate B). The root that signed Intermediate A is in the app's trust store. The app checks the chain like this. Step 1: the leaf names api.ledgerline.example and is valid until March 2027, so the name and date are fine. Step 2: it verifies Intermediate B's signature on the leaf. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: it verifies the root's signature on Intermediate A. Step 5: it finds that root in its trust store and accepts the leaf's public key. What is Step 3?
choices: It looks for Intermediate B in the trust store and stops if found
It confirms that Ledgerline is an honest, well-run business
It verifies the root's signature directly on the leaf certificate
It verifies Intermediate A's signature on Intermediate B
questions.why: A chain of trust is only unbroken if every link is checked, so the app must confirm that Intermediate A really signed Intermediate B before moving up to the root.

questions.prompt: A shopper visits greenleaf-garden.example. The browser shows a padlock because the site's certificate chain validated cleanly to a trusted root. What does this actually prove?
choices: A certificate authority the browser trusts confirmed that whoever holds this key controls greenleaf-garden.example
The website has been scanned and contains no malware or scam content
The certificate can never expire or be revoked while the padlock is shown
Greenleaf Garden is a legitimate, registered business that will ship the orders it takes
questions.why: A valid chain only shows that a trusted CA confirmed control of the name for that public key; it says nothing about the site's honesty or safety, and a scam site can hold a valid certificate.

questions.prompt: A team deploys a new certificate on portal.northwind.example. A developer tests it in their desktop browser and it works. The next day, many phone users report certificate errors on the same site. The leaf is unexpired and names the right domain. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The leaf certificate names the wrong website
The server sends only the leaf and not the intermediate, and the desktop browser had the intermediate cached
The phones' clocks are all set to a date before the certificate was issued
The root CA certificate has been removed from every phone
questions.why: Without the intermediate, a client cannot build the path from leaf to root unless it happens to have the intermediate cached, so the site works in some clients and fails in others.

questions.prompt: An attacker steals the private key for the certificate of billing.harborline.example. The certificate still has eight months before it expires. What should the site's owner do about that certificate?
choices: Leave it in place, since it will become invalid on its own in eight months
Have the CA revoke it so it is declared invalid before its expiry date
Ask users to reinstall the root CA in their trust stores
Ask the CA to sign the same certificate again with a later expiry date
questions.why: Whoever holds the stolen private key can pose as the site until the certificate is invalid, so it must be revoked, meaning the CA declares it no longer valid before it expires.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a certificate chain actually proves when a browser shows a valid connection to a site, walking through how the chain is checked, and name one thing it does not prove or one way it can fail in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: A certificate binds a name, like shop.example, to a public key. A certificate authority vouches for that binding by signing the certificate with its private key after checking the requester controls the name. The site sends its leaf certificate and usually an intermediate. The browser checks the leaf's name and expiry, verifies the intermediate signed the leaf, verifies a root signed the intermediate, and confirms that root is in its preinstalled trust store. If every link holds, the browser trusts the key. What that proves is only that a trusted CA confirmed the key holder controls the name. It says nothing about whether the site is honest, since scammers can get valid certificates. It can also fail operationally: an expired certificate breaks all clients, and a missing intermediate breaks some clients but not others.
rubricPoints: A certificate binds a name to a public key and is signed by an issuer.
A certificate authority checks control of the name and signs to vouch for it.
Trust flows from a preinstalled root through intermediates to the leaf, each link checked by signature.
A valid chain proves name-to-key control, not that the site is trustworthy.
Names a practical failure such as expiry, a missing intermediate, or a compromised key needing revocation.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine exercises certificate chains, and the unit's mastery goal is to explain precisely what a chain proves and does not prove.

lessons.plain: Computers talk to each other through a stack of layers, each with one job. The TCP/IP model names four: one moves data across a single local network, one routes it between networks, one delivers it to the right program on a machine, and the top one is the language programs actually speak, like web pages or email. Think of mailing a letter. There is the local carrier, the postal routing system, the apartment number, and the letter's content. An attacker can tamper at any of those points. Knowing which layer an attack targets tells you which defense can even see it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are on café Wi-Fi and someone at the next table wants to secretly read your traffic. Would it be easier for them to trick your laptop about which device is the local router, or to break into the website you are visiting? Why?
lessons.teach:
The TCP/IP model describes network communication as four stacked layers. The link layer moves frames, or chunks of data, between devices on the same local network, using hardware addresses called MAC addresses. The internet layer moves packets between networks using IP addresses, and routers forward them along the way. The transport layer delivers data to the right program on a machine, which is identified by a port number. It uses TCP, a reliable connection protocol, or UDP, a fire-and-forget one. The application layer holds the protocols programs speak: HTTP for the web, DNS for turning names into IP addresses, and SSH for remote login.

Attacks sort by layer because each layer trusts something different. At the link layer, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) maps IP addresses to MAC addresses without checking who is answering. In ARP spoofing, an attacker claims to be the router and sits in the middle of your traffic. At the internet layer, IP spoofing forges the sender's address, and ICMP floods bury a target in control messages. At the transport layer, attackers use port scanning and SYN floods. At the application layer, you find DNS cache poisoning, password brute force against SSH, and injection into web apps.

Here is a SYN flood traced step by step. Normally TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake: the client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK and stores a half-open entry, and the client answers ACK. In a flood, the attacker first sends thousands of SYNs from spoofed addresses. The server then sends each SYN-ACK to an address that never replies. Its half-open table fills up, and real clients get dropped. One transport-layer defense is SYN cookies, which encode the connection details in the reply so the server stores nothing until the ACK arrives.

A common mistake is thinking TLS (the encryption behind HTTPS) protects every layer. It protects application data in transit, but it does not stop floods or port scans. In a running system, a site can have HTTPS and still be knocked offline.

questions.prompt: A public library's IT team sorts three overnight security alerts by TCP/IP layer, so each one goes to the right defense. Alert 1: a laptop on the guest Wi-Fi keeps answering ARP requests, claiming to be the gateway router. This is a link-layer attack, because it abuses the unchecked mapping of IP addresses to MAC (hardware) addresses on the local network. Alert 2: 40,000 password guesses hit the library's SSH (remote login) server. This is an application-layer attack, because SSH is a protocol that programs speak. Alert 3: one outside address sends probes to ports 1 through 1024 on the library's mail server and records which ones reply. Which classification and reasoning complete Alert 3?
choices: Internet layer, because the probes come from an outside IP address and routers forward them between networks.
Link layer, because the probes must arrive at the server's network card, which is identified by a MAC address.
Application layer, because the target is a mail server, and mail is a program running at the application layer.
Transport layer, because this is port scanning, and port numbers identify which program on a machine receives data.
questions.why: Probing a range of ports to see which reply is port scanning, and ports belong to the transport layer, which delivers data to the right program.

questions.prompt: A small design studio runs a file server and a chat server on the same machine. When data arrives at that machine, which piece of information decides which of the two programs receives it, and which TCP/IP layer uses it?
choices: The port number, used by the transport layer
The MAC address, used by the link layer
The DNS name, used by the application layer
The IP address, used by the internet layer
questions.why: The transport layer delivers data to the right program on a machine, and it identifies that program by its port number.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing company serves every page over HTTPS. During a big concert sale, its servers stop accepting new connections. The logs show about 200,000 SYN messages from many random addresses, and almost none of them are followed by an ACK. Which defense targets this problem most directly?
choices: Require longer passwords on the SSH servers the operations staff use to log in
Turn on SYN cookies, so the server stores no half-open entry until a client's ACK arrives
Filter the server's DNS replies so that its cache cannot be poisoned with false addresses
Replace the TLS certificate with a stronger one so that the HTTPS encryption cannot be broken
questions.why: This is a transport-layer SYN flood that fills the half-open table, and SYN cookies stop the server from storing anything until the handshake completes.

questions.prompt: A credit union tells its members: "Our online banking portal uses HTTPS, so it is protected against network attacks." Which attack could still succeed against the portal despite HTTPS?
choices: Reading members' account numbers from the encrypted portal traffic while it crosses the internet
Knocking the portal offline with an ICMP flood that buries it in control messages
Quietly changing the contents of a portal page in transit without the encryption detecting it
None of these attacks, because TLS protects every layer of the TCP/IP model
questions.why: TLS (the encryption behind HTTPS) protects application data in transit, but it does not stop floods, so a site with HTTPS can still be knocked offline.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how the four TCP/IP layers map to common attacks, using one example per layer. Then name a limit: what can a defense working at one layer not see?
lessons.modelAnswer: TCP/IP splits networking into four layers. The link layer is the local network, using MAC addresses. The internet layer routes packets between networks by IP address. The transport layer uses TCP or UDP to deliver data to a program by port. The application layer is protocols like HTTP, DNS and SSH. Each layer trusts something, so each has its own attacks. ARP spoofing abuses unauthenticated address lookups on the local network. IP spoofing forges the sender's address. A SYN flood fills a server's half-open connection table. DNS poisoning or SSH brute force hits the application layer. The limit is that a control only sees its own layer. TLS encrypts application data but does nothing about a SYN flood or a port scan. SYN cookies stop the flood but cannot catch injection inside a valid web request. So you usually need defenses at several layers, and naming the layer tells you which tool fits.
rubricPoints: Names the four layers and what each one moves or identifies.
Gives a correct attack example for each layer.
Explains why attacks cluster by layer: each layer trusts something an attacker can abuse.
Traces or describes at least one attack mechanism, such as the SYN flood handshake.
States that a control at one layer cannot see attacks at another, using an example like TLS versus a flood.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is placing an unfamiliar attack scenario on the right layer and picking a matching control, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations rather than any current mission.

lessons.plain: A firewall, an intrusion detection system (IDS) and an intrusion prevention system (IPS) are three kinds of network guards that each watch different things. A firewall is like a building's front desk with a guest list: it checks who is coming in, from where, and to which door, then lets them in or turns them away. An IDS is like a security camera with someone reviewing the footage: it watches what visitors actually do and raises an alarm when something looks wrong. An IPS is that same watcher standing in the doorway with the power to stop someone on the spot.
lessons.guessPrompt: A firewall rule allows web traffic on port 443 to reach your company's web server. An attacker sends a harmful request to that server over port 443. Do you think the firewall will stop it, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A firewall is a filter that decides whether network traffic may pass, based mainly on addresses and ports. A packet is one small chunk of network data. Each packet carries labels: the source and destination address, and a port, which is a number identifying the service, such as 443 for secure web traffic. Firewall rules say things like "allow anyone to port 443, block everything else." A stateful firewall also remembers open conversations, so it can let replies come back without needing a separate rule. A firewall mostly reads these labels, not the message inside.

An intrusion detection system (IDS) inspects traffic contents and behaviour, then alerts a human. It uses signatures, which are known patterns of attacks, and anomaly detection, which flags traffic that differs from normal. An IDS usually watches a copy of the traffic, so it cannot block anything. An intrusion prevention system (IPS) does the same inspection but sits inline, meaning traffic actually flows through it, so it can drop bad packets.

Worked example: an attacker sends a web request to port 443 containing text crafted to trick the database. Step one, the firewall checks the labels: port 443 is allowed, so it passes. Step two, an IDS compares the content to its signatures, finds a match, and sends an alert; the request still reaches the server. Step three, with an IPS instead, the match causes the packet to be dropped, and the server never sees it.

A common mistake is believing a firewall stops attacks that ride on allowed ports. It does not, because it is not reading the content. Another limit: if traffic is encrypted and the IDS or IPS cannot decrypt it, it cannot read the content either.

In a running system, the tradeoff is the false positive, meaning legitimate traffic wrongly flagged. An IDS false positive wastes an analyst's time; an IPS false positive blocks real customers, so IPS rules must be tuned carefully.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain runs an online ordering site. Its firewall rule is "allow anyone to port 443, block everything else," and an IPS (a device that inspects traffic contents and sits inline, so all traffic flows through it) is placed in front of the web server. The ordering traffic is encrypted, and the IPS has not been given any way to decrypt it. An attacker sends an encrypted request to port 443 hiding a known attack pattern. Step 1: The firewall reads the labels, sees destination port 443, which is allowed, and passes the packet. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The web server receives the attacker's request. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The IPS cannot read the encrypted contents, so no signature matches and it lets the packet continue to the server.
The IPS sends an alert to an analyst but cannot drop the packet, because an IPS only watches a copy of the traffic.
The IPS matches the hidden pattern against its signatures and drops the packet, so it never reaches the server.
The IPS blocks the packet because encrypted traffic always differs from normal and triggers anomaly detection.
questions.why: An IPS can only match signatures against content it can read, so encrypted traffic it cannot decrypt passes through unrecognised, which is why the server receives the request in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A city water utility puts a security device in its network so that every packet must physically pass through it. The device compares packet contents with known attack patterns and discards matching packets. Which kind of device is this?
choices: An intrusion detection system (IDS)
A stateful firewall
A firewall that only reads ports
An intrusion prevention system (IPS)
questions.why: Inspecting contents against signatures and dropping packets while traffic flows through it (inline) is exactly what an IPS does.

questions.prompt: An employee at a design studio opens a web page, which sends a request out to a remote server. The studio's firewall has no rule allowing inbound traffic from that server, yet the page's reply arrives normally. What best explains this?
choices: An IDS saw the reply and alerted a human, who allowed it through.
The firewall is stateful, so it remembers the open conversation and lets the reply back in.
Replies to web requests never pass through a firewall at all.
The firewall read the reply's contents and judged them safe.
questions.why: A stateful firewall remembers conversations that were started from inside, so it can let replies return without a separate inbound rule.

questions.prompt: A ticket-sales company switches a rule from its IDS to its IPS. The rule wrongly flags about 2% of normal purchase requests as attacks. What is the most likely consequence after the switch?
choices: The firewall begins blocking port 443 to stop the flagged requests.
Nothing changes, because false positives only matter on an IDS.
About 2% of real customers now have their purchases blocked.
Analysts receive more alerts, but every purchase still goes through.
questions.why: An IPS sits inline and drops what it flags, so a false positive there blocks legitimate customers instead of just creating an alert for an analyst.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a firewall, an IDS and an IPS each actually look at, and why you might still choose an IDS over an IPS for some traffic. Name at least one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: A firewall filters traffic by its labels: where it comes from, where it is going, and which port or service it targets. It is good at shutting doors you never use, but if port 443 is open, an attack hidden inside a normal-looking web request walks right through. An IDS reads the contents and behaviour of traffic, matching known attack signatures or spotting unusual patterns, and raises an alert, but it only watches a copy, so it cannot stop anything. An IPS does the same inspection while sitting inline, so it can drop the bad packet. The tradeoff is false positives: when an IDS is wrong, someone reads a useless alert; when an IPS is wrong, real users get blocked. So for sensitive or business-critical traffic you might start with detection only until the rules are tuned. Both IDS and IPS are blind to encrypted content they cannot decrypt.
rubricPoints: A firewall decides allow or block mainly from addresses, ports and connection state, not message content.
An IDS inspects content and behaviour using signatures or anomaly detection and only alerts.
An IPS performs similar inspection but sits inline and can block traffic.
Attacks carried over an allowed port pass a firewall unless something inspects content.
False positives cost analyst time for an IDS but block legitimate users for an IPS.
Encrypted traffic that cannot be decrypted hides content from IDS and IPS.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning through attack scenarios to say which of the three controls would see, alert on, or block each one, which an exam-style situation exercises better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Defense-in-depth means protecting something valuable with several separate layers of protection, so that when one layer fails, another still stands in the way. Think of a bank: a locked front door, a guard, cameras, a vault, and a time lock on the vault. A thief who picks the door lock still faces the guard and the vault. The key idea is that every layer is expected to fail sometimes, so the layers must not all fail for the same reason. Simply piling on more of the same lock is not defense-in-depth. Different, independent layers are.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company protects its customer database with one very strong password and nothing else. Another protects it with a decent password, a rule that only the app server can reach the database, and an alert when unusual amounts of data are read. If the password leaks in a phishing email, which company is still protected, and why?
lessons.teach:
Defense-in-depth is a design principle: place multiple independent controls along every path an attacker could take to an asset, assuming each control will eventually fail. A control is any measure that reduces risk. Controls come in types: preventive (stop the attack, like multi-factor authentication, MFA, which requires a second proof such as a phone code), detective (notice the attack, like an alert on unusual logins), and corrective (limit or undo damage, like restoring from backups).

Why it works: if each layer has some chance of failing, an attacker must defeat all of them, and the chance that independent layers fail together is much smaller than any one failing. That only holds if the layers are independent, meaning they do not share a single cause of failure.

Worked example: protecting a customer database. Step 1, an attacker phishes a developer's password. Step 2, MFA on remote access blocks the login, unless the developer approves a fake prompt; assume they do. Step 3, network segmentation (splitting the network so only the app server can talk to the database) means the developer's laptop cannot reach the database directly. Step 4, if the attacker pivots through the app server, the app's database account has least privilege (only the permissions it needs), so it cannot export every table. Step 5, monitoring flags the unusual query volume, and the team responds. Each layer bought time or reduced damage.

Common mistake: stacking layers that fail together. Two firewalls from the same vendor with the same rules, or five systems all unlocked by one shared admin password, look layered but collapse at once. That is the slogan version.

Consequence in a running system: every layer adds cost, complexity, and friction for users and operators, and a misconfigured layer can cause outages or a false sense of safety. Good design picks a few diverse layers on the most likely attack paths rather than the most layers possible.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain protects the admin panel of its online ordering site, which can change prices and issue refunds. A control is any measure that reduces risk. Step 1: an attacker sends a fake email and steals the store manager's password. Step 2: the admin panel only accepts connections from the head-office network (a preventive control, meaning it tries to stop the attack). The attacker is outside, so they are blocked unless they first take over a head-office PC. Assume they do. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: any refund over $200 needs a second staff member to approve it, which caps how much money the attacker can move. Step 5: a nightly backup of the price table lets the team restore correct prices (a corrective control, meaning it limits or undoes damage). Which Step 3 adds a detective control (one that notices the attack) and does not share a cause of failure with Steps 1 and 2?
choices: A second rule on the same head-office network gateway, copying the existing allowed-address rule
An alert to the owner's phone whenever the admin panel is used from a device or at an hour never seen before
Turning off the nightly backups so the saved money can pay for a second network rule
A second login page that asks for the same manager password again before the panel opens
questions.why: The unusual-use alert notices the attack even after the stolen password and the office-network check have both failed, because it relies on neither of them.

questions.prompt: A public library's e-book system keeps an activity log. A daily rule flags any account that borrows more than 50 e-books in one hour so staff can look into it. The rule does not block the borrowing or undo it. What type of control is this?
choices: Preventive, because it stops the attack
Corrective, because it undoes the damage
Detective, because it notices the attack
Not a control, because it does not block anything
questions.why: The rule's job is to notice suspicious activity, which makes it a detective control. It still reduces risk even though it does not block anything.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic says it has three security layers: a remote-access gateway, a file-server login, and a patient-records app login. All three accept the same single-sign-on password, which means one shared credential, and none of them asks for anything else. Why is this the slogan version of defense-in-depth rather than the real design principle?
choices: The layers are all preventive. Defense-in-depth bans preventive controls.
Three layers are too few. The principle requires at least five.
One stolen password defeats all three at once, so the layers are not independent.
Remote-access gateways are never allowed to count as a security layer.
questions.why: Layers only multiply protection when they do not share a single cause of failure. A shared password is exactly that kind of shared cause.

questions.prompt: A 12-person startup is choosing protections for its code repository. One engineer proposes nine overlapping tools: three sign-in checks, three scanners, and three network filters. Another proposes three layers that work differently from each other, each placed on the attack paths the team thinks are most likely. Following the teaching on running systems, which choice is better, and why?
choices: The nine tools, because a misconfigured layer can never cause an outage
Neither, because defense-in-depth only applies to large companies
The three diverse layers, because every layer adds cost and friction, and diversity matters more than count
The nine tools, because more layers always lowers risk regardless of how they fail
questions.why: Good design picks a few independent layers on the most likely attack paths. Extra overlapping layers add cost, complexity, and misconfiguration risk without matching benefit.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes defense-in-depth a real design principle rather than a slogan, using an example system, and name one limit or tradeoff of adding layers.
lessons.modelAnswer: Defense-in-depth means putting several controls between an attacker and an asset, on the assumption that any single control will fail. What makes it real is independence and diversity: the layers must not share a common failure, and they should mix preventive, detective, and corrective types. For a customer database, I would combine MFA on remote access, network segmentation so only the app server reaches the database, a least-privilege database account, and alerts on unusual data reads. If a password is phished, the attacker still faces segmentation, limited permissions, and a team that gets alerted. The slogan version is just adding more of the same thing, like two identical firewalls or many systems behind one shared admin password, which all fall together. The tradeoff is that every layer costs money, adds complexity, and creates friction, and a badly configured layer can cause outages or false confidence, so you prioritize the likeliest attack paths.
rubricPoints: Defines defense-in-depth as multiple controls along attack paths, assuming each can fail.
Stresses that layers must be independent so they do not fail for the same reason.
Mentions mixing control types such as preventive, detective, and corrective.
Traces a concrete example where a later layer catches what an earlier one missed.
Identifies the slogan failure: redundant or shared-dependency layers that collapse together.
Names a tradeoff such as cost, complexity, user friction, or false confidence.

suggested.rationale: The skill is judging which independent layers matter for a given system, which is best practiced by reasoning through an exam-style scenario and defending the chosen controls.

lessons.plain: Threat modeling means sitting down with a sketch of a system and asking, before anyone attacks it, what could go wrong and what you will do about it. A framework such as STRIDE gives you a fixed set of questions so you do not rely on whatever happens to come to mind. Think of a home inspector who checks every room against the same list: wiring, plumbing, roof, foundation. Because the list is fixed, a room never gets a pass just because it looked fine. You end up with a ranked list of threats and the protections, called controls, that address them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Picture a simple website login: your browser sends a username and password across the internet to a server, which checks them against a database. Without any training, name as many different ways as you can that someone could abuse this setup. Do your ideas fall into a few distinct kinds of problem?
lessons.teach:
A threat-modeling framework is a structured way to ask what could go wrong with a design before an attacker finds out for you. STRIDE, which came out of Microsoft, is the best-known framework. Each letter names a category of threat, and each category breaks one security property.

Spoofing means pretending to be someone or something else. It breaks authentication, which is proving who you are. Tampering means changing data or code without permission. It breaks integrity. Repudiation means denying you took an action when the system cannot prove you did. It breaks non-repudiation, which trustworthy logs usually restore. Information disclosure means exposing data to people who should not see it. It breaks confidentiality. Denial of service means making the system unavailable to real users. It breaks availability. Elevation of privilege means gaining rights you were never granted. It breaks authorization, which is deciding what a known identity may do.

Why it works: you first draw a data-flow diagram. This is a sketch of the processes, the data stores, the outside actors, and arrows showing how data moves between them. Then you mark trust boundaries, the lines where data passes between parts that trust each other differently, such as the internet and your server. Next you walk each element and each boundary crossing through all six letters. The letters give you breadth, and the diagram makes sure you cover every part of the system.

Worked example: a browser sends a login to a web server, which checks a user database.

Step 1: the browser-to-server arrow crosses a trust boundary.

Step 2: run through the six letters. S: an attacker logs in with stolen passwords, so add multi-factor login. T: traffic is altered in transit, so require encryption with TLS (the encryption that puts the lock icon in a browser address bar). R: a user denies changing their email, so log the change with its time and source. I: the database leaks, so store passwords only as slow, salted hashes (scrambled values that cannot be turned back into the password). D: a flood of login attempts, so throttle each source. E: injected input grants admin rights, so use parameterized queries and least privilege.

Step 3: rank the threats by likelihood and impact, and fix the top ones first.

Comparable frameworks exist. PASTA is risk-driven and focuses on attacker goals. LINDDUN targets privacy. Attack trees break one attacker goal into the steps needed to reach it.

Common mistake: reciting STRIDE as six words instead of applying it to every element and every flow. When you do that, whole paths go unexamined. In a running system, an internal admin interface nobody modeled is a typical place for a breach to begin.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company runs a driver app that sends order-status updates and GPS locations over the internet to a dispatch server, which writes them to an orders database. The team has drawn a data-flow diagram and marked the driver-app-to-dispatch-server arrow as a trust boundary crossing, because it links the public internet to the company's server. They are walking that crossing through STRIDE. S: someone logs in as a driver using a leaked password, so require multi-factor login for drivers. T: status updates are altered in transit, so send all traffic over TLS. R: MISSING STEP. I: the orders database leaks customer home addresses, so restrict who can query it and encrypt the stored data. D: a script floods the server with fake location updates, so throttle each source. E: a crafted request lets a driver account reach dispatcher-only functions, so check permissions on every request and grant least privilege. Which entry correctly fills in the R step?
choices: R: a driver's phone sends false GPS coordinates to look closer to a restaurant, so cross-check locations against other signals before accepting them.

R: a driver insists they never marked an order as delivered and nothing can prove otherwise, so record every status change with its time, the driver's identity and the source in a log that drivers cannot edit.
R: a driver insists they never marked an order as delivered, so encrypt the connection between the app and the server with TLS.
R: the dispatch server stops answering during the dinner rush, so add spare servers that take over automatically.
questions.why: Repudiation is someone denying an action the system cannot prove, and a trustworthy log of who did what, when and from where restores non-repudiation; the other choices describe tampering or spoofing, denial of service, or the right threat paired with a control that does not prove anything.

questions.prompt: At a mid-sized accounting firm, an attacker sends staff emails crafted to look exactly as if they came from the firm's internal payroll system, asking them to confirm their bank details. Which STRIDE category is this, and which security property does it break?
choices: Tampering, which breaks integrity
Repudiation, which breaks non-repudiation
Spoofing, which breaks authentication
Information disclosure, which breaks confidentiality
questions.why: Pretending to be another party, here the payroll system, is spoofing, and it defeats authentication, the proof of who a sender really is.

questions.prompt: A warehouse company's security team writes a threat model that lists the six STRIDE categories with a definition of each. They apply the categories only to the public online storefront. They never draw the barcode scanners, the inventory database or the staff-only stock-adjustment web page. Months later an attacker gets in through that stock-adjustment page. What is the main flaw in how the team used STRIDE?
choices: They should have used PASTA, because STRIDE does not cover internal web pages.
They ranked the threats by likelihood and impact before fixing any of them.
They chose the wrong six categories; STRIDE needs a seventh category for internal systems.
They treated STRIDE as a list of six words instead of applying all six categories to every element and every data flow in a complete data-flow diagram, so whole paths went unexamined.
questions.why: STRIDE only gives full coverage when every process, data store, actor and boundary crossing on a data-flow diagram is walked through all six categories, and an unmodeled internal admin interface is a typical place for a breach to begin.

questions.prompt: A startup is designing a fitness-tracking wristband that collects heart rate, sleep patterns and location. Its main worry is how users' personal data could be linked, identified or exposed. Which threat-modeling framework is aimed most directly at that kind of concern?
choices: PASTA, because it is designed around privacy threats
STRIDE, because its six categories are only about privacy
LINDDUN, because it is designed around privacy threats
Attack trees, because they break one attacker goal down into the steps needed to reach it
questions.why: LINDDUN is the framework that targets privacy, while PASTA is risk-driven around attacker goals, attack trees decompose a single goal, and STRIDE covers six broad security properties.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use STRIDE (or a comparable framework) to threat-model a service you have never seen before. Include what you draw first, what each letter checks, and one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd start by drawing a data-flow diagram: the users, the processes, the data stores, and the arrows between them. Then I'd mark the trust boundaries, such as where internet traffic reaches our server. Next I'd take each element and each boundary crossing and ask all six STRIDE questions. Spoofing: can someone fake an identity? That's an authentication problem. Tampering: can data be changed? That's integrity. Repudiation: could someone deny an action we can't prove? That needs logs. Information disclosure: could data leak? That's confidentiality. Denial of service: could it be knocked offline? That's availability. Elevation of privilege: could someone gain extra rights? That's authorization. Finally I'd rank the threats by likelihood and impact and pick controls for the top ones. One limit is that STRIDE only covers what is on the diagram, so a missing flow means missed threats. It can also produce a long, flat list unless you prioritize it. And it is weaker on privacy, where LINDDUN fits better.
rubricPoints: Starts from a data-flow diagram with trust boundaries marked.
Applies the framework to each element and flow, not just as a memorized list.
Names all six STRIDE categories and the security property each one breaks.
Ranks threats by likelihood and impact before choosing controls.
States a limit, such as coverage depending on the diagram or the need to prioritize a long list.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine walks a learner through threat-modeling a system, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios with a diagram and defending a ranked set of controls builds the skill this unit asks for.

lessons.plain: Many attacks work the same way: the attacker sends data that the system mistakes for instructions. Injection tricks a program into running attacker-written commands, for example against a database. Cross-site scripting (XSS) sneaks attacker-written code into a web page so that other visitors' browsers run it. A buffer overflow writes more data into a fixed-size slot of memory than it can hold, and the extra spills into neighbouring memory that controls what the program does next. Picture a form whose 'name' box will act on anything written inside it, so someone writes 'and also hand me the keys' there.
lessons.guessPrompt: A login page builds its database question by pasting in whatever you type as your username. What could go wrong if someone types special characters that have meaning to the database instead of a normal name?
lessons.teach:
All three attack classes break the boundary between data, which should only be stored or shown, and code, which gets executed.

Injection happens when untrusted input is glued into a command that an interpreter runs. An interpreter is a program that reads and executes text commands, such as a database engine running SQL (the language used to query databases) or a shell running system commands. Here is a worked example. The app builds: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'INPUT'. An attacker types: x' OR '1'='1. The final query becomes WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'. Since '1'='1' is always true, every row matches, and the login check passes.
