The fix is a parameterized query, which sends the command and the data separately so the database never reads the data as SQL.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) is injection aimed at the browser. A site stores a comment containing a script, which is a small program the browser runs, and later displays that comment to other users. Their browsers run the script with the site's trust, so it can steal session cookies (small tokens that keep a user logged in). The fix is output encoding, which converts special characters into harmless display text before they reach the page.

A buffer overflow happens in languages like C that do not check memory limits automatically. A buffer is a fixed-size block of memory. If a program copies 200 bytes into a 64-byte buffer, the extra bytes overwrite nearby memory, sometimes including the return address, which tells the program where to continue after a function finishes. An attacker can point it at their own code. The defences are bounds checking (refusing to write past the end), memory-safe languages, and operating-system protections that make memory harder to abuse.

A common mistake is relying on blocklists that strip out 'bad' characters, or on validation done only in the browser. Attackers find encodings that slip past the filter, and they can skip the browser entirely. In a running system, any one of these flaws can mean leaked databases, hijacked user accounts, or full control of a server.

questions.prompt: A city library's self-service kiosk lets patrons check a book's status. Behind the scenes, the app hands this text to a shell (a program that reads and runs system commands): lookup BOOKID, where BOOKID is whatever the patron typed. Step 1: The app glues the patron's input straight into the command text. Step 2: An attacker types: 4471; cat /etc/passwd. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The shell runs the lookup, then prints the server's account file to the screen. Step 5: The fix is to pass the book ID to the program as a separate argument, so the shell never reads it as part of the command. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The extra characters run past the end of a fixed-size memory block and overwrite the return address.
The shell treats the whole string 4471; cat /etc/passwd as one book ID, so it searches for a book with that strange name.
The patron's browser runs the typed text as a script with the library site's trust and sends it to the server.
The final command becomes lookup 4471; cat /etc/passwd, and the shell reads the semicolon as the end of one command and the start of a second one.
questions.why: Because the input was glued into the command text, the shell sees two commands where it should see one piece of data. That is injection: untrusted data crossing over into code.

questions.prompt: A small firmware tool written in C copies a device name sent over the network into a 32-byte buffer (a fixed-size block of memory). It does not check the length. An attacker sends a 120-byte name. What is the main danger?
choices: The database reads the long name as SQL and returns every row in the device table.
The name is shown to other users, and their browsers run it as a script that steals session cookies.
The 88 extra bytes overwrite nearby memory, possibly including the return address, which could send the program to code the attacker supplied.
C automatically cuts the name down to 32 bytes, so the only effect is a shortened device name.
questions.why: C does not check memory limits automatically. Writing past the end of a buffer overwrites neighbouring memory, and if that includes the return address, the attacker can redirect execution.

questions.prompt: A recipe-sharing website shows each reviewer's display name next to their review. An attacker sets their display name to a small script. Every visitor who opens the recipe page then has their session cookie sent to the attacker. Which defence most directly stops this attack?
choices: Adding bounds checking to every memory copy in the web server
Checking the display name with JavaScript in the attacker's own browser before it is submitted
Output encoding: converting special characters in the display name into harmless display text before the page is built
Switching the page's database lookups to parameterized queries
questions.why: This is cross-site scripting (XSS): stored data reaches other users' browsers as code. Output encoding turns that data back into plain display text, so the browser shows it instead of running it.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking startup protects its search box by having JavaScript in the browser remove the characters ' and ; before the form is sent. The server then builds an SQL query from whatever it receives. Why is this protection weak?
choices: It is strong enough, because those two characters are the only ones an attacker could ever use for injection.
It only fails for programs written in C, because other languages check memory limits automatically.
Attackers can send requests directly to the server and skip the browser check, or use encodings the filter misses. The server still mixes data into the SQL command.
It is weak only because it runs slowly, and a delay in the browser gives attackers time to read session cookies.
questions.why: Browser-only checks and blocklists can be bypassed. The real fix is a parameterized query, which keeps data and command separate on the server.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what injection, XSS and buffer overflow have in common, how the main fix for each works, and one limit of a defence such as input filtering.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three happen when a system treats data from an attacker as if it were instructions. In SQL injection, input pasted into a query changes the query's logic. For example, adding OR '1'='1' makes a login check always true. The fix is parameterized queries, which keep the command and the data in separate channels. XSS is the same idea in a browser. A stored comment containing a script runs in other users' browsers with the site's trust and can steal their sessions. Encoding output before it is displayed turns it into harmless text. A buffer overflow writes past the end of a fixed-size memory block and can overwrite the return address, which redirects the program to attacker code. Bounds checking or a memory-safe language prevents this. Filtering bad characters is a weak defence on its own. Attackers use alternate encodings to get around filters, and browser-side checks can be bypassed completely. Filtering is one extra layer, never the main fix.
rubricPoints: Names the shared root cause: untrusted data gets executed as code or instructions.
Describes injection with an example of input changing a query or command.
Describes XSS as script running in other users' browsers under the site's trust.
Describes a buffer overflow as writing past a fixed-size memory block, which can hijack where the program goes next.
Matches each attack to its main fix: parameterized queries, output encoding, and bounds checking or memory safety.
Names a limit, such as blocklist filters being bypassable or browser-side validation being skippable.

suggested.rationale: The objective is conceptual, and being able to explain the shared data-versus-code root cause and match each attack to its fix is the skill a security course will test.

lessons.plain: A security framework is a big, organized checklist of what a well-defended organization should be able to do. You use it as a lens. Hold a system up against it, and you see which areas are covered and which are blank. Think of a home inspector's form. It covers the roof, wiring, plumbing and foundation, so nobody forgets the basement just because the front door has great locks. The US standards body NIST publishes two widely used frameworks. One is a short high-level framework with six broad goals. The other is a long, detailed catalogue of specific safeguards grouped into families.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team says their web app is secure because it has strong passwords, a firewall and encrypted connections. All three try to stop attackers from getting in. What important kinds of defense might be missing if an attacker gets in anyway?
lessons.teach:
A security framework is an organized catalogue of the outcomes a well-defended organization should achieve. You use it as an evaluation lens: you map a system's defenses onto it and look for empty areas. Two frameworks from NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, are standard vocabulary.

The Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) sorts outcomes into six functions. Govern means deciding who owns risk and sets policy. Identify means knowing your assets and risks. Protect covers safeguards that prevent harm. Detect means noticing when something goes wrong. Respond means acting on an incident. Recover means restoring normal service.

Special Publication 800-53 is far more detailed. It is a catalogue of individual controls, meaning specific safeguards. They are grouped into families with two-letter codes. Examples are AC (access control), AU (audit and accountability, essentially logging), IA (identification and authentication), CM (configuration management), IR (incident response), CP (contingency planning, such as backups and restores) and SC (system and communications protection, such as encryption in transit).

Why this works: a threat model tells you what could go wrong. A framework checks that your defenses span the whole lifecycle, not just prevention, so blind spots show up as blank areas.

Worked example: a small team runs a public web API with a database.
Step 1: list their controls. They have multi-factor login, a firewall and encrypted connections (TLS).
Step 2: map them. Multi-factor login is Protect/IA. The firewall and TLS are both Protect/SC.
Step 3: check the other functions. There are no central logs, so Detect/AU is empty. There is no incident plan, so Respond/IR is empty. Backups exist but have never been test-restored, so Recover/CP is weak.
Step 4: prioritize. The next effort goes to logging and restore testing, not a second firewall.

Common mistake: treating the framework as a compliance checklist to tick. Then a policy document nobody follows counts as done. Another version of the mistake is adopting hundreds of controls regardless of risk. In a running system, the result is an attacker who slips past the protective layer and works unseen for weeks, and a team that cannot restore cleanly afterward. A framework organizes judgment; the threat model still sets the priorities.

questions.prompt: A city library runs an online catalogue where members reserve books, backed by a member database. Use the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) functions and the 800-53 control families to evaluate it. Step 1, list controls: staff log in with multi-factor authentication, staff permissions are limited by role, all traffic uses TLS (encrypted connections), all servers send logs to one central place that alerts on failed logins, and nightly backups are test-restored every quarter. Step 2, map them: multi-factor login is Protect/IA (identification and authentication). Role permissions are Protect/AC (access control). TLS is Protect/SC (system and communications protection). Central logs with alerts are Detect/AU (audit and accountability). Tested backups are Recover/CP (contingency planning). Step 3, check the remaining functions for gaps. The team admits there is no written plan and no named person for what happens after an alert fires. [MISSING STEP: what does the check reveal?] Step 4, prioritize: the next effort goes to closing that gap. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Recover/CP is weak, because backups are only nightly, so a second backup site comes first.
Respond/IR is empty, because nobody knows who acts or what to do when an alert fires.
Detect/AU is empty, because logs only record events and do not stop an attacker.
Nothing is empty, because a control exists for every family the team has listed so far.
questions.why: Alerts tell the team that something went wrong, but with no incident plan and no owner, the Respond function and its IR (incident response) family have nothing in them.

questions.prompt: In NIST Special Publication 800-53, controls are grouped into families with two-letter codes. Which kind of safeguard belongs in the CP (contingency planning) family?
choices: Requiring a second factor, such as a phone code, at login
Keeping backups and proving they can actually be restored
Recording who did what in central logs for later review
Encrypting data as it travels between a client and a server
questions.why: CP covers contingency planning, meaning backups and restores. Encryption in transit is SC, a second login factor is IA, and logging is AU.

questions.prompt: A delivery startup has strong login rules, two firewalls and encryption on every connection. It keeps no central logs, and nobody would notice if an attacker were active inside its systems. Using the CSF as an evaluation lens, what should the next security effort be?
choices: Add central logging and alerting to fill the empty Detect function (AU family)
Add more login factors, because IA is the family that stops most attacks
Write a policy document so the Govern function can be marked as complete
Add a third firewall to strengthen the Protect function even further
questions.why: Every existing control sits in Protect, so Detect is a blank area. Filling that blank matters more than piling on more prevention.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm's security team marks Respond as covered because a 40-page incident policy exists on a shared drive. No one on call has read it, and it has never been practiced. They also plan to adopt all 800-53 controls at once, whatever their risks are. What mistake is the team making, and what is the likely result in a running system?
choices: They are treating the framework as a checklist. As a result, an attacker can work unseen and recovery can fail.
They are using the CSF instead of 800-53. As a result, auditors will reject the policy.
They are mapping controls to functions too early. As a result, the threat model cannot be written.
They are relying too much on threat modeling. As a result, the firm ends up with too few controls.
questions.why: Ticking boxes counts an unused document as done and ignores risk. This leaves real gaps that an attacker can exploit for weeks, followed by a messy recovery.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use NIST CSF and the 800-53 control families to evaluate a system you have never seen. Include one limit of relying on a framework.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd start by listing the system's existing controls and mapping each one to a CSF function: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond or Recover. For finer detail, I'd tag each control with an 800-53 family, like AC for access control, AU for logging, IR for incident response or CP for backups and recovery. The point isn't to tick boxes. It's to see the shape of the coverage. Most teams pile everything into Protect and leave Detect, Respond and Recover thin. That means a single bypass goes unnoticed and recovery is improvised. Those gaps become my priorities, ranked by the threat model's most likely and most damaging threats. The limit is that a framework says what areas to cover, not how much risk each gap carries. Treated as a compliance checklist, it rewards paperwork over working defenses and can bury a small team under irrelevant controls.
rubricPoints: Defines a framework as a catalogue used to map controls and expose gaps.
Names the CSF functions, including Detect, Respond and Recover rather than only Protect.
Describes 800-53 as detailed controls grouped into families, with at least one example family.
Uses the threat model or risk to prioritize the gaps found.
Names a limit, such as checklist compliance replacing real security or controls applied without regard to risk.

suggested.rationale: This skill is best built by reasoning through an exam-style scenario: mapping a described system's controls to CSF functions and 800-53 families, then defending which gaps to close first.

lessons.plain: Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics are ten general rules of thumb for judging whether an interface is easy to use. They were written by usability researcher Jakob Nielsen. Each one names a common way people get stuck, such as not knowing what the system is doing, being unable to undo a mistake, or meeting a confusing error message. Think of them like a home inspector's checklist. The inspector does not live in the house, but knows the usual places where things go wrong. A reviewer can walk through a screen with the list and spot likely trouble before real users ever hit it.
lessons.guessPrompt: You click Save in an app and nothing visibly changes: no message, no spinner, no tick. What problem does that cause you as a user, and what one small change would fix it?
lessons.teach:
Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics are broad rules of thumb for spotting problems in an interface. Usability means how easily people reach their goal with a product. A heuristic is a shortcut rule that guides judgement rather than a strict law. Reviewing a design against these rules is called heuristic evaluation.

The ten, in plain words:
(1) Visibility of system status: always show what is happening.
(2) Match between system and real world: use the user's words and familiar conventions, not internal jargon.
(3) User control and freedom: offer undo, cancel and a clear way out.
(4) Consistency and standards: the same thing looks and works the same everywhere and follows platform norms.
(5) Error prevention: make mistakes hard to make, for example by confirming destructive actions.
(6) Recognition rather than recall: show the options instead of making people remember them.
(7) Flexibility and efficiency of use: give experts shortcuts without confusing beginners.
(8) Aesthetic and minimalist design: remove anything that competes with what matters.
(9) Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors: write plain messages that say what went wrong and how to fix it.
(10) Help and documentation: provide searchable, task-focused help for when it is needed.

They work because each one names a recurring failure type. That gives a reviewer a structured checklist instead of vague personal taste.

Worked example, a file-upload page, traced step by step:

Step 1. The user clicks Upload and nothing changes for 20 seconds. That breaks heuristic 1, so add a progress bar.

Step 2. The upload fails with the message 'Error 0x80042'. That breaks heuristic 9 and also 2, so change it to 'File is over 10 MB; compress it or choose a smaller one.'

Step 3. There is no way to stop an upload in progress. That breaks heuristic 3, so add a Cancel button.

Each finding names the heuristic, the evidence and a concrete change.

Common mistake: citing heuristics without evidence, or forcing all ten onto every screen. Name only the ones the interface actually breaks, and rate how severe each problem is. Heuristics are expert judgement, not proof. They find likely problems cheaply but can miss what real users struggle with, so they complement testing with real people rather than replace it.

questions.prompt:
A reviewer runs a heuristic evaluation of a city bus-ticket kiosk. Each finding should name the heuristic, the evidence and a concrete change.

Step 1. The rider taps Pay and the screen stays frozen for 8 seconds with no sign of activity. That breaks heuristic 1 (visibility of system status), so add a 'Processing payment...' indicator.

Step 2. The main button reads 'Initiate fare transaction token' instead of words riders use. That breaks heuristic 2 (match between system and real world), so relabel it 'Buy ticket'.

Step 3. On the saved-cards screen, tapping 'Remove card' deletes the stored card at once with no prompt, and riders often hit it by accident. [Missing step: which heuristic is broken and what concrete change fixes it?]
choices: Heuristic 4 (consistency and standards): restyle the Remove card button to match the other buttons on the kiosk.
Heuristic 7 (flexibility and efficiency of use): add a quick shortcut so frequent riders can remove cards faster.
Heuristic 5 (error prevention): ask 'Remove this card? Yes / No' before deleting so the accidental tap cannot happen silently.
Heuristic 9 (recognize, diagnose and recover from errors): rewrite the error message so it explains in plain words what went wrong.
questions.why: An unconfirmed destructive action that riders trigger by accident is an error-prevention failure, and a confirmation prompt makes the mistake hard to make.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a heuristic evaluation of a user interface?
choices: Asking users to rate how attractive they find a design and averaging their personal preferences.
Watching a large group of real users complete tasks and timing each one to prove where the design fails.
Reviewing a design against broad rules of thumb to find likely usability problems quickly and cheaply.
Checking the code behind an interface against a strict standard that every screen must pass.
questions.why: Heuristic evaluation means checking a design against rules of thumb (heuristics) that guide expert judgement; it finds likely problems cheaply but is not proof and is not user testing.

questions.prompt: In a recipe-planning app, to add an ingredient the user must type its internal code, such as 'ING-4471' for tomatoes, from memory. No list or search of ingredients is shown. Which heuristic does this most directly break, and what change fits it?
choices: Heuristic 10 (help and documentation): publish a manual listing every ingredient code.
Heuristic 1 (visibility of system status): show a loading bar while the ingredient is saved.
Heuristic 8 (aesthetic and minimalist design): remove extra text from the ingredient screen.
Heuristic 6 (recognition rather than recall): show a searchable list of ingredient names to pick from.
questions.why: Forcing people to remember codes instead of showing the options breaks recognition rather than recall, so displaying a pickable list is the direct fix.

questions.prompt: A team evaluates a library's online book-checkout site. Their report lists all ten heuristics as broken on every page, gives no examples of where or how, assigns no severity, and they decide user testing is now unnecessary. What is the main problem with their approach?
choices: They should have used fewer heuristics overall, because only the first five apply to websites.
Nothing is wrong, because a heuristic evaluation is proof of usability problems and replaces user testing.
They should have rated severity, but listing all ten heuristics on every page is the recommended practice.
They should cite only heuristics the site actually breaks, with evidence and a severity rating, and still test with real users.
questions.why: Findings need evidence and severity and should name only the heuristics actually broken, and because heuristics are expert judgement that can miss real user struggles, they complement rather than replace user testing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Nielsen's heuristics are and how you would use them to review a screen they built. Include one example finding tied to a named heuristic, and name one limit of this kind of review.
lessons.modelAnswer: Nielsen's heuristics are ten rules of thumb for spotting usability problems. Examples include showing system status, matching the user's language, offering undo and escape, staying consistent, preventing errors, and writing error messages that explain how to recover. To review your screen, I'd walk through the main tasks and note only the places where a heuristic is actually broken. For each one, I'd record the evidence and propose a specific fix. For example, your delete button removes a record instantly with no confirmation and no undo. That breaks error prevention and user control and freedom, so I'd add an undo option or a confirmation step. I'd also rate each issue by severity so we fix the worst first. The limit is that this is expert judgement, not evidence from real users. It catches common problems quickly and cheaply, but it can miss what actual users find confusing, so we should still test with people.
rubricPoints: Defines the heuristics as general rules of thumb for finding usability problems, not strict laws.
Names several of the ten heuristics accurately in plain words.
Ties at least one concrete finding to a named heuristic with a specific design change.
Applies only the heuristics the interface actually breaks, ideally with a severity rating.
States that heuristic review is expert judgement and does not replace testing with real users.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine involves interfaces, and the unit goal is applying the heuristics unprompted to an unfamiliar screen, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style interface scenarios.

lessons.plain: Information architecture is how the content of a website, app or document set is grouped, named and connected so people can find what they need. It decides which categories exist, what goes inside each one, what the menu labels say, and how you move between pages. Think of a supermarket: if pasta sits next to the sauce under a sign that says 'Pasta & Sauces', you find it fast. If it is filed under 'Imported Goods' because that is how the buying department works, you wander. The products did not change; the structure did, and the structure decided whether you found them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A grocery website files oat milk under 'Beverages > Specialty' instead of near regular milk. Where do you think most shoppers will look first, and what will happen when it is not there?
lessons.teach:
Information architecture (IA) is the design of how content is organized, labeled and connected so people can find it. Findability is how easily a person can locate a specific item. IA has four main parts. An organization scheme is the rule for grouping, for example by topic, by task, by audience or alphabetically. Labels are the words used for categories and links. Navigation is the set of menus and links that let people move through the structure. Search is the text box fallback when browsing fails.

It works because people do not read a whole site; they scan labels and pick the one that most likely leads to their goal, a habit sometimes called following the scent of information. Each click is a guess. Clear groups and familiar words make each guess right; vague or insider labels make guesses fail, and people often give up after one or two dead ends.

Worked example: a user wants oat milk. Step 1, the top menu shows Fresh, Pantry, Beverages, Specialty. Step 2, they think 'milk is fresh' and open Fresh, then Dairy. Step 3, oat milk is not there because the store filed it under Beverages > Specialty. Step 4, they back out and try Specialty, which lists imported cheeses. Step 5, they either search or leave. A fix is to place oat milk under Dairy & Alternatives, or list it in both places with one link, matching where users expect it. Two common ways to check expectations are card sorting, where users group items themselves, and tree testing, where users try to find items in a bare text menu.

A common mistake is mirroring the company's internal structure, such as departments or database tables, instead of how users think about their tasks. In a running product this shows up as low task completion, heavy reliance on search, and support tickets asking where things are, even though every feature technically exists.

questions.prompt: A city council website. A resident wants to report a pothole. Step 1: the top menu shows Departments, Council, Services A-Z, News. Step 2: the resident opens Services A-Z and looks under R for 'Report'. Nothing is there. Step 3: they try Departments, then Public Works, then Highway Maintenance Division. They finally find a form called 'Carriageway Defect Notification'. Step 4: the diagnosis is that the site is grouped by council department and uses insider wording, so the resident's guesses kept failing. Step 5: ??? Which change best completes Step 5 as a fix that matches how residents think?
choices: Keep the structure but make the search box larger, since search is where residents should go first
Rename the form 'Report a pothole', put it in a task-based 'Report a problem' group, and link it from Services A-Z under P and R
Move the form into the Council section, because councillors are responsible for road budgets
Add two more levels of subcategories under Highway Maintenance Division so the form is filed more precisely
questions.why: It replaces the insider label with residents' own words and adds a task-based group and links where people actually look, which fixes both the scheme and the labels instead of relying on search or adding more department detail.

questions.prompt: A banking app's menu has a section called 'Instruments'. Customers kept missing it, so the team renamed it 'Accounts & cards'. Nothing else changed: the same items sit in the same place, reached the same way. Which part of information architecture did the team change?
choices: Organization scheme, the rule for how items are grouped
Navigation, the set of menus and links for moving around
Labels, the words used for categories and links
Search, the text-box fallback when browsing fails
questions.why: Only the wording of the category changed, and wording is what labels are; the grouping, menus and search all stayed the same.

questions.prompt: An HR team has drafted a new menu structure for its staff intranet. Before building any pages, they want to know whether employees can find the 'Parental leave policy' item. They plan to show employees a bare text-only version of the menu and ask them to locate it. Which method is this?
choices: Mirroring the org chart so each HR sub-team owns a menu branch
Card sorting, where users group the items themselves
Tree testing, where users try to find items in a bare text menu
Adding a prominent search box so browsing matters less
questions.why: Asking users to find a specific item in a plain text version of the menu is tree testing; card sorting instead asks users to create the groups themselves.

questions.prompt: A software company's help docs are grouped under the names of its internal engineering teams, such as 'Team Falcon' and 'Platform Core'. Every feature is documented. Yet about 70% of visits go straight to search, and support gets many tickets asking where to find setup instructions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The structure mirrors the company's internal organization instead of how users think about their tasks
The search box is too easy to reach, which discourages people from browsing
Users rarely scan labels, so no menu structure would change how they behave
Some features are missing from the docs, so users cannot find them by any route
questions.why: Heavy reliance on search and 'where is it' tickets, even though everything technically exists, are the classic signs of an architecture built around internal teams rather than user tasks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what information architecture is and why moving content between categories can change whether users succeed, and name one tradeoff, such as deep versus shallow menus or listing an item in more than one place.
lessons.modelAnswer: Information architecture is how we group, label and link content so people can find it. Users don't read everything; they scan labels and click whichever seems most likely to hold their goal, so every category name and grouping is a bet on how they think. If we organize by our internal departments, users guess wrong, hit dead ends and fall back to search or quit, even though the content exists. Moving an item to where users expect it, like oat milk under Dairy & Alternatives, can fix that without building anything new. There are tradeoffs: a shallow menu with many top-level choices is quick to reach but harder to scan, while a deep menu is tidy but adds clicks and more chances to guess wrong. Listing an item in two places helps findability but can clutter menus. We should check with card sorting or tree testing rather than opinion.
rubricPoints: Defines information architecture as organizing, labeling and connecting content for findability.
Explains that users scan labels and guess, so structure determines whether they find things.
Notes that organizing by internal company structure instead of user expectations is a common failure.
Names a concrete tradeoff such as breadth versus depth or duplicate listings versus clutter.
Mentions validating the structure with users, for example card sorting or tree testing.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises site structure, so reasoning through a realistic menu-restructuring scenario best builds the judgment this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Interaction design principles are rules of thumb for making a product easy to use without instructions. Affordance means an object's look suggests what you can do with it, like a door handle that invites pulling. Feedback means the system tells you, quickly, that your action happened. Consistency means similar things look and behave the same everywhere, so learning one part teaches you the rest. Error prevention means designing so mistakes are hard to make in the first place. Think of a well-designed kitchen: knobs that look turnable, burners that glow when on, every knob working the same way, and a child lock on the oven.
lessons.guessPrompt: You click Save in a web form and nothing on the screen changes. What are you likely to do next, and what problem could that cause?
lessons.teach:
Interaction design principles describe properties an interface should have so people can act correctly without being taught. This lesson covers four of them.

Affordance is the set of actions an object makes possible. A perceived affordance, often called a signifier, is a visual cue that tells the user an action is possible. A raised, shaded button signals that you can press it. Plain grey text that is secretly clickable has the affordance but hides it.

Feedback is the system's prompt, visible response to an action. Examples include a spinner, a changed colour or a message saying what happened. Feedback works because people cannot see inside software and need evidence that their action landed.

Consistency means the same words, icons, placement and behaviour mean the same thing across the product, and match conventions users already know from other software. It works because users reuse what they have learned instead of relearning each screen.

Error prevention means removing chances to make mistakes before they happen. Techniques include disabling invalid options, using constraints such as a date picker instead of free text, and asking for confirmation before destructive actions.

Worked example: a payment form has a Pay button. Step 1, the user clicks Pay. Step 2, nothing visibly changes for four seconds, so there is no feedback. Step 3, the user assumes the click failed and clicks again. Step 4, two charges are sent. The fix applies two principles together. Feedback: the button immediately changes to read Processing and shows a spinner. Error prevention: the button is disabled after the first click, so a second submission cannot happen.

A common mistake is treating these principles as purely visual polish and adding them last. They change behaviour, so missing them causes real failures. In a running system, missing feedback produces duplicate submissions, retries and support tickets. Inconsistent labels lead users to press the wrong control, and missing prevention lets a single misclick delete real data.

questions.prompt: A city library lets people reserve study rooms online. The date field is a free-text box. Step 1: a visitor types 03/04, meaning 3 April. Step 2: the system reads it as 4 March. Step 3: the room is reserved for the wrong day, and the visitor arrives to find it already taken. Step 4 (missing): the design change that uses error prevention so this mistake cannot happen in the first place. Which change belongs in Step 4?
choices: After saving, show a message that says Reservation saved.
Replace the free-text box with a date picker that shows a calendar with month names.
Make the Reserve button raised and shaded so it clearly looks pressable.
Rename the Reserve button to Book so it matches the word used on other library pages.
questions.why: A date picker is a constraint that only accepts real, unambiguous dates, so the wrong-date mistake is removed before it can happen. That is what error prevention means.

questions.prompt: In a music streaming app, tapping a song's title opens its lyrics. The title is shown as plain grey text with no underline, icon or other visual cue, so most users never discover the lyrics. Which principle is weakest here?
choices: Perceived affordance (signifier), because the action exists but nothing signals it
Error prevention, because users can tap the wrong song
Consistency, because the lyrics panel uses a different font
Feedback, because the app does not respond after the tap
questions.why: The tap action is possible, so the affordance exists. Nothing visible tells users it is possible, which means the signifier (perceived affordance) is missing.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse inventory tool, a trash-can icon means archive on the Products screen, so the item can be restored. The same icon means permanently delete on the Suppliers screen. Staff who learned the icon on one screen lose supplier records on the other. Which principle is violated?
choices: Error prevention only
Consistency
Feedback
Affordance
questions.why: Consistency requires the same icon to mean the same thing everywhere in a product. Here one icon has two different meanings, so what users learned on one screen leads them into mistakes on another.

questions.prompt: A concert ticket site's team decides that feedback and error prevention are just visual polish, and they postpone them until after launch. At launch, clicking Submit order shows no visible response for several seconds. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: Nothing changes in how people behave; the only complaints are that the page looks plain.
Users assume the click failed and click again, which causes duplicate orders, retries and support tickets.
Users learn the interface faster, because there is less on the screen to distract them.
Pages load more slowly, because the missing spinner frees up fewer resources.
questions.why: These principles change how people behave, not just how a page looks. Without feedback, users cannot tell whether their click landed, so they retry, which produces duplicate submissions and support tickets.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what affordance, feedback, consistency and error prevention mean, using one example screen, and name one tradeoff or limit of applying them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Affordance is about whether a control looks like what it does. A button should look pressable, and a link should look clickable. Feedback means every action gets a quick, visible response, such as a spinner or a 'Saved' message, so users aren't left guessing. Consistency means the same label, icon or position always means the same thing, so skills carry over between screens. Error prevention means making mistakes hard to make, for example by disabling Submit until required fields are valid or by confirming before a delete. On a checkout page, disabling Pay after one click and showing 'Processing' stops double charges. One tradeoff is that heavy prevention, such as confirmation dialogs everywhere, slows experts and trains people to click through without reading. Consistency can also clash with a better but unfamiliar design, so you have to weigh the cost of breaking a convention users already know.
rubricPoints: Defines affordance as cues that signal what action is possible.
Defines feedback as a timely, visible response to an action.
Defines consistency as the same elements meaning the same thing everywhere and matching conventions.
Defines error prevention as designing so mistakes are hard to make, not just reported afterwards.
Gives a concrete example such as a double-submit fix.
Names a tradeoff, such as confirmation fatigue or convention versus innovation.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises interface design, and the core skill is naming the principle behind a design flaw and justifying the fix in words.

lessons.plain: When you use any tool, two gaps can trip you up. The first is between what you want and knowing how to make the system do it: you want to mute the TV but cannot find which button does that. That is the gulf of execution. The second is between what the system did and understanding whether it worked: you pressed something and the screen gives no sign whether the TV is muted or broken. That is the gulf of evaluation. Think of crossing a river twice, once to send your request over and once to bring the answer back. Good design builds a bridge on both trips.
lessons.guessPrompt: You click 'Save' in a web form and nothing on the screen changes. Is your trouble in knowing how to act, or in knowing whether your action worked, and what single change would fix it?
lessons.teach:
Don Norman, a cognitive scientist who studied everyday design, described interaction as a loop between a person's goal and the system's state. The gulf of execution is the distance between what a person intends to do and the actions the system actually offers. It is wide when the user cannot tell which control to use, what order to use them in, or whether the action exists at all. The gulf of evaluation is the distance between the system's new state and the person's ability to perceive and interpret it. It is wide when the system gives weak, hidden or confusing signals about what happened.

The model works because it splits one vague complaint, 'this is confusing', into two diagnosable failures with different fixes. To narrow execution, you make the available actions visible and clearly labelled and map them to the user's words. To narrow evaluation, you show clear, prompt feedback (the system's response to an action) and make the current state visible.

Worked example: a user wants to share a document with a colleague. Step one, intention: 'let Sam edit this.' Step two, finding the action: the share option is hidden in an unlabelled three-dot menu, so the user hunts for a minute. That delay is a wide gulf of execution. Step three, acting: they type Sam's address and press Enter. Step four, perceiving: the dialog closes with no message. Step five, interpreting: did Sam get access, and was it view or edit access? The user cannot tell. That is a wide gulf of evaluation. Fixes: a labelled Share button for execution, and a confirmation reading 'Sam can now edit' for evaluation.

A common mistake is to treat every problem as execution and add more buttons, when users actually acted correctly but could not see the result. In a running system, a wide gulf of evaluation causes repeated clicks, duplicate submissions and support tickets from users who cannot tell their action already succeeded.

questions.prompt: A patron at the Riverside Public Library wants to renew 3 borrowed books at a self-service kiosk. Trace it with Norman's model. Step one, intention: 'keep these books for longer.' Step two, finding the action: the home screen has a large button labelled 'Renew my items', so the patron finds it in about two seconds. The gulf of execution here is narrow. Step three, acting: they scan their library card and tap 'Renew all'. Step four, perceiving: after a two-second spinner the kiosk returns to the home screen. No message appears and no due dates are shown. Step five, interpreting: the patron cannot tell whether any of the 3 books were renewed, or until when. Missing step, diagnosis and fix: which completion is correct?
choices: Both gulfs are narrow: the kiosk returned to the home screen, which already tells the patron the renewal worked.
Wide gulf of execution: add a second 'Renew' button on the card-scan screen so patrons can find the action faster.
Wide gulf of evaluation: after renewing, show a confirmation listing each of the 3 books with its new due date.
Wide gulf of execution: the patron acted wrongly, so rename 'Renew all' to match the library's internal term 'loan extension'.
questions.why: The patron found and performed the action easily but could not perceive or interpret the result, so the gulf of evaluation is wide, and clear feedback showing the new state narrows it.

questions.prompt: In Don Norman's model of interaction, what does the gulf of execution describe?
choices: The distance between the system's new state and the person's ability to perceive and interpret that state.
The number of steps a designer removes when simplifying a task flow.
The distance between what a person intends to do and the actions the system actually offers to do it.
The time a system takes to finish processing an action after the user has submitted it.
questions.why: The gulf of execution is the gap between the user's intention and the actions available. The gap in perceiving and interpreting the result is the gulf of evaluation.

questions.prompt: At Harbor Credit Union, members using the mobile app want to move money into their savings account. The transfer screen works. It shows a clear 'Transfer complete: $250 moved to Savings' message afterwards. But the field for choosing where the money goes is labelled 'Destination ledger', and many members give up before they find it. Which change best targets the actual problem?
choices: Add a larger, more colourful confirmation message after each transfer so members notice it.
Show a running balance on every screen so members can see their current state.
Add a pop-up after every transfer asking members to confirm they saw the result.
Relabel the field 'Send to account (e.g. Savings)' so the available action matches the members' own words.
questions.why: Members cannot work out which control matches their intention, which is a wide gulf of execution. Labelling the action in the user's words narrows it. The feedback after the transfer is already clear.

questions.prompt: A city parking app finds that about 40% of payments are charged twice. Logs show drivers tap 'Pay now' correctly, but the screen gives no visible sign that the payment went through, so they tap again. The product team proposes adding a second 'Pay now' button lower on the page. Why is this proposal a mistake?
choices: It treats the issue as a gulf of execution, which is the right diagnosis, but the second button should go at the top instead.
It narrows the gulf of evaluation, but adding buttons is too costly compared with relabelling the first one.
It is fine: duplicate payments always mean users cannot find the pay action, so more buttons will help.
It treats the issue as a gulf of execution, when drivers already act correctly and actually need clear feedback that payment succeeded.
questions.why: Drivers perform the action correctly but cannot see that it succeeded, which is a wide gulf of evaluation. Adding buttons is the common mistake of treating every problem as execution, and it does not stop the repeated taps.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between the gulf of execution and the gulf of evaluation, using an interface you have used, and name one limit of this model when diagnosing a usability problem.
lessons.modelAnswer: The gulf of execution is the gap between what I want to do and figuring out how the interface lets me do it. The gulf of evaluation is the gap between what the system did and me being able to tell what happened. On a parking-payment app, I wanted to extend my time but the option was buried under 'Account', so execution was the problem. After paying, the timer did not update for a while, so I paid twice. That second problem was evaluation. Splitting them helps because each gulf has a different fix: clearer, visible controls for execution, and prompt visible feedback and state for evaluation. One limit is that the model tells you where the breakdown is but not how common or severe it is. You still need to watch real users to know which gulf actually hurts people. Also, one bad screen can widen both gulfs at once, so the split is a diagnostic lens, not a strict category.
rubricPoints: Defines the gulf of execution as the gap between intention and knowing which available action achieves it.
Defines the gulf of evaluation as the gap between the system's state and the user perceiving and interpreting it.
Gives a concrete example that correctly assigns a problem to one gulf.
Links each gulf to a matching fix, such as visible controls versus clear feedback.
Names a real limit, such as the model locating problems without measuring their frequency, or both gulfs overlapping.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine exercises interface design, and the core skill is diagnosing a breakdown and explaining which gulf it belongs to.

lessons.plain: When people struggle with a product, it is tempting to say they used it wrong. In usability work, which is the study of how easily people can get things done with a design, that is almost never a useful conclusion. If many reasonable people make the same mistake, the design invited the mistake. Think of a door with a big flat handle that you are supposed to push. People keep pulling it. Blaming them changes nothing, because tomorrow new people arrive and pull too. Fixing the handle fixes everyone. Treating errors as clues about the design, not as flaws in the person, is how better products get made.
lessons.guessPrompt: In one week, 40 different customers type their phone number with dashes into a signup form, and every one of them gets the message 'invalid input'. Is the most likely problem the customers or the form, and what single change would you try first?
lessons.teach:
'The user is wrong' is a diagnosis that puts the cause of a failure on the person using the system. Designers should almost never accept it, because people's behavior is largely predictable, so a repeated error is a pattern the design produces. A user error is any action that does not match what the designer intended. A mental model is the person's internal picture of how the system works. Errors happen when the system does not match the mental model it encourages.

Why blame fails: you cannot retrain every future user, but you can change the design once. Blaming also ends the investigation early. You stop asking what the person saw, what they expected and why their choice seemed sensible to them.

Worked example. A payroll tool has two buttons side by side, 'Save draft' and 'Submit payroll', in the same color and size. Step 1: support logs show 12 accidental submissions this month. Step 2: the easy diagnosis is 'careless staff'. Step 3: instead, ask what users saw. The buttons look the same and sit close together, so a quick click on the wrong one is likely. Step 4: change the design. Make Submit visually distinct, move it away from Save, and add a confirmation step that shows the totals. Step 5: measure again. If the accidental submissions drop, the design was the cause.

A common mistake is reading the principle as 'users are always right about what they want.' It says something narrower. Their behavior is evidence about the design. Their stated opinions still need checking against what they actually do. Rare cases of true misuse, such as deliberate abuse, also exist, but they should be a conclusion reached after looking at the design, never the starting assumption.

In a running system, blaming users has real costs. Support tickets keep coming, workarounds spread, data gets corrupted by repeated wrong entries, and for safety-critical tools the same 'operator error' recurs until someone gets hurt. Treating each error as a symptom of the design turns a recurring cost into a one-time fix.

questions.prompt: A city parking app lets drivers pay by typing the 4-digit zone number shown on a street sign. When the app opens, the zone field is already filled in with the last zone the driver used. Last month, 300 drivers paid for the wrong zone and were fined. Step A: the operator's first reaction is 'drivers are not paying attention.' Step B: (missing). Step C: the team removes the pre-filled number and shows the zone's street name for the driver to confirm before paying. Step D: next month they count wrong-zone payments again to see whether the number falls. Which choice best fills Step B?
choices: Email every driver a reminder to double-check the zone number before paying, so future mistakes are the driver's responsibility
Ask what drivers saw and expected: a filled-in zone that looks as if the app detected their location, so accepting it seemed sensible
Survey drivers about which zone-entry screen they prefer and build whichever design gets the most votes
Accept the first diagnosis, because 300 drivers is a small share of everyone who uses the app each month
questions.why: Instead of stopping at blame, Step B investigates what drivers saw and why their choice seemed sensible to them, which reveals the pre-filled field as the cause the design change then targets.

questions.prompt: In user-centred design, what is a 'mental model'?
choices: A person's internal picture of how the system works, which guides what they expect it to do
The list of features users say they want when asked in an interview
The designer's technical diagram of how the system's components connect
A record of every action a user took, used to find who caused an error
questions.why: A mental model is the user's own internal picture of how the system works, and errors arise when the system does not match the model it encourages.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse, workers keep scanning parcels into the wrong storage bin. The bin labels for 'A-12' and 'A-21' are printed in tiny identical type next to each other. A manager proposes formally warning anyone who mis-scans. Which is the strongest argument against relying on that approach?
choices: Warnings are unfair because users are always right about what they need
Mis-scans are rare enough that they do not cost the business anything worth fixing
Workers should instead be asked which label colours they like best, and that answer should decide the fix
A repeated error is a pattern the design produces; you cannot retrain every future worker, but you can redesign the labels once
questions.why: Because behaviour is largely predictable, a recurring error points to the design, and changing the design once fixes it for every future user, unlike repeated warnings or retraining.

questions.prompt: A team interviews users of a note-taking app, and most say they love the new 'tag cloud' feature. Usage logs show almost nobody ever opens it. Applying the principle that 'the user is wrong' is rarely the right diagnosis, how should the team treat this?
choices: Trust the interviews, since the principle says users are always right about what they want
Assume users are deliberately giving false answers, so ignore all user research from now on
Conclude the users are misusing the app and leave the feature as it is
Treat what users actually do as evidence about the design, and check their stated opinions against that behaviour
questions.why: The principle is narrower than 'users are always right': their behaviour is evidence about the design, while their stated opinions still need checking against what they actually do.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says a confusing settings page is fine because 'people just need to read the instructions.' In your own words, explain why blaming the user is usually the wrong diagnosis, and name one limit of the idea, a case where the user really might be the cause.
lessons.modelAnswer: If lots of people make the same mistake, that pattern is telling us something about the page, not about them. People skim. They don't read instructions, and they act on the picture of the system the design gives them. We can't retrain every future user, but we can change the page once and fix it for everyone. Blaming users also stops us from asking the useful question: why did that choice look reasonable to them? So I'd look at where people go wrong and redesign that spot, for example clearer labels or a sensible default, then check whether errors drop. There is a limit. Sometimes the cause really is the person, like a deliberate abuser or someone using the tool for a job it was never meant to do. Even then, we should conclude that only after looking at the design. A single odd case doesn't justify a redesign, but a repeated pattern does.
rubricPoints: Repeated errors across many users point to a design cause, not individual carelessness.
Fixing the design once scales better than trying to change every user.
Blaming the user ends the investigation before asking why the action seemed sensible.
Users' behavior is evidence, but their stated opinions still need checking.
Names a real limit, such as deliberate misuse or rare one-off errors, reached only after examining the design.

suggested.rationale: This objective is a mindset shift whose core skill is arguing it persuasively to a teammate who wants to blame users, and no listed mission or engine covers interface design.

lessons.plain: User research is how designers learn what real people do and need, instead of guessing. It comes in two flavours. Qualitative research collects words, observations and stories from a small number of people, and it answers why and how: why did she give up on checkout? Quantitative research collects numbers from many people, and it answers how many and how much: what share of visitors abandon checkout? Think of a doctor. Talking with one patient about their symptoms is qualitative. Counting how many patients in a city have a fever is quantitative. Good research usually needs both, because numbers spot a problem and stories explain it.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop sees that 40% of people who start checkout never finish. Would watching five shoppers try to check out, or sending a survey to 2,000 shoppers, better tell you why they quit? Which would better tell you whether a fix actually lowered the 40%?
lessons.teach:
Qualitative user research gathers non-numeric data: what people say, do and feel. Common methods include interviews, which are open conversations about goals and frustrations. Another is the think-aloud session, where a person narrates their thoughts while using a product. A third is field observation, which means watching people in their real setting. Samples are small, often five to fifteen people, because each one yields rich detail. The output is themes and explanations.

Quantitative user research gathers numeric data from many people. Examples are analytics, which are logs of clicks and page visits, and large surveys with fixed answer scales. Another is the A/B test, where two versions of a design are shown to separate random groups and an outcome is compared. Samples are large, so results can be generalised and checked for statistical significance, meaning the difference is unlikely to be chance. The output is rates, averages and comparisons.

This split works because the two methods answer different questions. Numbers tell you what is happening and how big it is. Observation tells you why it happens and what to change.

Here is a worked example. Step one: analytics show 40% of users abandon checkout at the shipping page. That finding is quantitative, and it locates the problem. Step two: you run think-aloud sessions with six users. Four hesitate because shipping cost appears only at the last step. That finding is qualitative, and it explains the problem. Step three: you redesign the flow to show the cost earlier. Step four: an A/B test with 10,000 visitors shows abandonment falls to 28% for the new version. That finding is quantitative again, and it confirms the fix worked.

A common mistake is treating one method's strength as a substitute for the other. One example is claiming '60% of users hate the menu' because three of five interviewees said so. That sample is too small to support a percentage. The opposite mistake is A/B testing many variants without understanding the cause. Either way, a team can ship confident-looking changes that rest on weak evidence and wastes development time.

questions.prompt: A city library's mobile app team is investigating why few people finish creating an account. The team follows a sequence of steps. Step one: app logs from 22,000 sign-up attempts show that 52% of people quit at the screen asking for their library card number. This is quantitative, and it locates where the problem is. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the team adds an option to sign up without a card and get one later. Step four: they show the old and new sign-up flows to two separate random groups of 8,000 visitors each. Quitting at that screen falls to 31% in the new version, a difference unlikely to be chance. This is quantitative, and it confirms the fix worked. Which step two best completes the sequence?
choices: Test six different versions of the card screen on random groups to see which one scores best
Interview four people and report that 75% of all users dislike entering card numbers
Watch seven people narrate their thoughts while signing up; five stall because they have no card yet
Send a fixed-scale survey to all 22,000 users that asks them to rate the card screen from 1 to 5
questions.why: The logs only show where people quit, so the next step is a small qualitative think-aloud session that explains why, and that explanation is what the redesign in step three depends on.

questions.prompt: A hospital software team spends two days watching nurses use a shift-scheduling tool on a real ward. They take notes on workarounds and points of frustration. What kind of research is this, and what output should the team expect?
choices: Qualitative field observation; themes and explanations of why nurses struggle
Quantitative field observation; rates and averages for the whole nursing workforce
Qualitative A/B testing; a comparison of two scheduling designs
Quantitative analytics; logs of clicks that can be checked for significance
questions.why: Watching people in their real setting is field observation, which gathers non-numeric detail from a small group and produces themes and explanations rather than numbers.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company with 300,000 weekly users wants to know whether putting the 'Reorder' button at the top of the home screen raises repeat orders compared with the current layout. Which method fits this question best?
choices: Think-aloud sessions with eight users trying the new layout
An A/B test showing each layout to a separate random group and comparing repeat-order rates
Interviews with ten frequent customers about their ordering habits
Field observation of people ordering food at home
questions.why: The question asks how big a difference one design makes across many users, so a large randomised A/B test is the right tool because it gives a comparable rate that can be checked for statistical significance.

questions.prompt: A product manager at a fitness app interviews four users. Two say they find the workout search confusing. She then tells leadership, '50% of our users find search confusing.' What is the main problem with this claim?
choices: Interviews produce numeric data, so she should have reported an average instead of a percentage
She should have used field observation, because interviews cannot reveal frustrations
The claim is fine because qualitative samples of five to fifteen people are designed to be generalised
Four interviews are far too small a sample to support a percentage about all users
questions.why: A small qualitative sample gives rich explanations but cannot support a population percentage, so the claim treats an interview's strength as if it were a quantitative result and could push the team to change things based on weak evidence.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between qualitative and quantitative user research, when you would pick each, and one limit of each method.
lessons.modelAnswer: Qualitative research collects observations and words from a few people, through interviews or think-aloud sessions. It tells us why users struggle and suggests what to change. Its limit is that the sample is small, so we can't say how common a problem is or report percentages from it. Quantitative research collects numbers from many people, through analytics, surveys or A/B tests. It tells us what is happening and how much, and it can confirm whether a change made a measurable difference. Its limit is that it rarely explains the cause. A drop-off rate shows where users leave but not why. So I'd usually use them in a loop. First, numbers locate a problem. Then, observation explains it. Finally, numbers verify that the fix worked. Picking one alone risks either over-generalising from anecdotes or optimising blindly.
rubricPoints: Qualitative research means rich, non-numeric data from a small sample that answers why and how.
Quantitative research means numeric data from a large sample that answers what and how much.
Each comes with a concrete example method, such as interviews or think-aloud for qualitative and analytics, surveys or A/B tests for quantitative.
Small qualitative samples cannot support percentages or generalisation.
Quantitative data shows patterns but usually not their causes.
The two methods are often combined: numbers locate a problem, observation explains it, and numbers verify the fix.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine covers user research, and the core skill is articulating when each method fits and what it cannot show.

lessons.plain: A persona is a short, realistic portrait of a typical user: a name, a goal, a situation, a few frustrations. A user journey is a step-by-step story of how that kind of person moves through a task, from first need to finished outcome, including what they feel and where they get stuck. Teams use both to keep real people in mind while designing, like a novelist keeping a character sheet on the desk. But they are summaries and stories, not proof. A persona built from guesses only looks like evidence.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team writes a persona called 'Busy Maria, a nurse who checks shift schedules on her phone' without talking to any nurses. Would you trust a design decision justified only by 'Maria would want this'? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A persona is a fictional but grounded description of a user type, usually including a goal, a context of use, skills, and pain points (recurring frustrations). A user journey, or journey map, is a timeline of the stages a person goes through to reach a goal. Each stage lists their actions, the touchpoints (places they interact with the product or service), their thoughts and emotions, and the moments where things go wrong.

These artifacts work because they turn scattered research into something a whole team can share and remember. Arguing about 'the user' in the abstract invites everyone to picture themselves. A named persona with a stated goal makes people ask whether a feature actually serves that goal. A journey map shows where pain clusters, so effort goes to the worst steps.

Worked example. Suppose researchers interview eight commuters about buying train tickets. Step one: they notice most interviewees buy tickets while walking to the platform, one-handed, in a hurry. Step two: they write a persona, 'Dev, a commuter who needs a ticket in under 30 seconds.' Step three: they map Dev's journey: open app, find route, pay, show ticket at the gate. Step four: they mark the low point. Several interviewees said payment re-asks for card details every time. Step five: the team prioritizes saved payment. This decision traces back to observed behavior, not to the persona itself.

That last point sets the limit. A persona is only as good as the research behind it. Personas and journeys compress and simplify. They hide variation, minority users, and edge cases. They can also go stale as behavior changes.

A common mistake is the proto-persona treated as fact: a persona invented in a meeting from assumptions, then cited as if users had said it. The consequence in a shipped product is confident design built on fiction. That means features nobody needed, and real pain points nobody saw. Personas guide empathy and focus. Testing with real users is what supplies evidence.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain's researchers interview ten customers about refilling prescriptions online. Step 1: they notice most customers request refills late at night on their phones, after their children are asleep. Step 2: they write a persona, 'Rosa, a parent who wants to request a refill in under two minutes before bed.' Step 3: they map Rosa's journey (a timeline of stages toward her goal): log in, find the prescription, confirm the pickup store, receive a 'ready' notice. Step 4: ______. Step 5: the team prioritizes keeping customers signed in on their phones. Which step 4 makes the Step 5 decision trace back to observed behavior?
choices: The team agrees Rosa would probably hate logging in, so they label login as the journey's low point.
They mark the low point: several interviewees said the app signs them out and demands a password on every visit.
The team adds three more personas so that every customer type is covered before choosing anything.
The designers name the step they personally find slowest, and that step becomes the low point.
questions.why: Only this choice grounds the low point in what real interviewees reported, so the prioritized fix rests on evidence rather than on the persona or the team's own assumptions.

questions.prompt: A team builds a journey map for a gym membership service. A touchpoint is a place where the person interacts with the product or service. Which item from their map is a touchpoint?
choices: The member's frustration that evening classes are always full
The stage labeled 'decide whether to renew'
The front-desk kiosk where members scan in
The member's goal of exercising three times a week
questions.why: The kiosk is a point of direct interaction with the service; the other items are a goal, a pain point, and a stage of the journey.

questions.prompt: At a budgeting-software startup, the product team writes the persona 'Maya, a freelancer who wants cryptocurrency tracking' during a kickoff meeting without speaking to any users. Over the following months, they cite Maya in roadmap debates as proof of what users want. What is the main risk?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because the persona includes a goal, which is all a persona needs.
The team may confidently build features nobody needed and miss the real pain points.
Giving the persona a name makes the team too emotionally attached to one user.
The persona will be too detailed for engineers to remember during planning.
questions.why: This is a proto-persona treated as fact: it was invented from assumptions, so design built on it rests on fiction, not on evidence.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency built a single rider persona from interviews with 40 riders, most of whom were daily commuters. Later, a wheelchair user reports that the trip planner never shows elevator outages. What best explains why the persona-driven roadmap missed this need?
choices: Interviewing 40 people produces too much data to fit into one persona.
Personas compress and simplify, so they tend to hide minority users and edge cases.
The persona was not detailed enough to replace testing with real users.
Journey maps record only emotions, so access problems cannot appear on them.
questions.why: A persona summarizes the common pattern, so less common users such as wheelchair riders disappear from view; real-user testing, not the persona, is what supplies evidence.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what personas and user journey maps are for, and why 'our persona would like it' is not enough to justify a design change. Name at least one limit.
lessons.modelAnswer: A persona is a realistic sketch of a user type: their goal, context, skills and frustrations. A journey map lays out the stages someone goes through to reach a goal, with their actions, touchpoints, feelings and pain points at each stage. Both help a team share one picture of who they're designing for, so we stop designing for ourselves. They also help us spot which steps hurt most. But they are summaries of research, not research. If a persona was invented in a meeting, it just repackages our assumptions. Even a well-researched persona averages people out, hides edge cases and minority users, and can go out of date. So 'Dev would like this' tells us where to look. Whether the change actually works has to come from observing or testing real users.
rubricPoints: Defines a persona as a grounded portrait of a user type with goals, context and pain points.
Defines a user journey as stages of a task with actions, touchpoints, emotions and pain points.
States their purpose: shared focus, empathy, and prioritizing the worst pain points.
Notes they are only as valid as the research behind them, so assumption-based personas are not evidence.
Names a limit such as oversimplification, hidden edge cases or minority users, or going stale.
Says design claims should be checked with real user research or testing.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises user research artifacts, and the core skill is articulating what personas and journeys are good for and where they stop counting as evidence.

lessons.plain: Usability testing means watching real people try to do real jobs with a product, so you learn where it confuses them instead of guessing. You give someone a goal, such as booking a ticket, and observe without helping. Three tools are common. Think-aloud asks the person to say their thoughts out loud as they work. Task success rate counts how many people actually finished the goal. Time-on-task measures how long each attempt took. It is like watching a friend follow your hand-drawn map to your house: the moment they hesitate at a corner tells you more than asking them whether the map looked clear.
lessons.guessPrompt: You ask five people to change their delivery address on a shopping site. Three manage it, two give up. Before any teaching, what single number would you report, and what would you most want to know about the two who gave up?
lessons.teach:
A usability test is a session where a participant, meaning a person representative of the real users, tries to complete set tasks with an interface while a facilitator, the person running the session, watches and records. A task is a realistic goal phrased without hinting at the answer, for example "You moved house; make sure your next order goes to the new address" rather than "Click Account Settings."

The think-aloud protocol asks participants to narrate what they are looking for, expecting and feeling as they work. It works because it exposes the reasoning behind each click, so you learn why someone went the wrong way, not just that they did. Task success rate is the share of attempts that reached the goal: successes divided by attempts. Time-on-task is how long an attempt took from start to finish. Together, success rate tells you whether people can do it, time tells you how efficiently, and think-aloud tells you why.

Worked example. Five participants attempt the address task. Three succeed, so success rate is 3 out of 5, or 60 percent. Their times are 45, 60 and 240 seconds. The median, the middle value when sorted, is 60 seconds; the mean is 115 seconds, pulled up by one slow attempt, so the median better describes a typical success. Think-aloud notes show both failures saying "I expected this under my profile, not under Orders." That points to a concrete fix: move or link the address setting where people look.

A common mistake is the facilitator helping or asking leading questions when a participant stalls. This turns a failure into a fake success and hides the very problem you were testing for. A related trap: talking aloud slows people down, so treat time-on-task from think-aloud sessions as rough, not precise.

In a live product, skipping these checks means a confusing flow ships, and the cost shows up later as support tickets, abandoned purchases and frustrated users.

questions.prompt: A city library tests its renewal flow. Eight participants each get the task "A book you borrowed is due tomorrow, but you have not finished it. Make sure you can keep it another two weeks." Step 1: Five of the eight succeed, so the task success rate is 5 divided by 8, or 62.5 percent. Step 2: The five successful times, in the order they were recorded, are 70, 30, 310, 50 and 40 seconds. Step 3: [missing] Find the median time-on-task for a typical success. Step 4: The mean is 100 seconds, pulled up by the one 310-second attempt, so the team reports the median. Step 5: Think-aloud notes from the three failures all include "I thought renewing would be on the book's page, not in My Loans," so the team adds a Renew button to the book's page. What is the correct result for Step 3?
choices: 40 seconds, because it is the middle of the four ordinary times once the slow outlier is dropped
310 seconds, because it is the middle value of the list as recorded
50 seconds, because it is the middle value once the times are sorted (30, 40, 50, 70, 310)
100 seconds, because the median is the total divided by the number of attempts
questions.why: The median is the middle value after sorting, and sorting 30, 40, 50, 70, 310 puts 50 in the middle.

questions.prompt: A bank tests its mobile app's "freeze a lost card" task. There are 12 attempts, and 9 of them reach the goal. What is the task success rate?
choices: 25 percent
133 percent
75 percent
300 percent
questions.why: Task success rate is successes divided by attempts, and 9 divided by 12 is 75 percent.

questions.prompt: During a usability test of a travel booking site, a participant stalls on the task of changing a flight date. The facilitator says, "Maybe try the Manage Trip link at the top?" The participant then finishes the task. What is the main problem with this?
choices: It only makes this participant's time-on-task slightly less precise, so the result is still valid
It is acceptable because think-aloud sessions are supposed to be a conversation between the facilitator and the participant
It is acceptable as long as the hint is given after the participant has been stuck for over a minute
It turns what was really a failure into a fake success, which hides the very navigation problem the test was meant to find
questions.why: A facilitator's hint or leading question turns a failure into a fake success and hides the problem being tested for.

questions.prompt: A food delivery company runs think-aloud sessions on its new checkout. The team then claims the new design is exactly 4 seconds faster than the old one, based on time-on-task from those sessions. What is the weakest part of this claim?
choices: The claim is fine, because think-aloud makes participants concentrate and so produces the most precise times
Think-aloud only reveals whether people succeeded, so it should not be combined with timing
Time-on-task cannot be measured at all when participants are asked to talk
