questions.why: 24,000 sensors each sending once every 60 seconds gives 24,000 ÷ 60 = 400 writes per second, and 400 × 86,400 seconds in a day is about 34.6 million rows.

questions.prompt: An online ticket shop sends the seat price from the browser to its checkout API. A user edits the request on the way so that a $90 seat arrives at the server marked as $9. Using the STRIDE checklist, which threat is this?
choices: Spoofing, because the user is pretending to be someone else.
Denial of service, because the shop loses revenue.
Tampering, because data was altered as it crossed the trust boundary into the server.
Repudiation, because the user can later deny having bought the ticket.
questions.why: Tampering means altering data, and the price was changed as it moved from a less-trusted browser to the more-trusted server.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company collects ride sensor data from a phone app and mines its history store to find which stations run empty. The security team adds a rule that riders must log in again every 10 minutes during a ride, and no one reviews the app for usability. What is the most likely effect on the running system?
choices: Nothing changes for the data, because usability only affects how the screens look.
The data becomes more accurate, because every point comes from a freshly logged-in rider.
The history store fills up faster, because re-logins create extra rows.
Riders get annoyed and stop the tracking, so the data has gaps and the empty-station findings become quietly wrong.
questions.why: A design that is secure on paper but frustrating to use leads people to switch tracking off, leaving gaps that silently distort the mining results.

questions.prompt: A public library keeps a history store of every e-book each member has borrowed for several years. A reviewer says only the data lens applies to this store, because it is a back-end layer that people never see directly. Which review of this store is better?
choices: The mining lens can find patterns such as popular topics or unusual borrowing spikes, and the threat lens flags information disclosure, since reading history is personal, so retention and access should be limited.
The threat lens applies only as denial of service, since a stored archive cannot leak anything once it is written.
Only the usability lens applies, because members care most about how quickly the catalogue loads.
Only the data lens applies: count the rows per day and choose the storage size; security is handled at the login page.
questions.why: Each lens should be applied at every layer, and a stored personal history is both a source of patterns to mine and a disclosure risk that calls for limits on retention and access.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how threat modeling, usability, and a big-data/mining lens each apply to one architecture you know, layer by layer, and name one place where two lenses pull against each other.
lessons.modelAnswer: I take one architecture, for example phone to ingest API to queue to processor to stores to dispatcher map, and walk every layer three times. With the threat lens I look at the trust boundaries and run through STRIDE. Devices must authenticate so no one can spoof them, the queue needs rate limits against floods, and location history counts as sensitive data. With the usability lens I ask whether drivers and dispatchers can do their jobs: the app should buffer offline, save battery, and the map should show how old each position is. With the big-data lens I estimate volume and velocity, choose partitioning, and decide what to mine, such as delay hotspots. The lenses conflict. Mining wants to keep all history forever, while threat modeling wants short retention. Strict re-authentication helps security but hurts usability. I have to state the tradeoff I chose instead of saying "the cloud handles it."
rubricPoints: Defines each lens: threat modeling (abuse and trust boundaries), usability (users completing tasks), and big data/mining (volume, velocity, patterns).
Applies all three lenses to more than one layer of the same architecture, not one lens per layer.
Gives a concrete example of each lens, such as device spoofing, showing data age, or a rough throughput estimate.
Names a tradeoff between lenses, such as data retention versus privacy or security friction versus usability.
Notes a running-system consequence, such as users bypassing the system and corrupting the data that gets mined.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is articulating, layer by layer, how three different lenses read the same architecture and where they conflict, which is best practiced by explaining it back.

scenarios.title: Duplicate Checks and Route Counts at Lumen Parcel
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Lumen Parcel, a fictional delivery company, as a junior engineer. Your team lead asks you to review three short Python functions before a busy holiday season, when the daily list of parcel IDs grows from about 1,000 entries to about 1,000,000.

A few terms first. An algorithm is a finite, step-by-step procedure that turns an input into an output. Input size, usually called n, is the number that measures how big the input is, such as how many items a list holds. Correctness means the algorithm gives the right answer for every valid input. Efficiency means how much time and memory it uses as n grows. Time complexity counts the basic steps an algorithm takes as a function of n. Auxiliary space is the extra memory it needs beyond the input itself, including memory used by pending function calls. Big-O gives an upper bound on growth (it grows no faster than this), Big-Omega gives a lower bound (it grows at least this fast), and Big-Theta gives a tight bound (both at once). Common growth rates, from slowest to fastest, are constant (1), logarithmic (log n), linear (n), linearithmic (n log n), quadratic (n squared), exponential (such as 2 to the n), and factorial (n!).

Function A, has_duplicate_slow(ids): an outer loop sets i to every position in the list. Inside it, an inner loop sets j to every position after i. If ids[i] equals ids[j], it immediately returns True. If both loops finish, it returns False. It creates no new lists or other collections.

Function B, has_duplicate_fast(ids): it creates an empty set called seen. A set is a collection that stores each value once and, on average, can check whether a value is already inside in constant time. The function loops once over ids. For each id, if it is already in seen it returns True; otherwise it adds the id to seen. After the loop it returns False.

Function C, count_routes(k): if k equals 0 it returns 1. Otherwise it returns count_routes(k - 1) + count_routes(k - 1). A function that calls itself like this is recursive. Each call that has started but not yet finished occupies a frame on the call stack, which is the memory area that tracks unfinished calls.

Your sub-tasks:
1. For Functions A and B, state what the input size n is, and explain whether the two functions differ in correctness, in efficiency, or both.
2. Give the worst-case time complexity of Function A using Big-Theta, describe its best case using Big-Omega, and state its auxiliary space. Justify each answer by counting steps.
3. Give the time complexity and auxiliary space of Function B, then explain the trade-off between A and B for the holiday list of 1,000,000 IDs.
4. Give the time complexity and auxiliary space of Function C in terms of k, tracing how many calls happen for a small k, and suggest a simple change that makes it far faster.
subParts: Function A: time bounds and space
Function C: recursive analysis and fix
modelAnswer: For both A and B, the input size n is the number of parcel IDs in the list. Both functions are correct: each returns True exactly when some ID appears twice and False otherwise, for every list. They differ only in efficiency. A compares pairs of items, so its work grows much faster as n grows, while B passes over the list once. Two algorithms can give identical answers and still differ hugely in time and memory, which is why correctness and efficiency are judged separately. A common mistake is assuming the faster function must be less reliable, or that a correct function is automatically good enough.

Worst case (no duplicates, or the only duplicate is at the very end): the inner loop runs n-1 times, then n-2, and so on down to 0. The total is n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which grows like n squared, so the worst-case time is Theta(n squared), meaning quadratic. Best case: the first two items match, so it returns True after one comparison no matter how large n is. Every run does at least one step, so the running time is Omega(1) overall, and the best case is Theta(1), meaning constant. Auxiliary space is Theta(1): only the counters i and j are stored, and no collection grows with n. Consequence: at 1,000,000 IDs the worst case is about 500 billion comparisons, far too slow for a daily job.

B loops over the list once, and each set check and insert is constant time on average, so its time is Theta(n), linear, on average. The best case is still constant if the first two IDs match. Auxiliary space is Theta(n) in the worst case, because with no duplicates every ID is added to the set. Trade-off: A uses constant extra memory but quadratic time, while B uses linear extra memory to get linear time. For 1,000,000 IDs, B does about a million steps instead of about 500 billion, and storing a million IDs is usually affordable, so B is the better choice. A common mistake is reporting only time and forgetting that B's speed is paid for with memory that grows with n; on a memory-limited machine that memory could matter.

Each call with k greater than 0 makes two calls with k-1. Tracing k = 2: count_routes(2) calls count_routes(1) twice, and each of those calls count_routes(0) twice, giving 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 calls. In general there are 1 + 2 + ... + 2 to the k = 2 to the (k+1) minus 1 calls, so the time is Theta(2 to the k), which is exponential. Each increase of k by 1 roughly doubles the work. Auxiliary space is Theta(k), linear, because at most one chain of calls is unfinished at once, from k down to 0, so the call stack holds k+1 frames at its deepest. A common mistake is assuming space is also exponential; the calls happen one branch at a time, so the frames do not all exist together. Fix: make the recursive call once, store the result in a variable, and return that result times 2 (or simply compute 2 to the k). This gives k+1 calls, so Theta(k) time, which is linear.

scenarios.title: Choosing data structures for a parcel dispatch service
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Parcelwise, a fictional courier start-up, as a junior engineer. The dispatch service runs in memory on one server and tracks about 2 million active parcels. A data structure is simply a way of arranging data in memory so that certain operations are fast. We describe the speed of an operation with Big-O notation, which says how the work grows as the number of items, n, grows. O(1) means roughly constant work no matter how big n gets. O(log n) means the work grows very slowly, about one extra step each time n doubles. O(n) means the work grows in step with n.

The service has three jobs. First, when a customer types a tracking ID such as PW-88213, the service must find that parcel's record instantly. Second, couriers ask for the next job, and the service must always hand out the parcel with the earliest deadline, while new parcels arrive constantly. Third, a supervisor dashboard needs to list, in order, every parcel whose deadline falls between two times, for example 14:00 to 15:00.

A teammate, Dana, has proposed storing everything in one plain linked list. A linked list is a chain of items where each item holds a pointer, meaning a stored memory address, to the next item. Dana also says that if you switch to a hash table, lookups are guaranteed O(1). A hash table is a structure that runs each key through a hash function, a formula that turns the key into a slot number in an underlying array, so the item can be found by jumping straight to that slot. Your lead asks you to write a short design note answering the following.

1. For tracking-ID lookup, choose a data structure. Name the expected cost of lookup, insert and delete, and explain what it would cost to use Dana's linked list or a sorted array instead. A sorted array is a block of consecutive memory slots kept in key order.

2. Respond to Dana's claim that hash-table lookups are guaranteed O(1). Explain why the cost is O(1) only on average, what can make it worse, and what that would mean for the running service.

3. For handing out the earliest-deadline parcel, choose a data structure. State the rule it must always keep true, and give the cost of adding a parcel and removing the earliest one. Compare this with keeping a fully sorted list.

4. For the deadline-range dashboard, choose a data structure. Explain what 'balanced' means for it, and what happens to its performance if it is not kept balanced and parcels happen to arrive in deadline order.
subParts: Tracking-ID lookup structure and rejected alternatives
Why hash-table O(1) is average, not guaranteed
Earliest-deadline dispatch structure and its invariant
modelAnswer: Use a hash table keyed by tracking ID. Lookup, insert and delete are O(1) on average, because the hash function turns the ID straight into a slot number, so the service jumps near the right place instead of searching. Space is O(n) plus some spare empty slots, since the table is kept partly empty to limit collisions. Dana's linked list has no way to jump to an item. Every lookup walks the chain from the start, so search is O(n), which can mean up to 2 million steps per customer request. Inserting at the head is O(1), but deleting a given parcel still needs an O(n) search to find it first. A sorted array allows binary search, which repeatedly halves the range being searched, so lookup is O(log n), about 21 steps for 2 million items. However, insert and delete are O(n), because every item after the change point must shift over by one slot to keep the order. With parcels arriving and leaving all day, that shifting is costly. The hash table wins because this job needs exact-key lookup only, with no ordering.

Dana is wrong that O(1) is guaranteed. A collision happens when two different keys hash to the same slot. The table must then keep several items at that slot, for example in a small list, or probe nearby slots, and a lookup has to check each of them. With a good hash function and a table that is not too full, collisions are rare and short, so the average cost is O(1). In the worst case, for example with a poor hash function, a flood of keys that hash alike, or someone deliberately crafting IDs that collide, many keys pile into one slot, and lookup degrades to O(n), no better than the linked list. A second effect is resizing. When the table gets too full, it is rebuilt into a bigger array and every item is re-inserted. That single insert costs O(n), although averaged over many inserts it still works out to O(1) each, which is called amortized cost. For the running service, this means most tracking lookups are instant, but there can be occasional latency spikes during a resize. A bad or attacked hash function could slow every lookup badly. Mitigations are a good, well-mixed hash function, keeping the load factor (items divided by slots) low, and watching for slow lookups.

Use a min-heap ordered by deadline. A heap is a binary tree, meaning each node has at most two children, that is stored compactly in an array. Its invariant, the rule that must always stay true, is the heap property: every parent's deadline is earlier than or equal to its children's deadlines. As a result, the earliest deadline is always at the root, the top node, so peeking at it costs O(1). Adding a parcel places it at the next free spot at the bottom and then swaps it upward while it is earlier than its parent. That costs O(log n), because the tree's height is about log n. Removing the earliest parcel moves the last item to the root and then swaps it downward with its earlier child until the rule holds again, also O(log n). Space is O(n). A fully sorted list would make removing the earliest item O(1), but each new parcel would need O(n) work to find its place and shift or relink items. With constant arrivals, the heap is far cheaper overall. Its trade-off is that it does not keep everything in full order, which this job does not need.

Use a balanced binary search tree keyed by deadline, for example a red-black or AVL tree, which are self-balancing kinds. A binary search tree keeps the rule that everything in a node's left subtree is earlier and everything in its right subtree is later. That lets the service find the start of a range by following one path down, then walk forward in order, listing the k matching parcels in O(log n + k). Insert, delete and search are O(log n). Balanced means the left and right sides of every node stay roughly equal in height, so the tree's total height stays about log n, around 21 levels for 2 million parcels. Self-balancing trees restore this after each change by doing small rearrangements called rotations. If the tree is not balanced and parcels arrive already in deadline order, each new node becomes the right child of the previous one. The tree degenerates into a long chain, effectively a linked list, with height n. Search, insert and range lookup then fall to O(n), and the dashboard would slow down steadily as the day went on. A hash table is rejected here because hashing scatters keys with no order, so a range query would have to scan everything, O(n). A heap is rejected because it only knows the minimum, not the full order.

scenarios.title: Checking the Restart Rule at Brightwell Logistics
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the platform team at Brightwell Logistics, a fictional freight company. Only some staff may restart the shipment-tracking service, and the rule is written in a design document in symbolic logic.

First, some terms. A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. A predicate is a statement with a variable in it, such as Admin(u), meaning "user u is an admin". A predicate becomes a proposition once you fill in a specific user. The symbol ∀u means "for every user u". The symbol ∨ means OR, ∧ means AND, ¬ means NOT, and → means "if ... then". In P → Q, P is called the hypothesis and Q the conclusion. The rule uses four predicates: Admin(u), OnCall(u) (u is on the on-call rota), Contractor(u) (u is an outside contractor), and CanRestart(u) (u is allowed to restart the service). The rule is:

∀u [ Admin(u) ∨ (OnCall(u) ∧ ¬Contractor(u)) ] → CanRestart(u)

Two colleagues have each rewritten the rule in plain English. Write P(u) for the bracketed part and Q(u) for CanRestart(u). Priya wrote: "If a user cannot restart, then the bracketed condition is false for them," which is ¬Q → ¬P, called the contrapositive. Marco wrote: "If a user can restart, then the bracketed condition is true for them," which is Q → P, called the converse. Two statements are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row of a truth table. A truth table is a grid listing every true/false combination of the parts.

The team also keeps user lists as sets. A set is an unordered collection with no repeats. The admins are A = {ana, ben}, the on-call staff are O = {ben, dee, eli}, and the contractors are C = {dee, fay}. The union X ∪ Y holds everything in X or Y or both. The difference X \ Y holds what is in X but not in Y.

Finally, when a restart fails, the service retries and waits longer each time: 1 second before the first retry, 2 before the second, 4 before the third, and so on, doubling each time. A teammate claims that after n retries the total waiting time is 2^n − 1 seconds. Mathematical induction is a proof method with two parts. The base case shows the claim holds for the first value. The inductive step assumes the claim for some value k and shows it must then hold for k + 1.

1. Translate the rule into one plain-English sentence. Then evaluate the bracketed condition for Dee, who is on call and a contractor but not an admin, and say what the rule tells you about whether Dee may restart.
2. Decide whether Priya's version and Marco's version are each logically equivalent to the original P → Q. Justify your answer using truth-table rows.
3. Using the sets given, compute O \ C and then A ∪ (O \ C). Explain what the final set means for the restart rule.
4. Prove by mathematical induction that 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(n−1) = 2^n − 1 for every whole number n ≥ 1.
subParts: Translate the rule and evaluate it for Dee
Induction proof of retry waiting time
modelAnswer: Plain English: "Every user who is an admin, or who is on call and not a contractor, is allowed to restart the service." For Dee, Admin(dee) is false, OnCall(dee) is true and Contractor(dee) is true, so ¬Contractor(dee) is false. Then OnCall ∧ ¬Contractor is true AND false, which is false. The whole bracket is false OR false, which is false. An implication with a false hypothesis is true no matter what the conclusion is. So the rule is satisfied whether or not Dee can restart. It does not grant Dee permission and does not forbid it either; the rule simply says nothing about Dee. A common mistake is reading the rule as "only these people may restart", which is a different statement.

Priya's contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P is equivalent. Marco's converse Q → P is not. Check all four rows. Row P=T, Q=T: P→Q is T, ¬Q→¬P (F→F) is T, Q→P is T. Row P=T, Q=F: P→Q is F, ¬Q→¬P (T→F) is F, Q→P is T. Row P=F, Q=T: P→Q is T, ¬Q→¬P (F→T) is T, Q→P (T→F) is F. Row P=F, Q=F: all three are T. The contrapositive matches P→Q in every row, so it is equivalent. The converse differs in rows 2 and 3, so it is not. Row 3 is exactly Dee's kind of situation: someone who does not meet the condition but can restart. The original rule allows that case, but Marco's version forbids it. Treating the converse as the same rule would wrongly lock out or flag such users in a running system.

O \ C keeps the on-call users who are not contractors. Of ben, dee and eli, only dee is in C, so O \ C = {ben, eli}. Then A ∪ (O \ C) = {ana, ben} ∪ {ben, eli} = {ana, ben, eli}. Ben is listed once because sets have no repeats. This set mirrors the bracketed condition Admin(u) ∨ (OnCall(u) ∧ ¬Contractor(u)): union matches OR, and difference matches AND NOT. So these are exactly the users the rule guarantees can restart. Ana, ben and eli must be allowed. Dee and fay are not covered by the rule, so it neither grants nor denies them.

Claim: S(n) = 1 + 2 + ... + 2^(n−1) = 2^n − 1 for all n ≥ 1. Base case, n = 1: the left side is just 2^0 = 1, and the right side is 2^1 − 1 = 1. They match, so the claim holds. Inductive step: assume for some k ≥ 1 that 1 + 2 + ... + 2^(k−1) = 2^k − 1. This assumption is the inductive hypothesis. For n = k + 1, the sum is (1 + 2 + ... + 2^(k−1)) + 2^k. By the hypothesis this equals (2^k − 1) + 2^k = 2·2^k − 1 = 2^(k+1) − 1, which is the claim for k + 1. Since the base case holds and each case implies the next, the claim holds for every n ≥ 1. Check with n = 3: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 = 2^3 − 1. A common mistake is skipping the base case or assuming the k + 1 statement directly. Practical consequence: the total wait grows exponentially, so 10 retries already add up to 1023 seconds, about 17 minutes.

scenarios.title: Sorting Shipment Records at Harborlight Freight
scenarios.scenario:
Harborlight Freight is a fictional shipping company. You have just joined its routing team as a junior engineer. Your lead, Priya, gives you a short team note and four problems from this week's backlog.

The team note says: A sorting algorithm puts records in order by a key, which is the field you sort on. A comparison sort decides the order only by asking questions like 'is record A's key smaller than record B's?' A sort is stable if records with equal keys come out in the same relative order they went in. A sort is in-place if it needs only a small, fixed amount of extra memory beyond the array (the list of records) itself.

Insertion sort walks through the array from left to right and slides each record back into its correct spot. It is stable and in-place. It takes about n^2 steps in the worst case, where n is the number of records, but it is fast when the data is already nearly sorted. Merge sort splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively (defined below), then merges, meaning it combines the two sorted halves into one sorted list. It is stable and takes about n log n steps even in the worst case, but it needs an extra buffer, a second storage area about the size of the array, so it is not in-place. Quick sort picks a pivot, which is one chosen element, moves smaller keys to its left and larger keys to its right, then recursively sorts each side. It is in-place apart from the memory its recursion uses, and it usually takes about n log n steps. If the pivot keeps turning out to be the smallest or largest element (for example, always picking the first element of data that is already sorted), it slows to about n^2 steps. It is not stable. Heap sort first builds a heap, a tree-shaped arrangement stored inside the array where every parent key is at least as large as its children's keys, then repeatedly moves the largest remaining key to the end. It is in-place and takes about n log n steps even in the worst case, but it is not stable.

Recursion means a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of that problem. The base case is an input small enough to answer directly, without another call. Without a base case, the calls never stop. Every call that has started but not finished waits on the call stack, a region of memory that holds one frame per active call. A frame is a small record of that call's variables and the place to return to when it finishes. If too many calls are waiting at once, the program runs out of stack memory and crashes with an error called a stack overflow. A recurrence is an equation that describes an algorithm's running time, written T(n), in terms of its running time on smaller inputs. Big-O notation, as in O(n log n), describes how the work grows as n grows, ignoring constant factors.

One last known result: in the worst case, any comparison sort must make on the order of n log n comparisons. This is written Omega(n log n), meaning 'at least about this much.' The reason is that n distinct items can be arranged in n! (n factorial, meaning n times (n-1) times ... times 1) possible orders. Each yes/no comparison can at best cut the remaining possible orders in half. So you need about log2(n!) comparisons to pin down the one correct order, and log2(n!) grows like n log n.

1. The dispatch screen shows today's 40,000 shipment records, already sorted by pickup time. Dispatchers now want them grouped by depot code, but within each depot the records must stay in pickup-time order. A colleague proposes re-sorting by depot code with quick sort. Say whether that is safe, name a sort from the note that does work well, and explain why, using the term stability.

2. The handheld scanners have very little spare memory, and an audit requires a guaranteed worst-case time of about n log n. Pick the best sort from the note, and explain why each of the other three sorts fails at least one of the two requirements.

3. A teammate's recursive merge sort is described by the recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn, with base case T(1) equal to a constant, where c is a fixed amount of work per record. Explain what each part of the recurrence means. Trace it for n = 8 to find the total merge work, and state the total in big-O. Then say about how deep the call stack gets, and what happens if the base-case check is accidentally deleted.

4. A vendor pitches a 'next-generation comparison sort' that it says sorts any list of n distinct keys using only O(n) comparisons in the worst case. Using the lower bound from the note, explain why you should doubt this claim, and support your answer with a small worked example.
subParts: Keep time order within each depot
Low memory with a worst-case guarantee
Interpret and trace the merge sort recurrence
Evaluate the O(n) comparison sort claim
modelAnswer: It is not safe. Quick sort is not stable, so when two records have the same depot code it may swap them. That would scramble the pickup-time order inside a depot. Use merge sort instead. Merge sort is stable: records with equal depot codes keep the relative order they already had, and they already had pickup-time order. Grouping by depot therefore preserves time order within each depot automatically, and merge sort's worst case is about n log n, which is fine for 40,000 records. Insertion sort is also stable, but its worst case is about n^2 steps. For 40,000 records that is around 1.6 billion steps, so it is a poor fit here because the data is not already nearly sorted by depot. A common mistake is to sort by depot with any fast sort and assume the time order survives. That only holds if the sort is stable. In a running system, the consequence would be dispatchers seeing pickups within a depot out of time order.

Heap sort is the best choice. It is in-place, so it needs almost no extra memory, and its worst case is about n log n, which meets the audit. Merge sort fails the memory requirement because it needs an extra buffer about the size of the array. Quick sort fails the guarantee because, with unlucky pivots (for example, a first-element pivot on already-sorted data), it slows to about n^2. Its recursion also uses stack memory. Insertion sort is in-place but fails the guarantee because its worst case is about n^2. Heap sort is not stable, but stability was not a requirement here.

In T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn, the term 2T(n/2) means the algorithm makes two recursive calls, each on half the records. The term cn is the work to merge the two sorted halves, which is proportional to n. T(1) = constant is the base case: a single record is already sorted, so no further calls are needed.

Trace for n = 8. At the top level, one merge of 8 records costs 8c. At the next level, two merges of 4 records each cost 4c + 4c = 8c. At the level below that, four merges of 2 records each cost 8c. Below that are 8 base cases of size 1, which need no merging. That gives log2(8) = 3 levels of merging, each costing 8c, for a total of 24c. In general, there are log2 n levels, each costing cn, so the total is cn log2 n, which is O(n log n).

Call-stack depth: only one chain of calls is active at any moment (8, then 4, then 2, then 1), so the stack holds about log2 n + 1 frames. For n = 8, that is about 4 frames, which is very shallow.

If the base-case check is deleted, a call on 1 record keeps splitting and calling itself forever. Frames pile up on the call stack until memory runs out, and the program crashes with a stack overflow.

The claim contradicts the Omega(n log n) lower bound. Any comparison sort must, in the worst case, make about log2(n!) comparisons, and log2(n!) grows like n log n. Because n log n eventually exceeds c times n for any fixed c, no comparison sort can guarantee O(n) comparisons in the worst case.

Small example with n = 3: there are 3! = 6 possible orders. Each comparison has two outcomes, so 2 comparisons can distinguish at most 2 x 2 = 4 orders, which is fewer than 6. At least 3 comparisons are needed in the worst case. At larger scale, for n = 1,000, log2(1000!) is about 8,530, so the worst case needs roughly 8.5 times n comparisons, and that ratio keeps growing as n grows.

The vendor's claim must therefore be wrong, or it is really describing something else. For example, the method might not be comparison-based (it might exploit special properties of the keys), or the O(n) figure might be a best case or a case that only holds for special inputs rather than a worst case for any input.

scenarios.title: Mapping service dependencies at Kettlebrook Software
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined the platform team at Kettlebrook Software, a fictional company that runs an online shop. The shop is built from six small programs called services, and some services call others to get work done. Your lead, Priya, wants you to model these calls as a graph so the team can answer questions during outages.

A graph is a set of vertices (the things, here the services) connected by edges (the links between things, here one service calling another). In a directed graph each edge has a direction, from caller to callee. In an undirected graph an edge works both ways. In a weighted graph each edge carries a number, such as a cost or a delay. In an unweighted graph every edge counts the same. A hop is one step along one edge.

The six services are Gateway, Auth, Orders, Inventory, Billing and Email. Each service calls the services listed after it, in this order. Gateway calls Auth, then Orders. Auth calls Email. Orders calls Inventory, then Billing. Inventory calls Billing. Billing calls Email. Email calls nothing. No call has a cost or delay attached.

Two ways to store a graph are on the table. An adjacency list keeps, for each vertex, a list of only the vertices it has edges to. An adjacency matrix is a V-by-V grid of yes/no cells, where V is the number of vertices. Cell (row X, column Y) says whether there is an edge from X to Y.

Two ways to walk a graph are also on the table. Breadth-first search (BFS) starts at one vertex and uses a queue, a first-in, first-out waiting line. It visits all vertices 1 hop away, then all vertices 2 hops away, and so on outward. Depth-first search (DFS) starts at one vertex and follows one path as deep as it can go before backing up to try the next branch. DFS uses recursion or a stack, a last-in, first-out pile. Both searches keep a visited set, a record of vertices already seen, so that no vertex is processed twice.

Priya asks you to do the following.

1. Describe this graph. Give the number of vertices and edges, and say whether it is directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted. Then recommend an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix for storing it, and explain why.

2. When Email breaks, the team wants to know the fewest hops from Gateway to Email. Choose BFS or DFS for this job and justify your choice. Then trace the search step by step from Gateway, following neighbours in the order given above. Give the hop count to every service and the shortest path to Email.

3. Before restarting Orders, the team needs every service that Orders depends on, directly or indirectly. Use DFS from Orders, following neighbours in the order given. Trace the visit order and give the final set. Then explain what goes wrong if you forget the visited set, both in this graph and in a graph that contains a cycle (a path that leads back to where it started).

4. Next year the shop will have about 2,000 services and 9,000 calls. State the time complexity of BFS or DFS using an adjacency list and using an adjacency matrix. Estimate the work for each and say which storage choice the team should keep.
subParts: Describe the graph and choose a representation
BFS for fewest hops to Email
DFS for everything Orders depends on
modelAnswer:
The graph has 6 vertices: Gateway, Auth, Orders, Inventory, Billing and Email. It has 7 edges: Gateway to Auth, Gateway to Orders, Auth to Email, Orders to Inventory, Orders to Billing, Inventory to Billing, and Billing to Email.

It is directed, because a call goes from caller to callee. Orders calls Billing, but Billing does not call Orders. It is unweighted, because no edge carries a cost or delay, so every hop counts the same.

Recommend an adjacency list. An adjacency list stores only the edges that exist, so its memory grows with V + E, here about 6 + 7 entries. An adjacency matrix always stores V times V cells, here 6 x 6 = 36 cells, and only 7 of them say yes.

This graph is sparse, meaning it has far fewer edges than possible pairs. For sparse graphs the list saves memory. It also lets a search jump straight to a vertex's real neighbours instead of scanning a whole row of mostly empty cells.

A matrix is mainly worth it when the graph is dense or you need very fast answers to the question 'is there an edge from X to Y?'.

Choose BFS. BFS explores in layers: everything 1 hop away first, then everything 2 hops away, and so on. In an unweighted graph, the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it has reached it by a path with the fewest hops. DFS does not promise this, because it may wander down a long branch first.

The trace runs like this. Start with Gateway at 0 hops, mark it visited, and put it in the queue. The queue is [Gateway].

Take Gateway from the queue. Its neighbours Auth and Orders are unvisited, so mark them at 1 hop and add them. The queue is [Auth, Orders].

Take Auth. Its neighbour Email is unvisited, so mark it at 2 hops and record that it was reached from Auth. The queue is [Orders, Email].

Take Orders. Inventory and Billing are unvisited, so mark both at 2 hops. The queue is [Email, Inventory, Billing].

Take Email. It has no neighbours. Take Inventory. Its neighbour Billing is already visited, so skip it. Take Billing. Its neighbour Email is already visited, so skip it. The queue is now empty and the search ends.

The hop counts are: Gateway 0, Auth 1, Orders 1, Email 2, Inventory 2, Billing 2. The shortest path to Email is Gateway, then Auth, then Email, which is 2 hops.

A common mistake is using DFS here. DFS may report a longer route, such as Gateway, Orders, Inventory, Billing, Email at 4 hops, as if it were the answer.

Start DFS at Orders and mark it visited. Go to its first neighbour, Inventory, and mark it visited. From Inventory go to Billing and mark it visited. From Billing go to Email and mark it visited.

Email has no neighbours, so back up to Billing. Billing has nothing left, so back up to Inventory. Inventory has nothing left, so back up to Orders. Orders' next neighbour is Billing, which is already visited, so skip it. The search ends.

The visit order is Orders, Inventory, Billing, Email. The set Orders depends on is {Inventory, Billing, Email}. Gateway and Auth are not included, because no edge leads from Orders to them.

If you forget the visited set in this graph, Billing is reached twice: once through Inventory and once directly from Orders. Email is reached twice too. The work is repeated and the dependency list contains duplicates. In a bigger graph, this kind of repeated work can grow very quickly.

If the graph had a cycle, for example if Email also called Orders, the search would go Orders, Inventory, Billing, Email, Orders, and round again forever. On a running system that means a hung tool or a crash from running out of memory or stack, at the very moment the team needs the answer.

With an adjacency list, BFS and DFS each take O(V + E) time. Each vertex is handled once because of the visited set, and each edge is examined once when its starting vertex is processed.

With an adjacency matrix, both take O(V^2) time. To find the neighbours of a vertex you must scan its entire row of V cells, and you do this for all V vertices.

At the new scale, V = 2,000 and E = 9,000. The list costs about 2,000 + 9,000 = 11,000 basic steps. The matrix costs about 2,000 x 2,000 = 4,000,000 steps, and it also needs 4,000,000 stored cells, almost all of them empty.

The graph stays sparse, so the team should keep the adjacency list. Traversals will run roughly hundreds of times faster than with a matrix and use far less memory. This matters when a search runs during an outage.

scenarios.title: Release Pipelines and Delivery Routes at Tallowbrook Freight
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Tallowbrook Freight, a fictional regional shipping company, as a junior engineer. Your team lead hands you four small problems from the same week. Each one can be modelled as a graph, which is a set of items called nodes joined by connections called edges. In a directed graph, each edge points one way. In a weighted graph, each edge carries a number called its weight, such as a cost or a distance.

Problem A is the nightly software release. It has five steps: Fetch (download the code), Compile (turn the code into a runnable program), Test, Package (bundle the program for shipping), and Deploy (put it on the live servers). The rules are: Fetch before Compile, Compile before Test, Compile before Package, Test before Deploy, and Package before Deploy. Each rule is a directed edge from the earlier step to the later one.

Problem B: a colleague proposes one extra rule, "Deploy must finish before Compile," so that the previous release is live before new code is built.

Problem C is truck routing between depots W, X, Y and Z. These are one-way roads, with costs in dollars: W to X costs 4, W to Y costs 1, Y to X costs 2, X to Z costs 1, and Y to Z costs 6. The team uses Dijkstra's algorithm. This method finds the cheapest route from one start node to every other node. It does this by repeatedly locking in, or finalizing, the unfinished node with the smallest known cost. Later, finance suggests adding a new depot V with a road from W to V costing 5 and a fuel-rebate road from V to Y with weight -5, because the company is paid to use that road.

Problem D is loading. Pallets come in sizes of 1, 3 and 4 units, and a truck bay holds exactly 6 units. The goal is to fill the bay using the fewest pallets. A teammate suggests a greedy approach. A greedy approach makes the choice that looks best right now and never revisits it; here, that means always taking the largest pallet that still fits.

Your tasks:
1. For Problem A, give a valid topological order of the five steps. A topological order lists every node so that each edge points from an earlier item to a later one. Briefly explain how you found it.
2. For Problem B, explain whether the extra rule makes the release schedule impossible. Describe one method that would detect the problem automatically.
3. For Problem C, trace Dijkstra's algorithm from W to find the cheapest cost and route to Z on the original roads. Then explain what goes wrong once the -5 rebate road is added, and what that means for the routing system.
4. For Problem D, show whether the greedy approach gives the fewest pallets. Classify the problem as greedy, divide and conquer, or dynamic programming, and defend your choice. Divide and conquer means splitting a problem into separate, non-overlapping smaller problems, solving each, and combining the results. Dynamic programming means solving overlapping smaller problems once each and reusing the stored answers; storing those answers is called memoization.
subParts: Dijkstra trace and the negative rebate
Greedy vs dynamic programming for pallets
modelAnswer: One valid order is Fetch, Compile, Test, Package, Deploy. Swapping Test and Package (Fetch, Compile, Package, Test, Deploy) is also valid. One method is to count each step's incoming edges, meaning the number of steps that must come before it. Fetch has zero, so it goes first. Removing Fetch drops Compile to zero, so Compile goes next. Removing Compile drops both Test and Package to zero, and either can go next. Deploy reaches zero only after both Test and Package are removed, so it goes last. Every rule points forward in the final list, which is the definition of a topological order. A common mistake is ordering by name or by a guess and forgetting that Deploy needs both Test and Package.

Yes, the extra rule makes the schedule impossible. It creates a cycle, which is a path of edges that returns to where it started: Compile to Test to Deploy to Compile (Compile to Package to Deploy to Compile is a second one). Every step in the cycle would have to come before itself, so no topological order exists and no release could ever start. The incoming-edge counting method detects this automatically. After Fetch is removed, Compile still has an incoming edge from Deploy, so no remaining step reaches zero. If the method gets stuck before all steps are placed, the graph has a cycle. A second method is a depth-first search, which follows edges as deep as possible before backing up. It marks each node as unvisited, in progress, or done. Reaching a node that is still in progress means you have looped back onto your current path, which is a cycle. For a running system, the pipeline should reject the rule with a clear error rather than hang forever or run the steps in a broken order.

Original roads, starting from W. Set W = 0 and all others to unknown. Finalize W (cost 0); this updates X = 4 and Y = 1. The smallest unfinished node is Y (1), so finalize it. Through Y, X becomes min(4, 1+2) = 3 and Z becomes 1+6 = 7. Finalize X (3); through X, Z becomes min(7, 3+1) = 4. Finalize Z (4). The cheapest cost is $4 by the route W, Y, X, Z. This works because, when every weight is zero or more, no route that is not yet explored can make an already-smallest cost even smaller, so locking it in is safe. With the rebate road added, the run starts the same way: W gives X = 4, Y = 1 and V = 5. Y is finalized at 1, which fixes X at 3 and then Z at 4. When V (5) is finally processed, the route W, V, Y costs 5 + (-5) = 0, which is cheaper than the 1 already locked in for Y. Because Y was already finalized, Dijkstra does not go back and update X and Z. It reports Z = 4, but the true cheapest route is W, V, Y, X, Z at 5 - 5 + 2 + 1 = $3. The negative weight breaks Dijkstra's core assumption that locked-in costs can never improve. As a result, the routing system would quietly give wrong, more expensive routes with no error. The team should either keep all weights nonnegative (for example, by modelling the rebate separately) or switch to a shortest-path method designed to handle negative weights, such as Bellman-Ford.

Greedy takes 4 first, leaving 2. A 3 does not fit, so it takes 1 and then 1, for 3 pallets. But 3 + 3 also fills 6 using only 2 pallets, so greedy is not optimal. Grabbing the 4 early looked best at the time but blocked the better combination, and greedy never revisits a choice. This is dynamic programming. Let best(n) be the fewest pallets that fill exactly n units, with best(n) = 1 + the smallest of best(n-1), best(n-3) and best(n-4), skipping any that go below 0, and best(0) = 0. Building up gives best(1) = 1, best(2) = 2, best(3) = 1, best(4) = 1, best(5) = 1 + min(best(4), best(2), best(1)) = 2, and best(6) = 1 + min(best(5), best(3), best(2)) = 2. So the answer is 2 pallets, using 3 + 3. It is not divide and conquer, because the smaller problems overlap rather than being separate. For example, best(2) is needed both when working out best(5) and when working out best(6). Memoization stores each best(n) once so it is never recomputed. Without it, a plain recursive version would solve the same smaller problems again and again, and its running time would grow very quickly for large bays. Using greedy in production would waste truck space on every load where it guesses wrong.

scenarios.title: Brightkettle Sensors: Debugging a Tiny Thermostat Chip
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightkettle Sensors, a fictional company that builds small smart thermostats. Each thermostat has a simple processor, or CPU (central processing unit), the part of a computer that runs instructions one after another. Your team lead, Priya, asks you to help debug a test board. She gives you some background first.

Computers store everything as binary, meaning base 2, written only with the digits 0 and 1. Each single 0 or 1 is called a bit. Because long binary strings are hard to read, engineers often write them in hexadecimal (hex), meaning base 16, using the digits 0-9 and then A-F for the values 10-15. One hex digit stands for exactly four bits. For example, hex 2 is binary 0010 and hex D (13) is binary 1101. Hex values are often written with the prefix 0x, so 0x2D means hex 2D. Bits in a byte (8 bits) are numbered from the right, starting at bit 0.

AND is a Boolean logic operation, meaning it works on true/false values written as 1/0. AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1. When you AND two binary numbers bit by bit, that is called a bitwise AND. Engineers use it to test a single bit with a mask, which is a number that has a 1 only in the position you care about. If the result is not zero, that bit was set (equal to 1). XOR (exclusive OR) is another Boolean operation that outputs 1 only when its two inputs are different.

The thermostat has a status register. A register is a tiny, very fast storage slot inside the CPU that holds one value. In the status register, bit 2 means the temperature sensor is ready and bit 1 means an error has occurred. Right now the status register reads 0x2D.

Priya also shows you a five-instruction test program stored in RAM (random-access memory, the main working memory where programs and data live). The CPU has a program counter (PC), a special register holding the address of the next instruction to run. It also has two general registers, R1 and R2, and an ALU (arithmetic logic unit), the circuit that does the actual adding and logic operations. The CPU runs the fetch-decode-execute cycle. It fetches the instruction at the address in the PC, decodes it to work out what it means, then executes it. After each instruction the PC normally goes up by 1. Each instruction takes one address. The PC starts at 0 and both registers start at 0.

Address 0: LOAD R1, 5 (put the number 5 into R1). Address 1: LOAD R2, 3 (put 3 into R2). Address 2: ADD R1, R1, R2 (the ALU adds R1 and R2 and stores the result in R1). Address 3: XOR R2, R1, R2 (the ALU does bitwise XOR of R1 and R2 and stores the result in R2). Address 4: HALT (stop running; the PC is not advanced).

Finally, Priya explains two kinds of circuits. Combinational logic is a circuit whose output depends only on its current inputs, like an adder made from gates. It has no memory, so the moment the inputs change, the old output is gone. Sequential logic is a circuit whose output depends on its current inputs and also on stored state, meaning remembered past values. Sequential logic is built from storage elements called flip-flops, which hold one bit each, and it updates on the tick of a clock, a steady timing signal. A register is a group of flip-flops.

She also mentions interrupts. An interrupt is a signal from hardware, such as a button, that tells the CPU to pause what it is doing and deal with an event. When an interrupt arrives, the CPU finishes its current instruction and saves its place: the PC and the register values. It then jumps to an interrupt handler, a short routine for that event. The operating system (OS) is the core software that manages the hardware. When the device starts up, the OS installs these handlers and records their addresses. When the handler finishes, the saved state is restored and the original program carries on where it left off. The alternative is polling, which means the program keeps checking the button over and over in a loop.

1. The status register reads 0x2D. Convert it to binary. Then use a bitwise AND with the right mask to decide whether the sensor-ready flag (bit 2) is set and whether the error flag (bit 1) is set. Show the masks you used.
2. Trace the five-instruction program through the fetch-decode-execute cycle. Give the values of R1, R2 and the PC after each instruction, and state the final values in both decimal and binary for R1 and R2.
3. A junior colleague wants to count how many times the thermostat button is pressed by wiring the button straight into an adder circuit, with no register. Explain why this will not work, using the difference between combinational and sequential logic, and say what the running device would actually show.
4. A user presses the thermostat button while the CPU is in the middle of running a program. Describe step by step what the CPU does using an interrupt, say where the OS takes part, and give one reason an interrupt is better than polling here.
subParts: Hex to binary and flag masking
modelAnswer: 0x2D splits into hex 2 = 0010 and hex D = 1101, so the binary value is 0010 1101 (45 in decimal). To test bit 2, use the mask 0000 0100 (0x04). 0010 1101 AND 0000 0100 = 0000 0100, which is not zero, so the sensor-ready flag is set. To test bit 1, use the mask 0000 0010 (0x02). 0010 1101 AND 0000 0010 = 0000 0000, which is zero, so the error flag is not set. The sensor is ready and there is no error.

Start: PC=0, R1=0, R2=0. Fetch address 0, decode LOAD R1,5, execute: R1=5, PC=1. Fetch address 1, LOAD R2,3: R2=3, PC=2. Fetch address 2, ADD: the ALU computes 5+3, so R1=8 and PC=3. Fetch address 3, XOR: R1=8 is 1000 and R2=3 is 0011, and 1000 XOR 0011 = 1011, so R2=11 and PC=4. Fetch address 4, HALT: the CPU stops and the PC stays at 4. Final values: R1 = 8 (binary 1000), R2 = 11 (binary 1011, hex 0x0B), PC = 4.

An adder on its own is combinational logic. Its output depends only on its inputs at this moment, and it has no memory. A count needs state: the circuit must remember the previous total so it can add 1 to it. Without a register (flip-flops updated on a clock tick) to hold the total and feed it back into the adder, nothing is stored. The running device would show only what the current inputs produce, something like 1 while the button is held down and back to 0 when it is released. It would never build up a total. The fix is sequential logic: store the count in a register and, on each press, load the register with the adder's output of old count + 1.

The button sends an interrupt signal to the CPU. The CPU finishes the instruction it is currently executing and saves its place: the PC and the register values. It then jumps to the interrupt handler for the button. The OS takes part because it installed that handler and recorded its address when the device started, and the handler is OS code that deals with the event, for example recording the press. When the handler finishes, the saved PC and registers are restored and the original program resumes exactly where it stopped, as if nothing happened. An interrupt is better than polling because with polling the CPU wastes time and power checking the button over and over. Polling can also miss or delay a press if the program is busy elsewhere. With interrupts, the CPU does useful work and responds only when an event actually happens.

scenarios.title: Lanternfish Tickets: The Double-Sold Seat and the Frozen Refund
scenarios.scenario:
Lanternfish Tickets is a small fictional company that sells seats for local concerts. Its booking service runs as one process. A process is a running instance of a program, with its own private memory called its address space. Inside that process are two threads. A thread is an independent path of execution inside a process. Threads in the same process share the same memory, so both can read and write the same variables.

Both threads handle customer purchases. Each purchase runs four steps on a shared variable called seats_left. First, read seats_left into a local copy. Second, check that the copy is greater than 0. Third, subtract 1 from the copy. Fourth, write the copy back to seats_left. The scheduler is the part of the operating system that decides which thread uses the CPU next. It can pause one thread between any two of these steps and run the other thread. A context switch is that move of the CPU from one thread to another: the system saves the paused thread's registers (its small set of working values inside the CPU) and loads the other thread's. When a program's result depends on the unlucky timing of threads that share data, and at least one of them writes to it, the bug is called a race condition.

On Friday, seats_left was 1 and two customers clicked Buy at the same moment. Both received a confirmation email. The logs later showed seats_left as 0, not -1. The venue had to turn one customer away at the door.

A developer, Priya, added a mutex. A mutex (short for mutual exclusion lock) is an object a thread must lock before it enters a critical section, which is the stretch of code that touches shared data. The thread unlocks the mutex when it leaves. If another thread already holds the mutex, the second thread blocks, meaning it waits without running, until the mutex is released. Priya wrapped the whole read, check, subtract and write sequence in a mutex called seat_lock. Overbooking stopped. Under heavy load, though, the number of purchases completed per second (throughput) dropped slightly.

A week later a refund feature arrived. Purchases now lock seat_lock first and then ledger_lock, a mutex that protects the payment ledger. The new refund thread locks ledger_lock first and then seat_lock. During a busy sale the service froze. CPU use was near 0%, no errors were logged, and nothing made progress.

A deadlock is a situation where two or more threads each wait forever for something another one of them holds. A deadlock can only happen when four conditions all hold at once. Mutual exclusion means a resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Hold and wait means a thread keeps what it already holds while it waits for more. No preemption means the system cannot forcibly take a lock away from a thread. Circular wait means there is a cycle of threads, each waiting on a resource held by the next. Remove any one of the four conditions and a deadlock cannot occur.

Your tasks:
1. Trace, step by step, one ordering of the two purchase threads' steps that explains how both customers got a seat while seats_left ended at 0. Name this kind of bug.
2. Explain why Priya's mutex fixes the overbooking, and why throughput dropped slightly.
3. Explain how the purchase thread and the refund thread froze the service, showing how each of the four deadlock conditions is met.
4. Propose one change to the locking code that prevents this deadlock, and say which of the four conditions your change removes.
subParts: Why the mutex fixes it and costs speed
modelAnswer: Call the threads A and B. seats_left starts at 1. Thread A reads seats_left, so its local copy is 1. A context switch happens and B runs. B reads seats_left, and its copy is also 1, because A has not written anything yet. B checks that 1 is greater than 0, which passes. B subtracts to get 0, writes 0 to seats_left and confirms a seat. The scheduler switches back to A. A still holds its old copy of 1, so its check passes too. A subtracts to get 0, writes 0 and also confirms a seat. Two seats were sold, but seats_left only went from 1 to 0, because A's write overwrote B's result with the same stale value instead of going to -1. This is a race condition. The outcome depended on the timing of two threads accessing shared data, with at least one of them writing.

The mutex makes the read, check, subtract and write sequence a critical section that only one thread can be inside at a time. If B tries to lock seat_lock while A holds it, B blocks until A finishes and unlocks. B then reads the updated value 0, the check fails, and B correctly refuses the sale. Each thread now always sees the other's completed write, so the stale-copy interleaving can no longer happen. Throughput drops because purchases that used to overlap now take turns: a thread that finds seat_lock held must wait instead of doing useful work. There is also a small extra cost to lock and unlock, and to the context switches that happen when a blocked thread later wakes. The trade-off is slightly lower speed in exchange for correct results.

Here is one interleaving that freezes the service. The purchase thread locks seat_lock. The refund thread locks ledger_lock. The purchase thread now tries to lock ledger_lock and blocks, because refund holds it. The refund thread tries to lock seat_lock and blocks, because purchase holds it. Neither thread can continue, so CPU use sits near 0% with no errors. Mutual exclusion holds because each mutex can be held by only one thread. Hold and wait holds because each thread keeps its first lock while it waits for its second. No preemption holds because nothing forcibly takes a lock away from either thread. Circular wait holds because purchase waits on refund and refund waits on purchase, which forms a cycle. All four conditions are present, so this is a deadlock.

Make every thread take the locks in one agreed order, for example always seat_lock first and then ledger_lock. In practice that means changing the refund code to lock seat_lock before ledger_lock. Now whichever thread gets seat_lock first can also get ledger_lock, while the other thread waits on seat_lock and holds nothing. No cycle can form, so this removes the circular wait condition. Other answers are acceptable if they are justified. One is to protect both resources with a single lock, so no thread ever holds one lock while waiting for another. Another is for a thread that fails to get its second lock to release its first lock and retry. Both of these remove the hold and wait condition.

scenarios.title: Fixing the order database at Kettle & Crumb
scenarios.scenario:
Kettle & Crumb is a small fictional online shop that sells baking supplies. Its order data lives in a relational database, which is a system that stores data in tables (also called relations), where each row is one record and each column is one named fact about that record. You have just joined the engineering team, and four problems have landed on your desk.

First, the whole shop runs on one table called Orders, with these columns: order_id, order_date, customer_id, customer_name, customer_email, product_id, product_name, product_price, quantity. One order can contain several products, so an order with three products takes up three rows, each repeating the customer's name and email. Last month a customer changed her email address, and support updated only some of her rows. Now the database shows two different emails for the same person.

Second, the customer service screen runs a query (a request for data) that finds all orders for one customer_id. It now takes several seconds because the database reads every row in the table to find the matches. This is called a full table scan.

Third, two warehouse workers sometimes update the stock count for the same product at the same moment. Each person's app reads the current count (say 10), subtracts what they packed (2 and 3), and writes back the result. Sometimes the final count is 8 or 7 instead of the correct 5. One person's change silently overwrites the other's. This bug is called a lost update.

Fourth, the product team wants two new features. The first is a box saying "customers who bought this also bought", which works by following links from a product to its buyers and then to their other purchases. The second is a search bar that should find products from loose text, such as "gluten free flour", even when the words are misspelled or appear in a different order. To handle more traffic, the team also plans to add a replica. A replica is a second copy of the database that receives changes from the main copy a moment later, and the shop would send read requests to it. The process of copying changes to a replica is called replication.

Your tasks:
1. Identify the keys and normalize the Orders data. A primary key is a column, or a set of columns, whose value uniquely identifies each row. A foreign key is a column in one table that holds the primary key of a row in another table, linking the two tables. Normalization means splitting tables so that each fact is stored in exactly one place. Third normal form (3NF) means that every non-key column depends on the whole primary key and on nothing but the key. Propose a set of tables in 3NF, name each table's primary key and any foreign keys, and explain how your design prevents the two-emails problem.
2. Speed up the customer lookup. An index is a separate, sorted structure that lets the database jump straight to the rows it needs, much like the index at the back of a book. Most relational databases build indexes as a B-tree, which is a balanced tree where each node holds many sorted keys and every lookup walks from the top (the root) down to the bottom level (a leaf) in a small number of steps. The query planner is the part of the database that decides how to run a query, for example by scanning the whole table or by using an index. Say which index you would add and why it helps. Describe roughly how a B-tree lookup finds the matching rows. Name one cost of adding the index.
3. Stop the lost update. A transaction is a group of database operations treated as one unit. ACID names its four guarantees. Atomicity means all of the steps happen or none do. Consistency means the data's rules hold before and after. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work. Durability means a committed change survives a crash. An isolation level is a setting for how strictly transactions are kept apart: stricter levels prevent more anomalies but allow less parallel work. Locking means a transaction claims a row so that others must wait before changing it. MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) means the database keeps older versions of a row so that readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers. Explain why the lost update happens. Then give two ways to prevent it, using the terms above.
4. Choose data systems for the new features and judge the replica. A graph database stores items as nodes and the links between them as edges, so following chains of links is fast. A search-oriented system builds an inverted index, which is a map from each word to the items that contain it, and ranks the results by relevance. It often tolerates typos. Say which kind of system suits each feature, and whether the relational database should stay the main record for orders. Then explain one consistency-versus-latency risk of sending reads to the replica, given that the replica runs a moment behind (this delay is called replication lag). Suggest one way to handle that risk.
subParts: Index and B-tree for customer lookup
Transactions and preventing the lost update
Choosing data systems and replica tradeoffs
modelAnswer:
Split the data into four tables. Customers(customer_id PK, customer_name, customer_email). Products(product_id PK, product_name, product_price). Orders(order_id PK, order_date, customer_id FK to Customers). OrderItems(order_id FK to Orders, product_id FK to Products, quantity), with the composite primary key (order_id, product_id).

Why this reaches 3NF: in the original table, customer_name and customer_email depended only on customer_id, and product_name and product_price depended only on product_id. They did not depend on the whole row's key, so these facts were repeated on many rows. After the split, every non-key column depends only on its own table's key. Quantity depends on the pair (order_id, product_id), which is the whole key of OrderItems.

Because the email is now stored once, in one Customers row, changing it means updating one row. Two conflicting emails cannot exist. A strong answer may note that the price paid at order time is a separate fact from the current catalog price. You can store it on OrderItems as unit_price_at_purchase so that later price changes do not rewrite old orders. Credit any reasonable equivalent design that names correct primary and foreign keys and removes the repeated customer and product facts.

Add an index on Orders.customer_id. Without it, the database must read every row (a full table scan), so the work grows with the size of the whole table. With a B-tree index, the lookup starts at the root node. The database compares the wanted customer_id against the sorted keys in that node and follows the matching branch down. It repeats this at each level until it reaches a leaf. The leaf holds that customer_id and pointers to that customer's rows. Each node holds many keys, so the tree stays shallow, and even millions of rows need only a few steps. The query planner sees the index and chooses it instead of the scan, because it estimates this will read far fewer rows.

Cost: every insert, update, or delete on Orders must also update the index. Writes therefore get a bit slower, and the index uses extra storage. Credit any answer that names the customer_id index, describes the root-to-leaf sorted search, and gives one real cost (slower writes or extra space).

Why it happens: each worker reads the count (10), then writes back a result calculated from that old value. Nothing stops the second read from happening before the first write. Both start from 10, and the last write wins, giving 8 or 7 instead of 5. The two changes are not isolated from each other.

Any two of these fixes are acceptable. (a) Wrap the read and the write in one transaction and lock the row when reading it, for example by reading it 'for update'. The second worker then waits until the first commits, reads 8, and writes 5. (b) Make the change atomic inside the database with a single statement, such as 'set stock = stock - 3', so that no stale value is ever carried in the app. (c) Run the transactions at a stricter isolation level, such as serializable. Under MVCC, the database detects that two transactions changed the same row from the same snapshot, rejects one of them, and the app retries it. (d) Use an optimistic check: store a version number and only write if the version is unchanged, otherwise retry.

The answer should connect the fix to isolation and atomicity in ACID. It should also note the tradeoff: locking makes workers wait, while optimistic or MVCC approaches avoid waiting but require retries.

"Also bought" suits a graph database, or a graph-style model, because the feature follows chains of links from a product to its buyers and then to their other products. A graph stores those links directly as edges, so each hop is cheap. In a relational database, each hop needs another join, which gets slow and awkward as the chain grows.

The search bar suits a search-oriented system with an inverted index, because it needs word matching, ranking by relevance, and tolerance for typos and word order. A relational index does not do these well.

The relational database should stay the main source of truth for orders and stock, because orders need ACID transactions, keys, and constraints. The graph and search systems can hold copies that are updated from it.

Replica risk: because of replication lag, a read sent to the replica may return stale data. For example, a customer places an order, refreshes the page, and does not see it yet. Or a stock count read from the replica is out of date. Reading from replicas lowers latency and spreads the load, but gives weaker consistency.

Acceptable mitigations include sending a user's reads to the main database for a short time after they write (read-your-writes), always reading from the main database for critical data such as stock or payments, or checking that the replica has caught up before reading from it. Credit any answer that matches each feature to a fitting system with a reason, keeps orders on the relational database, and names stale reads from lag along with one sensible fix.

scenarios.title: Brightleaf Books: Checking the Math Behind a New Recommendation and Fraud System
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightleaf Books, a fictional online bookstore, as a junior engineer on the data team. Your lead, Priya, wants you to sanity-check four pieces of math before a new feature goes live. She gives you short definitions to work from.

Recommendations. Each book is stored as an embedding. An embedding is a list of numbers, called a vector, that places an item in a space so that similar items land close together. To compare two vectors, the team uses cosine similarity. Cosine similarity measures how closely two vectors point in the same direction. It ranges from 1 (same direction, very similar) through 0 (unrelated) to -1 (opposite). The formula is: cosine similarity = (dot product of A and B) divided by (magnitude of A times magnitude of B). The dot product multiplies matching positions and adds the results. For example, (1,2) dot (3,4) = 1x3 + 2x4 = 11. The magnitude, or length, of a vector is the square root of the sum of its squared entries. For example, the magnitude of (3,4) is the square root of (9 + 16), which is 5. A reader just finished Book A, whose embedding is (3, 4). The two candidates are Book B with (4, 3) and Book C with (-4, 3).

Fraud flags. A conditional probability, written P(X | Y), is the chance that X is true given that Y is already known to be true. Bayes' theorem lets you flip a conditional probability around: P(X | Y) = P(Y | X) x P(X) / P(Y). The overall chance of Y can be found by adding up every way Y can happen: P(Y) = P(Y | X) x P(X) + P(Y | not X) x P(not X). At Brightleaf, 2% of orders are fraudulent. The fraud checker flags 90% of fraudulent orders. It also wrongly flags 5% of legitimate orders.

Training. A model learns by adjusting a number called a weight, w, to make its loss smaller. The loss is a score of how wrong the model is, and lower is better. The derivative of the loss tells you the slope at the current w. The slope is how much the loss changes when w increases a little. With many weights, the list of these slopes, one per weight, is called the gradient. Gradient descent is the method of repeatedly stepping against the slope: new w = old w - (learning rate x derivative). The learning rate is a small number that sets the step size. The team's toy loss is L(w) = (w - 3)^2, whose derivative is 2(w - 3). The current weight is w = 5 and the learning rate is 0.1.

Evaluation. Data is split into three parts. The training set is what the model learns from. The validation set is held back to check and tune the model during development. The test set is used once at the very end to give an honest final score. Overfitting means the model has memorized quirks of the training data instead of general patterns. It shows up as high training accuracy but much lower validation accuracy. This is also called high variance, because the model's behavior swings with the particular data it saw. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple and scores poorly on both sets. This is also called high bias. Common remedies for overfitting include using a simpler model or fewer features, gathering more training data, and stopping training earlier. Brightleaf's book-genre classifier scores 99% accuracy on the training set and 71% on the validation set.

Your tasks:
1. Compute the cosine similarity between Book A and Book B, and between Book A and Book C. State which book should be recommended and why.
2. Use Bayes' theorem to find the probability that an order is actually fraudulent given that it was flagged. Explain in one sentence what this means for the support team that reviews flagged orders.
3. Perform one step of gradient descent from w = 5 and show the new weight and whether the loss went down. Then say what would happen if someone set the learning rate to 1.5 instead.
4. Diagnose the genre classifier's problem using the terms above. Suggest two remedies, and name one thing the team must not do with the test set.
modelAnswer: A and B: the dot product is 3x4 + 4x3 = 24. The magnitude of A is sqrt(9+16) = 5 and the magnitude of B is sqrt(16+9) = 5. Cosine similarity = 24 / (5x5) = 0.96. A and C: the dot product is 3x(-4) + 4x3 = -12 + 12 = 0. The magnitude of C is sqrt(16+9) = 5. Cosine similarity = 0 / 25 = 0. Recommend Book B: its similarity is close to 1, meaning it points in nearly the same direction as Book A. Book C scores 0, meaning it is unrelated. A common mistake is comparing raw numbers or forgetting to divide by the magnitudes.

Let F = fraud and G = flagged. Then P(F) = 0.02, P(not F) = 0.98, P(G|F) = 0.90 and P(G|not F) = 0.05. P(G) = 0.90x0.02 + 0.05x0.98 = 0.018 + 0.049 = 0.067. P(F|G) = 0.018 / 0.067, which is about 0.27, or roughly 27%. So about 73% of flagged orders are actually legitimate. The support team should treat a flag as a reason to review the order, not as proof of fraud. Blocking every flagged order automatically would hurt many honest customers. The common mistake is to assume the answer is 90%, which confuses P(G|F) with P(F|G).

The derivative at w = 5 is 2(5 - 3) = 4. New w = 5 - 0.1x4 = 5 - 0.4 = 4.6. The loss before was (5-3)^2 = 4. The loss after is (4.6-3)^2 = 1.6^2 = 2.56, so the loss went down and w moved toward the minimum at w = 3. With a learning rate of 1.5: new w = 5 - 1.5x4 = -1, and the loss becomes (-1-3)^2 = 16. That is worse, because the step overshot the minimum, and repeated steps of this size can bounce around or grow without ever settling. A common mistake is adding the derivative instead of subtracting it, which moves uphill.

The classifier is overfitting (high variance). It scores 99% on training data but only 71% on validation data, so it has memorized training quirks rather than learned general patterns. It is not underfitting, because underfitting would show low scores on both sets. Any two of these remedies are acceptable: use a simpler model or fewer features, gather more training data, or stop training earlier. The team must not use the test set to tune or repeatedly adjust the model, since validation data exists for that. The test set should be used once at the end, otherwise its score is no longer an honest estimate of performance on new data.

scenarios.title: Securing the Driver Portal at Larkspur Freight
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Larkspur Freight, a fictional regional trucking company, as a junior engineer. The team is reviewing the security of the Driver Portal, a website where drivers log in to see their routes and upload delivery photos. Your lead, Priya, asks you to check four decisions before the portal goes live.

Some terms you will need. Encryption scrambles data so that only someone holding the right key can turn it back into readable form. Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key to both lock and unlock. Asymmetric encryption, also called public-key encryption, uses a key pair: a public key anyone may see and a private key only the owner keeps. A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint, called a hash. It is one-way: you cannot run it backwards to recover the input. A salt is a random value stored next to each password and mixed into it before hashing. A slow hash, such as bcrypt or Argon2, is a hash function deliberately designed to take noticeable time and effort for each guess. A digital signature is a value made with a private key that anyone can check with the matching public key. A certificate is a small file that binds a name, such as portal.larkspurfreight.example, to a public key, and that is signed by a certificate authority (CA). A CA is an organisation whose signature browsers are set up to trust. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol behind the padlock in a browser. It protects data while it travels between the driver's phone and the server.

Here is what the team has built so far. First, passwords are stored as plain SHA-256 hashes. SHA-256 is a fast, general-purpose hash function. No salt is used. A teammate says, "Hashing is one-way, so even if the database leaks, the passwords are safe." Second, when a driver's phone connects, the server sends a chain of three certificates. The first is for portal.larkspurfreight.example and is signed by "Northgate Issuing CA". The second is for Northgate Issuing CA and is signed by "Northgate Root CA". The third, Northgate Root CA, is already stored as trusted inside the phone's operating system.
